en: The Sūtra of the Flower Hand Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One; also titled the Sūtra on Gathering All Roots of Goodness.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha under Imperial Order during the Later Qin Dynasty.
Chapter One: Introduction (I). Introduction, Chapter One.
Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove. It was a place secluded and tranquil, suitable for cultivating detachment, and the proper dwelling for those who practice the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra arose from meditative concentration in the late afternoon, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākātyāyana, Mahākauṣṭhila, Mahākapphiṇa, Mahācunda, Subhūti, Mahāraṭṭha, Vakkula, Nanda, Nandika, Gavāmpati, Ānanda, Kambala, Nārada, Vāsiṣṭha, Aniruddha, and Upāli—these five hundred bhikṣus, among others, all arose from meditative concentration at the hour of *pradoṣa* (late afternoon) and went to where the Buddha was. They prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat down to one side.

At that time, there were also the bhikṣus Yaśas, Rāṣṭrapāla, Devapūjita, Yaśakāma, Gaṇakāma, and Icchāntika; five hundred such bhikṣus, having completed their summer retreat in Śrāvastī, proceeded toward Rājagṛha, went to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva, together with thirty thousand bodhisattvas, having completed the summer retreat in the kingdom of Campā, came to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa, the Bodhisattva Śāstṛ, the Bodhisattva Jyotirasa, the Bodhisattva Naradatta,
the Bodhisattva Indradatta, the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, the Bodhisattva Brahmādeva,
the Bodhisattva Balasena, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva Jayamati, and the Bodhisattva Vardhamāna...
The Bodhisattva Maticitra, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśin, the Bodhisattva Supratisthita, the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta,
the Bodhisattva Nityodyukta, the Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura, the Bodhisattva Sūryagarbha, the Bodhisattva Lokadhara,
the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara, the Bodhisattva Amṛtarasadhara, and the Bodhisattva Susthitamati.
Bodhisattva Immeasurable Intention, Bodhisattva Firm Intention, Bodhisattva Transcending the Three Realms,
Bodhisattva Boundless Power, Bodhisattva Immeasurable Power, Bodhisattva Vajra Power, Bodhisattva Peerless Power, Bodhisattva Unshakable Power,
Bodhisattva Swift Eloquence, Bodhisattva Sharp Eloquence, and Bodhisattva Profound Eloquence.
The Bodhisattva Sāgara, the Bodhisattva Anantapratibhāna, the Bodhisattva Amitapratibhāna,
the Dharma Prince Mañjuśrī, the Dharma Prince Puṣpaketu, the Bodhisattva Dharmodgata, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, the Bodhisattva Ratnadhara,
the Bodhisattva Aparimitakalpavyūhavikurvaṇa, and the Bodhisattva Strīvyañjanapraṇidhivikurvaṇa.
The Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Male Aspect, the Bodhisattva Who Transforms the Aspect of Sentient Beings, the Bodhisattva Boundless Sovereignty,
the Bodhisattva Immeasurable Sovereignty, and the Bodhisattva Sovereign in Destroying Self-Arisen Conditions—
these bodhisattvas are able to follow the conduct and vows of immeasurable sentient beings and deliver them.

Having each completed the summer retreat in their respective locations, they traveled through various kingdoms and encountered one another midway; together they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the great assembly had all gathered like clouds, employed his supernatural powers to cause the long-resident bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās of the kingdom of Magadha to go to the Bamboo Grove, prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and sit to one side.

At that time, the Elder Mahākāśyapa was staying in the Śakra Cave on Mount Vaidehaka, together with five hundred bhikṣus. They all practiced the dhūta austerities: they lived on alms, wore robes made of discarded rags, observed the practice of constant sitting, stayed wherever a tree provided shade, were of few desires and easily satisfied, and delighted in the practice of seclusion.
At that time, by the Buddha’s supernormal power, Mahākāśyapa suddenly vanished from that stone chamber and appeared in the Bamboo Grove, proceeding to where the Buddha was.
Seeing him from afar, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Behold, this Mahākāśyapa is now coming here from that place.”

This person constantly practices the conduct of an araṇya-dweller: begging for food, wearing rag-robes, possessing only the three coarse and tattered robes, dwelling in remote and distant borderlands, having few desires and being content, delighting in the practice of seclusion, and with a mind that does not conjoin with any phenomena;
he is fully endowed with all the virtues of a śrāvaka. Among my disciples, none can equal him in these dharmas.
"You should know, O disciples, that even this Mahākāśyapa does not delight in conversing with the devas, much less with humans!
At that time, the World-Honored One called out to him from afar: "Welcome, Kāśyapa!"
After a long time they met again, and [the Buddha] said, "You should take this half-seat of the Tathāgata.

When the Buddha shifted his body, the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great radiance shone everywhere throughout the world, and a great sound was heard everywhere, like the striking of a golden bell.
Mahākāśyapa bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in prostration, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Buddha is the Great Teacher, and I am his disciple."
Whatever robes, alms bowls, or seats belong to the Buddha should not be used by his disciples according to the Dharma. Why is this?
For the robes of the Tathāgata are objects of worship and reverence for all the devas and humans in the world, like ancestral shrines or temples.

In the past, I received the saṃghāṭī robe from the Buddha; out of reverence and respect, I never dared to wear it. Since that time, I have not given rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of anger, or thoughts of malice, nor have I produced the fever of desire, the fever of hatred, or the fever of delusion to burn and afflict myself.
“World-Honored One!
To speak briefly, when I received the robe of the World-Honored One while still on the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), the moment I placed it upon my head, I became one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Although I received the Tathāgata’s robe in accordance with the teaching, I truly did not dare to give rise to thoughts of superiority or inferiority.”
I merely hold it in my hand and do not let it touch my body;
even when my hands have not been washed, I do not dare to grasp it, so how could I ever presume to treat it with such negligence as to place it beneath my head?
It is always with me, never departing for even a moment.
I carry this robe with the same reverence as the *śarīra*.

Since the Buddha gave it to me, I have not dared to wear it; yet from the moment I brought it here, my mind has constantly been mindful of the Buddha, except when I entered other meditative concentrations.

When entering other meditative absorptions, there are no signs of earth, water, fire, or wind, nor are there signs of this world or future worlds. Regarding all that is seen, heard, sensed, or known—the range of mental activity—within it there is neither perception nor non-perception.
“World-Honored One!

Regarding all non-conceptual formations and the attainment of non-conception—which transcend all conceptual formations, transcend the attainment of non-conception, and transcend all manifold conceptual formations—I do not perceive therein any training or non-training, nor do I perceive a Tathāgata, the qualities of a Tathāgata, or the conduct of a Tathāgata.”

For example, space has various names; it is called "space," yet it is deceptive, non-abiding, and non-existent. It is without grasping, without relinquishing, without contention, and without receiving.

It is also called "suchness" and termed "pure. It is without color, without form, and cannot be seen. Although it is designated by these various names, the characteristic of space cannot be demonstrated as being large or small, high or low, finite or infinite.
“World-Honored One!

Noble wisdom is called that which can know all things; yet this noble wisdom cannot know the numerical divisions of space, nor its various forms and colors, nor such characteristics as its objects of perception.”
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata is likewise; sometimes he is called the Buddha, sometimes the Great Teacher, and again the World-Honored One;

he is the torch, the lamp, the refuge, the savior, the shelter for the world, the illuminator, the guide, the healer of all ailments, the one who reveals the path, the one who has reached the ultimate path, and the All-Knowing One.”
Although I employ such conventional, provisional names to praise the Tathāgata, within this I do not perceive any dharma; there is nothing to be received and nothing to be attained. Why is this?
Because all dharmas are fundamentally empty from the very beginning.
It is like a magician who conjures by illusion a consecrated universal monarch (cakravartin), complete with the fourfold army and the seven treasures, traveling through the four continents.
"World-Honored One! Although those various people perceive diverse physical forms and manifold voices,
the Wheel-Turning King does not form such a thought:"
"I am honorable and noble; leading the fourfold army, I travel throughout the world.
Yet those fourfold armies likewise do not think:
"The king is our master, and we are his followers."
"Although there is that which is performed, there is no mental conception.
World-Honored One!
The characteristics of these dharmas are likewise thus: there is no Tathāgata, nor are there śrāvakas—whether those in training or those beyond training—nor pratyekabuddhas, nor ordinary persons."
“World-Honored One!
Within these characteristics of dharmas, the dharmas of a Tathāgata and the characteristics of a Tathāgata are all unobtainable, unknowable, and cannot be grasped.”

The Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha and the characteristics of the Pratyekabuddha, the Dharma of the Śrāvaka and the characteristics of the Śrāvaka, and the mental dharmas of ordinary beings and the characteristics of ordinary beings—all these are unobtainable; they cannot be known and cannot be grasped. Within these characteristics of dharmas, the characteristic of form and the dharma of form are both unobtainable, being without knowledge and without grasping. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—the dharma of consciousness and the characteristic of consciousness—are likewise unobtainable, being without knowledge and without grasping.
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, regarding this mark, that which is called the emptiness of form is empty for such reasons; in this state, the emptiness of form is entirely unobtainable.
The emptiness of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is empty for such reasons; in this state, the emptiness of consciousness is likewise unobtainable.”
“World-Honored One!
Furthermore, within these characteristics, it is said that the Tathāgata is empty and the dharmas of the Tathāgata are empty.
For this reason, both emptiness and the locus of this emptiness are unobtainable.”
Even up to ordinary beings and the dharmas of ordinary beings, they are empty; for this reason they are empty, and even this state of emptiness is unattainable.

It is like a magically conjured wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*) and his fourfold army: therein there is truly no wheel-turning sage king, no fourfold army, no illusion nor the products of illusion, no earth nor the element of earth, no water, fire, or wind nor the elements of water, fire, or wind, and no space or consciousness nor the elements of space or consciousness.
“World-Honored One!
I observe that all dharmas are likewise thus. From the very beginning, I have not been within these dharmas, nor do I harbor any discrimination regarding them.”
I take this Dharma as the means for recollecting the Buddha’s merits; this is called the Right Path.
World-Honored One!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family enters such a path yet practices other dharmas, following other teachers and reverently complying with their instructions, claiming to possess right view—this is impossible.
“World-Honored One!
I have no doubts regarding this Dharma.

Having entered this gate, I know that all dharmas are of a single characteristic—that is to say, the characteristic of being detached from characteristics and the characteristic of having nothing to be received.”
"I was dwelling in the stone chamber of Śakra when, having received the World-Honored One’s command, I came here desiring to inquire about my doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma.
Now, as the Tathāgata has looked upon me and invited me to share his seat, and the great trichiliocosm shook in six ways, I immediately reflected:
'How rare is the Tathāgata!'"
Having accomplished the profound and pure Great Dharma, he spontaneously attained the Unsurpassed Way without a teacher. Abiding in great compassion, he has toppled the banner of arrogance.
Now, he looks upon his disciples and offers them a seat, like a poor and lowly man who, with a heart of reverence, beholds a Wheel-Turning King;
when that Wheel-Turning King commands him to sit together, this poor man feels a sense of rare wonder.
I find it already difficult even to behold a noble wheel-turning monarch, let alone to share his couch and sit with him!

It is the same with the Buddha: he is an omniscient being of great majesty and virtue; a Dharma King who was self-enlightened without a teacher, whom none among the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can surpass, much less any other beings in the world, whether devas, humans, or asuras.
"It would already be a great benefit for me to now see, approach, and consult with him; how much more so to be invited to share his seat!
This is truly rare! I then thought:
"The Tathāgata is profoundly endowed with great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity; he does not boastfully exalt himself as the most honored or the supreme in the world."
"The virtues of the Tathāgata manifest of themselves; this is called that which is not shared with any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised Kāśyapa, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
It is as you have said.

The Tathāgata is immeasurable, and he is also able to accomplish immeasurable great dharmas; namely, such an amount of giving constitutes the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā), such an amount of upholding precepts constitutes the perfection of morality (śīla-pāramitā), such an amount of patience constitutes the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā), such an amount of diligence constitutes the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā), such an amount of meditative concentration constitutes the perfection of concentration (dhyāna-pāramitā), such an amount of wisdom constitutes the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), such an amount of samādhi constitutes the perfection of samādhi (samādhi-pāramitā), such an amount of merit constitutes the perfection of merit (guṇa-pāramitā), such an amount of conduct and vows constitutes the perfection of conduct and vows (caryā-praṇidhāna-pāramitā), such an amount of skillful means constitutes the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā), such an amount of liberation constitutes the perfection of liberation (vimukti-pāramitā), and such an amount of knowledge and vision of liberation constitutes the perfection of knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-pāramitā).
Kāśyapa! The Tathāgata has attained the four incomparable knowledges and is able to roar the true lion’s roar amidst the great assembly.
What are these four?

"The category of morality is peerless; the category of concentration is peerless; the category of wisdom is peerless; and the Buddha-dharmas are peerless. These are called the Tathāgata’s four peerless knowledges.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The wisdom of all Buddhas is peerless, Inconceivable to the world.
Because the karma of his mind is pure, he is able to roar the true lion’s roar.
He shall let out that lion’s roar to terrify all the non-Buddhists;
upon hearing the Buddha’s most profound Dharma, they shall fall into a great abyss.
If a person dwells in the mark of a self, And dwells in the mark of sentient beings,
I declare that such a person regarding the Buddha-dharma Is a follower of external paths.
If a person relies on the mark of phenomena, Or relies on the marks of "self" and "what belongs to self,"...
Such a person, regarding the Buddha’s Dharma, I declare to be a follower of external paths.
If a person is greedily attached to precepts and other various merits,
or is conceited due to their extensive learning, I declare them to be a follower of external paths.
If a person clings to small desires, yet practices contentment and seclusion,
wearing even coarse and tattered robes, I call them a non-Buddhist. Like space,
which is without obstruction and cannot be defiled by smoke or dust, [so is the one who is free from attachment].
I have taught that the dharma of the śramaṇa is likewise unstained.
It is like a person who offers name-flowers, ointments, and incense to space; space does not give rise to joy.
If it is defiled by dust and grime, the nature of space remains unstained;
because its intrinsic nature is pure, so too is the dharma of the śramaṇa.
Even if one reviles it with harsh words, space harbors no resentment.
The Dharma of the śramaṇa is unstained; its metaphor is likewise so.
If a person, regarding this Dharma, has already studied it or is now studying it, and their mind is free from attachment, they are called a true śramaṇa.
Just as space is without obstruction, And smoke or dust cannot defile it, So too is the Dharma of the śramaṇa: Fundamentally pure and without change.
Just as the moon in the sky Has its radiance unobscured,
Nor does he give rise to this thought: "My light can illuminate everything.
When a bhikṣu enters another's home, he is unstained by the eight worldly dharmas;
like the moon, he is free from such thoughts: "I am able to remain unstained."
When a bhikṣu enters another's home, he should not harbor conceit, arrogance, or a sense of self-importance; if such thoughts arise, they must all be extinguished.
He should instead maintain a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, free from desire and without seeking anything for himself.
He shall preach the Dharma extensively for the great benefit [of beings], purifying his conduct within the world.
Chapter Two: Supernatural Powers (Ṛddhi-varga) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
“Take your seat and ask whatever you doubt; I shall explain it for you so that you may attain joy and understanding.”
At that time, Kāśyapa rose from the ground, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down in his place.

Then, the World-Honored One again manifested his supernatural power, causing all the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās from all the lands to come to the Bamboo Grove by the power of the Buddha; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit on one side.

At that time, the fourfold assembly—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others—entered the Bamboo Grove and all saw it as vast and spacious, without any mutual obstruction.

At that time, the World-Honored One again manifested his supernormal power, causing all the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven within this trichiliocosm to follow the Buddha’s power and proceed to the Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha. There they joined their palms in salutation to the Buddha and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One again employed his supernatural power to cause the dragon kings Sāgara, Anavatapta, Khaṇḍa, Śveta, Kṛtaka, Nanda, Upananda, Maṇasvin, Takṣaka, Sundara, and Elāpattra—along with billions of other such dragon kings—to come to the Bamboo Grove by virtue of the Buddha’s supernatural power. They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, all came into the Bamboo Grove by the power of the Buddha; together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās already seated there, they were all accommodated without any mutual obstruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:

"Prepare a high seat for the Tathāgata; I shall now preach the Sūtra for Severing the Doubts of Sentient Beings, which fully knows the deep intentions of all sentient beings and causes them all to rejoice and enter the ocean of Dharma."

He spoke of the practices of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and their deeds of purifying buddha-fields and transforming sentient beings; he also spoke of the accomplishment of the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, dhyāna-pāramitā, and prajñā-pāramitā; and he further spoke of the accomplishment of the practices of all dharma-gates, which enable one to know the faculties of all sentient beings and what is possible and impossible for them, causing all bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and others to attain great joy.
"Regarding my past karmic conditions, retributions, and mental vows, my wisdom is unimpeded; I shall now explain a small portion of them for you.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and prepared a seat for the Buddha that reached as high as the Brahma Heaven.

Furthermore, he created a place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*) in mid-air, adorned with the seven treasures and as soft, supple, and smooth as *kācalindika* cloth. It was one thousand worlds in length and seven hundred *yojanas* in width. Both the walking and sitting areas were provided with windows, arranged in sevenfold rows, surrounded by sevenfold jewel grottoes, sevenfold railings, and sevenfold jeweled nets arrayed all around.

To the left and right of that seat, rows of jewel-trees were arrayed, composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. The golden trees had silver leaves, crystal flowers, and lapis lazuli fruits; the silver trees had golden leaves, lapis lazuli flowers, and crystal fruits; the lapis lazuli trees had silver leaves, golden flowers, and crystal fruits; and the crystal trees had golden leaves, silver flowers, and lapis lazuli fruits.

Between all the jewel trees there are bathing pools, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities. On the four sides of each pool are stairways made of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; their bottoms are covered with golden sand, and various lotus flowers of blue, yellow, red, and white spread across the surface of the water, while flocks of mandarin ducks and other birds warble in harmony.
Latticed nets of the seven treasures covered the various ponds, with various banners and streamers erected and manifold famous incenses burned.
At the places for walking meditation, the flowers reached a depth of seven fathoms; upon these many flowers were manifested bhikṣus, all resembling Maudgalyāyana.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having finished creating seats by means of his supernormal powers, returned to the place where the Buddha was and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have already prepared the seats; may the Holy One know the proper time."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“Although these seats have been prepared, the Tathāgata will not preach the Dharma to the assembly from upon a transformation seat.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Anantapratyaya:
“You shall prepare the Dharma seat for the Tathāgata; I shall now sit upon it and preach the Sūtra on Severing the Doubts of Sentient Beings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Manifesting Immeasurable Conditions, having received the Buddha’s instruction, desired to arrange the Dharma seat.
At that time, the bodhisattvas within the trichiliocosm each piled their upper robes to form high seats.
Then the Tathāgata had this thought:

"I shall now manifest the power of my supernormal knowledges so that these bodhisattvas may personally realize their vows, resolve to practice the Way, purify buddha-lands, and bring sentient beings to maturity."

Furthermore, at the time of his attainment of Buddhahood, the purity and adornment of his land shall be such; the number of his assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas shall be such; the manner in which he expounds the True Dharma to deliver sentient beings shall be such; the length of his lifespan and the nature of his Buddha-dharma shall be such; his physical form, marks of excellence, and right conduct shall be such; and the duration for which the Dharma shall remain after his parinirvāṇa shall be such.
He causes each of the bodhisattvas to see these matters within their own robes, so that they may sever all their doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One rose with composure and ascended the high seat, entering a Buddha-samādhi called "Manifesting Immeasurable Conditions.

Then, within their own robes, each of the bodhisattvas saw the pure and adorned lands they would attain upon realizing the Unsurpassed Way; they saw the number of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in those assemblies, the length of their lifespans and their physical appearances, the nature of their diligent practice and meritorious virtues, the manner in which they would expound the True Dharma to deliver sentient beings, the way their relics would be distributed after their parinirvāṇa, and the duration for which the Dharma would remain unimpaired. Thus did each of them see such matters within their own robes.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas simultaneously raised their voices and spoke in verse:
"The Most Honored One of pure conduct, Sovereign among all dharmas,
Adorned with merit, With unimpeded power of meditative concentration."
The Holy Lord is free from flattery and crookedness, Free from arrogance and frivolity;
Having attained holy, luminous liberation, He dwells in profound samādhi.
Abiding in the Buddha’s profound samādhi, He manifests unsurpassed, holy supernormal powers.
With unimpeded wisdom, you manifest all future events.
Having seen this ourselves, our minds are peaceful and unmoving;
we have thus sat at the site of enlightenment, subduing Māra and possessing samādhi.
We have thereby attained the unsurpassed eye of all Buddhas;
with this unsurpassed eye, we see that all phenomena are empty.
It is called an "eye" yet is without obstruction; it is called "seeing" yet there is no seeing.
To penetrate all phenomena without obstruction— this is called the unsurpassed eye.
To maintain an impartial mind toward existence and non-existence, one thereby attains the Buddha-eye,
which can perceive throughout the triple world universally and without hindrance.
Because the Buddha has entered samādhi, he has enabled me to obtain this eye,
as well as all the gates of dhāraṇī, whereby I may universally enter into all phenomena.
It is only now that we have beheld the Buddha’s inexhaustible wisdom.
This was obtained through the practice of immeasurable, pure conduct in the past;
it could not have been reached through minor acts of giving, morality, or wisdom.
Therefore, he sits upon the lion throne, his radiance illuminating the ten directions.
Causing all devas, nāgas, and spirits to know that I have become a Buddha,
and likewise to fully know the causes and conditions of our original practices;
the Buddha, seated upon the fearless throne, preaches the Dharma to sever the doubts of the multitude.
Like the lion king, dwelling in the forest and roaring alone,
Having cultivated and gathered this wisdom throughout immeasurable kalpas,
Now, by the power of samādhi, he causes all devas and humans to know it.

Because he originally sought to benefit both himself and others, he cultivated immeasurable generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he practiced these for the sake of sentient beings.
By virtue of these causal practices, he now sits upon the lion throne.
We now join our palms in reverence; we pray only that you will sever our doubts.
Whether the Dharma remains for long or short, may the assembly attain the light of the Dharma, completely severing the net of all doubts and penetrating all phenomena.

At that time, within the assembly, there was a son of the Dharma named Puṣpadharagarbha. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and thought to himself:

"I wish to ask the Buddha about the various gateways of the Dharma, the gateway of vajra-words, the gateway of repeated words, the gateway of uninterrupted words, and the gateway of words for the cultivation and accumulation of all dharmas."
If good sons or good daughters study this gateway of phrases, they shall attain the skillful means of unimpeded eye-knowledge regarding all gateways of dharmas.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will observe the roots of goodness I have planted in past lives, as I seek the Way with a profound mind and have donned the great armor of adornment.

At that time, the Tathāgata, having observed this bodhisattva’s planting of roots of goodness from the first moment he resolved his mind upon enlightenment, and his profound aspiration for the path and great adornment, looked toward the assembled multitude and emitted a wondrous light from his mouth like a blazing flame. It illuminated immeasurable and boundless worlds; mountains, forests, walls, earth, water, fire, wind, and the realm of space all became a single golden color, flowing and spreading without obstruction throughout the eight directions, above, and below.

At that time, all sentient beings throughout the trichiliocosm saw their own bodies as the color of pure gold. Those sentient beings who had mostly been scorched by the fire of desire spontaneously perceived that the lustful intentions within their bodies had subsided;
those who had mostly been scorched by the fire of hatred spontaneously perceived that the hateful intentions within their bodies had subsided;
and those who had mostly been scorched by the fire of delusion spontaneously perceived that the deluded intentions within their bodies had subsided.
By the power of the Buddha’s supernatural faculties and his original vows, all sentient beings suffering within the great hells throughout this entire trichiliocosm have obtained temporary rest.

At that time, the sentient beings within this trichiliocosm were shrouded by karmic obstructions, retributive obstructions, and afflictive obstructions; yet, through the spiritual power of the Buddha and the power of the original vows of Puṣpakuṇḍalagarbha, all these obstructions were temporarily suspended.

At that time, from all the pores of the Tathāgata’s body, immeasurable rays of light resulting from karmic retribution were universally emitted, causing all sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness.
These emitted rays of light passed beyond immeasurable, boundless, *asaṃkhyeya* lands in the eastern direction, equal in number to the sands of the Ganges;
the same was true for the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.
After the Buddha had emitted this light, he raised his voice and cleared his throat; the sound was heard throughout all worlds. **Chapter 3:

Jālinīprabha (Part 1)** At that time, to the east, beyond immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) worlds, there was a land named Eka-cchattra. Therein dwelt a Buddha named Ekaratnavyūha, who was currently preaching the Dharma. He bestowed upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Jālinīprabha the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, saying:
"Now, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva shall, immediately after me, attain Buddhahood."
At that time, Jālinīprabha addressed that Buddha, saying,
"Who is it that has produced this great light and this great sound?
That Buddha replied:

"To the west, passing from here through immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, there is a world named Sahā. The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni, who currently resides and teaches for the sake of bodhisattvas the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, which encompasses all dharmas, severs the doubts of sentient beings, and brings joy to the multitude."
In that world there is a bodhisattva named Kusumagarbha, who wishes to inquire of that Buddha regarding the dharma-gate of gathering all dharmas and giving rise to immeasurable merit.

Jālinīprabha, you should know that all the bodhisattvas in that world have made great vows and practice boundless conduct; they have all gathered in that assembly, for in other worlds there are few who possess such magnificent adornments as these.
“If even those among that assembly of bodhisattvas who merely see or hear his name obtain such great benefit, how much more so for those who make offerings to him, attend upon him,
and consult him! At that time, Jālinīprabha said to that Buddha,
“Indeed, so it is.”
"Blessed One!
I wish to go to that Sahā world to make offerings to, pay homage to, and visit Śākyamuni Buddha, and to see the assembly of bodhisattvas who fully adorn that land."
That Buddha replied, "You yourself know the proper time; you should travel to that land with a single-minded focus. Why is this?"
"The majestic power of those bodhisattvas is difficult to surpass.
The Buddha Ekaratnavyuha gave a multitude of lotus flowers to Jālinīprabha and said:

"With these flowers, you shall make an offering to that Buddha and, expressing my intention, pay him homage and inquire after his well-being, saying: 'The Tathāgata Ekaratnavyuha, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha, pays homage to the Tathāgata Sālendrarāja, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha.'"
"Are you free from affliction and illness? Is your daily life light and easy, and is your physical strength at peace?

Net-Light Bodhisattva prostrated at the feet of that Buddha, circumambulated him three times to the right, and immediately, surrounded before and behind by an immeasurable assembly of bodhisattvas, vanished from that land as suddenly as a strong man bends and extends his arm, arriving here in this world.
He went to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “Indeed, World-Honored One,
I am Jālinīprabha.”
The Buddha said,
“Excellent! Are you at peace now?”
After Jālinīprabha Bodhisattva had prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, he withdrew to stand to one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The Buddha Ekaratnavyūha inquires after the World-Honored One:
Are you free from affliction? Are you free from illness? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vigor at peace?”
"Offer this lotus flower to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha immediately accepted it and passed it on to Maitreya.
Having received it, Maitreya addressed the five hundred bodhisattvas, including Bhadrapāla, saying:
“O virtuous friends!
The Tathāgata gave me these lotus flowers, and now I give them to you.”

At that time, there were five hundred bodhisattvas—namely, the bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, Ratnakūṭa, Nārāyaṇa, Jyotirasa, Varuṇadeva, Suvikrāntaśrī, Mahāmati, Jayamati, Vardhamānamati, Amoghadarśin, Sthitamati, Balātikrānta, Sadāparihīṇa, Anikṣiptadhura, Sūryagarbha, Lokadhara, Pṛthivīdhara, Trailokyavikrāmin, Anantabala, Vajrabala, Dṛḍhamati, and Anantavikrāmin—as well as others such as these, who had all received lotus flowers from Maitreya.
They addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Our original vow is that if there are sentient beings who hear our names or behold us, they shall all attain certainty regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.”
“World-Honored One!

Maitreya Bodhisattva gave these flowers to us. We now scatter them before all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present in the eastern direction, and likewise offer them to all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir. May these scattered flowers reach every single one of the infinite worlds throughout the ten directions. Should any sentient beings therein see these flowers or smell their fragrance, may they—by virtue of our original vows and the power of our profound practice of never abandoning any sentient being—all surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

At that time, the bodhisattvas wished to scatter these lotuses throughout the ten directions. The Buddha stroked each flower with his hand, and within every flower, the body of a Buddha appeared in its entirety. These emanated Buddhas departed through the air, and likewise spoke these words:

"If there are sentient beings who do not believe that all dharmas are empty like illusions and transformations, signless and without conditions—these sentient beings do not have a Buddha as their teacher, nor are they disciples of the Buddha."
Then he spoke these verses:
"All phenomena are empty and signless; Without grasping and without an object of perception, All are like illusions and transformations, And also like the moon reflected in water."
It is not empty because of emptiness; its nature is fundamentally and eternally so.
This is what the Buddha has taught as the most supreme and subtle Dharma.
All phenomena are empty and signless, and likewise, they are devoid of a self.
If a person understands in this way, they will be free from greed and contention.
If a person delights in this Dharma, the Buddha is their teacher;
by the power of the Buddha, we shall travel throughout the ten directions.
At that time, each of the emanated Buddhas spoke this verse, which reached throughout the ten directions.
Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The original vows of these bodhisattvas are pure and reach the level of the unprecedented; they are able to cause all sentient beings suffering in this land, as well as those with many afflictions in other worlds, to attain the certainty of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon merely hearing their names.
However, Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas should not be born in such a world of mixed evils.
Why is this? It is like a priceless mani-jewel, which can eliminate all the decline and afflictions of sentient beings and enable them to attain peace and happiness.

Suppose there were a wise person who was well-versed in the characteristics of jewels; having heard that this precious gem possessed great merit, he contemplated it with his mind and traveled everywhere in search of it. He found it lying within a pit of impure filth, where various craftsmen, impoverished laborers, and lowly, wretched people lived nearby. Yet even they did not know the name of this precious gem, much less could they know its inherent merits.
At that time, the seeker of jewels, having seen this, spoke these words:
"This jewel should not remain in such a defiled place.
Then the poor and lowly man said to this person:
"What is this jewel? Where is it now?
At that time, the seeker of the treasure pointed to the jewel and showed it to him.
Those people, lacking wisdom and unable to recognize the characteristics of the jewel, spoke thus:
"Although you praise this precious gem in such a manner, we do not perceive any merit in this jewel."
"Who would believe your words that they are not real?

At that time, the seeker of jewels immediately took the pearl from that place and departed. Thereafter, the poor man encountered various misfortunes and afflictions; he suffered from illness, disputes, and many other pains, remaining in a state of unrest.
“World-Honored One!

The Sahā world is also like this; its inhabitants all devour one another, are impoverished and lowly, and have accomplished evil dharmas. It is also like a precious jewel: wherever it dwells, filth and impurity abound.”
“World-Honored One!

This maṇi jewel can extinguish decline and affliction while bestowing universal peace and happiness; one should know that this refers to the Buddha and this world, where the assembly of bodhisattvas is fully adorned.
As for the poverty and lowliness on the four sides of the precious jewel, one should know that these represent the various evil sentient beings of the Sahā world.”
When those men and women heard of the merits of the jewel, they went forth to search for it; finding it in a place of filth, they spoke thus:
"This jewel should not be in such a place."

"Thus, it is because we have heard the Buddhas currently residing in the lands of the ten directions extol the World-Honored One, as well as this world’s assembly of great bodhisattvas endowed with perfect adornments, that we have come desiring to see, pay homage to, and inquire after his health;
yet we see that this land is filled with sentient beings who abound in suffering and affliction, turbidity and disorder, and the defilement of sin, and who possess meager merit."
World-Honored One!

Just as this precious jewel does not manifest its radiance when in an impure place, so too do the Tathāgata and the assembly of great Bodhisattvas of Great Adornment not manifest their merits in this land at present.
Just as a mani jewel, though situated in a foul place, can still provide some benefit to the poor and lowly;

so too, although the World-Honored One now manifests a great light in this world, the Tathāgata’s true radiance—his physical form, merit, power, sovereign supernormal faculties, and the power of his original vows—all remain unmanifested.
“World-Honored One!

The sentient beings of this land have meager roots of goodness; they cannot even believe in the merit of the light manifested by the Tathāgata, let alone believe in the merits possessed by the great bodhisattvas—such a thing is impossible.”
World-Honored One!

It is like a seeker of jewels who, having extracted this precious gem from an impure place and taken it away, subsequently encounters various misfortunes and afflictions, illnesses, disputes, and many sufferings of unrest.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who read, recite, and cultivate such a sutra as this will be reborn in other lands; for in this world there will be great decline and affliction, to the point that even the name of the Buddha-dharma will not be heard.

Why is this? Because these sentient beings delight in dwelling among unwholesome dharmas, preying upon one another, and are submerged in various great misfortunes and afflictions; lacking pure conduct, meritorious conduct, and wise conduct, they lose the great benefit.
“World-Honored One!
If good sons and good daughters desire to seek excellent benefit and attain the Buddha-way, they should not be born here;
even those seeking the state of a śrāvaka should not be born in this world, let alone bodhisattvas!”

Why is this? Just as in the Avīci Hell, the Saṃjīva Hell, the Kālasūtra Hell, the Pratāpana Hell, the Tapana Hell, and so forth, the sentient beings therein do not experience even a moment of pleasure.
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata and the bodhisattvas of that land view the sentient beings of this Sahā world as if they were here in these various hells undergoing manifold sufferings and afflictions.
The sentient beings of that land are born with constant joy; if I were to describe it, no one would be able to believe it, for they have never experienced such a thing.”
“World-Honored One!
I have come to the presence of the Buddha to hear the Dharma and enter the gate of the pure Dharma; what need is there to speak of the bliss of that land? Why is this so? [Because]...”
All suffering and pleasure are entirely impermanent and lack any fixed characteristic.

We wish to hear that there is neither suffering nor pleasure; neither permanence nor impermanence; neither conceptualization nor discrimination; neither cultivation nor non-cultivation; neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned; neither speech nor non-speech; neither the mundane nor the supramundane; neither the outflowing nor the non-outflowing; neither reality nor unreality; neither awakening nor the factors of awakening; neither power nor weakness; neither darkness nor light; neither the path nor the non-path; neither fruit nor non-fruit; neither arising nor abiding; and no place of arrival.
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
We now wish to hear this Dharma. Why is that? Because—”
All pleasant things appear in the world due to causes and conditions of illusory merit.

The Dharma of the Tathāgata is empty; it is formless and signless. It possesses neither the ten powers nor the four fearlessnesses; it has no supernatural powers, nor does it preach the Dharma. It is without suffering and without pleasure, transcending all mental stirrings and the activities of the mind. Because it has attained this mark of suchness (*tathatā*), it is called the Tathāgata.

All those who give rise to discursive thoughts [distinguish between]: what is real and what is unreal; what is with outflows and what is without outflows; what is called mundane and what is supramundane; what is precept and what is non-precept; what is power and what is non-power; what is fear and what is fearlessness; what is a holy field of merit and what is not a holy field of merit; what is called the Tathāgata, the assembly of bodhisattvas, the various śrāvakas, and the pratyekabuddhas; and what is supernormal power and what is aspiration.
The Tathāgata has completely severed all such conceptual proliferations.
By virtue of this power of non-obstruction and fearlessness, he is able to let out the lion’s roar and manifest the great voice of a Buddha amidst the great assembly.
“World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata is also able to give rise to the perception of non-disgust within disgust, and to give rise to the perception of weary detachment within that which is not disgusting; furthermore, he can remain equanimous by departing from both. This is called the Buddha’s practice, the noble practice of mastery, and the practice not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.”
“World-Honored One!
This practice that is not shared with others cannot be equaled by any other, nor can it be destroyed. Why is this so? [Because]...”
The intellectual power of other beings cannot reach or know such various categories of conditioned phenomena of the Buddha-Bhagavāns—so profound, so causal, so quiescent, and so blissful.
“World-Honored One!
The various practices of the Tathāgata are non-practice, which sentient beings are unable to practice.
For this reason, World-Honored One!”
The various practices of the Tathāgata are not within the capacity of any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha to perform.
That which is not within their capacity is neither practice nor non-practice; for all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fundamentally lack the power of practice regarding this Dharma.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
the conduct of the Tathāgata is called "boundless conduct. As for boundless conduct,
it is that which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have fundamentally aspired to and delighted in, being without limit or boundary.
“World-Honored One!
This Dharma cannot be explained by means of written words; to explain it by means of written words is to depart from this practice.
This Dharma is named the ‘Dharma-Gate of Essential Meaning’ (Arthapraveśa), which can open sixty-six thousand Dharma-gates and cause them all to be illuminated.”
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha One-Jewel-Adornment constantly expounds this Dharma-gate for the sake of sentient beings.

When this gate was being spoken, seventy-seven thousand bodhisattvas all attained this unimpeded Dharma-gate and were able to accord with the conduct of the Tathāgata. These bodhisattvas then cried out in unison:
"We have now already attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Sixty thousand sentient beings all resolved their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
At that moment, the Tathāgata immediately bestowed predictions of their future buddhahood upon them.
Eighty quadrillion nayutas of beings, amidst all dharmas, distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, there were thirty thousand bhikṣuṇīs who, no longer grasping at any dharmas, attained the liberation of mind through the exhaustion of outflows.
At that time, the Buddha smiled, emitting a great radiance that illuminated the world universally, and the earth shook violently.
Thereupon, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"For what cause and for what reason do you manifest a smile, emit a great radiance that illuminates the world universally, and cause the earth to shake so violently?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“When the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha preached this Dharma-gate, seventy-seven thousand bodhisattvas all attained this gate.
Within the expanse of space in this world, the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha had previously heard this Dharma-gate from eighty thousand Tathāgatas.”
Having heard this, they attain this Dharma-gate of non-obstruction; having attained this gate, they are constantly able to travel and transform within immeasurable Buddha-lands.

Chapter Four: The Nature of Suchness (1) At that time, to the east, passing through seven hundred and eighty thousand *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, there was a world named Single Jewel Heap (*Ekaratnākara*). There dwelt a Buddha named Infinite Jewel Power (*Anantaratanabala*), who currently resides there, surrounded by a vast assembly of immeasurable beings who pay him respectful homage as he preaches the Dharma for them.
The Buddha Anantaratnabala conferred upon the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avandhyacaryābala the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, saying:
"This Bodhisattva shall next attain Buddhahood after me."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amogharatnācāra, seeing a great radiance and hearing a great sound within that assembly, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Whose radiance and whose voice is this?"
That Buddha replied:

"To the west, passing from here through seven hundred and eighty thousand *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni, who is currently present, preaching for the sake of the Greatly Adorned Bodhisattvas the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra* that Severs the Doubts of Sentient Beings and Brings Joy to the Multitudes."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amoghadarśanabala addressed that Buddha, saying:
"I wish to go to that Sahā world to make offerings to and pay homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, and to see the assembly of bodhisattvas in that land who are fully adorned with great majesty."
That Buddha replied:
"You yourself know the proper time; you should travel to that world with a single-minded focus. Why is this? Because—"
Those bodhisattvas possess great majesty and virtue; they are difficult to overcome and difficult to equal.
On my behalf, you should inquire after that Buddha, asking:
"Are you free from affliction? Are you free from illness? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vigor at peace?"
"Offer this lotus flower to that Buddha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Aviruddhacāritrabala rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and circumambulated him three times to the right. Immediately, together with seventy-eight thousand bodhisattvas, he vanished from that buddha-field and arrived in this world.

He caused all the trees in this trichiliocosm to produce flowers and fruit out of season; a rain of various famous flowers fell, their fragrance wafting everywhere, while exquisite music played simultaneously.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Amogharatnākara approached the Bamboo Grove, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, rubbed the Buddha’s feet with his hands, and three times declared:
"I am the Bodhisattva Amogharatnākara."
The Buddha said:
"Cease for now! I recognize the sincerity of your heart."
Then, the Bodhisattva Avitathacaryabala bowed his head to the ground in prostration and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha Anantaratnabala inquires after the World-Honored One:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy, and is your physical strength robust?”
"With this lotus flower, I offer worship to the World-Honored One.
After the Buddha had accepted the flower, he asked him:
"Is the Buddha Anantaratnabala at peace and free from ailment? Is his physical strength robust?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
The Buddha Anantaratnabala has little affliction and little illness; he is at ease and unconditioned.”
The Buddha gave these flowers to Maitreya Bodhisattva.
At that time, Maitreya took the lotus flower in his hand and spoke these words:

"By the power of the roots of goodness, merit, and karmic conditions of this lotus flower, may good men or good women who resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* obtain a pure buddha-field and bring sentient beings to maturity."

Why is this? If sentient beings have not planted roots of goodness, they are difficult to transform; if they are not endowed with roots of goodness, they are difficult to transform; if their roots of goodness are feeble and shallow, they are difficult to transform; and those who delight in inferior teachings are difficult to transform.

Why is this? Within these various flowers, if anyone wishes to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, they shall see them all; they will also be able to see the assembly of bodhisattvas in the world-system Jewel-Heap of the Buddha Boundless Jewel-Power, as well as the great assembly of śrāvakas there who have attained common liberation, the three knowledges, and the six supernormal powers.
“World-Honored One!

These flowers are born as the retribution for the causes and conditions of profound roots of goodness; therefore, I now offer them to the Buddhas so that those among the assembly who have resolved to seek the Buddha-way may attain freedom from all obstacles, and even those who have not yet resolved may likewise be inspired to do so.”
"Just as the Tathāgata has realized all dharmas, attaining the Unsurpassed Way through the characteristic of non-disruption, I too, with this mind, hold these flowers to offer in worship.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"What is meant by 'dharmas' such that the Tathāgata, through Suchness, realizes them as non-disruptive and thereby attains the Unsurpassed Way?"
Bhadrapāla addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
There is no such dharma; it is by means of the Tathāgata’s penetration of Suchness (tathatā) and the attainment of the indestructible that he achieves the Buddha-way."
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata does not apprehend the characteristics of these dharmas.
If the Buddha does not apprehend them, they are neither called "dharmas" nor called "non-dharmas."
World-Honored One!
If there were any dharma within that which is non-apprehensible, it would constitute the Tathāgata giving rise to this characteristic of dharmas. Why is this so?
All characteristics that arise do so because of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Since even the Tathāgata does not perceive these bases, how much less could he perceive characteristics within that which is non-apprehension!
To have such an observation is itself to create a characteristic; therefore, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without grasping, without rejecting, and without following after.
Because those who practice accordingly attain this mark, they are called Tathāgatas.
Why is this? All dharmas that the Buddha desires are within the *tathatā* (suchness); if one grasps at various dharmas, one destroys the *tathatā*.
Just as there is no Tathāgata, yet because of the *tathatā* (suchness), he is called the Tathāgata;
this *tathatā* is signless, and because it is signless, he is called the Tathāgata;
this *tathatā* is inexhaustible, and because it is inexhaustible, he is called the Tathāgata.
This Suchness is indestructible; because it is indestructible, one is called the Tathāgata.
All phenomena are according to reality; because they are according to reality, one is called the Tathāgata.
Therefore, World-Honored One!
The suchness of all phenomena is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the suchness of all phenomena.
Therefore, World-Honored One,
the meaning of "Tathāgata" is that there is no place of abiding, because he does not abide even in correct penetration.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "If a person neither grasps nor rejects, neither conforms to nor disputes the Dharma, this one is called a field of merit for all the world.
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"Abiding in what state are you able to speak thus?"
He replied: “World-Honored One!
I dwell within all the various abodes throughout the world, and there I speak in this manner:”
“World-Honored One!
I do not greedily cling as ordinary people dwell. Why is this?”
The dwelling place of ordinary worldlings is precisely attachment to the signs of decay and ruin.
If one clings to these signs of decay, such a person will themselves undergo decay and transformation.
World-Honored One!

The true nature of reality does not abide as the world abides; within these worldly characteristics, the noble ones are without contention and without duality, which is called "abiding in the world," whereas ordinary beings have no sphere of activity therein.
The world is like a mirage, for it transcends all sense bases;
the world is impermanent, for it arises from conditions;
the world is impure, for it gives rise to evil karma.
Therefore, the world, the abode of the world, and the characteristics of the world’s destruction all abide within that which has no abode.
For this reason, I abide in the non-dual Dharma and am able to make such a statement.
At that time, the Buddha said to Bhadrapāla:
"Do you abide in this Dharma and speak thus? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the Dharma attained by the Buddha, none but the Tathāgata himself is able to know it. “Bhadrapāla!”
"What dharma have I attained?
[The Buddha replied: "Indeed so, World-Honored One!
Regarding the dharma attained by the Buddha while seated at the site of enlightenment—whether it be 'dharma' or 'non-dharma,' such a thing is impossible."
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla: "Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said."

The Dharma attained at the Tathāgata’s place of enlightenment is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Regarding this Dharma, my wisdom cannot function within it, my eyes cannot see it, and there is no sphere of activity for it; it is not penetrated by insight and cannot be fully understood by clarity. When questioned, there is no answer; within this Dharma, there is no receiving and no grasping, no defilement and no purity.

If I were to speak of this Dharma that I have realized for myself, and if anyone were to practice this Dharma by means of signs or mental formations, they would all become confused and distressed. Bhadrapāla!

Regarding this Dharma, with the exception of the Buddhas who bear witness to it, even those bodhisattvas who manifest in their final birth cannot realize it; hearing such a Dharma, they still harbor fear and trepidation—how much less so those below them who could possibly bear witness to it!
Chapter 5: On Lack of Faith (1) The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:

"In future ages, there will be bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate the mind, do not cultivate ethical discipline, and do not cultivate wisdom. Upon hearing this sutra—which explains that the bodhi of all Buddhas is without gain, without loss, without discrimination, without defilement, and without ignorance, and which accords with suchness as entrusted by the Buddhas—they will lack faith."
Startled, doubtful, and terrified, they feared falling into a great abyss and thought to themselves:

"The Tathāgata is said to have attained all-knowledge (sarvajñatā), yet this sutra says that wisdom does not function, insight cannot penetrate, clarity cannot comprehend, there is no answer to questions, and there is no characteristic that can be known."

"When these people see someone reading, reciting, or preaching this sutra, they instead treat them with pity, or give rise to anger and pride, conceiving thoughts of enmity and hostility. Bhadrapāla!"
Observe the final age: there are those who are thus perverted and rebellious toward me;

these thieves of the Dharma instead attain honor and nobility, while those capable of expounding the Tathāgata’s true wisdom are treated with contempt and are not permitted to dwell in monasteries or vihāras.

By means of this Dharma, I am naturally without a teacher and let out the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly. These wicked people do not recognize the Tathāgata or the Dharma of the Tathāgata; because they do not recognize them, they conceive thoughts of praise regarding things that deserve censure, and they conceive thoughts of reproach regarding things that deserve praise.
What is meant by "reproachable"?

If a person grasps at or clings to any phenomena, even wholesome dharmas, this is what the Tathāgata reproaches. If such a person gives praise to that which is reproachable, they are called a thief among śramaṇas, a defiler of śramaṇas, a caṇḍāla among śramaṇas, and a dregs-like ruin within the Saṅgha; they follow after external paths with deep calculations of annihilationism and eternalism, giving rise to a mind of attachment and discrimination toward dharmas.

"Bhadrapāla! The Right View of the world spoken of by the Tathāgata consists of dharmas that are subject to conceptual proliferation and accord with the principles of birth and death, intended to cause sentient beings to know the retribution of karma. Yet these deluded people conceive of these dharmas as being supreme."

"Bhadrapāla! The matted-hair brahmins also speak of the causes and conditions of worldly transgressions and blessings; if one who knows them thus were called an 'enlightened one,' then those brahmins should have attained enlightenment."

Bhadrapāla! Such a brahmin, after my parinirvāṇa, will personally perceive faults within what he knows and sees, thereby giving rise to a mind of weary detachment; he will seek to go forth as a renunciant within my Dharma, and once he has gone forth, he will be able to attain the Buddha-dharma.
"Bhadrapāla! Observe the future world:

these deluded people will not even equal the fire-worshipping brahmins. Such deluded people shall be like Makkhali Gosāla, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, and others, who will take the mundane right view taught by me—which accords with the principles of birth and death and the karmic retribution of causes and conditions—and treat such discursive arguments as supreme wisdom."
Such a person slanders the Tathāgata and the Dharma of the Tathāgata; they are unable to see or know the essential means for transcending birth and death.
I say that such a person is not a fit vessel for the Path.

Why is this? Because such a person destroys the Buddha-dharma accumulated by me over immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable eons through a minor cause; such a person commits an offense against the Tathāgata and is a thief of the Tathāgata.
"Bhadrapāla! Who is it that is said to praise the Tathāgata and preach the Dharma in accordance with the Tathāgata’s intention?

It is one who, regarding all dharmas, is without greed and without contention, without arising and without action, signless and unconditioned; who transcends the three periods of time while expounding the Dharma—such a person is called one who praises the Tathāgata and acts according to his will. They are called a son of the Buddha, born from the Buddha’s mouth and transformed by birth from the Dharma."

“Bhadrapāla! Such a person is able to read, recite, inquire about, and respond to sūtras such as these; they are called one who acts according to their will, one who speaks in accordance with the Dharma, and one who practices in accordance with the Dharma, and I shall augment them with my spiritual power.”

This person has previously received my instruction and was exhorted by me; they are able to establish the banner of the Dharma, blow the great conch of the Dharma, beat the great drum of the Dharma, and unfurl the banner of the Dharma, and are known to all the Tathāgatas.

Such a person adorns themselves with the flower garland of merit, dwells in the realm of permanence and bliss, and subdues all demonic adversaries. Rare in this world, those who behold them gain benefit; they are worthy vessels capable of upholding the unsurpassed Way, are mindful of by all Bodhisattvas and Buddhas, can purify the Dharma-eye, encounter no obstacles regarding any phenomena, and bring joy to the Buddhas' minds.

The Buddha permits such a person to draw near, pay homage, serve, and receive the True Dharma. Adorned with all merits, their wisdom is profound and far-reaching; they rain down the great Dharma rain for all students, increasing the Buddha-dharma and spreading the flowers of the awakening mind. They bring forth the fruit of liberation and sit upon the site of enlightenment, attaining Buddha-enlightenment to show the path to sentient beings, and being able to perform the gift of Dharma to fulfill the vows of all beings.

"Bhadrapāla! I shall now briefly describe the merits of such a person; were I to describe them in detail, few would be able to believe and accept them. Such a person is called one who extols the Tathāgata and praises the Buddha-dharma."
“Bhadrapāla! It is like a person who has not seen Lake Anavatapta; upon seeing another lake, they say:
‘This is equal to that great lake, no different at all.’”
"Although these people wish to praise that pond, they instead bring it to ruin.

Bhadrapāla! These deluded people possess none of these merits; they lack such Dharma and such wisdom. With merely mundane, outflow-tainted right views and through their defiled attachment to birth and death, they praise me, saying these words:"
"The Tathāgata’s wisdom has no obstruction within this Dharma.
Although they wish to praise me, in reality they disparage me.

It is like a foolish person who hears that gold is yellow, but later, upon hearing someone describe the superior characteristics of Jambūnada gold, refuses to believe or accept it, saying to that person:
"Cease, do not speak! This true golden color is yellow, not as you describe.
These deluded people are likewise thus—blind and in darkness, devoid of sight.

"If one hears others speak of the names of Buddhas and the names of Dharmas, and further hears that the Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, was born into a royal family with a full retinue of kin, left home to study the Way and became fully endowed with precepts and meditative concentration, yet does not hear of the true Dharma-body of the Buddha or the true characteristics of the Dharma, but merely takes these names of dharmas to be 'All-Knowledge' and calls him 'Tathāgata'—[this is called the second stage]."
Furthermore, they have not heard the Tathāgata’s exposition on why, by what characteristics, all dharmas are non-dharmas.
Consequently, when such persons occasionally hear these sūtras explaining the true body of the Buddha and the reality of the Dharma-characteristics, they give rise to doubt and wonder.
Does such a phenomenon exist?

Is it not so? Is it not like that blind man who, having heard that the color of gold is yellow, later hears people speak of Jāmbūnada gold and conceives doubt, failing to believe it—is it not just like this?

"Furthermore, it is like a foolish person who hears it said that the great ocean is thirty thousand yojanas in breadth and eighty-four thousand yojanas in depth; that it contains immeasurable treasures, and its water is of a single flavor, neither increasing nor decreasing."
Such people do not believe it, and they think to themselves:
"All the streams flow into it; how could it not overflow?
It is so deep and vast—though there be precious treasures therein, who could possibly obtain them?"
One might then claim that the great ocean lacks such virtues.

Foolish people are just like this: they hear others speak of the name of the Buddha and the name of the Dharma, yet they do not hear of its profound merits, wisdom, or the true nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

Or, they may hear others speak of such sūtras as these—which describe ultimate nirvāṇa, the immeasurable treasures of the Dharma, and the attainment of great liberation that enables sentient beings to obtain the unobstructed eye of a Buddha.

Regarding all phenomena, there is neither increase nor decrease; all wisdom is boundless and limitless; its merit is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom, such that no other beings can measure it, nor can anyone destroy it.

For example, just as the great ocean does not harbor dead corpses, so too is the Buddha-dharma: those with wrong views, evil persons, and those who have lost their life of wisdom may not dwell therein.
Furthermore, just as the great ocean has a single salty taste, so too is the Buddha-dharma: it leads to the same nirvana and possesses the single flavor of liberation.
Foolish people, upon hearing this, are unable to believe or understand it; they claim that such a thing does not exist and is not the true Dharma. "Bhadrapāla!
Observe these foolish people: they do not even know from where birth comes, nor to what place death leads."
Regarding the past, what conduct did one practice?
One does not know the karmic conditions nor the retribution. Regarding the future world, what dharma will one practice?
What retribution will one obtain?
Are you practicing the path of wisdom or the path of consciousness?

If such a deluded person conceives the notion of non-Dharma regarding this Dharma, and conceives the notion of reality regarding the teachings I have censured, they will be unable to rely upon such sūtras after my parinirvāṇa.

“Bhadrapāla! In my sutras I have said that if, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there are those who slander the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha, you should not harbor anger, resentment, or distress. You should instead think:
‘If we give rise to a mind of anger and resentment, we are no longer śramaṇas, nor do we abide in the dharma of a śramaṇa, and we do not accord with the Path.’”
"If one is a śramaṇa but does not follow the Dharma, one will ultimately be unable to attain faith, understanding, and penetration into the dharma of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha-spoken *Kusuma-hasta Sūtra*, Scroll One.
The Buddha-spoken *Kusuma-hasta Sūtra*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Six: The Foundations of Mindfulness (2). Chapter Six: The Foundations of Mindfulness.
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"At that time, all virtuous persons should think thus:
'We ourselves shall rely upon the four foundations of mindfulness.
As for the four foundations of mindfulness, within the Noble Dharma, all phenomena are termed foundations of mindfulness."

Why is this? Because all dharmas abide eternally in their own nature and cannot be destroyed; they are the gateway of the foundations of mindfulness, the gateway where dharmas reside, the initial gateway for entering the Dharma, the gateway of the Eightfold Noble Path, and the gateway of the three doors of liberation.
Regarding the gates of liberation: by means of the dharma of non-duality, one abandons the two extremes and attains noble liberation.
The dharma of non-duality is that which is non-existent;
if it is non-existent, it is inexhaustible, and this is called right view.
To be far removed from the two extremes means that the extremes themselves are empty by nature and lack any reality.
Bhadrapāla, you should know that the Tathāgata does not attain freedom from extremes by perceiving extremes; because there were originally no extremes, it is called "freedom from extremes."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are detached from all phenomena; the wise do not perceive them as ordinary people do.
Bhadrapāla! The true mark of dharmas cannot be found when sought; therefore, it is called "detachment. These dharmas are illusory, with neither gain nor loss.
"Bhadrapāla! For this reason, in the past there was a deva who came and asked me:
'Is it well with you, śramaṇa?'"
I immediately replied:
"What have I obtained that I should have joy?
He asked again:
"Are you grieved? I replied again,
"For the loss of what thing would there be grief?"
He asked again,
"Are you neither joyful nor sorrowful? He replied:
"So it is," the deva said. "Excellent!"
"I am neither joyful nor sorrowful.
He then asked the deva,
"What is your intention?"
The deva said:
"I thought that śramaṇas dwell in tranquil extinction.
"Bhadrapāla! [the Buddha continued.]
Observe this deva who has swiftly attained my Dharma.

The deva at that time is now present in this assembly; knowing that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is quiescent, you should know that because this deva formerly made offerings to five hundred Buddhas, he has swiftly attained thorough penetration within my Dharma.

Therefore, the Buddha said: "Those who have not planted roots of goodness, or whose roots of goodness are not yet mature, cannot even understand the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, much less be able to swiftly penetrate my Dharma!"

Bhadrapāla! If one hears this Dharma and can quickly understand it, their merit will be exceedingly slight—yet it would still be as though they had planted the roots of all manner of goodness under a thousand Buddhas. Why is this?
"Only those whose roots of goodness are vast can penetrate such profound wisdom.

At that time, the bodhisattvas Bhadrapāla, Ratnakūṭa, Nāyaka, Jyotirasa, Narada, Indradeva, Varuṇadeva, Suvikrāntaśakti, Mahāmati, Upakāramati, Vardhamānamati, Amoghadarśin, Susthitamati, Balātikrānta, Nityodyukta, Anikṣiptadhura, and Sūryagarbha—these five hundred bodhisattvas each scattered various flowers upon the Buddha as an offering and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!..."
If there are sentient beings who seek such sutras as these and manage to hear them, may they all be made certain to attain the path to Buddha-enlightenment.

Furthermore, by this cause, may the present Buddhas of the ten directions be entreated to remain for a long time and preach the Dharma, and may the assemblies be fully endowed with the factors that assist enlightenment.
At that time, the Buddha asked Bhadrapāla:

"What benefit do sentient beings derive from you, such that you are able to make this great vow for their sake, and to entreat the Buddha to remain long and preach the Dharma, so that the multitude may be fully provided with the aids to the path of enlightenment?"
Bhadrapāla addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I do not generate this adornment because of the loss or gain to myself caused by sentient beings; I do not form the thought:
'Because these sentient beings have benefited me, I shall cause them to abide in the Buddha-dharma.'"
"It would be a detriment to me, and I would not abide in the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, the bodhisattvas do not adorn themselves with such conceptual discrimination.
"For example, World-Honored One!"

When the flowers and leaves of the Pārijātaka-kubera tree were in full bloom, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, seeing its flourishing splendor, felt great joy and amused themselves beneath the tree with the five kinds of music.

"Bhagavān! What benefit or harm does this king of trees bring to the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, such that their hearts are filled with love and delight, and they constantly go beneath it to amuse themselves with the five desires, obtaining incomparable joy and bliss upon seeing it?"
The Bodhisattvas are likewise; they do not cultivate their adornments out of concern for whether sentient beings will benefit or suffer loss, but rather think:
"When shall I attain the wisdom of a Buddha, so that I may become the refuge for the immeasurable sentient beings of the worlds in the ten directions?"
"Just as those celestial trees bloom with flowers that bring joy to the devas,
so shall I cause sentient beings to delight themselves in the Dharma-joy of the Buddha’s five faculties, just as the devas beneath that king of trees delight themselves in the five pleasures."
"Furthermore, World-Honored One,
one generates adornment by being detached from sentient beings, yet does not apprehend sentient beings;
one generates adornment by being detached from the self, yet does not apprehend a self."
One generates adornment by way of detachment from dharmas, not by attaining any dharmas;
one generates adornment by way of detachment from the aggregates, not by attaining any aggregates;
one generates adornment by way of detachment from the elements, not by attaining any elements.
One generates this adornment by way of detachment from the sense bases (*āyatana*), not by attaining them.
World-Honored One!

Within this adornment there are no fruits; because the adornment is detached, it is empty of such fruits. Therefore, one should generate this adornment regarding all phenomena without grasping or abandoning.
"Bhagavān! Such marks of adornment are unapprehendable; the locus of adornment and that for which there is adornment are both unapprehendable, Bhagavān!"
If there is anything attained, then one has attained a self.
Therefore, a bodhisattva does not crave or accept either a self or non-self;
if one accepts non-self, that itself becomes a self, and it cannot be called "non-self" or "one who has nothing received."
“World-Honored One!
By this principle, this Great Adornment manifests in the world; within this adornment, there is no distinction between ‘this’ and ‘that.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"What benefit is there in seeing such adornments? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"

Having set forth this adornment, I do not perceive that the dharmas of ordinary persons and those in training are distant from me, nor do I perceive that the Buddha-dharmas are near; furthermore, I do not perceive these Buddha-dharmas as being "Buddha-dharmas" in such a way.
"Bhagavān! I have set forth this adornment, within which I perceive neither gain nor loss.
It is by virtue of these characteristics that such an adornment manifests in the world."

At that time, the various flowers scattered by the bodhisattvas manifested supernatural powers, reaching everywhere throughout the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas and to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to abide in the Buddha-dharma.

Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Turning the Wheel of Dharma upon the Initial Resolve (2).
