At that time, to the east of this world, passing through immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands, there was a world named Saṃbhāra-viśeṣa. There, a Buddha named Nirnimitta-ghoṣa currently dwelt, teaching the Dharma.

He was bestowing the prediction of supreme enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) upon the Bodhisattva Citta-utpāda-dharmacakra-pravartana, saying: "After me, this Bodhisattva shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
At that time, this bodhisattva, seeing a great radiance and hearing a great sound, addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Whose radiance and sound is this?"
That Buddha replied:

"To the west, passing from here through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is titled Śākyamuni; he is currently present there, and this is the light and voice of that Buddha."

Now that Tathāgata is preaching for the bodhisattvas the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*—which severs the doubts of sentient beings and brings joy to the multitude—and those bodhisattvas have achieved immeasurable and perfect adornments.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Instantly Turning the Wheel of Dharma upon Resolving His Mind addressed that Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I wish to go to that Sahā world to make offerings to, pay homage to, and visit Śākyamuni Buddha and the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
"Why is this? It is difficult even to behold these great beings, let alone to draw near to them!
That Buddha replied:
“You yourself know the proper time.
Having received this permission, the Bodhisattva rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
At that time, the Buddha Voice of Signlessness gave him a lotus flower and addressed him, saying:
"Take this flower and give it to Śākyamuni.

Within this lotus, behold the merits cultivated by the Buddha Voice of Signlessness when he was originally a bodhisattva; let such flowers as these fill that world so that all sentient beings may enjoy them."
At that time, the Bodhisattva received the flowers from the Buddha and came to this land.

At that moment, all the vegetation of this world—its grasses, trees, flowers, leaves, fruits, and even down to the finest hairs—appeared within the hand of the Bodhisattva Fa-chuan-ju-lun (Turning the Wheel of Dharma upon Resolving the Mind). Furthermore, all the voices of sentient beings there issued forth the sounds of the Dharma: the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; and the sounds of the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the path, meditative concentrations, liberations, and various samādhis.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I now behold the Tathāgata’s great power of supernormal faculties.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "This was not done by me.

To the east from here, passing through immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds, there is a world named Saṃbhāra-guṇa-lakṣaṇa; the Buddha there is named Alakṣaṇa-ghoṣa, who currently dwells and teaches the Dharma."

There is a bodhisattva named Instantaneous Turning of the Wheel of Dharma upon Arousing the Mind, who has come from that realm to this world; this is due to the power of that bodhisattva’s original vows, the fruition of his merit, and his supernormal abilities.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness did the Bodhisattva ‘One Who Turns the Wheel of Dharma upon Arousing the Mind’ plant in past lives, such that he is able to possess such karmic rewards and supernormal powers?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “Excellent, excellent!
By the power of the Buddha, you are able to question the Tathāgata. The Bodhisattva Whose Resolve Immediately Turns the Wheel of Dharma has planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas.”
Now, listen with single-minded attention to the roots of virtue planted by this bodhisattva in past lives.

When the Buddhas of the ten directions sat at the site of enlightenment and first attained Buddhahood, this bodhisattva—whether as a Brahma King, a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or a seer possessing the five supernatural powers—would come to the site of enlightenment to make offerings to those Buddhas and request them to turn the wheel of Dharma; how many times did he do so?
“Śāriputra! When I first attained the unsurpassed path, the Brahmā King came to entreat me, saying:
‘I only pray, World-Honored One!’”
He turns the Wheel of Dharma.
There are sentient beings who, having deeply practiced wholesome dharmas in past lives, possess sharp faculties and wisdom such that they can understand the Buddha’s intention;
if they do not hear the Dharma, would they not suffer eternal loss?

“Śāriputra! This Bodhisattva ‘The One Who Turns the Wheel of Dharma upon Generating the Mind’ exhorts all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma; these various merits serve no other purpose than to request the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma.”
“Śāriputra! I shall now speak a parable to clarify this meaning, for the wise attain understanding through parables.

Suppose there were a single vessel, shaped like a sea trench, containing the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system: ten billion suns and moons, four hundred billion great oceans, ten billion sets of four continents, four hundred billion nayutas of minor kingdoms belonging to those four continents, ten billion Sumeru kings of mountains, and ten billion Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa). This vessel were filled to the brim with mustard seeds, sesame seeds, or rice grains. A powerful giant were to take them all up and scatter them in the four directions, and a great wind were to blow everywhere so that each single mustard seed fell upon a single world-system.”
"What do you think?
Are the worlds into which those mustard seeds have fallen many? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
It is exceedingly much;
it is immeasurable and beyond calculation.”
“Śāriputra! I shall now clarify this matter for you.
Suppose all those worlds where as many mustard seeds have fallen were joined together into a single vessel, its length, breadth, height, and depth being exactly equal.”
Its walls are solid and firm; suppose such a great vessel were filled with fine sand, like measuring rice or flour with bushels and pecks.
Would the number of grains of sand in it be considered many?
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
It is beyond measure and cannot be numbered.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"The number of grains of sand in these rivers may still be counted and known; however, the number of times these bodhisattvas have exhorted the Buddhas at the sites of enlightenment to turn the wheel of Dharma and deliver sentient beings is incalculable—and yet, they have not yet dedicated these roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, the number of times they have offered wheels of the seven precious jewels to the Buddhas, requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma, is many times greater than that."
Furthermore, they offered wheels of various precious jewels to the Buddhas, requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma, in numbers even more than doubled;
they also offered wheels of incense to the Buddhas, requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma, in numbers that increased yet further.

How much more so when one uses gold, silver, colored paintings, or wooden wheels to make offerings to the Buddhas and entreat them to turn the wheel of Dharma, yet does not dedicate this root of goodness toward the path of the Buddha’s Bodhi, but only for the purpose of requesting the Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma!
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
After this, there will be a Buddha named Overpowering Wisdom (Jñānabala).
At that time, there will be a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Renowned Power (Yaśobala), who possesses sovereign majesty over a great trichiliocosm."

While he was amusing himself with the five desires in the gardens and pavilions of the inner palace, and as the various court ladies sang praises, sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity spontaneously emerged in accordance with those sensual matters; the king was immediately struck with fear and gave rise to a mind of weary detachment.
He then went to visit the Buddha Overpowering Wisdom (Atijñānabala). The Buddha Overpowering Wisdom caused him to recollect the roots of goodness he had planted in the past.
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king thought to himself:
"The wisdom of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is truly unprecedented and unimpeded; it enables me to know the various roots of goodness I have planted in the presence of so many Buddhas."

My mind was overwhelmed by the five sensual pleasures of self-indulgence, and being entangled in the myriad affairs of governing the state, I did not even know that I had planted various roots of goodness under a single Buddha.

Although in the past I planted many roots of goodness under all those Buddhas, I did not dedicate them toward the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; thus, these roots of goodness remained within the state of uncertainty.
I shall now employ the roots of goodness I have accumulated for the sake of the unsurpassed path and to benefit sentient beings; wherever I am born, I shall travel through the lands of all Buddhas.

Therein, the speech of all sentient beings shall be sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and from all the grasses, trees, forests, flowers, leaves, and fruits throughout those worlds, there shall likewise issue forth the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
"I share these roots of goodness with all sentient beings, so that they may attain the wisdom now possessed by the Buddha Overcoming Power.
Having formed this thought, he rose from his seat, stood before the Buddha, and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
"Now I offer all my kingdoms to the Buddha and the Saṃgha; I only pray that you will accept and enjoy them.
Having made this offering, he left the household life to pursue the Way.

Upon hearing this, the fourfold army also followed him into the homeless life; forty *nayuta* of court ladies likewise followed him into the homeless life, as did eighty billion *nayuta* of other people.
The fourfold assemblies of the Buddha Jñānabala increased and expanded.

All those who had left the household life attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). Each, by means of their supernatural power, traveled to buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, where they exhorted immeasurable Buddhas seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma and deliver sentient beings.

In the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, he likewise exhorts and entreats immeasurable Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, to turn the wheel of Dharma and deliver all sentient beings; it is exactly the same for all of them.

From that time forward, King Yaśaḥprabha was never again conceived in a womb, nor did he ever take birth in impure lands; in every world where he traveled, all the sentient beings, grasses, trees, and forests produced the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

“Śāriputra! Do you think that the King Renowned Power at that time—who, having personally heard from Buddha Transcendent Wisdom Power the roots of goodness he had planted in previous lives, left the household life to practice the Way and attained the five supernormal powers, and who traveled through immeasurable worlds in the ten directions to exhort all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma and deliver sentient beings—was anyone other than this? It was none other.”
“The one who has now given rise to this mind is none other than the Bodhisattva Dharmacakra-pravartaka.

Chapter 8: Manifesting Transformations (2) At that time, the Bodhisattva Dharmacakra-pravartaka arrived at the city of Rājagṛha and went to the Bamboo Grove. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Buddha Animittasvara sends his greetings to the World-Honored One.”
"Are you free from affliction and illness? Is your daily life light and easy, and is your physical strength robust?
Accept this great lotus flower as an offering to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha then accepted the flower and addressed him, saying:
"Is the Buddha Aśvaghosa well and at ease? Is his teaching of the Dharma successful?
He replied, "World-Honored One!"
The Buddha Animittasvara possesses robust physical strength, and sentient beings are easily delivered.
Why is this? Within that world, when the great assembly gathers, there are four dharmas of purity.
What are the four? They are:
the purity of the roots of goodness for the sake of awakening;
and the purity of immeasurable precepts through the correct formulation of vows.
The purity of immeasurable vision arises from not apprehending dharmas;
the purity of what is observed arises from not grasping at signs.
World-Honored One!
In that assembly, there are none who violate prohibitions, break precepts, or corrupt their dignified conduct; nor is even the name of these three transgressions known there.
The beings of that land regard all sentient beings in this world as if they were being tortured in a prison. I now entreat you to return; I only pray that the Tathāgata will go to that world.
At that time, the Buddha said to him: "Stop!
Son of good family!"
"What do you intend to do upon reaching that world?
I, too, am now transforming sentient beings here.
Bodhisattva Instantaneously Turning the Wheel of Dharma then made a fervent request three times:

"I only pray that the Tathāgata will come to that world; if you do not deign to visit us, I shall myself, by means of the supernatural power obtained as a karmic reward, take this world and, in the space of a single thought-moment, place it within the expanse of space in that land."

At that time, the Buddha remained silent, granting this bodhisattva permission to manifest the sovereign power of great supernatural penetrations; he did so desiring to cause sentient beings to be fully endowed with roots of goodness, and also to demonstrate the power of his knowledge and vision for deliverance.
At that time, this bodhisattva immediately severed and took up the trichiliocosm with his right hand, just as a potter turns a wheel with a staff, and carried it away.
At that time, Śāriputra perceived that this trichiliocosm was all shaking violently, and he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Take this world and us with you; take this world and us with you."

At that time, the World-Honored One, with a voice of wisdom that was gentle, harmonious, and elegant—pleasing to the hearts of the assembly, profound and far-reaching, neither too high nor too low, concise yet not disordered, and capable of revealing the underlying meaning—replied to Śāriputra: "This was not done by me."
The sound of his voice was heard throughout the great trichiliocosm.

At that time, there were sentient beings who were greedily attached to the notion of self and relied upon the view of existence; they were all struck with great terror and attained a mind of weary detachment.

As for the rest of the fourfold assembly, they saw only the Tathāgata surrounded by bodhisattvas as he preached the Dharma, like a wheel-turning monarch seated upon his throne, or like the Great Brahmā King amidst the host of Brahmās.

At that time, the Bodhisattvas who had just resolved their minds to attain enlightenment took all the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions and gathered them together in one place to show them to sentient beings.

Then, by the power of his supernatural penetrations, the World-Honored One caused a great wind to arise and blow upon those worlds, so that they struck and collided with one another until they were torn asunder, shattered, and completely dispersed and extinguished.

The Buddha manifested his supernatural power, and the Great Brahma Kings and all the Brahma devas—who had regarded the dharmas they saw and heard as permanent and indestructible—now beheld their own Brahma palaces being shattered and destroyed. They were struck with great terror and gave rise to a mind of weary detachment, each thinking:
"These palaces were previously established of themselves, yet now they are all being crushed and ruined together, like water waves tossed by the wind that form into foam."
"If even water, when exhausted by the sun's heat and the blowing wind, is completely worn away and destroyed, this is the mark of our own impermanence.
With hearts filled with trepidation, they all joined their palms and paid homage to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"Since long ago, I have constantly taught you that the world is illusory and lacks any reality.

It is as if someone were contending with empty space; so it is with the world, existing only through the power of recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination—unstable and unsubstantial, like a mass of foam."
The world is like an illusion, capable of deceiving sentient beings;
the world is like a mirage, lacking substantial reality and unable to quench craving;
the world is like a shadow, which cannot be grasped.
"The world is like an echo, arising from false and deceptive karma;
the world is according to reality, its nature being without inversion. Śāriputra!"

Seated at the site of enlightenment, I have realized things as they truly are: I know that the characteristics of the world are empty, non-existent, and without any basis of support; through the absence of obstruction, I have attained the realization of the world's characteristics.

“Śāriputra! Originally, as long as I did not know the gratification of the world, the peril of the world, and the escape from the world, I did not proclaim for myself that I had attained the path of a Buddha.”

Having realized the nature of the world as it truly is, as well as its origin, its cessation, and the path leading to its cessation, I have proclaimed for myself: "I have attained the Way of the Buddha."
“Śāriputra! What is called the world?
That which is the world refers to the five aggregates.”
What are the five? They are the aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness. “Śāriputra!
What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)? There may be sentient beings who think:
"That which is past is not called form; that which is future or present is not called form. Therefore, the Buddha taught that all forms whatsoever—whether in the past, future, or present;"

Whether internal or external, coarse or subtle, beautiful or ugly, near or far—all these are called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), yet this aggregate of form is in reality devoid of any intrinsic characteristic.

For example, the aggregate of space, the aggregate of wind, the aggregate of fire, the aggregate of water, and the aggregate of earth exist only as names; the aggregate of form, the aggregate of sensation, and likewise the aggregates of perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also thus. It is for these reasons that we speak of the existence of the aggregates.

“Śāriputra! Ordinary people are ignorant and deluded; they are greedily attached to the body and do not understand the characteristics of form (rūpa). They claim that form is the self or belongs to the self, grasping at signs and making discriminations that give rise to a mind of attachment. It is the same for feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).”
“Śāriputra! When I sat at the site of enlightenment, regarding this matter, I did not conceive of it as existent, nor did I conceive of it as non-existent, and thus the Dharma-eye arose.

Yet ordinary beings give rise to craving and attachment toward these dharmas that do not exist; when these dharmas disintegrate, they give rise to sorrow and affliction. Because such people are deeply attached and have lost what they were attached to, their delusion increases further and they repeatedly initiate dark karma.”
If one uses tiles, stones, staffs, whips, swords, spears, or various other weapons to inflict mutual harm upon others, such karmic offenses arise due to delusion and confusion.
Because the Tathāgata has realized the equality of all phenomena and the equality of all views, he teaches right view.
That which is called right view is equal, upright, and without high or low.
Because those who practice the path rightly, those who cultivate rightly, and those who attain liberation rightly obtain this view, it is called right view.
“Śāriputra! What the Buddha calls right view cannot be explained to you in words; it can only be practiced in accordance with what has been taught. Śāriputra!”

"You all should practice in accordance with the Dharma; you shall thereby attain immeasurable and boundless wisdom. This is called one gate among the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, namely, the characteristic of all conditioned arisings as being non-arising."
When the Tathāgata taught this Dharma-treasury gate, seventy-seven thousand nayutas of Brahmā kings, having become free from dust and defilement regarding all dharmas, attained the pure Dharma-eye.

An assembly of eighty-four thousand nayutas of devas from the desire realm attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena; and immeasurable other people likewise attained the pure Dharma-eye, free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena.

Within the ten billion Jambudvīpas, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas all attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*) in this assembly; furthermore, immeasurable and boundless sentient beings all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers, and the fourfold assembly, the Brahmās of the Brahma-world, the Brahma-abodes, and the Brahma-multitudes, as well as the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans of the desire realm, all saw themselves return to this world.
Chapter Nine: The Powers of the Tathāgata (2) At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the World-Honored One:

"It is unprecedented! This Bodhisattva 'Setting in Motion the Wheel of Dharma upon Resolving the Mind' possesses such great supernormal power that he has taken this Sahā world-system and the Tathāgata, and placed them within the midst of another world-system."
“World-Honored One!
When you carried me there and brought me back here, at that time my very spirit was not present, let alone possess any supernormal powers!
I then further gave rise to this thought:”
"This Bodhisattva now possesses great supernormal powers, escorting me back and forth while I am entirely unaware of whether it was slow or fast, far or near.
I further thought to myself:
"If this Bodhisattva already possesses such spiritual power before attaining the Way of the Buddha, how much more so once he has attained Buddhahood!"
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Do not harbor the thought that this Bodhisattva 'Setting Forth the Wheel of Dharma upon Resolving the Mind' is able to escort the Tathāgata with coming and going."

Why is this? Because I do not see any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, arhat, pratyekabuddha, or any other sentient being—whether deva, nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, asura, garuḍa, kiṃnara, mahoraga, human, or non-human—who could move even a single corner of the Tathāgata’s robe, let alone lift it up and carry it to another world before returning it here; such a thing is impossible.
Maudgalyāyana!

Setting aside all the devas and humans of this world, suppose every sentient being in this trichiliocosm—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception; whether visible or invisible—were simultaneously to obtain a human body, leave the household life out of faith, and attain arhatship, possessing the six supernormal powers just like yours, Maudgalyāyana.
"What do you think?
Is the power of these supernormal knowledges and wisdoms not great?
"It is exceedingly great."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“These arhats could take up the trichiliocosm with their hands and travel through the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
Suppose the Tathāgata were to place a single mustard seed in mid-air; even the great śrāvakas endowed with supernormal powers would be unable to move it by so much as a hair’s breadth.
Maudgalyāyana!

Let us set aside for a moment this assembly of those with great supernormal powers; suppose there were a single person possessed of great supernormal power whom the Buddha permits to blow upon a great trichiliocosm with a single breath, causing it all to disintegrate and scatter its atoms so that they pervade immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
and suppose further that with another single breath, he could cause those atoms to reconstitute a great trichiliocosm once again.
Maudgalyāyana! What do you think?
Does this person possess great supernormal power?
“Very great, World-Honored One! “Maudgalyāyana!

Suppose there were people who all possessed such great supernormal powers, filling this trichiliocosm as densely as a grove of sugarcane, rice, hemp, or bamboo; even if they were all of one mind to manifest their supernatural powers simultaneously, they would still be unable to move even a corner of the Tathāgata’s robe, let alone lift the Tathāgata and place him in another realm before returning again.
“Maudgalyāyana!

While I am seated here, I can shake immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and asaṃkhyeya worlds in the eastern direction. Yet the sentient beings therein do not perceive at all that there is any coming or going; these beings cannot even perceive the formation, destruction, or dissolution of the world.”
Maudgalyāyana! You should know that the supernatural power manifested by the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each being.

There may be sentient beings who are to be delivered upon seeing the body of a Buddha; there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered upon seeing the body of a deva; there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered upon seeing the body of a nāga; there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered upon seeing the bodies of yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, or mahoragas; there may be those who are to be delivered upon seeing a male body or a female body; and there may be those who are to be delivered upon seeing a large body or a small body.
Maudgalyāyana!
You should know that all the powers, fearlessnesses, and sovereign supernormal faculties possessed by the Tathāgata are entirely contained within this sutra.
It is likewise in the south, west, and north, in the four intermediate directions, and in the zenith and nadir.
“Maudgalyāyana!
If you were to behold the conduct of the Tathāgata and his great supernormal powers, you would be unable to engage in question and answer.
Maudgalyāyana!”

I have taught Ānanda the dharanī-gateways so that he may receive and uphold the twelve divisions of the scriptures—sūtra, geya, vyākaraṇa, gāthā, udāna, nidāna, avadāna, itivṛttaka, jātaka, vaipulya, adbhutadharma, and upadeśa—so that he shall not forget them; yet even now, Ānanda is still unable to fully comprehend the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.

Why is this? Because even if all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas were to spend one eon, a hundred thousand million eons, or even immeasurable asaṃkhyeya eons reading, reciting, receiving, upholding, contemplating, and expounding a single word, a single letter, or a single phrase spoken by the Buddha, they would still not be able to exhaust them; how much less could they fully know the great supernormal powers exercised by the Tathāgata? Such a thing is impossible.
“Maudgalyāyana!
For the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings and expounding the Dharma, the Tathāgata employs various causes and conditions, various modes of conduct, and various gateways to the Path.”

When he merely puts on his robes, even all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot know how many sentient beings are benefited therein or how he preaches the Dharma; how much less could they possibly know the Tathāgata’s conduct, the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers, or the Tathāgata’s wisdom? Such a thing is impossible.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having received the lotus flowers from the Bodhisattva Who Turns the Wheel of Dharma upon Generating the Mind, addressed the Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla, the Bodhisattva Ratnākara, the Bodhisattva Śāstṛ, the Bodhisattva Jyotirasa, the Bodhisattva Naradatta, the Bodhisattva Indradatta, the Bodhisattva Varuṇadeva, and the Bodhisattva Suvikrāntabala—those such as these who are able to protect the treasury of the Dharma in future ages:
"O sons of good family!
“Are you able to protect the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, and to well believe in, understand, and expound the conduct of the Tathāgata?
“Indeed we are, World-Honored One!”
"We are all capable of this," they replied. The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, whenever you have something to say, first contemplate the Tathāgata’s underlying intention and the Dharma-gate he has entered, and only then speak."
If someone were to ask,
"What is meant by being fully endowed with the Buddha's wisdom?
you should first contemplate the conduct of the Tathāgata according to sūtras such as these, and only then provide an answer.
If you hear any of the gates of teaching that have been spoken, you should in all cases observe the intentional conduct of the Tathāgata, for it was for this purpose that he taught such a Dharma.

If you see the conduct of sentient beings, you should likewise observe the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata; that is to say, when sentient beings possess such conduct, the Buddha employs that very conduct to transform and eliminate it.

"Regarding the practice of sentient beings, there are ninety-nine thousand faculties; the Tathāgata fully knows those with a predominance of desire have such faculties, those with a predominance of hatred have such faculties, those with a predominance of delusion have such faculties; those who resemble those with much desire have such faculties, those who resemble those with much hatred have such faculties, those who resemble those with much delusion have such faculties; those who resemble those with much desire and hatred have such faculties, those who resemble those with much desire and delusion have such faculties, those who resemble those with much hatred and delusion have such faculties, and those who resemble those with much desire, hatred, and delusion have such faculties."

In this way, these faculties can purify the path and give rise to all things; in this way, these faculties arise from fundamental conditions; in this way, these faculties are obtained through habitual practice.

There are faculties of karmic action that initiate black karma, white karma, or both black and white karma; these faculties accord with the Path, accord with meditative concentration, accord with wisdom, and accord with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); these faculties are compliant with the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, and these faculties accord with the Truths.
“O sons of good family!
Within this, there are twenty thousand faculties; through the power of the causes and conditions from previous lives, they are able to give rise to various karmas, whether black or white.”

By means of these karmic conditions, one obtains various colors—whether black, white, neither black nor white, superior, or middling—and such colors consist of twenty thousand faculties that can produce all bodies, whether long, short, coarse, fine, or of medium size.
There are two hundred thousand faculties capable of manifesting internal characteristics within the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body, by which one knows:

"This person has a mind of greed; this person has a mind of anger; this person has a mind of delusion. One also knows: "This person is free from greed; this person is free from anger; this person is free from delusion."

There are thirty thousand distinctions of karmic retribution regarding the sense faculties; that is to say, when a person dies, their consciousness becomes bewildered and faints, their physical form undergoes transformation, their hands and feet contract and shrivel, the various faculties become disordered, and the joints of the limbs separate from one another.

When exhaling the breath, one knows that these faculties are destined for the hells; likewise, these faculties are destined to fall among animals; these faculties are destined to be born as hungry ghosts; these faculties are destined to be born among devas or humans; these faculties are destined to be born in other Buddha-fields to behold the Buddhas; and these faculties are destined to sever the continuity of birth and death so as not to undergo further existence.

There are seventy thousand faculties; by the power of faith and understanding, one can gather the roots of goodness, while twenty thousand faculties gather unwholesome dharmas—this can be known at the time of death.
O sons of good family!

"This is called the power of the Buddha; it is the practice of the Tathāgata and the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata. Abiding herein, the Tathāgata can expound all dharmas without increase or decrease. Chapter Ten:
On Merit (2) At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Resolute Mind (*Dṛḍhamati*). He rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
I have attained the light of the Dharma through this gateway; therefore, I shall cultivate this gateway so that it may be brought to full perfection. Why is this?

I shall now give rise to such adornments, seeking, practicing, and perfecting this Dharma without ever becoming weary or ceasing, so that in future ages I may once again hear the Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Dṛḍhamati, "Excellent, excellent!
You are able to diligently seek the great Dharma accumulated by all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, over immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable kalpas."

“Dṛḍhamati! Suppose all sentient beings in this trichiliocosm—whether they be of the form realm or the formless realm, with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—were at once to obtain human bodies. If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to provide all these beings with every requisite for happiness, giving them whatever they required of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and could indeed provide them all;”

He takes all these sentient beings and places them entirely within his palm; for the duration of a kalpa, or slightly less than a kalpa, he uses one hand to remove their filth and cast it far away to another place.
Dṛḍhamati! What do you think? Is what this person has done not indeed great?
“Very great, World-Honored One! “Firm Resolve!

Furthermore, if there should be a person who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whether while the Buddha is present or after his parinirvāṇa, who is able to seek such *bodhisattva-piṭaka* sūtras that assist toward enlightenment, and forms this thought:

"I shall cultivate and collect this Mahāyāna treasury of the Dharma and preach it for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may sever greed, hatred, and delusion, and be freed from birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction."

When seeking in this manner, if one obtains even a single four-line verse of this sutra and is able to read, recite, and explain it for the sake of sentient beings, compared to the merit of the former [action], it does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part; indeed, it is beyond the reach of any analogy.
In this way, by seeking the causes and conditions of such profound dharmas, a bodhisattva is able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
"Firm Mind! Who would be able to believe this?"
Only the Buddhas possess ultimate and thorough understanding.
Yet, noble disciples and others who have resolved to seek the Buddha-way are able to believe and accept it. Why is this so?

When the bodhisattvas first resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they make this vow: "I shall act as a protector for sentient beings who have no protector; I shall be an island for those without an island; I shall be a path for those without a path."
I shall cultivate this Mahāyāna—the wisdom of the Buddha—and cause immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to abide in the outflow-free Dharma.
Resolute Mind!

Suppose this person, from dawn until mealtime, were to heap up various precious jewels as high as Mount Sumeru and give them to each and every individual; and at midday, in the afternoon, and during the first, middle, and last watches of the night—throughout their entire lifespan, day and night during the six periods—were to bestow such a mass of jewels upon sentient beings.
Dṛḍhamati! What do you think?
Would these sentient beings attain satisfaction of mind?
"No, World-Honored One! It may even be because of this that one falls into the three evil realms."
The Bodhisattva reflects:

"I shall diligently seek the unsurpassed, sublime Dharma, and cause all sentient beings to view the heaps of jewels in the trichiliocosm as being like mucus and saliva, thereby engendering in them a sense of dread."

“The Bodhisattva of Great Wisdom contemplates this heap of jewels as being entirely sentient beings of the three poisons and afflictions; it is the root of suffering in the cycle of birth and death, of wandering through the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans; it is the root of suffering when seeking them, the root of suffering when guarding them, and the root of all manifold sufferings arising from enmity, hatred, contention, and the commission of various sinful karmas.”
In this way, the bodhisattva develops a sense of weary detachment toward the great mass of jewels and further reflects:
"This is not a mass of jewels, but rather a mass of suffering and affliction in the evil realms; because some sentient beings are greedily attached to it, they fall into the three evil paths."
“Dṛḍhamati! Let alone all the sentient beings in this trichiliocosm.

Suppose the sentient beings in immeasurable *gaṅgā*-sands of lands throughout the ten directions—whether they be of the form realm, the formless realm, those with perception, those without perception, or those with neither perception nor non-perception—were all at once to obtain human bodies. If there were a single person who, having resolved their mind, wished to provide them with all manner of articles of pleasure, and could immediately grant them whatever they required, such as forms, sounds, fragrances, and tastes; and if, whether placing them upon his head or carrying them on his shoulders, he were to do so for a full kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, allowing them to sit or lie down as they pleased, and furthermore, using one hand to remove their filth and cast it far away to another place.”
Dṛḍhamati! What do you think? Is what this person has done not indeed much?
“Very much so, World-Honored One! “Firm Resolve!

I now tell you this sincere word: if a son of good family or a daughter of good family resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seeks such *bodhisattva-piṭaka* sūtras that assist the factors of enlightenment, the merit of taking even a single step toward it is immeasurable; even upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it could not be fully exhausted. Compared to the previous merit, it does not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor can it even be reached by analogy.

Why is this so? Those former requisites of pleasure are the causes and conditions for the outflows (*āsrava*) of all fetters (*saṃyojana*); they cannot bring about the ultimate liberation from suffering or absolute peace.

In contrast, the causes and conditions through which Bodhisattvas seek the Dharma increase the categories of morality (*śīla-skandha*), concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), and wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). They can also fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, attain immeasurable and inconceivable powers of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), and bring sentient beings to maturity while purifying Buddha-fields.
Therefore, Resolute Mind!
The Buddha has taught that it is through the causes and conditions of a bodhisattva’s seeking of the Dharma that one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!"

Suppose the four continents were filled with Tathāgatas, as dense as a grove of sugarcane, rice, or hemp; and suppose there were a person who, for the duration of their entire life, provided them with all necessary requisites such as clothing, bedding, and medicinal decoctions.

After these Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, stupas made of the seven precious substances—each one yojana in height and adorned with banners and spires—are erected; and they are honored with flowers, incense, flags, canopies, and the lighting of lamps for a hundred kalpas, or even more than a hundred kalpas.
Dṛḍhamati! What do you think?
Would the merit obtained by this person be great or not?
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
It is immeasurable and boundless.”
“Dṛḍhamati! I now tell you these sincere words:

suppose a person were to make offerings to that many Tathāgatas, erect that many stūpas, and perform various kinds of offerings for that many kalpas; yet if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek such *bodhisattva-piṭaka* sūtras that assist in awakening, and were to receive, uphold, read, and recite them—the former merit would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or even a hundred-thousand-millionth part of this [latter] merit, and it would not even be comparable by way of analogy.”
Why is this? Because among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is foremost; among all forms of seeking, the seeking of Dharma is foremost.
Therefore, Resolute Mind!

In the final five hundred years, you who uphold, receive, read, and recite such sutras as these shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit, which will not be exhausted even upon attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Dṛḍhamati! I now wish to speak a parable to roughly clarify this matter; you should believe and accept it.
Suppose the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system were made into a single vessel, filled with mustard seeds like black sesame or rice.”
"What do you think?
How many mustard seeds are there in this? "Very many."
“World-Honored One!
They are incalculable. “Firm Mind!”
Suppose again that as many great trichiliocosms as there are mustard seeds were joined together to form a single vessel, filled to the brim with fine sand.
How many would these fine grains of sand number?
“Very much so, World-Honored One!
It is immeasurable and boundless.”
“Dṛḍhamati! Suppose there were a man of great strength who took this fine sand and scattered it in the four directions.
Then a great wind arose and blew these grains of sand, so that each one fell into a separate world-system.”
"What do you think? How many worlds are there? "Very many."
“World-Honored One!
They are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable. “Firm Mind!

I now declare to you clearly: the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the power of immeasurable supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom; he can leap over all those realms in a single step, yet remains seated in his original place without moving from his dignified posture, for even such supernormal powers are not yet fully manifested.

Dṛḍhamati! Suppose the Tathāgata were to take one such grain of sand as one kalpa; let that many kalpas constitute one day, let that many days constitute one month, and let that many months constitute one year. Traveling eastward in this manner for a thousand years without ceasing—[such is the distance he would traverse].
The same applies to the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir.

If a good man or a good woman, wishing to hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, were to take even a single step, the merit thereby obtained—if it were to have a physical form—could not be contained within all the lands traversed by the Tathāgata; for the Tathāgata knows only that the merit of such a person is immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.
“Dṛḍhamati! This merit cannot be known through words or calculation; this merit is contained within immeasurable numbers. **Chapter 11:

Generating the Resolve (Cittotpāda)** At that time, to the east, beyond incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands, there was a world named Mahāyaśas. The Buddha there was named Meru-skandha, who currently resides and bestows the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the Bodhisattva Prabhā-tejo-rāśi, speaking thus:
"This Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-tejo-rāśi shall, after me, attain Buddhahood.

At that time, while that Buddha was surrounded by a great assembly and preaching the Dharma, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-tejo-rāśi, being present in that gathering, saw a great radiance, heard the sound of a cough, and observed the earth shaking violently.
He asked that Buddha, "World-Honored One!"
"Whose light and voice is this? That Buddha replied:

"To the west, passing from here through incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) lands, there is a world named Sahā. The Buddha there is named Śākyamuni; he is currently present, preaching the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra."

The bodhisattvas in that assembly are fully endowed with great adornments; even now, among the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, there are few such multitudes of great bodhisattvas.
If one merely hears the names of these bodhisattvas, one still attains great benefit, let alone seeing them with one's own eyes, drawing near to them, and making offerings to them.
At that moment, the Bodhisattva Prabhāsa-tejo-rāśi addressed the Buddha Meru-skandha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to go to that Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha, to pay homage to him and make offerings to him, and also to see that assembly of great Bodhisattvas who are fully adorned.”
That Buddha replied, "Go as you wish. Then,
that Buddha gave seven lotus flowers to the Bodhisattva Light-and-Virtue-Mass (Prabhāsa-tejo-rāśi) and addressed him, saying:
“Take these flowers and present them to Śākyamuni Buddha, and on my behalf inquire after that Buddha’s health:
‘Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and at ease in your daily life? Is your strength robust?’”

Then that bodhisattva took those flowers, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he vanished from that buddha-field and suddenly appeared in this world.
Arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he proceeded to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Buddha Sumerumdhara inquires after the World-Honored One:
Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy? Are your physical strength and vitality robust?"
"With this lotus flower, I make an offering to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Buddha accepted the flower and asked him:
"Is the Buddha Sumerukalpa free from illness and affliction? Is his physical strength and vigor well?"
He replied, “World-Honored One!
The Buddha Meru-skandha is at peace and free from ailment in that world.”
The Buddha gave these flowers to Maitreya and said:
"Ajita! You should take these flowers and plant them as the causes and conditions for the roots of goodness that assist the Buddha-way."
Then Maitreya Bodhisattva received the flowers from the Buddha and gave them to Bhadrapāla Bodhisattva,

The Bodhisattva Cāritramati, together with seventy-seven thousand such bodhisattvas, spoke these words:
"O virtuous friends!..."

"I have received these flowers from the Buddha and now offer them to you; take these flowers as an aid for the path to Buddhahood, and all of you should with one mind together resolve upon the Great Vow."
At that time, seventy-seven thousand bodhisattvas took these lotus flowers and simultaneously made great vows of skillful means, returning them to the Buddha.
Having compassionately accepted them, the Buddha addressed Maitreya, saying:
"I shall now bring peace and security so that you may plant the roots of great goodness."
Ajita! Buddhas are difficult to encounter, and Bodhisattvas likewise are difficult to meet. Why is this so?
"The dharmas I have attained all arise from the practices of a bodhisattva. What do you think?
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, would the ten powers appear in the world?"
"No, World-Honored One. "Ajita!
What do you think?
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, would there be the appearance in the world of the four fearlessnesses?
"No, World-Honored One. "Ajita!"
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would there have been great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity appearing in the world?
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, would there have been the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) that transcend the world?"
"No, World-Honored One.
"If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, would there have been the appearance in the world of the Dharma of Non-False Practice?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, would the Elephant King Avalokita have appeared in the world?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would the *siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi* have appeared in the world?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would the mark of the invisible crown of the head have appeared in the world?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, would the Wheel of Dharma with its three turnings and twelve aspects have appeared in the world?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would there have been anyone in the world who appeared with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would there have appeared in the world hundreds of thousands of immeasurable dharmas?"
"No, World-Honored One!
If the Tathāgata had not originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, would there have been a great assembly of śrāvakas appearing in the world?"
"No, World-Honored One! Therefore, Ajita!"

One should know that all the merits of the Buddhas reside within the initial resolve to tame the mind; therefore, Bodhisattvas are difficult to encounter in this world, and Buddhas are likewise difficult to meet.
“Ajita! For example, if there are no cows, there is no clarified butter (sarpis); likewise, if there are no bodhisattvas who resolve their minds [on enlightenment], there is no lineage of Buddhas.
If there are cows, there is clarified butter; likewise, if there are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds, the lineage of Buddhas will not be severed.”
“Ajita! Just as there are flowers and fruits when there are seeds, so too, if a bodhisattva gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, the lineage of the Buddhas will not be severed.
Therefore, you should know that giving rise to this aspiration is difficult; because giving rise to this aspiration is difficult, a Buddha is also difficult to encounter.”

“Ajita! For example, among the treasures of the ocean, those of incalculable value are few while other jewels are very numerous; likewise, among sentient beings, there are few who are able to give rise to the bodhicitta, while many conceive the aspiration of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.”

Therefore, you should know that the bodhisattva mind is the most difficult to attain; it appears only once in a great while, like the udumbara flower. This precious jewel-like mind is beyond price; this mind is as exceedingly high and great as Mount Sumeru; this mind is indestructible, like space; this mind is deep and unfathomable, like the ocean; and this mind is peerless and supreme, surpassing the maṇi jewels that fill the trichiliocosm.
Ajita! If this mind were to possess form and color, all the devas, humans, asuras, and others in the world would pay it homage.
Therefore, you should diligently apply yourselves with vigor and give rise to a profound aspiration for the sake of producing this mind.

12. Chapter on Aśoka (3). Chapter Twelve: On Aśoka.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: “Ajita!
What is called the true bodhisattva mind?
The bodhisattva mind is inconceivable and cannot be fully described; I shall now provide a simile to illustrate and verify this mind.

"Ajita! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King of Peace (*Anarāja*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. This Buddha King of Peace lived for eighty-four thousand years and held three great assemblies:
at the first assembly, when he preached the Dharma, seventy billion people attained arhatship."
At the second great assembly, nine billion people attained arhatship;

at the third great assembly, a full ten billion people attained arhatship, their outflows exhausted and their tasks accomplished. Having laid down the heavy burden and achieved their own benefit, they were liberated through right knowledge, having severed all fetters of existence.
“At that time, there was a consecrated great king named King Siṃhaghoṣa (Lion-Virtue). His chief queen had two crown princes born at the same time:
the first was named Aśoka (Sorrowless), and the second was named Vigatāśoka (Free from Sorrow).”
While these two princes were playing together in the palace hall, they saw King Anāthapiṇḍada entering the city of Priyadarśanā, surrounded by a great assembly.
At that moment, Aśoka said to Vigataśoka,
"Do you see King Anāthapiṇḍada coming from there?"
Vītarāga said, "I see it. Then Aśoka said:
"We shall act just as King Prasenajit Buddha did.
They then spoke this verse for the sake of Vigataśoka: "Vigataśoka!..."
Behold, this World-Honored One, King Ananda, surrounded and revered by the great assembly, approaches from there with serene dignity.
I have conceived such a thought: I wish to seek the unsurpassed path in order to deliver all suffering sentient beings from birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Due to greed, envy, anger, and pride, they commit various sinful deeds;
having committed these various sinful deeds, they transmigrate through the various evil realms.
I shall seek the path of the Buddha to deliver such sentient beings.
"Vītaśoka, you too should give rise to this unsurpassed mind;
for Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower.
At that time, Vītaśoka replied with a verse:
“Words accomplish nothing; in the world, many speak but do not act.
I do not rely on words, but practice bodhi solely with my mind.”
In the world, many speak of becoming a Buddha, yet they cannot practice according to their words;
such people are all speakers of empty words, and in the end there will be no real fruit or retribution.
If one could attain the path of Buddhahood merely through verbal discourse, [there would be no need for practice].
"All who engage in speech, Should all be able to become Buddhas.
At that time, Aśoka spoke again in verse:
"If you have resolved your mind in such a way, This is indeed stinginess and greed."
Out of fear of being asked for alms, he resolved his mind but remained silent.
The Great Being invited all sentient beings and bestowed upon them an equal share of wealth and Dharma;
without the slightest stinginess, he desired only to achieve Bodhi.
If one who has thus resolved their mind is called "lazy," fearing they will not act according to what they have said, that indeed is shameful.
You doubt the Unsurpassed Way; it cannot be accomplished alone, however immeasurable the difficulties may be.
"Having previously given rise to such thoughts, I did not dare to speak.
Then Viśoka said, "We should go together to question the Tathāgata King of Peace; among us who have resolved our minds, whose resolve is the true one?"
"If you have heard it from the Buddha, you shall know it yourself.

Having spoken these words, Vimukta immediately descended the stairs; for the sake of making an offering, he took pearl slippers and a garment of the finest jewels worth one hundred million, and went to where the Buddha was.

At that time, Aśoka immediately threw himself down from the palace roof; his body was uninjured, and he stood there safe and sound. He went to where the Buddha was, removed the precious robes from his body, untied the bright pearl from his topknot, and offered them to King Anāthapiṇḍada Buddha.
The Buddha compassionately accepted it.
Viśokā followed from behind to where the Buddha was; seeing Aśoka standing by the Buddha’s side, she immediately asked him, "By which path have you come?"
Aśoka replied, "I threw myself down from atop the palace; my body was uninjured, and I stood safely before the Buddha.
Vigatāśoka then offered a priceless precious robe and mani-jewel sandals to the Buddha Prabhūtaratna, and spoke these verses:
“I have obtained the sight of the World-Honored One, yet I have been traveling by a non-path;
now I shall cultivate the right path, which is praised by all Buddhas.”
At that time, Aśoka spoke again in verse:
“If a person cherishes their own body and life, yet comes as you do to seek the Way,
such a person acts for their own benefit and is unable to benefit sentient beings.”
I do not begrudge my body or life; I am willing to undergo all manner of hardships for the benefit of sentient beings, to deliver those who suffer from manifold afflictions.
To see the Buddha is itself the Way; one should seek nothing else beyond this.
Ordinary people practice the right path, yet in truth they fall into deviant ways.
Sentient beings dwell in deviant paths; though they perceive what is right and what is wrong, their greedy attachment is the bondage of Māra, whereby they remain far removed from the right path.
May I always encounter the Buddhas; may I always aspire to leave the household life;
may I constantly and purely cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya); may I deliver sentient beings in every lifetime;
may I always dwell securely in wholesome dharmas; and may I always uphold the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma.
By means of these upheld dharmas, he brings great benefit to sentient beings;
constantly exerting himself with diligence, he understands the meaning upon hearing the Dharma;
abiding eternally in meditative concentration, he is exalted and honored because of his merit.
"Ānanda! After these two princes had spoken this verse, they left the household life to practice the Way under the Buddha King of Peace.
They said to one another:
"I shall become a Buddha first!
At that time, the bhikṣu Aśoka said to Vigataśoka,
"By what practice do you intend to become a Buddha first?"

Vītarāga replied, "I have resolved that for the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall undergo the sufferings of hell for ten trillion kalpas without regret, until I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

Adorned with such firm resolve and possessing a mind of patience and gentleness, even if someone were to come from the east carrying jars of excrement, fire, feces, urine, and poison, and bind them upon my head, at that time I would not give rise to anger or resentment; I would neither look upon them with an evil eye nor revile them, but would think only this:
"I now practice patience for the sake of seeking the Buddha-dharma, to give birth to the wisdom of a Buddha, and because I desire to bring this person to nirvāṇa."
If I harbor anger and resentment, how am I any different from them?
I am a practitioner, whereas they are not; I should not give rise to the karma of one who is not a practitioner.

The karma of a practitioner is that which I ought to undertake: namely, to sever my own anger and resentment, and likewise to sever the anger and resentment of immeasurable sentient beings while preaching the Dharma for them.
"I have adorned myself in this way for the sake of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, Aśoka asked Vigataśoka:
"Do you perceive this mind, or do you know this mind as that which has given rise to the adornment?"
Vigatāśoka replied, "If this mind does not exist, then there is no adornment.
If there is no adornment, how could there be a bodhisattva practicing the path?"
"Therefore, you should know that it is because this mind exists that Bodhisattvas cultivate the path and emerge from the world.
The Bhikṣu Aśoka said to Vigataśoka: "Do not speak thus;
it is precisely because this mind exists that there is adornment."
Why is this so? Because the mind is empty like an illusion, arising and ceasing from moment to moment.
If it is empty like an illusion, arising and ceasing from moment to moment, then these phenomena are without marks, nor are they without the absence of marks.

Vītarāga! Whether it be existence or non-existence, both are termed "views. If there is such a view, it is entirely a false view; if it is a false view, it is a false path and is not called bodhi. Such a person is far removed from the path of bodhi and has nothing to hope for.
Therefore, one should know that phenomena such as existence and non-existence are all mere conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
A Bodhisattva should not associate with or cultivate such proliferating phenomena.
What, then, are the phenomena that a Bodhisattva should associate with and cultivate?
A Bodhisattva should not cultivate or associate with such things.
Why is this? If a phenomenon is something that can be cultivated, it is not the true Dharma; therefore, a Bodhisattva should not take delight in or become attached to any phenomena.
Why is this? Because this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is not a phenomenon to which one can become attached.
If a bodhisattva attains such understanding, that too is not a phenomenon.
Why is this? Because the non-attainment of the characteristics of liberation is what is called bodhi.
Furthermore, for a bodhisattva who knows in this way and contemplates in this way, they likewise fall into non-dharma.
Why is this? That which lacks the characteristic of liberation is called bodhi.
If a bodhisattva practices in this manner, thinking, "I shall realize this dharma in such a way," they immediately fall into what is not the Dharma.
"Why is this? Because that which is without nature and without description is called bodhi.
At that time, Vigataśoka said to Aśoka:
"If awakening exists, you should say it exists; if it does not exist, you should say it does not exist.
For what reason do you say nothing at all regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?"
Aśoka replied: "O virtuous friend!
That which is called 'Bodhi' is a dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); do not proliferate concepts regarding whether it exists or does not exist."
"Why is this? All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are not bodhi; that which is without conceptual proliferation is itself bodhi.
At that time, Vigataśoka said:
"O virtuous friend!
I do not understand the meaning of what you have said: that all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) are not bodhi, and that the dharma of non-proliferation is itself bodhi."
Aśoka replied, "O virtuous friend!
Let us go together to the Buddha and request a resolution for our doubts."
Then the two bhikṣus went together to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
The bhikṣu Vigataśoka recounted in detail to the Buddha the discussion they had previously held.
Then, King Śānta Buddha approved Aśoka’s words, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Having thus granted his approval, he addressed Vigatāśoka:
As Aśoka said: "All conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is not bodhi; the dharma of non-proliferation is bodhi. Why is this so?"
Freedom from all conceptual proliferation is called bodhi.
What is meant by "freedom"?
It is the complete quiescence of all conceptual proliferation.
What is called conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)?
It is the conceptual proliferation of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and the conceptual proliferation of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
it is the conceptual proliferation of the category of ethical discipline, the category of meditative concentration, and the category of wisdom.

Having few desires and being content, practicing asceticism and the dhūtas, being easy to satisfy and easy to support, and dwelling in empty and quiet places—all these are conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).
From where do these conceptual proliferations arise?
All arise from recollection, conceptualization, and discrimination (*vikalpa*).
What is meant by discrimination?

It refers to the discrimination of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and the discrimination of the categories of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and all meritorious qualities such as fewness of desires and contentment.

If one discriminates form, that is itself non-form; within such discrimination, there is no aggregate of morality, concentration, or wisdom, nor is there few desires, contentment, or the practice of the dhūtas.

Within such discrimination, there is also no emptiness of form. Furthermore, if one discriminates feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, that is itself non-consciousness; within such discrimination, there is no aggregate of morality, concentration, or wisdom, nor is there few desires, contentment, or the practice of the dhūtas. Within such discrimination, there is also no emptiness of consciousness.
To be able to know in this way, that wisdom itself is also empty.
Within such emptiness, there are no characteristics—whether of identity or difference—and this is called bodhi.

At that time, Vigataśoka, upon hearing this Dharma being taught, attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) and further came to understand this bodhicitta; because of this mind, he was named a Bodhisattva.

At that time, the two bodhisattvas contemplated these dharmas with faith, understanding, and compliance; for eighty thousand years they constantly applied themselves with diligence, walking back and forth without ceasing and never sleeping or reclining. These two bodhisattvas, having passed away from this life, were immediately reborn in the presence of the Buddha Wondrous Shoulder (*Suśṛṅga*) in the thousandth world-system below; they both left the household life together, recognized their own past lives, and practiced with diligence as before.

This is called the mind of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva: it neither comes nor goes, has no attachment, is without birth or cessation, and is without abiding or movement.

If they cannot even attain it themselves, how much less could they cause sentient beings to hear it?

Whether mundane or supramundane, all instruments of happiness—

Behold this mind and the retribution it yields:
even throughout immeasurable and incalculable eons, one could never reach its limit.
You should observe this mind: in every thought-moment it constantly arises and ceases;
like an illusion it has no inherent existence, yet it attains great karmic fruition.
This mind depends upon various conditions and possesses not a single determinate characteristic.
Thus, this indeterminate mind can attain a great fruition.
This mind does not abide within conditions, nor is it separate from various conditions;
neither existent nor non-existent, it is yet able to give rise to a great fruition.
The wise know that this mind is able to give birth to the wisdom of a Buddha;
who would not hold it in high esteem,
except for those who are greedily attached?
If a person relies on form, and relies on feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness,
they create dualistic marks regarding phenomena and bind themselves with falsehood.
It is like a person in open space who says to themselves, "I am bound."
Because this person binds themselves, they are constantly fettered within the retribution of their fruits.
Therefore, know that the nature of the mind is deceptive and non-existent;
one should not give rise to views of doubt, for this mind has no fixed characteristic.
This mind and its manifold conditions are all empty and devoid of intrinsic nature;
if one understands them thus, one will never retreat from Bodhi.
If the nature of phenomena is itself empty, then those phenomena are unborn.
All dharmas are without arising; this is called the seed of true wisdom.
If a person knows thus, I grant them the prediction of enlightenment (bodhi-vyākaraṇa).

If one knows that all phenomena are signless, And does not even grasp at this wisdom,

Regarding harsh words, various insults, and manifold sufferings such as swords and staves—

One who can establish themselves in this patience, extinguishing the two extremes of existence and non-existence,

In that world there are immeasurable jeweled ponds, within which are various thousand-petaled lotuses of blue, yellow, red, white, and diverse colors; all are vast and wide, emerging from the water and rising eighty-four thousand yojanas high, each petal emitting a thousand rays of light that shine universally throughout the ten directions.
All the streets and lanes were perfectly level and even, with jeweled cords stretched continuously to demarcate the sides of the roads.
Within these streets stood jewel-trees, each seven thousand yojanas in height, their branches and foliage so vast that they could cover eighty-four thousand yojanas.
Upon each and every tree there were eighty billion *maṇi* jewels serving as fruit.
Such trees were immeasurable and innumerable.
The radiance of the lotuses constantly illuminated the world, yet it was entirely eclipsed by the pure light of Śākyamuni Buddha, so that it no longer appeared at all.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Puṇyarājavairocana, seeing this great light, asked the Buddha Anantaguṇajñānavairocana:
"World-Honored One!
What is this radiance that illuminates this realm?"
That Buddha replied:

"To the west of here, passing beyond eleven thousand *asaṃkhyeya* world-systems, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni, who is currently present, preaching for the sake of the bodhisattvas the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* titled 'Severing the Doubts of Sentient Beings and Causing Them to Rejoice. This is his radiance."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Puṇyarājasuprabha addressed the Buddha Anantaguṇajñānaprabha, saying:
"I wish to go to the Sahā world to see Śākyamuni Buddha, to pay homage to him, and to make offerings."
That Buddha replied,
"Go as you wish. At that time,
he immediately gave him a large lotus flower and said:
“Take these flowers and present them to Śākyamuni, and in my name, inquire after that Buddha’s health:
‘Are you free from illness and affliction? Are you light and agile in your daily activities, and are your movements at ease?’”

Then that bodhisattva, like a strong man bending and extending his arm, suddenly vanished from that buddha-field and arrived at this world, reaching the city of Rājagṛha. He proceeded to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side;
he then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata Anantaguṇajñānaprabha inquired after the World-Honored One, asking:
"Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your physical strength and well-being secure?
He then presented these lotus flowers to the World-Honored One.
After the Buddha had accepted the flowers, he asked him:
"Is the Tathāgata Anantaguṇajñānaprabha free from much illness and affliction in that world? Is his gait healthy and at ease?"
That bodhisattva said:
"The World-Honored One of Boundless Merit and Wisdom-Light is dwelling in peace and health in that world.
