Chapter Sixteen: Scattering Flowers (4). Chapter Sixteen: Scattering Flowers. From the land of Susaṃskṛta, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a world named Samantaguṇasamudgata. In it dwells a Buddha named Sarvapratyayeṣu Vaśavartivibhaktabuddhalakṣaṇa, who is currently present, bestowing the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Buddhadhyānasamādhi-kuśalamūla-vyūha.
At that time, this bodhisattva, seeing a great radiance and hearing a great sound, addressed the Tathāgata Sarvālambana-vibhūti-nirmita-buddha-lakṣaṇa, saying:
"World-Honored One!
"Whose light and voice is this? That Buddha replied, "Good son!"

To the west, passing from here through twelve thousand *asaṃkhyeya* world-systems, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha titled Śākyamuni, who is currently present, preaching for the sake of the bodhisattvas the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* entitled "Severing the Doubts of Sentient Beings and Causing All to Rejoice."
"This is the light and the voice of that Buddha.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Adorned with the Roots of Goodness from the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha took various flowers in his hand and scattered them from afar toward this realm. By the power of the causes and conditions of his original vows, he encountered no obstacles in any of the lands as he proceeded directly to this Sahā world, arriving at Rājagṛha city and entering the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the fourfold assembly in the gathering marveled at this unprecedented event. These lotus flowers circled the Buddha three times and came to rest before him; each spoke a single verse in praise of the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas, saying:
“The World-Honored One possesses boundless great wisdom, Spontaneously awakening to immeasurable dharmas.
He manifests unimpeded supernormal powers, Universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.”
The great Bodhisattvas of brilliant wisdom, skilled in question and answer and free from fear,
have heard the Buddha’s name from afar and, desiring to make offerings, have gathered here universally by means of their supernormal powers.
All have succeeded to the position of honor in this single lifetime;
With courageous and steadfast great adornments, their fame heard afar throughout the ten directions, They have all come to gather here in this Sahā world.

Able to give rise to the Great Mind for the sake of sentient beings, Profoundly generating the adornments of fearlessness, we now inquire of the World-Honored One: How may one realize the Unsurpassed Way?
"How does one cultivate and gather all Buddha-dharmas, To be able to destroy the armies of Māra and attain the Buddha-way?
At that time, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Spoke these words to the later-arriving transformed flowers:
"The assembly of flowers beheld the Buddha’s body, peerless; Furthermore, from the Buddha they heard the essential true words."
He immediately gave rise to a heart of courageous joy and sympathetic appreciation; prostrating in homage to the Buddha, he stood to one side and instantly vanished from that place.
When the assembly saw this, they were all struck with wonder and doubt:
“Who was this person, and from where did they come, that having questioned the World-Honored One, they immediately vanished?
At that time, the fourfold assembly, revering his majestic countenance, none dared to question the Buddha to resolve their doubts.
The Buddha immediately manifested as the likeness of a bhikṣu, appearing like Ānanda, and spoke to prompt a question:
“Who is this person who questioned the World-Honored One, yet vanished as soon as the inquiry was made?”
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will resolve the doubts of the assembly: for what reason and by what cause has this come to be?
The Buddha said:
“These flowers have come from the east, passing through worlds beyond calculation. Behold, it is the work of the supernatural powers of the Bodhisattva Vīravikrāntagāmin.”
When this Bodhisattva originally practiced the Way, he deeply gave rise to such great adornments;
therefore, for those who seek the Buddha-way, if they maintain mindfulness, they will certainly attain it.
If one is seen by such as these, one will immediately take deep delight in all wholesome dharmas,
abandon all indolence, and purely uphold the precepts; with vast and extensive learning like the great ocean,
one will skillfully cultivate and learn expedient means, never again receiving a womb-born existence but always being born through transformation.
Throughout successive lifetimes wandering in birth and death, may they never forget the mindfulness of the True Dharma;
wherever they are born, may they encounter the Buddhas and assemble together with the multitude of noble sages;
may they always give rise to a mind of weary detachment from the five desires and be able to leave the household life with faith in the Buddha-dharma.
At the very moment of seeing him, one obtains this benefit, as well as other benefits that cannot yet be fully described.
The various virtues of such Great Beings are inexhaustible if one wishes to extol them.
If there be a woman who, with a mind of faith, hears of this Great Adornment of the Bodhisattva,
she shall never again receive a female body and will surely become a supreme honor among sentient beings.

If there be a man or a woman who, upon hearing his name, feels joy in their heart and makes a vow wishing to see this Bodhisattva, then at the dissolution of the body after death, they shall be reborn there.
If any men, women, or other sentient beings, upon hearing of these great merits of the Bodhisattva,
are able to believe and rejoice with a pure mind, they shall immediately become non-retrogressive from enlightenment.
If there are sentient beings who have entered the stage of the Dharma and hear this wondrous and extraordinary name of the Bodhisattva,
though such persons may not yet attain the Way of the Buddha, they shall nonetheless obtain immeasurable merits.
There is a medicinal tree named "Joyful to Behold," which can cure the hundreds of thousands of ailments of sentient beings.
For a distance of one yojana all around, it cannot be scorched by the fierce flames of calamitous fires;
if any venomous insects enter within its reach, their poisonous vapors are instantly extinguished.
If one smells the fragrance wafting from this tree, one immediately faints and loses one's life;
its roots, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all silent, inactive, and do nothing at all.
Yet its power is effective, for it completely eliminates all poisons and harms;
this tree can even from afar dispel various ailments—how much more so when one takes its roots and trunk to ingest!

These great bodhisattvas are likewise; throughout the ten directions, the hearing of their names performs the work of a Buddha—how much more so for those who behold them with their own eyes, offer worship, and draw near to consult them, resolving all doubts.
Then the emanated Ānanda, who had been manifested by the Buddha, again increased his reverence and asked the World-Honored One:
"As for the great bodhisattvas whom the Buddha has described— those who can perform the work of a Buddha through their renown—
is there such a person in the Sahā world?"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
The Buddha said:

“My life will not remain much longer; the merit of these sentient beings now is slight and shallow. The Bodhi of the Buddhas is extremely difficult to believe in, and what the Tathāgata speaks is profoundly boundless.”
Ānanda, you should know that there are bodhisattvas present here now in this great assembly;
the great adornments of these bodhisattvas cannot be fully extolled by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Ānanda, behold this Bhadrapāla; behold also Ratnākara and Dharmākara, the Guide, the Wise One, and Jyotiska, as well as the Brahmin Narada.
Behold also the bhikṣu Śrīguṇa, Vairocana, and Varuṇa.
I also contemplate the great bhikṣu Śānabala; the practices and vows of these [sages] are inconceivable.
These bodhisattvas are called "Not in Vain," for they have all given rise to the great adornment that is not in vain.
If even those who merely see them obtain benefit, how much more so for those who draw near and receive their instructions!
If there are sentient beings who behold him, or again hear his great renown,
they will have no doubt regarding the Buddha-way and shall never again fall into the various evil realms.
Always able to initiate and practice diligent effort, Able to skillfully cultivate and gather true wisdom,
Always able to dwell securely in pure upholding of the precepts, And able to have deep resolve and delight in the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
Ānanda! All the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, currently residing throughout the worlds of the ten directions, together extol this Bodhisattva’s magnificent and great vows that have been made.
They extol these [Bodhisattvas] of wide renown, causing other Bodhisattvas to give rise to a sense of noble esteem;
all say they wish to see the Honored One Śākyamuni and those who are fully endowed with majestic adornments.

Immediately all the Buddhas granted their permission; having each prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and respectfully circumambulated him, they vanished from those buddha-fields and appeared here in this Sahā world.
Hearing that this bodhisattva was fully endowed with vows, he redoubled his diligence toward the unsurpassed path;
the Tathāgata then bestowed upon him the prediction that he would attain Buddhahood, specifying his land, lifespan, and name as follows.
Through the causes and conditions of all unwholesome karmas throughout these immeasurable and incalculable eons,
and by virtue of these very karmic causes and conditions, you were born with me in this turbid world.
Although I have now attained the unsurpassed path, I still do not rejoice in seeing the future age when there will be bhikṣus who break the precepts,
who are quick-tempered, foul-mouthed, and coarse in their speech.
When these bodhisattvas hear of this matter, they intensify their great adornment of diligence;
they practice great giving during times of famine and proclaim the true teaching when the Dharma is about to perish.
Now, before the Buddha, I make this vow: I shall surely, by means of the Unsurpassed Dharma, within the future terrors of the evil age, sacrifice my own body and life to benefit all sentient beings.
To even conceive such a vow is already difficult, let alone being able to accomplish practice in accordance with that vow!
Such sutras as these and those who uphold them will be treated with contempt in this evil age.
Ānanda, observing that world of perversion, hears such various sūtras and dharmas as these;
therein he conceives the thought that they are not the Dharma, saying, "All these teachings were not spoken by the Buddha."
Having attained offerings through my awakening, I shall instead diligently create conditions for the destruction of the Dharma;
in such an extremely evil and turbid age of chaos, who could endure remaining within it?
When this person heard these words from the Buddha, they immediately wept with tears streaming down;
thinking of the Dharma accumulated through countless eons by the Buddha’s practice, they wondered how it could so easily be dispersed and extinguished!

At that time, the various students gave rise to a mind of revulsion; realizing that conditioned phenomena have no fixed characteristics, they applied themselves with diligence as if their very heads were on fire, until—free from all outflows without remainder—they attained nirvana.
When the various devas heard that in this evil age the True Dharma would be destroyed, they were all filled with sorrow and grief, saying:
"We would rather end our lives now than witness such a time when the Dharma is ruined."
We now behold you as the World-Honored One, the one capable of bestowing the great gift of the Dharma and fearlessness;
gazing up at the Buddha before us, we shall listen to the teaching of the profound and unimpeded Dharma.
Furthermore, I see bhikṣus practicing the various dhyānas, having perfected concentration, wisdom, and supernormal powers;
yet in the future evil age when the Dharma is destroyed, such worthy sages will be difficult to encounter again.
"The wicked bhikṣus have become rampant in turn, while those who uphold the pure precepts lack power;
they shall not even be permitted to rest for a moment in the stūpas and temples.
At that time, all the devas were deeply distressed and cried out in sorrow:
"Alas! How tragic it is that the Buddha-dharma is being destroyed; it is truly a great pity.
For these beings, the Buddha practiced asceticism, yet he is now slighted and reviled by such evil people."
Forming factions and befriending one another, they slandered virtuous people by attributing faults to them;
claiming "The Buddha is our teacher," they yet acted contrary to the Buddha's intent and destroyed the True Dharma.
Forming an affinity with female lay devotees, they bind themselves by solemn oaths to engage in the same activities;
with one mind, they together destroy my True Dharma, harboring no reverence for the Buddha’s teachings.
These various evils and the like destroy the Triple Gem and are shunned by all the worthy sages;
they are like the sharp horns of a wild, runaway bull, which everyone avoids.
At that time, there will be wicked bhikṣus who, in turn, will mock those who cultivate goodness;
such perversity shall exist in future ages—therefore, one should give rise to weary detachment and not be negligent.
Exert yourself with diligent vigor within the Buddha-dharma;
do not behold such a turbid and chaotic world, nor encounter those like these, for dwelling together with them brings great suffering and distress.

"Are you free from illness and affliction? Is your physical strength at ease?

Between the world of the Buddha who can manifest the marks of a Buddha within all conditions and the next, there is the world of Boundless...
Within these conditions appeared the Buddhas Pratyutpanna, Lakṣaṇavyūha, Padmavikrāntabala,
Jālinīprabha, Anantaprabha, Kusuma, Ratnasāla, Citta-utpāda-dharmacakra-pravartana,

At that time, beyond immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds to the southwest, there was a world named Śubhavyūha. In it dwelt a Buddha named Kṣemaṅkara, who was currently present bestowing the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi upon the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvārthasiddhi.

To the northeast of here, passing beyond immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, there is a world named Sahā. In it dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni, who is currently present, preaching for the sake of the bodhisattvas the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* that Severs the Doubts of Sentient Beings and Brings Joy to the Multitude.”
Such are the light and voice of that Buddha.
In that world there are great bodhisattvas who have fully accomplished the adornment of inconceivable great vows;
if any sentient beings hear their names, they will certainly attain the stage of non-retrogression.
Then, the Bodhisattva Sarvarthasiddhi addressed that Buddha, saying:

That Buddha replied:
"If you wish to go, do as you please.
Convey my words to inquire after the health of Śākyamuni Buddha:"
"Are you free from much illness and affliction? Is your daily life light and easy, and is your movement secure?

At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvarthasiddha prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and suddenly vanished from that buddha-field. In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at this world.
Arriving at the city of Rājagṛha, he proceeded to the Bamboo Grove, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

“Are you free from much illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy, and is your walking comfortable?
Then the Buddha asked, “Is Tathāgata Kṣema well and practicing in peace?”
The Bodhisattva replied,
"The World-Honored One Kṣemaṃkara is dwelling in peace and good health in that world. Then,
having paid his respects and inquired after his well-being, the Bodhisattva Sarvārthasiddha sat down to one side.

In the northeast there is a world named Free from All Sorrow; therein dwells a Buddha named Vigataśoka, who is currently present, bestowing the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāprabha.

The rest is as described above.

Between the realm of Joyful Bliss (Ratiprīti) and this place, there is a world named Peaceful Security (Kṣema). The rest is as described above.

From the realm of Peaceful Security to this point, there is a world named Covered with Golden Nets. In it dwells a Buddha named Meru-uttara, who currently resides there, bestowing the prediction of unexcelled enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃha-meru.
The rest is as described above.

The remainder is as described above.

The rest is as described above.

The rest is as described above.

The remainder is as described above.

The rest is as described above.

From the realm of *Saṃjñāloka* (Many Lights) to this point, there is a world named *Candanagandha* (Sandalwood Fragrance). In it dwells a Buddha named *Candrasūryaprabhāsa* (Moon-Sun-Radiance), who currently resides there, bestowing the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment upon the Vaipulya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
The rest is as described above.

Between the world-system of Candanagandha and this [current] location, there is a world named Vairocana. In it dwells a Buddha named Daśadigvighuṣṭaśabda, who is currently present, bestowing the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Daśadigvyūhabala-rāja.
The rest is as described above.

From the world-system Luminous to this place, in the interval between them, there is a world named Moon. The remainder is as described above.

From the world-system Candravatī to this point, there is a world named Samantaprabhāsa. In it dwells a Buddha named Anantaprabha, who is currently present, bestowing the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vimalalakṣaṇa.
The rest is as described above.

Between the realm of Universal Bright Virtue and this place, there is a world named Fragrant Brightness. In it dwells a Buddha named Superior Fragrance Meru, who is currently present, bestowing the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment upon the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Selection.
The remainder is as described above.

Chapter Nineteen: On Samādhi (6) At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the great assembly had all gathered together, immediately entered the Buddha’s Śūraṅgama Samādhi while remaining on his seat;
emerging from the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Sublime Vajra Samādhi.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Wondrous Vajra, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Knowing the Distinctions of the Languages and Sounds of the Ten Directions;
emerging from the Samādhi of Knowing the Distinctions of the Languages and Sounds of the Ten Directions, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Immeasurable Adornments;
emerging from the Samādhi of Immeasurable Adornments, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Lion Moon.
Emerging from the Lion Moon Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Lion’s Display Samādhi;
emerging from the Lion’s Display Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Boundless Edge Samādhi;
emerging from the Boundless Edge Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Light King Samādhi.
Arising from the Light-King Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Sublime Dhāraṇī;
arising from the Samādhi of the Sublime Dhāraṇī, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Non-arising of Marks;
arising from the Samādhi of the Non-arising of Marks, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Lion’s Sovereign Power.
Arising from the Lion Sovereign Power Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Pure Moon Samādhi;
arising from the Pure Moon Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Adornment of the Single Mark Samādhi;
arising from the Adornment of the Single Mark Samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s Adornment of All Marks Samādhi.
Emerging from the Samādhi of Adornments of All Marks, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Boundless Light;
emerging from the Samādhi of Boundless Light, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Great Ocean;
emerging from the Samādhi of the Great Ocean, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Dharma-nature of the Ocean of All Dharmas Arising.
Emerging from the Samādhi of the Dharma-nature of the Ocean of All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Manifesting Boundless Vows and Conditions;
emerging from the Samādhi of Manifesting Boundless Vows and Conditions, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Producing All Boundless Sovereign Dharmas;
emerging from the Samādhi of Producing All Boundless Sovereign Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Non-abiding in Any Dharma.
Emerging from the Samādhi of Non-Abiding in All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Boundless Radiance and Lofty Flowers;
emerging from the Samādhi of Boundless Radiance and Lofty Flowers, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Pure Seal of the Contemplation of All Dharmas;
emerging from the Samādhi of the Pure Seal of the Contemplation of All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Stainless Seal of All Dharmas.
Rising from the Samādhi of the Stainless Seal of All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Manifesting the Sovereign Power of Boundless Buddhas;
rising from the Samādhi of Manifesting the Sovereign Power of Boundless Buddhas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Extinction-Characteristic of All Sentient Beings;
rising from the Samādhi of the Extinction-Characteristic of All Sentient Beings, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Practice of All Dharmas.
Emerging from the Tathāgata’s Samādhi of the Conduct of All Dharmas, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Adornment of Manifesting Boundless Sovereign Supernatural Powers;
emerging from the Samādhi of the Adornment of Manifesting Boundless Sovereign Supernatural Powers, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Unobstructed Nature of All Dharmas throughout the Three Times;
emerging from the Samādhi of the Unobstructed Nature of All Dharmas throughout the Three Times, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Attaining Mastery over All Dharmas.
Emerging from the samādhi of attaining sovereign power over all dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s samādhi of the seal of sovereignty that encompasses the ocean of all dharmas;
emerging from the samādhi of the seal of sovereignty that encompasses the ocean of all dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s adamantine samādhi;
emerging from the adamantine samādhi, he entered the Buddha’s samādhi of excellent penetration.
Emerging from the Samādhi of Skillful Penetration, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Immovability;
emerging from the Samādhi of Immovability, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Contemplating All Dharmas;
emerging from the Samādhi of Contemplating All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
Arising from the Samādhi of Universal Radiance, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Seal of Universal Observation;
arising from the Samādhi of the Seal of Universal Observation, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Darkness of Ignorance;
arising from the Samādhi of the Darkness of Ignorance, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Non-seeing.
Emerging from the Samādhi of Non-Viewing, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Non-obstruction and Non-grasping in All Dharmas;
emerging from the Samādhi of Non-obstruction and Non-grasping in All Dharmas, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Inexhaustible Marks;
emerging from the Samādhi of Inexhaustible Marks, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Inexhaustible Concentration.
Arising from the Samādhi of the Inexhaustible, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Inexhaustible Conditions;
arising from the Samādhi of Inexhaustible Conditions, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Single Jewel Mark;
arising from the Samādhi of the Single Jewel Mark, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Great Adornment.
Arising from the Samādhi of Great Adornment, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Boundless Adornment;
arising from the Samādhi of Boundless Adornment, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Freedom from Hatred;
arising from the Samādhi of Freedom from Hatred, he enters the Buddha’s Samādhi of Revealing the Roots of Goodness in All Sentient Beings.

Arising from the samādhi of manifesting the roots of goodness for all sentient beings, he enters the Buddha’s samādhi of the causes and conditions for planting the roots of goodness in all sentient beings;
arising from the samādhi of the causes and conditions for planting the roots of goodness in all sentient beings, he enters the Buddha’s samādhi of universal entry;
arising from the samādhi of universal entry, he enters the Buddha’s samādhi of pure practice in all dharmas.
Rising from the Samādhi of Pure Practice of All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of the Non-appearance of All Dharmas;
rising from the Samādhi of the Non-appearance of All Dharmas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Illuminating Adornment for All Bodhisattvas;
rising from the Samādhi of Illuminating Adornment for All Bodhisattvas, he entered the Buddha’s Samādhi of Purifying the Eyes of All Śrāvakas.
Emerging from the samādhi of purifying the eyes of all śrāvakas, he enters the Buddha’s samādhi of the unimpeded purification of the roots of goodness planted by all sentient beings;

emerging from the samādhi of the unimpeded purification of the roots of goodness planted by all sentient beings, he enters the Buddha’s samādhi of extinguishing the suffering and affliction of the three evil realms;

emerging from the samādhi of extinguishing the suffering and affliction of the three evil realms, he enters the Buddha’s samādhi of the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings within all buddha-fields.
Emerging from the samādhi of the roots of goodness planted by sentient beings within all buddha-lands, he entered the Buddha’s samādhi of immovable transformation.
The Buddha remained within this samādhi of immovable transformation.
At that time, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens praised him with these verses:
“The Buddha abides in immovable transformation; His majestic virtue is like Mount Sumeru.
He destroys the treatises of all non-Buddhist paths, Shining uniquely throughout the great trichiliocosm.”
His mind cannot perceive it; he enters the concentration of non-reliance.
Entering concentration without reliance—this is the inconceivable Buddha.
To destroy the net of doubts of the multitude, out of compassion, he preaches the Dharma.
"Without doubt you always dwell in meditative concentration, Having attained the three knowledges, you have transcended the three realms.
Bodhisattvas of great wisdom and virtue Have now all gathered for this assembly;
The Buddha is undoubtedly in concentration— We only pray that you will resolve the doubts of the multitude."
The Buddha’s concentration does not rely on the eye, nor is it that it does not rely on it;
being neither of these, it is free from the characteristics of the eye—this concentration is praised by the Noble Ones.
If the Buddha’s concentration relied upon the eye, he would be a deceiver.
Knowing that the eye is non-existent, the Buddha is therefore certainly without dependence.
The Buddha does not depend on the six sense organs, yet he is also not one who does not depend [on them].
Outsiders are confused by this teaching; it is something the world cannot understand.
**Chapter 20: Seeking the Dharma (6)** At that time, the World-Honored One arose serenely from the Samādhi of Immovable Transformation and addressed Śāriputra:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice four dharmas attain non-retrogressive wisdom; they acquire great compassion, various samādhis, and wisdom, and are also able to reach the ten powers of a Buddha without obstruction.

Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, they attain the wisdom of discernment and obtain unimpeded eloquence, uninterrupted eloquence, swift eloquence, joyful eloquence, profound eloquence, sharp eloquence, and unhindered eloquence. They attain all dhāraṇīs, constantly see the Buddhas, leave the household life out of faith, and reverently practice the True Dharma.”

In every lifetime they are born into, their wealth and profit shall never be exhausted; their retinue shall never diminish, and their physical appearance shall never lack luster. Their bodies shall be free from defects or impairments; their faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body shall remain unimpaired; their speech shall not be deficient, and their intellect and mind shall be free from darkness.
They shall not follow deviant paths, their resolve shall not be distracted, and their mindfulness shall be free from error.
They shall remember past events, attain a sense of superior shame and remorse, always engage in wholesome reflection, and remain far removed from all evil.

From lifetime to lifetime, as he transmigrates, he does not forget right mindfulness and does not lose his original vows. That is to say, regarding the immeasurable fruits and roots of all virtues planted by the Buddhas, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self; rather, they are shared with all sentient beings, yet without the mark of a "sentient being."
Although they discern phenomena, they have no basis for reliance;
because they have no reliance, neither Māra, nor his followers, nor any heterodox paths can obstruct or destroy them, and they will certainly reach the site of enlightenment.
Having sat upon the site of enlightenment, he dwells in the *sarvadharma-tulana-viśuddha-mudrā-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Pure Seal of the Contemplation of All Dharmas).
By means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta-prajñā*), regarding all dharmas that can be known, cognized, attained, abandoned, realized, or cultivated—
whether they be with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), mundane (*laukika*) or supramundane (*lokottara*)— [he perceives them all].
The world—whether near or far, coarse or subtle, long or short;
whether in the past, future, or present; whether within the range of the mind or the range of wisdom;
whether measured by the mind or measured by wisdom; whether an object of the mind or an object of wisdom—...
Regarding conditions: whether they are the characteristics of mental factors (*caitta*), or the objects characterized by wisdom;

whether they belong to the category of mental concomitants (*cittasamprayukta-saṃskāra*), or the category of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*), or the category of sentient beings (*sattva*); whether they exist as provisional designations (*prajñapti*) or as substantial dharmas (*dravyadharma*);

including their general and specific characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*, *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and all those who teach them—the causes for which they teach the Dharma, or the matters that are taught—for what reason?
How is it explained? "Whether by means of language, or by means of objective characteristics, or whether defiled or pure—
by all the various expressions of the world, such as the names for the eye, and those for the ear, nose, tongue, and body..."
Furthermore, regarding all names of the mind— such as head, feet, hair, body hair, and various limbs—
and all the various names for the different origins of the external phenomena of earth, water, fire, and wind,
as well as the names for the sun and moon, and Brahmā, Śakra, and the various devas.
The names of yakṣas are designated according to their characteristics and explained according to those same characteristics;
they correspond to what is conceptually differentiated and what is grasped through attachment— whether as causes or conditions, paths or practices, bonds or liberations,
skillful means or further progress, or as knowledge, wisdom, or the application of knowledge.
As for the various worldly arts and crafts, whether excellent or inferior— regarding such matters as these,
by abiding in the Samādhi of the Pure Seal of the Contemplation of All Dharmas, one penetrates them to their ultimate limit through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment,
severing the habitual tendencies of afflictions so that none remain.
What are the four? "Śāriputra, there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva who,
having established the mind of the Great Vehicle and for the sake of bringing profound benefit to many sentient beings, puts on the great armor and forms this thought:
"All sentient beings have their greed, anger, and delusion burning fiercely; they are devoid of wholesome deeds and, upon death, fall into the great abyss, with few who can be saved."

I shall now, for the sake of these sentient beings, gather the medicine of great wisdom to heal them, causing them to escape the triple world. I shall act as an uninvited teacher for sentient beings, treating them so that they attain the dharma of the indestructible marks—namely, the indestructibility of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—and further attain the path to indestructible nirvana.
When these bodhisattvas give rise to such a mind, they don the great armor for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
What is meant by "the Dharma"?

It refers to all that can assist in attaining unsurpassed bodhi and gathering the qualities of a Buddha—namely, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka sūtras that sever all doubts and bring joy to the multitude. One should read, recite, receive, uphold, and practice according to the teachings, expounding them to sentient beings in accordance with their faculties, whether sharp or dull.

When a bodhisattva thus single-mindedly seeks the Dharma, even if they obtain but a single four-line verse that possesses profound skillful means and essential significance as taught by the Buddha—whether they receive it, uphold it, recite it, transcribe it, or even explain it for the sake of a single person—they first make this vow: "I desire that this person may accord with this meaning, and that all sentient beings likewise attain understanding."
By means of these causes and conditions of teaching the Dharma, a bodhisattva shall attain the four dharmas that are supreme, permitted by the Buddhas, and praised by the wise.
What are these four?
First, attaining uninterrupted mindfulness and resolute mindfulness regarding the Buddha-dharma;
second, the body becoming a fit vessel capable of receiving the Dharma;
third, being empowered by all Buddhas to proclaim and manifest their transformative teachings.

Fourth, they are able to attain all *dhāraṇīs*, and in every successive rebirth they are able to give rise to the Buddha-dharma; wherever they are born, they do not fall into the gates of false views, and within the Buddha-dharma they always delight in leaving the household life and feel weary detachment toward the five desires.
These are the four dharmas.
"By means of these four dharmas as roots of goodness and causal conditions, a bodhisattva shall attain ten dharmas. What are the ten? They are:
being able to sever doubt and regret regarding all dharmas;"
He knows the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings;
he is able to attain the unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas;
by virtue of this liberation, from every single pore of the Buddha’s body, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless rays of light emerge.
Each ray of light illuminates hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya worlds;
within each ray there are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of asaṃkhyeya numbers of exquisite jewel lotuses;
upon each lotus sits a Buddha.

Each and every Buddha, by means of a single teaching, is able to deliver and liberate hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of countless sentient beings, causing them to attain the indestructible Dharma.

By virtue of this power of liberation, the light manifested from each and every pore of the Tathāgata emits hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of flames like Mount Sumeru, and also produces great flowing rivers as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

By virtue of this power of unimpeded liberation, he can place a trichiliocosm within a single pore and cast it away to another direction, beyond immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; yet all sentient beings therein suffer no harm or affliction, nor do they perceive any thought of coming or going.

“Śāriputra! By the power of this unimpeded liberation, one is able to understand the distinctions in the speech of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions; one also fully comprehends the continuous succession of mental thoughts of all sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
and one also severs the doubts of sentient beings in immeasurable asaṃkhyeya realms where the Buddha-dharma does not exist.”

Furthermore, by the power of unimpeded liberation, they are able to know the minds of sentient beings—whether they are to be disciplined, whether they are burning with passion, or their sequential states—and they know the distinct characteristics of all phenomena.
They also definitively know that all things are ultimately empty, and within this, there is no self or what belongs to a self; thus, they relinquish all conditioned marks.

Why is this so? Because when the Tathāgata investigated conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), he found them to abound in faults and defects while being devoid of virtues; not a single one was worth grasping.
It is by knowing them in this way that he attained this Dharma.
“Śāriputra, by virtue of this power of liberation, the Tathāgata further possesses four dharmas. What are these four?
First, he has completely severed all afflictions along with their residual tendencies;
second, when the Buddha walks, if there are sentient beings who touch his feet, they shall experience joy for seven days;
third, when the Tathāgata turns his body to the right, the earth at a depth of eighty-four thousand yojanas revolves like a wheel.
Fourth, they are constantly in meditative concentration, never once falling away from it. "Śāriputra!
To speak in brief, when a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma, they are fully able to encompass all the Buddha-dharmas."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If a person seeks the Buddha’s wisdom, And desires great compassion,
To reach the other shore of wisdom, They should deeply revere the Dharma."
If you wish to attain great supernormal powers, To be able to shake the trichiliocosm,
And to know the minds of sentient beings, You should deeply revere the Dharma.
If you wish, in a single thought-moment, To universally know all minds, [you should deeply revere the Dharma].
This mind has no form or color; like an illusion, it is not solid.
Because one reveres the Dharma, one constantly attains supreme retribution and is also able to realize the immeasurable and boundless teachings of all Buddhas.
Because of revering the Dharma, one always attains non-forgetfulness of mindfulness;
in whatever place one is born, right mindfulness constantly increases.
Because of revering the Dharma, one never loses a sublime physical form.
Those born shall always be handsome, with all their limbs complete.
They shall be able to encounter the Buddhas; encountering the Buddhas, their hearts will be filled with faith and joy.
Because their minds are pure, they are able to make profound offerings to the Buddhas.
In every place of birth throughout successive lifetimes, the power of faith constantly increases;
having abandoned the defilements of the five desires, one always delights in the practice of renunciation.
By virtue of this power of faith, one dwells securely within the observance of the precepts.
One seeks only meditative concentration, yet does not exalt oneself through precepts.
Always delighting in attaining the various dhyānas, one does not regard them as the ultimate Dharma;
rather, seeking true wisdom, one is able to sever and extinguish all outflows (āsravas).
Always delighting in the practice of wisdom, yet not grasping at the signs of wisdom;
by means of signless wisdom alone, they seek deeply into all Buddha-dharmas.
Having attained the luminous wisdom of all dharmas, they possess the dhāraṇī praised by the Buddhas.
Capable of serving as a vessel for the Dharma, protected by the Buddha’s supernormal powers,
these people, through the Buddha’s protection, attain the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
Possessing immeasurable eloquence, they preach the Dharma for the benefit of all beings.
The Dharma protected at the three times— beginning, middle, and end—
is always praised by the Buddhas; it brings great benefit to sentient beings,
is guarded by the devas, and is revered by the nāgas and spirits.
Protected and remembered by all Buddhas, their fame resounds throughout the ten directions.
Their renown never diminishes; they delight in performing all manner of wholesome deeds, never taking pleasure in what is contrary to the Dharma, and constantly practicing the path of the Buddha.
Constantly illuminating the light of the Dharma, Dispelling all doubts and suspicions,
Able to purify the nature of wisdom, And extinguishing the grief and affliction of sentient beings.
Abiding securely on the right path, Never speaking of deviant ways.
One practices the most supreme dharma, which is called the unsurpassed path.
This person does not rely on the mind, nor yet do they not rely;
knowing that the phenomena of the mind are like illusions, they have no place of reliance.
With this mind that has no dependence, one constantly practices the Buddha-way;
wandering among great assemblies, the mind remains unattached.
One delights in traveling to convert beings in all directions, finding comfort wherever there is no binding.
Not coveting fame, profit, or sustenance, Detached from kin and all worldly passions,
Free from every blemish or impurity, With a mind as pure as space—
who beholding such a Bodhisattva Would not pay them reverence?
Therefore, having heard this Dharma, one should study it with a single mind;
by attaining this Buddha-Dharma, one can greatly benefit sentient beings.
Within this sublime Dharma, there is nothing that is limited or obstructed.
I declare this to be the right path, which is studied only by the wise. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the Dharma, they should study extensive learning and the skillful means of extensive learning."
What is meant by "much learning" and the "means of much learning"? Śāriputra,
one who possesses much learning hears it from others.
Regarding the skillful means of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), one is able to reflect for oneself with single-minded right mindfulness.

As for that which is heard from others, it refers to the words conforming to the Path spoken by the Buddhas—namely, the *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, and *upadeśa*. These are what are called the words conforming to the Path heard from others.
"What is meant by reflection, single-mindedness, and right mindfulness?

It is the skillful means regarding the Dharma to thoroughly know the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as phenomena arising from conditions; to discern whether they are white or black, beautiful or ugly; and through such analytical discrimination, to realize that they all enter into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmanimitta*), and the fixed position of phenomena (*dharmasthiti*). To penetrate them in this way is called right mindfulness."

Why is this so? Śāriputra, it is because the Tathāgata, through skillful means, speaks of the five aggregates yet they are not the five aggregates; he speaks of the twelve bases and the eighteen elements yet they are not elements or bases; he speaks of the twelve links of dependent origination yet they are not dependent origination; he speaks of dharmas arising from conditions as having no fixed characteristics, making such proclamations for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
Therefore, you all should rely on the meaning and not rely on the words.
Ordinary people, lacking wisdom, follow after verbal expressions; the wise follow the meaning. "Śāriputra!
What is meant by "verbal expression"?

All vocal sounds and distinctions of written characters, which involve grasping at signs and seeking after them—whether they be things that can be known, recognized, seen, abandoned, realized, or cultivated; whether they possess signs or are signless; whether they follow the mind or its mental concomitants; or places where doubt and regret may arise; and all such phenomena as "this exists" or "that exists," which are analyzed and proclaimed—all these are termed verbal expression.
“Śāriputra, what is meant by ‘meaning’?
That which is indicated by verbal expression is called ‘meaning.’”
If one discriminates the meaning, it is then expressed through names and words. Therefore, Śāriputra,
you should know that meaning is inexpressible.
For this reason, I have said in my sūtras:
"The Tathāgata does not dispute with the world; it is the world that disputes with me. Śāriputra!

Only the Tathāgata is able to skillfully explain the aggregates (skandhas), the elements (dhātus), the sense bases (āyatanas), the twelve links of dependent origination, and phenomena arising from conditions; no one else is capable of doing so. Śāriputra!
In the Dharma taught by the Buddha and the Dharma selected by him, there is no dispute or contention.
What is meant by "Dharma"?
How does one select it?
Śāriputra! The eye is itself the Dharma; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are themselves the Dharma. Why is this so?
This eye is empty in the past and the future, how much more so in the present?
Why is this? Because the nature of the eye is inherently thus; therefore, it is called a dharma.
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are empty in their coming and going; how much more so in the present?
Why is this? Because the nature of the mind is inherently such, it is called "Dharma."
"What is meant by discernment?
To discern the eye: the eye arises from conditions; it is empty and lacks any fixed characteristic.
If it possessed a fixed characteristic, the eye would have to obtain the eye."
If the eye were to obtain the eye, there would be two eyes; likewise, there would also have to be a seer within, which would entail such a fault.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Such discernment is called the Dharma-eye.

Within this meaning, a Great Being of Right View should investigate the eye as a mere designation, the eye itself, and the phenomena of the eye (*cakṣurdharma*); among these three things, which one is real?
One should understand it thus:
these three things are all empty; there is only verbal expression, and not a single thing that is real. Why is this so?

All verbal expressions are the sphere of consciousness; all phenomena known by consciousness are mundane. If mundane phenomena were not supramundane, then that which is not supramundane would be the doctrine of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); if it were the doctrine of the non-Buddhists, it would not be the teaching of the Buddha.

Why is this so? Because that which the Buddha speaks of is supramundane; yet supramundane dharmas are beyond verbal expression, for the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished.
Therefore, although the Tathāgata speaks, he is without attachment;
nor does he definitively differentiate the characteristics of the eye as being produced from the causal conditions of wholesome or unwholesome karma.
Why is this so? Because the eye is "possessing parts" (sabhāga).
What is meant by "possessing parts"?
The three realms of existence arise from the twelve links of dependent origination. "Śāriputra,
for what reason is it called 'existence' (bhava)?"
One thinks to oneself: "I shall obtain such eyes.

One discriminates in various ways, delighting in the fruits of the eye to experience sensory objects, and becomes attached, thinking, "The eye is me; the eye is mine. Therefore, it is called "possessing parts" (sabhāga).
Furthermore, it wanes and then flares up again; all such afflictions—namely, the notions of "I" and "mine"—fall into the two extremes, and are therefore called "possessing parts" (*bhavāṅga*).
Śāriputra! It is like a bronze vessel that produces a sound when struck.
Do you think this sound comes from the outside, or does it exist within?
He replied: “World-Honored One!
This sound exists only from a multitude of causes and conditions; it is neither internal nor external.”
The Buddha asked Śāriputra,
"Have you already mastered this Dharma of multiple conditions? He replied:
"No," [Ananda] replied.
The Buddha said, "This sound originally does not exist; it merely deceives the faculty of hearing through the conjunction of various conditions."

In this way, ordinary people give rise to craving and attachment toward the eye within emptiness; yet, within the eye, the characteristic of an "eye" can ultimately never be found. Seeking in this manner, one finds nothing to which to be attached; this is called discernment.
"What is called 'no eye' is also the absence of the characteristic of an eye; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Though one speaks of the eye as impermanent, The eye is itself non-existent."
If the eye does not exist, who is impermanent?
Though it is said that the ear is impermanent, the ear itself does not exist; if the ear does not exist, who is impermanent?
Though it is said that the nose is impermanent, the nose is itself non-existent;
if the nose is non-existent, who is it that is impermanent?
Though it is said that the tongue is impermanent, the tongue is itself non-existent.
If the tongue does not exist, who is impermanent?
Although one says the body is impermanent, the body itself does not exist; if the body does not exist, who is impermanent?
Although it is said that the mind is impermanent, the mind itself is non-existent;
if the mind is non-existent, who is it that is impermanent?
Following these twelve bases (āyatana), there are thus twelve names.
If one follows the twelve names, there should be twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Because of the combination of earth, water, fire, and wind, it is called a "person.
Ordinary people follow after names and words, like a dog chasing after a tile or a stone.
If a person does not follow after names, nor discriminates a self,
knowing that "self" is merely a conventional designation, that person attains tranquility.
Within tranquility there is no dharma that can be called "tranquility."
Thus, there is speaking and no speaking; no speaking is itself quiescence (*śānti*).
Within this Dharma, there is no going, nor is there any goer.
If a person thoroughly penetrates this, they will know the characteristic of quiescence.
If one extinguishes the sphere of mental activity, Severs all paths of speech,
And realizes there is no self and no sentient beings— This is called "quiescence.
Not discriminating between existence and non-existence, Even this discrimination is empty.
If one conceives of nirvāṇa in the mind, that mind itself does not exist.
Not seeing anything distant in phenomena, nor seeing anything near—
those who attain this eye of wisdom know for themselves the meaning of quiescence.
If a person hears this Dharma and is able to contemplate it correctly, they shall sever all doubts and regrets;
the darkness of ignorance will be exhausted without remainder.
Free from doubt and free from regret, they will attain sublime tranquility and be without fear.
Firmly abiding in the true nature of reality, they encounter no obstruction regarding the dharmas.
These Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to eliminate the net of delusions within themselves;
out of compassion for sentient beings, they act to sever doubts concerning the dharmas.
By means of this sublime treatise, the true nature of phenomena is revealed;
to extinguish all conceptual proliferation, you should not give rise to doubt.
Verbal discourse leads to contention, and because of it, one falls into the evil realms.
If a person is greedily attached to this, they are unfit to expound the True Dharma.
Such is called "following the meaning"; thus one will have no sorrow or affliction, and will draw near to the Unsurpassed Way, for one is able to practice this meaning.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should apply diligent effort in four matters.
What are these four?
One practices diligence for the sake of renunciation;
one practices diligence in secluded places;
and one practices diligence within the Buddha's teaching.
Seeing sentient beings suffering, they apply themselves with diligent vigor so as to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi, thinking to themselves:
"When shall I obtain great wisdom to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings and preach the Dharma for them?"
“Śāriputra! I shall explain for you how bodhisattvas who practice with diligent vigor are able to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Listen attentively!”

“Śāriputra! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named King of Peace (*Anarāja*), whose lifespan was seventy thousand years, and who preached the Dharma for the assembly of śrāvakas on three occasions.”
In the first assembly, two billion people attained arhatship;
in the second great assembly, four billion people attained arhatship;
and in the third great assembly, six billion people likewise attained arhatship.

At that time, Jambudvīpa was extremely vast and expansive, measuring ninety thousand yojanas; within it were eighty-four thousand great cities, each twelve yojanas long and seven yojanas wide, composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearl, musaragalva, and agate.
That city was foremost in its pure and magnificent adornment; its population was flourishing, and it was prosperous, joyful, and peaceful.

The city had sevenfold walls and sevenfold moats, both likewise made of the seven treasures. Within each moat there were flowing waters that circled all around, upon which blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated lotuses were arrayed. Ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, swans, peacocks, and gibbons of various species frolicked therein.

Upon the banks of all the moats, there were sevenfold rows of trees made of the seven treasures. The golden trees had silver branches, agate stems, lapis lazuli leaves, crystal flowers, musaragalva fruits, and red pearl roots.
The silver trees had golden branches, crystal stems, lapis lazuli leaves, musaragalva flowers, agate fruits, and red pearl roots.
As for the lapis lazuli trees, they had coral branches, musaragalva stems, agate leaves, silver flowers, golden fruits, and crystal roots.
As for the *musāragalva* trees, they have agate branches, coral twigs, silver leaves, golden blossoms, crystal fruits, and lapis lazuli roots;
the agate trees have coral branches, silver twigs, golden leaves, crystal blossoms, lapis lazuli fruits, and *musāragalva* roots;
the coral trees have golden branches, silver twigs, crystal leaves, lapis lazuli blossoms, *musāragalva* fruits, and agate roots.
Each city has eighty thousand gardens, equal in length and breadth at twenty yojanas each, surrounded by sevenfold walls made of the seven precious substances.

Within these gardens are sevenfold pavilions made of the seven precious substances, with sevenfold railings and nets of the seven precious substances covering them above; they are adorned with sevenfold moats like those of a city.
In these groves there are various kinds of trees, namely sandalwood trees, various aloeswood trees, various fragrant trees such as the kāraṇa, and various musical-instrument trees;
there are also various flowering trees, fruit trees, trees that produce utensils, and trees that yield all kinds of food and drink.
Within it there were also trees of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musāragalva, agate, and coral. There were various kinds of flowers, namely:

the *atimuktaka* flower, the *campaka* flower, the *pāriyātra* flower, the *dhānukārī* flower, the *māndārava* flower, the *haritaka* flower, the *tālarī* flower, the *gotālarī* flower, the *mandārava* flower, the five-colored flower, and the moon-surpassing flower; such were the various kinds of flowers that existed there.
Within each garden there are seven hundred great ponds, five li in length and breadth, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.

These ponds are all adorned with the seven treasures; their bottoms are strewn with golden sand, and they have stairways made of the four treasures. They are covered by nets of jewels, and blue, yellow, red, white, and variegated lotus flowers spread across the surface of the water.

"At that time, there was a king of Jambudvīpa named Kṣemadatta, who established palaces in all eighty-four thousand great cities; in each palace, he had eighty-four thousand court ladies as his retinue."
Among all those cities, there was one great city, forty yojanas wide and eighty yojanas long, wherein King Kṣemadatta resided.
This city is adorned with the aforementioned seven supreme jewels; it is prosperous, joyful, peaceful, and secure, and filled with people.
Within this great city is a royal palace, ten yojanas square, composed of the wondrous seven jewels.
Within this palace and residence are various halls and diverse towers and pavilions;
among them is a great hall named the Dharma Hall, which is upright, majestic, and exquisite, like the Vaijayanta Palace of Śakra.
Within this palace-city there is a beautiful garden named Sudharma.
In this garden are various kinds of trees: flowering trees, fragrant trees, musical trees, as well as trees that produce necklaces, clothing, food, and drink.
Within it, there were also various trees made of the seven treasures adorning the garden.

This royal palace was square, orderly, magnificent, vast, and towering; it featured a great high terrace adorned with the seven treasures, within which curtains and canopies made of the seven treasures were set up.

“Śāriputra! The first queen of King Vīryaśrī gave birth to a crown prince who, having previously made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, was handsome and exquisite, beloved and respected by all. Possessing marks of great majesty and endowed with merit, the king granted him a great city and commanded him to dwell therein.”
On the day the Prince was born, four billion girls were born simultaneously within this city; the King immediately issued an edict ordering that they be provided to the Prince as his retinue.
The king and his consort assembled the various ministers and bestowed a name upon their son, calling him "Wondrous Virtue" (Miaode).
At the time of the prince's birth, all the devas rejoiced; they played various musical instruments and rained down *mandārava* flowers, all crying out with one voice:
"The Prince Wondrous Virtue has now appeared in the world! He has now appeared in the world!"
"Therefore, his name is Wondrous Virtue.
At that time, the prince gradually grew up; surrounded by a retinue of many court ladies, he entered a garden for recreation, boarding a sandalwood boat to enjoy himself with the five desires.

At that time, within the water, he beheld the Buddha’s physical form, supremely upright and handsome, purer than fire or gold, more radiant than the sun and moon, like a mass of pure gold, like the blaze of a golden mountain, like a magnificent jeweled pillar. Adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his body emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of rays of light as he sat amidst a circle of disciples, preaching the Dharma.
Having seen him, the Prince thought to himself:
"This man is so handsome, with such distinguished features; why should I not now obtain such a body?"
At the moment he resolved his mind [on awakening], the marks of a Buddha did not appear.

Because he did not see them, his heart was filled with grief and distress; he no longer took pleasure with the court ladies and stayed away from female beauty. Descending from the ship, he ascended a seven-jeweled tower and sat cross-legged, thinking to himself:
"When shall I attain such bodily marks as those of a Buddha?"

At that time, when the court ladies came forward wishing to entertain him, the Prince saw them from afar and felt a sense of weary detachment. He closed the door and would not let them approach, thinking to himself:
"These sentient beings have such blazing greed and are beset by many afflictions and sufferings."
I vow to attain this most supreme body of great wisdom!
If I were the same as these sentient beings afflicted by the disease of craving and desire, what distinction would there be?
I am a practitioner, whereas they are not practitioners.
These sentient beings are ablaze with anger and beset by many afflictions; I vow to attain this body of supreme and wondrous great wisdom!
If I were the same as these sentient beings afflicted by the disease of anger and resentment, what distinction would there be?
I am a practitioner, whereas they are not; therefore, I must discipline myself and not give rise to anger or resentment toward sentient beings.
"These sentient beings are filled with ignorance and beset by many afflictions and sufferings.
I vow to attain this great wisdom and most supreme, wondrous body!
If I were the same as these sentient beings who are ignorant and afflicted by illness, what difference would there be?"
I am a practitioner, whereas they are not; these sentient beings are entangled by stinginess and envy, and are beset by many afflictions and sufferings.
If I were the same as these stingy and envious beings, what difference would there be?
I shall extinguish all greed, hatred, and delusion, and give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings in order to seek the Right Path.
By means of this Right Path, I shall abandon all unwholesome states of mind, including greed, anger, ignorance, stinginess, and envy!
Having thus given rise to a mind of weary detachment, he took deep delight in the Dharma, no longer craving frivolous play; he sat alone in contemplation, far removed from all clamor and bustle.

At that time, King Kṣemadatta and the chief queen both heard that the crown prince took no pleasure in amusements, was weary of and detached from the five desires, and had seen to it that the female attendants were forbidden from entering. They then thought to themselves:
"Who could have acted improperly to disturb the crown prince?"
"Why has he come to no longer delight in the pleasures of the five desires and grown weary of beholding the forms of women?
We shall go ourselves to question him.
Having thought this, the king and the queen went to the prince's dwelling and spoke in verse, asking:
“Your Dharma-palace is pure, and it is filled with court ladies;
the grove is adorned with various trees—why, then, do you not rejoice?”
Within such a great city, the Dharma Hall is exceedingly high and vast, seeing clearly throughout the four continents;
why do you not rejoice? Who has done you wrong, or who is disturbing your mind?
You now dwell alone in sorrow, like a merchant who has lost his treasure.
I am your parents; you should answer us truthfully:
who is there now capable of healing you?
"Because I have attained mastery.
At that time, the Prince replied in verse:
"If there is no one who can do what is impossible, how could you speak such falsehoods?"
Do not inflict evil upon others; you should simply discipline your own mind.
As I was playing upon the water, I beheld the Buddha’s body with its excellent marks and signs, like a mass of Jambū-river gold, its radiance illuminating the ten directions.
The radiance of jewels, the sun and moon, The light of fire, lamps, and the stars— All these are eclipsed and do not appear When reflected by the Buddha’s light; such a sign I have seen.
At that moment, I made this vow: "May I attain such a body of wisdom!"
When you have crossed over old age, sickness, and death, and [delivered] sentient beings who suffer from delusion and affliction;
when you have attained the wisdom of the physical marks and inconceivable power,
you shall extensively benefit sentient beings and cause them to transcend birth and death.
I have stilled all desires for pleasure, including my consorts and retinue;
now I have left the home life to practice the Way, following [the Teacher] so as to become a Buddha.
Having left the home life and donned the Dharma robes, I diligently cultivate and practice wholesome dharmas.
Parents may go forth from home; together let us all cultivate this Way.
One should practice the True Dharma, for one is not at peace amidst the five desires.
Lustful craving harms the wholesome Dharma; the bonds of desire are most firm and strong.
No others have the power to sever it; only I alone am free from it.
Because I practice this detachment, I shall attain the wisdom of a Buddha.
If anyone creates obstacles for one who has gone forth within the Buddha-dharma, [they will suffer].
Such a person gains no benefit; it is out of compassion for them that I speak.
What use are kingdom, wealth, or children?
Wealth and nobility are all impermanent; if you do not relinquish them now, they will soon be scattered as well.
Because of having left the household life, one is able to give rise to many wholesome dharmas;
yet while wandering through birth and death, one undergoes manifold sufferings from lifetime to lifetime.
Thus revolving in succession, one remains empty and without a definitive son.
Lacking right contemplation of the Dharma, you cling only to provisional names.
Do not commit offenses on account of your son; we have both gone forth from home in the Dharma.
I have long been free from all calamities, and this is a time when we are both free from them.
"Having obtained this perfect human body, Only after a long time have we come to believe in the wholesome Dharma;
Now that we have met with the Buddha King of Peace, We may now go forth together into the homeless life.

After Prince Wondrous Virtue had spoken these verses, he immediately proceeded to the place where the Buddha King of Peace was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“I am born within the net of Māra, where all manner of wrong practices increase;
now I wish to tear it asunder—may the Buddha grant me permission to leave the household life.”
My father’s bonds are firm and strong; he himself dwells within the bonds of fear.
These possess no solid or real happiness, but are merely the root of all suffering.
Now I wish to untie these many bonds and tear asunder the net of Māra.
Having gone forth in the Buddha-dharma, may I become a Buddha, the Honored One among two-legged beings.
I deeply fear all sensual desires; there is never peace in receiving them.
Desire is a dharma of delusion and fear; I shall renounce it and practice the path of the Buddha.

“Śāriputra! At that time, King Śānta Buddha immediately granted permission for Sudhana to leave the household life and receive the precepts; eighty-four thousand people from the multitude, along with their other kinsmen and court ladies, all followed him in leaving the household life.”
Furthermore, ten billion spiritual friends also followed him into the homeless life.

When the king heard that the prince had left home to study the Way, he immediately arrayed the fourfold army and, accompanied by his various ministers, went to the Buddha An-rāja. Prostrating himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side and, joining his palms toward the Buddha, spoke these verses:
“Leaving home brings no affliction or fever; It is quiescent, peaceful, and immovable.”
This is the root of all happiness; I pray that you allow me to leave the home life under the Buddha.
Abandoning kingdom, wealth, wife and children, as well as cherished kinsmen—these desires one never tires of experiencing are by their very nature ever base and defiled.
If one indulges in the five exquisite sensual pleasures, it is the practice of those with ordinary and inferior wisdom;
But by cultivating the Dharma praised by the Buddha, one extinguishes all manifold sufferings.
Relinquishing all that belongs to the kingdom and cities, one gives them as offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
I pray that the Buddha grant me permission to leave the household life, so that I may become a Buddha, a World-Honored One seen by all.
For the great benefit of sentient beings, I wish to deliver them from all suffering and distress;
desiring to cause them to leave behind all calamities, and through leaving these calamities, to attain nirvana.
At that time, the Buddha rejoiced and praised him:
"Excellent is this resolve for the Great Mind!
You are able to revere the Buddha’s profound wisdom; welcome, come and listen, and go forth."
Having heard the granting of permission, the king’s heart was filled with great joy;
he would surely become a Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, for he had received the Buddha’s consolation.
Thereupon the king immediately went forth into homelessness, along with his fourfold army.
All have resolved upon the Bodhi-mind and shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
Having left the household life, this assembly has all attained the patience of non-arising;
passing away from this place, they shall all be reborn in the heavens.
Having encountered twenty billion Buddhas of great renown,
they all went forth under those Buddhas and practiced the True Dharma.
Always diligent in effort, they attained wisdom and fearlessness.
They are able to greatly benefit sentient beings, causing them to be liberated from immeasurable suffering.
All the Buddhas they encounter, they receive and uphold the True Dharma;
solely for the sake of its widespread dissemination, they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives.
Having attained such a great fruit— this most supreme and wondrous wisdom—
and having realized the inconceivable Dharma, who would not seek the Buddha-way?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Do you think that the King Kṣemadatta at that time was someone else?
He was none other than myself.
As for Prince Sumati, he is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dṛḍhamati."

In this way, Śāriputra, because Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas delight in the Dharma, they see all sentient beings oppressed by the suffering of afflictions and give rise to great compassion; they teach and transform them, causing them to abide in the causes and conditions of wholesome dharmas, whereby they gradually attain liberation.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, because the bodhisattva mahāsattvas delight in the profound Dharma, they seek the profound Dharma and also preach this profound Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
What is meant by the profound Dharma?
It is that which can be practiced by those who are diligent.
These diligent ones are the assembly of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who seek the unsurpassed path and do not regress; these individuals are all able to penetrate deeply into all dharmas.
What is meant by "profoundly penetrating"?
If one seeks the characteristics of the eye, this is merely a provisional designation and does not constitute profound penetration.
The characteristic of dharmas is defined as being neither internal nor external, neither self nor belonging to a self, neither defiled nor pure, and neither arising nor ceasing.
Why is this so? Because its nature is eternally such.
This dharma-nature is without action and not produced by action; this is called penetrating the profound dharma of the eye.
To seek for the characteristics of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind is merely a provisional designation; it does not constitute a profound realization.
The true characteristic of dharmas is that they are neither internal nor external, neither "I" nor "mine," neither defiled nor pure, and neither arising nor ceasing.
Why is this? Because its nature is eternally so.
Such a dharma-nature is neither created nor uncreated; this is called penetrating the profoundly deep meaning of the Dharma.
“Śāriputra! That which profoundly penetrates is the true mark of dharmas (*dharmatā*).

If one grasps at the emptiness of dharmas, that is a false grasping; if one grasps at signlessness (*animitta*), that constitutes a sign; if one grasps at wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), that likewise constitutes a wish.”

Śāriputra! The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally neither increasing nor decreasing; this is what is called profoundly penetrating all phenomena. Therefore, it is said that bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others are those who are diligent.
“Śāriputra! For what reason is one called a bodhisattva?
Because they are able to discern with precision that there are no dharmas of a sentient being, they are therefore called a bodhisattva.”
Furthermore, because the practice of this person is headed by wisdom, he is called a Bodhisattva;
moreover, because he causes sentient beings to know that all dharmas practiced are non-existent, he is called a Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The meaning of "non-existence" is the meaning of a bodhisattva; the meaning of "that which cannot be demonstrated" is the meaning of a bodhisattva. Therefore, the meaning of a bodhisattva is non-dual and peerless.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
that which neither transcends nor sinks is called a bodhisattva. Furthermore, Śāriputra:
Emptiness is bodhi.
What is meant by emptiness?
It is called emptiness because all dharmas are non-existent.

Śāriputra! If, within the Dharma, there were even the slightest mark of determinacy, that would be attachment to marks, attachment to a self, attachment to a person, attachment to the mark of sentient beings, and attachment to the marks of all phenomena. Since these various marks do not exist within this empty Dharma, it is called "empty.
Emptiness is itself bodhi; for this reason, all phenomena are called bodhi.
“Śāriputra! You should follow and practice according to the Tathāgata’s teachings;
do not oppose them. Why is this?
The bodhi of all Buddhas is foremost and most profound, beyond the reach of all ordinary persons.
Śāriputra, let us set aside ordinary persons for a moment.

All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas neither see nor contemplate it, nor can they penetrate the bodhi of all Buddhas, even though they have fully exhausted their knowledge and vision through the contemplation of the wisdom of non-arising.
By what dharma is "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna) so named?
There is no dharma that can be exhausted; all dharmas are free from exhaustion and have entered ultimate exhaustion. Therefore, it is called the knowledge of exhaustion.
Yet, one cannot know within each and every moment how much is being extinguished.
Because that which you have not yet exhausted remains, it is said that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot fully penetrate the bodhi of all Buddhas.

"Śāriputra, as for the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), within all phenomena there is not even the slightest arising; one who can know this is said to know the wisdom of non-arising. Yet, such a person cannot know, within every thought-moment, the extent of what has already arisen as non-arising and what has not yet become non-arising."
All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not possess such wisdom; therefore, the Buddha’s wisdom is called "unequaled," for nothing else can equal it.
Furthermore, this wisdom is equal in that it makes no distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, and is thus termed "equanimous."
“Śāriputra! The wisdom of the Tathāgata is perfectly awakened and exhaustive, free from all error; therefore it is called the Buddha-wisdom.
This Buddha-wisdom is boundless and immeasurable; it is attained only after seeking it for incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya-kalpa), and for this reason it is called awakening.”
“Śāriputra! For what reason is the Tathāgata called the Awakened One?

All sentient beings sleep long in birth and death; whether they pass away or sink, they are unable to attain penetration. Only the Bodhisattva alone is able to awaken; therefore, he is named the Awakened One.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, one is called an Awakened One (Buddha) because of having correctly awakened to all phenomena.
What is meant by 'correct awakening'?"

Knowing that all phenomena are neither dharma nor non-dharma, neither defiled nor pure, and neither past, future, nor present—one is called an Awakened One because of conforming to these characteristics.
Furthermore, one realizes that there is no dharma that arises, ceases, comes, or goes; therefore, one is called an "awakened one" (*buddha*).
"Śāriputra, this meaning of awakening is immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and its depths are difficult to fathom."

It is like the great ocean, whose water is of a single flavor, neither increasing nor decreasing; it receives all streams without overflowing, gradually deepening until it reaches the state of ultimate profundity.

Śāriputra! The great ocean of the Tathāgata is also like this: it is empty and devoid of arising or ceasing, possessing the single flavor of liberation. His sequential teaching of the Dharma is called "gradually turning deeper";
his attainment of all-knowledge is called "the profound first."
Because one thoroughly penetrates and fully realizes unsurpassed bodhi, being without error or deviation regarding all dharmas, it is called "without increase or decrease";
because no interrogations or challenges can exhaust it, it is called "difficult to diminish";
and because it can gather all virtuous merits, it is called "receiving the multitude of streams."
“Śāriputra! If I were to fully explain the meaning of the Tathāgata, who would be able to receive it?
It is like the dragon king Sāgara, who, when wishing to send down a great rain, pours it only into the great ocean; no other place is able to receive it.”
The Tathāgata is likewise: if he were to fully expound the Buddha’s wisdom, no sentient beings—not even Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—would be able to receive it;
only those Bodhisattvas who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind can receive and uphold it through the empowerment of the Buddha’s spiritual power.
“Śāriputra, there are four things in the world that are most difficult to obtain.
What are these four?
It is difficult to obtain a human body;
it is difficult to be born in a central land;
it is difficult to have faith in the Buddha-dharma.
Having already attained faith and understanding, you are able to ask what ought to be asked; this is exceedingly difficult.
You have now accomplished these four difficult tasks; you should now question the Buddha regarding your doubts concerning all phenomena.
I now grant you permission to ask whatever you wish, O devas and humans of all the worlds; the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa, so do not have cause for regret later.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to ask something; I only pray that you will grant me leave.
