The Buddha said, "I have granted leave. Now ask as you please, and I shall answer each of your questions for you."
Śāriputra said: “Indeed, World-Honored One!”
"I shall now, for the sake of the Bodhisattva Upariṣṭha, inquire of the Tathāgata.
He then spoke in verse:
"Abiding in supreme merit, Cultivating the pure path, most exalted and venerable,"
Delighting in gentle forbearance, one should inquire about such practice:
How does a bodhisattva give? Having given, how does the mind rejoice?
How does one generate a virtuous mind to bring great benefit to sentient beings?
How does one maintain pure precepts with a mind of patience and gentleness?
How does one practice diligence without retreating or resting?
Seeing sentient beings in suffering and distress, how does one exercise compassion toward them?
With a profound mind delighting in Bodhi, I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain:
How is it that throughout immeasurable kalpas, one adorns the path to Bodhi,
such that the mind never recedes or sinks, but instead gives rise to great joy?
How does one practice meditative concentration and cultivate wisdom?
How should one seek the Dharma to become a person of great learning?
What kind of Dharma should one listen to?
What dharmas should be taught?
The practice of generating the bodhicitta—this is what I now ask.
How does one seek the true Dharma, and how does one develop a deep longing for it therein?
How does one leave behind all desires, and having left them, how can one go forth?
How, at the time of going forth, can one give rise to a heart of joy?
Having gone forth, how does one become a person of towering and supreme merit?
How does one dedicate the mind so as to be able to give rise to the power of skillful means?
How can one, throughout every lifetime, never lose right mindfulness?
How is it that while dwelling within the womb, one constantly cultivates the bodhicitta?
How can one also behold all Buddhas without any obstruction?
How does one diminish greed and desire, and with a compassionate heart diminish anger?
How does one diminish delusion, so that the mind is always free from error?
How is it that one is born into a royal family, yet also manages the affairs of state,
and is able to remain free from all calamities, always being reborn in favorable realms?
How is it that while attending to worldly matters, the mind remains constantly joyful?
How is it that you have moved all the Tathāgatas, such that you are always able to see the Buddhas?
How is it that you possess a physical form so sublime and eternally foremost,
and are likewise endowed with a retinue, all of whom have resolved their minds upon Bodhi?
How does one, in whatever place they are born, always feel weary of and detached from family ties,
always delight in practicing renunciation, and remain free from a mind of greedy attachment?
Having gone forth, how can one be able to receive and uphold bodhi?
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, who will be able to protect the True Dharma?
How can one dwell in an age of turmoil yet maintain an undisturbed mind,
seeing sentient beings beset by afflictions and being able to comfort them all?
How does one hear and retain [the teachings], entering the gateway of dhāraṇī?
By means of unimpeded eloquence, how can one preach the unsurpassed Dharma?
How does one know the various and diverse minds of sentient beings?
How is it that one can discipline oneself in wholesome dharmas?
For the sake of all bodhisattvas, I ask the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings:
these practices of the bodhisattvas, I pray you, explain them in detail.
If a person, for the sake of the Buddha-dharma, Gives rise to the bodhicitta, That person,
upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, Will experience great joy.
Regarding all phenomena, The Buddha’s wisdom is without obstruction.
With my limited wisdom, I have questioned the World-Honored One.
Although I have asked what I could, I am unable to fully comprehend it all.
Regarding that which I cannot ask, I pray that the Buddha will explain it in full detail.
Chapter 21: Praising Virtue (6). Chapter Twenty-one: Praising Virtue. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”

That you are able to ask the Buddha about such matters as the profound practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas on the path to buddhahood, their abiding in pure merit, and their delight in gentleness and patience—your merit is immeasurable.
Why is this? Because bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to perform what is difficult to do.
For example, suppose there were a person who wished to take all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm and relocate them to a single place; would this task not be difficult?
Śāriputra said: "It is most difficult,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said:

"If one were to compare it to the difficult deeds performed by a bodhisattva, it would not equal even one part in a hundred; nor one part in a thousand, nor one part in ten million, nor even could it be reached by any analogy."
Śāriputra! Setting aside all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, suppose that at the time of the kalpa-ending conflagration, the three thousandfold world-system becomes a single mass of fire.

If a person were able to extinguish it with a single breath and restore it with another breath—such that the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Sumeru, and all other mountains, as well as the great oceans, all lands, palaces, gardens, groves, villages, and cities, were restored exactly as they were before.
"What do you think?
Is what this person has done not indeed difficult? Śāriputra said:
“It is most difficult,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"If one were to compare this to the difficult deeds performed by a bodhisattva, it would not equal even a hundredth part; nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousandth, nor even a millionth part; indeed, it cannot be reached even by way of analogy."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Suppose there were a person who wished to shatter and disperse the trichiliocosm with their fingernails; would this person be said to manifest great power?
He replied, “World-Honored One!
Its power is exceedingly great.”
The Buddha said:

“If one were to compare the great power manifested by a bodhisattva, it would not equal even a hundredth part; nor a thousandth, nor a hundred-thousand-millionth part, nor indeed could any analogy reach it.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is as if, in this trichiliocosm, the element of earth rests upon water, and water rests upon wind.

Suppose there were a person who, from the very limits of the wind, were to lift up this world and place it upon his head or carry it on his shoulder; using the joints of mosquitoes as a ladder, he would ascend it all the way to the Brahma-heaven without falling.
"What do you think? Is this person’s skillful means not a difficult feat? Śāriputra replied, "This person’s skillful means is indeed difficult:
to take up this trichiliocosm and ascend upon a ladder as thin as a mosquito’s leg as far as the Brahma Heaven without falling—this is truly most difficult."

“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata shall now speak these truthful words to you: if one were to compare the great power of a bodhisattva’s skillful means, it would not equal even one part in a hundred; nor one part in a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand million, nor could it be reached even by any analogy.”

Why is this so? Because all Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have accomplished immeasurable physical and mental diligence; they have deeply made great vows, practiced great skillful means, given rise to great wisdom, and achieved great power. They seek the great fearlessness and the clear eye of great awakening; they seek great compassion and non-empty practice; they seek such great dharmas of the Buddhas as the elephant-king’s backward glance, the lion’s majestic stride, and the mark of the invisible crown of the head. They also seek peerless and most supreme dignified conduct, incomparable merit, and incomparable gentleness; they practice incomparable giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means, thereby penetrating the characteristics of all phenomena.

The Tathāgata manifests the three wheels of incomparable and sovereign spiritual power; he thoroughly understands the deep intentions of all sentient beings and the activities of their minds. He vows to resolve the conventional designations of all sentient beings; he vows to resolve the liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation of all sentient beings; he vows to resolve the *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* of all sentient beings; he vows to resolve the paths practiced by sentient beings and the fruits they attain; he vows to know the various truths understood by sentient beings; he vows to resolve the myriad differences in the sounds and languages of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions; he vows to resolve the depth of sentient beings' attachments and their freedom from attachment; he vows to attain the wisdom of non-appropriation regarding all phenomena; and he vows to resolve the wisdom of the emptiness of karmic retribution regarding all phenomena.

“Śāriputra! To speak in brief, regarding all that the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek and vow for—wisdom and merit—as well as their practice in accordance with those vows and the fruits obtained through such practice: among these matters, there is nothing that can serve as a metaphor, nor any causal conditions by which they can be explained.
Such magnificent merit of great vows can only be known by a Buddha; only those who draw near to a Buddha can understand them.”
“Śāriputra! You śrāvakas enter according to faith, while the bodhisattvas know through resolute belief and understanding.
That you, who have performed such great meritorious deeds, have asked the Buddha about this matter—now I shall explain it to you in brief.”

Why is this? That which you have asked regarding the affairs of bodhisattvas cannot be fully explained in a single day, a month, a year, a hundred years, a thousand years, or ten million billion years; nor even in one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, or ten million billion kalpas.
"Śāriputra! You should know that this matter is immeasurable and boundless; it can only be explained after incalculable, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Śāriputra!"

The Tathāgata fully knows that the meritorious fruit and retribution of even a single inferior or lowly thought of initial resolve among bodhisattvas cannot be fully described even in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas; how much less could the meritorious fruit and retribution of all the thoughts accumulated over one day, one month, one year, or even a hundred years ever be fully described!
Why is this? When a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks great wisdom, they are able to give rise to the causes and conditions for immeasurable merit. Śāriputra!
"The practices of all bodhisattvas are inexhaustible, for they desire to cause all sentient beings to abide in the dharma of non-arising.
Śāriputra! The practices of all bodhisattvas are difficult to comprehend, for they seek the profound dharma."
The conduct of the bodhisattvas is profoundly deep because they do not rely upon any phenomena.
The conduct of the bodhisattvas is boundless and peerless because the wisdom of the Buddhas is boundless and peerless.

The practices undertaken by all bodhisattvas are inexhaustible and without limit; they do not practice giving for a certain duration and then cease, nor do they think, "this object may be given" or "this object may not be given," or "this person may receive it" or "this person may not receive it."
As for the bodhisattva’s giving, he relinquishes all things and bestows them equally upon sentient beings.

The bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts is likewise without limit; it does not consist merely of days, months, years, or even the duration of one's life, but rather consists of constantly practicing pure precepts throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas for the sake of all sentient beings in the ten directions and for the sake of the Buddha-way—this is the activity of a bodhisattva.

“Śāriputra! The activities of a bodhisattva mahāsattva cease all at once; that is to say, when sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and abiding in the samādhi of the pure seal of the contemplation of all dharmas, they thoroughly penetrate and fully comprehend all dharmas through wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment.”
Chapter 22: Examining Conduct (6). Chapter Twenty-Two: Examining Conduct. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"One should examine the mind of a bodhisattva by means of three matters."
What are these three?
First, being able to relinquish all that one possesses without expecting a reward—know that this is the true bodhisattva mind.
Second, seeking the Dharma without any greed or attachment, preferring to lose even one's body and life rather than abandon the Dharma; this is called the true bodhisattva mind.

Third, not to oppose the profoundly deep Dharma, and through the power of faith and understanding to give rise to no doubt or confusion regarding the Buddha’s bodhi—this also is called the true bodhisattva mind.
One examines the bodhisattvas by means of these three states of mind.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are another three matters that examine the mind of a bodhisattva."
What are these three? They are:
to always exert diligent effort and seek the Dharma without weariness—this refers to the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra;

by means of this sūtra, to increase one's own roots of goodness and also to be able to increase the roots of goodness of sentient beings; and to constantly follow the Dharma Master, honoring and making offerings to him.

If, after more than a thousand years, they are able to hear a single four-line verse associated with roots of goodness, having heard it, they accord with it—neither opposing, nor resisting, nor sinking, nor regressing—and they follow the Dharma teacher, increasing their reverence and constantly reproaching themselves:
"Because of the sins that obstructed the Dharma in my past lives, I have not been able to hear the Dharma; this is not the fault of the Dharma teacher."
"Now I shall draw near to and follow this Dharma Master, so that all my obstructing dharmas and sinful karmas may be completely extinguished!
This, too, is called the true Bodhisattva mind.
Therefore, you should know that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the Dharma with a profound mind and follows after a Dharma teacher, they will be able to accomplish all Buddha-dharmas. "Śāriputra!
In the distant past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a kalpa named *Suvidyā*.
At that time, there was a Buddha named *Samantaguṇavardhana-meghasvarapradīpa*, whose lifespan lasted five hundred kalpas.

The assemblies of śrāvakas were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; in each assembly, there were people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges who all possessed the three types of supernormal knowledge and had attained the great arhatship of shared liberation.

The assembly of bodhisattvas was equal in number to that of the śrāvakas; in each assembly, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) and dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression, while those who had first resolved their minds were beyond calculation.

When the Buddha Samantaguṇābhyudgata-meghasvara-pradīpa was about to enter nirvāṇa, he established a great Dharma master in each of the ten billion Jambudvīpas, all of whom were empowered with supernormal powers.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall remain for eight hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of years.

At that time, there will be a Dharma teacher established here in Jambudvīpa named Śabda-jñāna; empowered by the spiritual authority of that Tathāgata, he will protect the city of the Dharma and cultivate the bodhisattva practices as long as the Dharma remains in the world, attaining the patience of non-arising and dwelling on the stage of non-retrogression.

Eighty trillion years after that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma Master Śabdavidya traveled from country to country and from town to town, everywhere expounding the infinite and boundless Buddha-dharmas accumulated by the Buddha Samantaguṇottarameghasvarapradīpa over incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
“Śāriputra! At that time, on the borders of Jambudvīpa, there was a city named Dṛḍha.
In this city, there lived a householder named Dṛḍhasena.”
In his youth and vigor, while the king governed the various cities, he conceived this thought:
"How may I be able to accumulate wisdom?
By means of this wisdom, I shall enable sentient beings to practice the Dharma and abandon worldly occupations."
Having formed this thought, a deva immediately addressed him, saying: "Householder,
you should know that there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Samantaguṇottarameghasvarapradīpa, who has now entered parinirvāṇa."
At that time, when the householder heard the name of the Buddha, joy arose in his heart; yet upon hearing of his parinirvāṇa, he immediately wept with great sorrow.
A deva asked him, "For what reason do you first feel joy and subsequently weep with grief?"
The householder replied:
"When I heard from you that a Buddha had appeared in the world, my heart was filled with joy;
yet now, hearing of his parinirvāṇa, I weep because I have lost a great benefit."
The deva spoke again: "Do not grieve!

When the Buddha Universal Virtue Increasing Cloud Sound Lamp was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he empowered a Dharma master named Śabda-vidyā through his supernormal powers; this master fully received and upheld the Buddha’s treasury of Dharma, and was thus the one who knew that Buddha’s treasury of Dharma."
The householder asked,
"Where is the Dharma Master Śabdavidyā now? He replied:
“Householder! The Dharma Master is currently in the city of Kapilavastu, three hundred and sixty yojanas to the east of here.
Having heard these words, the householder Sthiramati that very morning took eighty billion pieces of gold and a thousand-jeweled necklace, and together with a large retinue, set out for that city.
Having arrived, he sought out the dwelling place of the Dharma Master.
Upon seeing the Dharma Master, he prostrated at his feet and stood to one side.

The Śabdavidyā Dharma Master preached for him the profound, pure, and wondrous Dharma—namely, this Mahāyāna sūtra which severs all doubts, brings joy to the assembly, and gathers all the roots of goodness of the bodhisattvas.

At that time, the householder, having heard the sutra, was filled with joy; out of reverence for the Dharma, he took a golden necklace and offered it to the Dharma Master, and he also personally provided for him with offerings and service.

“Śāriputra! For the sake of seeking the Dharma, the householder Drḍhamati diligently and with reverence makes offerings to the Dharma teacher, constantly following and attending him, desiring to obtain this sutra so that he may copy it, receive and uphold it, read and recite it, and practice its teachings.”

From the time he first heard it, for sixty billion years he constantly followed the Dharma Master; during that entire interval, he was not able to hear it again, let alone write it down, receive and uphold it, or read and recite it!

For all those years, the householder provided offerings to the Śabdavidyā Dharma Master without his mind ever turning away; he did not give rise to thoughts of desire, thoughts of anger, or thoughts of malice. He constantly remained outside the gate where the Dharma Master stayed, attending to him day and night, never once sleeping or reclining.

At that time, there was an evil Māra named Constantly Seeking an Opportunity, who, in order to seek out the faults of the layman Sthira-gaṇa, transformed himself into the body of the Dharma Master Śabda-vidyā and engaged in sexual acts with a woman.
Having performed this transformation, he said to the layman:
"Behold your teacher, whom you always claim is like a Buddha, foremost in wisdom, and as learned as the ocean."
Observe now that you yourself practice what is contrary to the Dharma; how can you teach others to cultivate pure precepts while you yourself violate the prohibitions?

Your teacher claims to be one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), yet he has ruined the holy life; he constantly teaches others to practice the profound and pure Dharma, so why do you now act unlawfully yourself?
"Householder, you should stop; abandon this person and do not take him as your teacher!

You maintain pure precepts, have few desires and are content, delight in seclusion and diligence, and are firm in mindfulness and wisdom. Having yourself accomplished such virtues, why would you take this man as your teacher?"
At that time, the householder Dṛḍhasena had this thought:
"While I was in my own home, a deva came to me and said:
'A Buddha has appeared in the world, named Samantaguṇavivardhanameghasvarapradīpa, and he has now entered parinirvāṇa.'"
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he bestowed his supernormal powers upon each and every Dharma master within ten billion Jambudvīpas.
In this Jambudvīpa, there was a Dharma master named Śabdavidyā.
"He is able to receive and uphold everything taught by that Buddha; he is a keeper of the Dharma-treasury of that Tathāgata.
You should go and attend upon him!
Upon hearing these words, I considered them a great benefit and immediately went to where this Dharma-master was.

At that time, the Dharma Master immediately expounded for me the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* titled *Cutting Through the Doubts of Sentient Beings and Bringing Joy to the Multitudes*, which guided my mind.
I was filled with joy and presented the Dharma Master with great offerings; I also served him with my own person as an offering, regarding this act as the ultimate truth.
Now that this person has come and pointed out such faults and improper conduct to me, the Dharma Master, you should know this to be the work of Māra.
Why is this? For one who is protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness and empowered by his spiritual authority, it is impossible for such a thing to occur.
"This may be a māra, or a follower of māra, or one sent by māra.
Why is this? For within the Dharma taught by the Dharma Master Śabdavidyā, such a thing does not exist."
I shall examine and seek the marks of a woman and the qualities of a woman, and I shall investigate the marks of a man and the qualities of a man.
If I were to follow these deceptive marks, there is no evil I would not do.
Why is this so? All sinful karma arises from recollective thought and conceptual discrimination.
If I, following the marks I perceive, harbor contempt or anger toward a Dharma teacher, I am likewise able to slander the Buddha and subvert the Buddha-dharma.
"This Dharma master has been empowered by the spiritual power of the Buddha Universal Virtue Supreme Cloud Sound Lamp.
I shall now make this vow:

If this Dharma master is indeed empowered by the spiritual power of that Tathāgata, and I too am one who deeply seeks the Dharma, then by these causes and conditions, these signs of impurity shall immediately vanish!"
Immediately, he joined his palms, focused his mind on the Buddha, and spoke these sincere words:
"At that moment, the woman's appearance vanished and did not manifest again. After the layman Jianzhong had eliminated the demonic interference, he thought to himself:

'I have sought the Dharma with such single-minded devotion, yet the Dharma Master Shengming has not taught it to me; this is surely the work of Māra, and furthermore, it is due to the karmic conditions of my own obstructive offenses from past lives, not the fault of the Dharma Master.'"
"I shall exert myself and practice with diligent perseverance!
Having thus contemplated and extinguished all demonic activities, he still followed the Dharma Master with reverence, giving rise to neither anger nor pride.
“Śāriputra! Observe this householder; his mind is pure, firm, and difficult to deter.
From the moment he first heard [the teaching] sixty billion years ago, even though he did not hear it again during that interval, he has nevertheless continued to follow with deep-seated reverence.”
Although Māra constantly sought opportunities to deceive him in this way, his mind remained unswayed; instead, his reverence increased and his faith became pure.

After sixty billion years had passed, the Elder Firm-Assembly (Jianzhong) died there and was reborn in the world-system named "Non-contention" (Avigraha), the one thousandth and tenth world in the upward direction.
In that land there is a Buddha named Mahāskandha. At one assembly he preached the Dharma, and his community of śrāvakas numbered nine hundred and sixty million.
A Bodhisattva named Drdhasena was born at that time into a royal family. Upon his birth, a deva came and said to him:
"By virtue of your single-minded pursuit of the Dharma, you have obtained this karmic fruit."
Having heard this, Drḍhasena thought to himself:
"If it is so, from this day forward I shall seek it again.
After living for a thousand years, he went forth into homelessness within the Dharma of Mahābāhu.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for them; through their original vows and the Buddha’s spiritual power, they attained the recollection of past lives and were able to receive and uphold the treasury of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata Mahāskandha.
During half an eon, he practiced the holy life and transformed immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, causing them all to dwell securely in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"After his life came to an end, he next encountered a Buddha named Sumeruketu.
Having reached the age of seven, he left the household life within that Buddha’s Dharma to seek the Way."

Because this person firmly maintains the causes and conditions of their original vow and through the spiritual power of the Buddha, they are able to receive and uphold the entire Dharma-treasury taught by the Buddha Sumerukalpa; furthermore, they remember without forgetting the teachings they requested from the Buddha Mahāskandha.

In this manner, through successive encounters, he met sixty hundred thousand million billion nayutas of Buddhas; he was able to receive, uphold, recite, explain, and practice all that these Buddhas taught.
From this time forward, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhasena’s erudition and wisdom shall be like the waters of the great ocean:
unturbid and inexhaustible, equal to space;
pure, profound, and wondrous, with a bottom so deep it is difficult to fathom.

“Śāriputra, you might think that after the householder Dṛḍhasena heard the voice from heaven, he took a golden necklace to the place of the Dharma teacher; having heard the Dharma with joy, he offered it to the Dharma teacher and also served him with his own person in reverence, constantly following the Dharma teacher for sixty billion years for the sake of seeking the Dharma, yet did not hear the Dharma again.

If one constantly seeks opportunities for Māra to thus deceive and delude them, yet upon seeing or hearing of the teacher's faults does not feel resentment or obstruction, but pursues him with single-minded devotion until the end of life—is this not a person of extraordinary character?
"Do not form such a view; he was none other than the Buddha Jvalanaprabha. Śāriputra!
Observe how the Bodhisattva, with a profound mind and diligent effort, sought the Dharma in this way and attained such a great fruit."
Therefore, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas seek the Dharma with a profound mind, they will swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Śāriputra!
The Dharma Master Śrīghoṣa still protects the Dharma for all Buddhas during the three periods of the day; he is now present in this assembly.
“Śāriputra, there are furthermore three matters that verify the mind of a bodhisattva:”
First, when a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma with single-minded devotion, they are able to universally practice all manner of deeds;
this is the initial resolve. Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva seeks the immeasurable Buddha-dharmas, hears the profound Dharma without alarm or fear, accepts it with faith and does not oppose it, and follows the profound Dharma as heard with a pure and unmoving mind—this is called the second true mind of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If someone comes to where a bodhisattva is and speaks thus:
"If there is anyone who has resolved upon the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, they should bestow happiness upon all sentient beings."
‘Now I am the foremost among those suffering; it should be given to me first, and only thereafter to all sentient beings.
If such a bodhisattva has the power to save them yet refuses to give, their mind becomes discouraged and they think:
‘If I cannot even bring happiness to this person, how much less can I save all sentient beings?’
"You should know that this is not the true bodhisattva mind.
If, upon seeing a seeker, one's mind does not retreat or sink, but instead gives rise to compassion and regards [the act] as joy, you should know that this is the true bodhisattva mind."

“Śāriputra! When giving various articles of pleasure to those who seek them, even if one is met with harsh words, abuse, and insults, one’s mind remains free from anger and resentment; instead, one gives rise to loving-kindness and compassion and provides whatever they seek.”

Being able to thus subdue the mind, one immediately eliminates the causes and conditions of immeasurable karmic offenses from birth and death, swiftly approaching the path of the Buddha. Within each and every thought-moment, one can encompass immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means of the profound mind, whose resolve is indestructible.
If a beggar speaks harshly or reviles him, the Bodhisattva then thinks:
"This person is bestowing the Buddha-dharma upon me.
Because he does not give rise to anger toward this, he draws near to the path of the Buddha; this is called the true mind of a Bodhisattva through skillful means.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If someone were to come to a bodhisattva and say:
'Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is a dharma that is exceedingly difficult; how can you possibly gather all the Buddha-dharmas?'"
If, upon hearing this, the bodhisattva’s mind gives rise to retreat or despondency, it is not a true mind.
If, upon hearing this teaching, the mind gives rise to a thought of adaptability, this is what is called the true mind of a bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If someone were to come and say to a bodhisattva:
'If one has resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, one does not have mastery over one's own body or life, much less over material wealth! "
“Good son! You should now abandon this mind; do not allow yourself to lose mastery over your body and life.
When a bodhisattva hears this and becomes attached to his body and life, thereby giving rise to regression and despondency, you should know that this is not the true mind of a bodhisattva.
If one hears of this matter, one should form this thought:
"All sentient beings cherish their bodies and lives, yet when old age, sickness, and death arrive, they will inevitably and forcibly seize them away."
Furthermore, because of being stingy with one's own life, one gives rise to various sinful karmas;
due to these sinful karmas, one will fall into the evil realms, and thus be unable to protect one's future existence.

If I were to covet and cherish my own body and life, creating the causes and conditions for transgressions, I would fall into the various evil realms and wander through birth and death; how would I differ from those foolish people?

I should no longer cherish or protect my own body and life; rather, I should only long for and cherish the wisdom of the Tathāgata, safeguarding the Buddha-dharma, and practicing with diligent vigor to deliver all sentient beings, while abandoning craving, attachment, and all afflictions!
"I shall now, for those who are neither bound nor liberated, expound the various dharmas for the sake of sentient beings.
Having reflected thus, he replied to that person, saying:
"As for your statement that body and life do not attain mastery, it is naturally so with all phenomena; whether one cherishes them or does not cherish them, both are devoid of mastery."
"Alas, O benevolent one!
All dharmas are empty and without a master; they have no basis of reliance, but exist only through conditions.
If one can thus correctly contemplate dharmas, you should know that this is the attainment of the true bodhisattva mind through skillful means.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Suppose someone were to come and say to a bodhisattva:
'You have resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; you should now serve as my servant for me.'"
The Bodhisattva replied:
"I do not serve as a servant for you alone; I ought to attend to all sentient beings. Why is this? Because..."

I bear the heavy burden for all sentient beings: the burden of peace and security, the burden of tirelessness, the burden of rebirth in auspicious realms, the burden of being able to encounter the Buddhas, the burden of hearing the Buddha’s Dharma, the burden of practicing in accordance with the Dharma, and the burden of attaining liberation. This burden does not cause weariness or exhaustion of body or mind; it does not afflict oneself with distress nor afflict others, for it neither brings suffering upon oneself nor brings suffering upon them.
"As you have said, you shall be my servant.
What do you require?
If that person should say:
"If you require my body and life," the Bodhisattva should say,

"I now have no stinginess regarding the protection of my body and life; rather, I pity and cherish you, so that you do not give rise to a sense of mastery within these dharmas— which are entirely empty, without a master, and without any basis— and thereby commit sinful karma."
By these causes and conditions, one falls into the various evil realms. Alas, O virtuous one!
It is my heart’s desire that you not give rise to such karmic conditions for sin and fall into the various evil destinies. Thus is my mind.
"If you do not believe me, I shall follow your wishes.
If one can thus disregard even body and life, know that this is the true Bodhisattva mind.

Such a person will then distance themselves from birth and death and draw near to the unsurpassed path of all-encompassing wisdom; they will teach and transform sentient beings, purify Buddha-lands, and further increase the roots of goodness for both themselves and others.
“Śāriputra! It is like refining a priceless maṇi jewel: when it is smelted in fire, its color shines forth accordingly, and the master jeweler who refines it gains great wealth and profit.”
This jewel can produce all manner of skills; whoever sees it cannot help but admire it and cherish it. Śāriputra, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this:

he is able to practice the equality of all dharmas and can manifest the true bodhisattva mind to sentient beings. According to the purity and clarity of his roots of goodness, he is constantly protected and remembered by all Buddhas; he is a joy for immeasurable sentient beings to behold, and is the refuge for all devas and humans in the world.
“Śāriputra! It is as if someone were to plant a medicinal tree, irrigating it at the proper times and shielding it from wind and sun, so that this medicinal tree gradually grows and flourishes.”
Once fully grown, it can extinguish the immeasurable ailments of sentient beings and is joyfully beheld by those who are aged and sick.

So too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: having resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and planted various roots of goodness, they single-mindedly seek the Dharma for the sake of Buddha-wisdom; they shield themselves from the works of Māra and all afflictions, and within the Buddha-dharma, they gradually achieve growth according to the deeds they perform.
Once it has grown, it can destroy the diseases of affliction of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, and it can gather the medicine of wisdom for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya multitudes.

When I attain Buddhahood, all sentient beings—whether defiled or undefiled—shall all delight in seeing me; among all the devas, humans, and asuras in every world, I shall be the most honored and noble.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, if someone should come and say to a bodhisattva:
'If you resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, this person shall be born in the great hells. "

Why is this? Because for as many sentient beings as one liberates, one should, for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, undergo all manner of sufferings in the great hells on their behalf; only thereafter shall one attain the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha and liberate sentient beings.
"If you are able to perform such deeds as these, you should seek *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva’s mind immediately recoils and sinks; he conceives the thought that it is difficult to attain. You should know that this is not the true mind of a bodhisattva.

If, upon hearing this matter, one conceives the thought that it is but momentary, the thought that it is not long-lasting, the thought that one is able to endure it, and the thought that one will not fall back or sink away, and forms such a resolve:

"If, by means of the causes and conditions for my entry into hell, I can cause all sentient beings to be free from all suffering and attain the Buddha-way, then for the sake of each and every sentient being, I shall pass through as many asaṃkhyeya kalpas as there are in those realms, enduring all manner of sufferings within the great hells."

Why is this? Because by means of this, one shall attain incomparable wisdom, incomparable Buddha-powers, and the fearlessnesses of a Buddha; furthermore, one shall attain incomparable Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, and be able to establish great Dharma assemblies for the sake of sentient beings, bestowing portions of the Dharma-treasure.

If a person hears this portion of the Dharma-treasure, they shall attain the severance of immeasurable and innumerable sufferings, as well as the severance of immeasurable afflictions throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of the future, and shall also obtain incomparable bliss free from desire.
"Therefore, I shall be capable of taking upon myself, one by one, all the sufferings of the hells for immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, without my mind ever sinking into despondency!

If, within this state, one conceives the thought that it is but a moment, the thought that it is not long or far-reaching, and the thought that one is able to endure it—know that this is the true Bodhisattva mind.
The Buddha-spoken *Kusuma-hasta Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
The Buddha-spoken *Kusuma-hasta Sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter 23: Attaining Mindfulness (7) Attaining Mindfulness Chapter Twenty-Three The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Do you wish to hear further concerning the mind of a bodhisattva?"
“Yes, indeed, World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time; you should further explain the true mind of the bodhisattva.”
"By means of this true mind, one is able to cultivate and accumulate unsurpassed bodhi.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named King of Virtue Radiance (*Guṇarājaprabhāsa*) Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
Śāriputra! This Buddha, King of Virtue and Radiance, has a great assembly of eighty-four thousand śrāvakas, and the number of the bodhisattva assembly is likewise.
At that time, within each of those assemblies of śrāvakas, eighty-four thousand people all attained arhatship.
In each of those assemblies, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Under the Buddha Śrītejorāja, there were as many great arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who had attained mastery over their minds; the number of *srotāpannas*, *sakṛdāgāmins*, and *anāgāmins* was twice that amount.
At that time, there was a prince named Smṛti who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Upon seeing the Buddha, the prince perceived his great majestic virtue and thought to himself:
"The Buddha is truly rare!"
"Having accomplished such profound merit, by what cause shall I attain this Buddha-wisdom and a body endowed with the marks and signs?
Then, following his thoughts, he questioned the Buddha in verse:
"I now behold the World-Honored One; I vow that I shall attain this wisdom."
By practicing what karmic causes and conditions did you attain this unsurpassed wisdom?
The Buddha’s physical form is foremost in color, like the moon among the stars;
his supernormal powers are peerless, able to preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings.
Your wisdom is peerless, like that of Śakra, the Honored One among the gods;
having attained mastery over all phenomena, I now ask about this matter.
The Buddha’s wisdom is pure and unimpeded, penetrating and reaching throughout the three times.
O Honored One by all the multitudes, please explain this matter to me.
World-Honored One, you have in the past beheld countless Buddhas and inquired about the causes of Bodhi; I pray that you will now explain them to me.
"Now I ask about unimpeded wisdom: how does one realize the Buddha-way, become the refuge for all multitudes, and attain deliverance from the suffering of birth and death? "Śāriputra!"
At that time, the Buddha King of Virtue and Radiance replied in verse:
“Young man, what you have spoken is indeed true;
I have seen various Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
I have seen Buddhas more numerous than the sands of the Ganges, their names and numbers beyond reckoning;
likewise, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, I have asked the Buddhas about such matters as these.
You have now resolved upon the Bodhi-mind and shall surely become a Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings.
Now listen to what I say; having heard it, practice according to these words.
Constantly practice giving without indolence, maintain the precepts without ceasing, never tire of hearing the Dharma, and cultivate true wisdom.
The Buddha briefly spoke this verse; seeing that the youth was tireless and desiring to lead him to the path of Buddhahood, he further explained it in detail:
"You practice giving without slackening; you maintain the precepts with purity and without weariness."
Question: The wise have no weariness; this is the causal condition for true wisdom.
True wisdom has no location and no place of permanent abiding.
By inquiring of the Buddhas regarding these causal conditions, one gives rise to true wisdom.
The Buddha’s wisdom does not rely on the eye, for the nature of the eye is itself empty;
therefore, one should not be attached to it, but should seek the Buddha’s wisdom.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These sense bases are all empty; there is no characteristic to which one may cling.
This body is a composite of the four great elements, the locus upon which the mind depends;
it arises from conceptualization, yet even that conceptualization does not exist.
If one does not rely on the body, nor rely on life,
nor rely on wealth and profit, then one can attain the Way of the Buddha.
One should always seek to leave the household life and always practice with diligent vigor.
Always loathing all desires, for the sake of leaving the evil realms behind;
the practice of giving you perform is for the sake of all sentient beings—
without discrimination toward the multitude, and without frivolous conceptualization regarding the gift.
At that time, Prince Smṛti, with a heart full of faith and joy, spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“The World-Honored One can sever all doubts And uproot one from the path of birth and death.
By preaching this profound and pure Dharma, He has brought me great benefit.”
I thought that I had already attained Buddhahood and was seated at the site of enlightenment,
having destroyed all the fetters of Māra, because I had heard the Dharma from the Buddha;
thus I became a leader of the multitude, able to shake the great trichiliocosm.
Manifesting various supernatural powers, it is because they have heard the Dharma from the Buddha.
It is said that they then relinquish their great life-span and have already entered nirvana;
for all phenomena are empty, and birth is true wisdom.
Knowing the characteristic of the cessation of phenomena, The phenomena that cease have no location;
All conditioned things are utterly extinguished, And this utter extinction is itself emptiness.
I now go to my parents To express my gratitude and take my leave.
Having gone forth in the Buddha’s Dharma for the sake of cultivating bodhi,
he immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; after circumambulating him three times,
he departed and proceeded toward his parents’ abode, meeting a wicked Māra along the way.
The Māra conceived this thought:
"The Prince intends to renounce the world; I shall create obstacles and disturb his mind to ruin his resolve.
He immediately stood in the middle of the road and addressed the Prince, asking:
"Where are you hurrying?
Stay a moment, for I wish to question you. The prince then replied:
"I have come from the presence of the Buddha and have heard the unsurpassed Dharma; now I wish to practice it.
Māra said, "Excellent!"
If you seek the Buddha-way with diligence, you should first experience sensual desires, and only thereafter leave the household life.
You were born into a place of honor and nobility, with immeasurable wealth and property;
you should first enjoy worldly pleasures, lest you feel regret later in life.
"In such a noble station, these wondrous five desires are difficult to obtain;
if you now abandon them to leave the household life, you will surely feel regret later.
At that moment, the prince said:
"The pursuit of sensual desires brings no lasting peace; with a perverted mind, you praise these empty and defiled dharmas.
You say that wealth and honor are difficult to attain, and that escaping the eight difficulties is even more difficult.
Now that I have encountered this opportune time, I shall leave the household life to cultivate the Buddha-way."
I have fully understood the realm of desire, as well as the faults of the realms of form and formlessness;
that the three realms are suffering and impermanent, and that by severing craving one attains nirvana.
I shall realize the unconditioned Dharma and bring great benefit to sentient beings.
"Deliver us from birth, sickness, and death, and from the manifold sufferings of the cycle of coming and going.
Then the Māra Lost Mindfulness said to the prince:
"Virtuous one, you yourself say that you aspire to seek the Buddha-dharma; I shall now likewise transform and benefit you."
Then Smṛtimat said: "Speak for me first; having heard it, I shall understand. Māra said:
"I shall speak for you once you have made a vow.
The prince replied, "Alas, O Benevolent One!"
"I previously told you that upon hearing it, you should know.
Māra said to Smṛtimat: "You should not say, 'Upon hearing it, I shall know'; rather, you should speak thus:"
"Simply observe their instruction and act accordingly! De-nian replied:
"I should not now follow the manner of a disciple by acting immediately upon an instruction."

Why is this? If you conceive of what is Dharma as non-Dharma, or conceive of what is non-Dharma as Dharma, and instruct me on that basis, I shall reflect upon it; if it is good, I will follow it, but if it is not good, I will discard it.
Therefore, this is the method of the wise; having heard it, you should understand it.
If you wish to have me first establish a formal vow so that I may act according to your instructions, this is the business of ordinary people, not the work of the wise.
"This is the work of Māra, not the Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, I do not follow your previous fixed vow, fearing that those with wisdom might reproach me, saying:
'How can one make a vow and then later violate it oneself?'"
Then Māra thought to himself:
"This prince is now intelligent and wise; since he is unwilling to make a vow, he is difficult to deceive.
Having had this thought, he spoke to Smṛtijñānakīrti, saying:
"Excellent, Prince! It is not the way of the wise to make a vow beforehand.
Nevertheless, I shall now instruct you; you should receive it with faith."
"In what matters should one see many faults and abandon them, and in what matters should one see few faults and draw near to them?
Having heard this, the prince immediately said to Māra: "Alas, O man!"
You should not speak in such a manner now.
Why is this? One should not associate with either those who have many faults or those who have few faults!
For example, just as a large amount of poison can harm a person, even a small amount can do so.
It is like the food of a wheel-turning monarch containing poison being able to harm people; likewise, the food of a lowly person containing poison can also harm people.
Therefore, you should know that those of profound wisdom should abandon both many faults and few faults.
The dharmas frequented by the wise are free from all defects; they are without fever, without affliction, unshakable, and quiescent, leading to ultimate peace and happiness.
At that time, Māra thought to himself:
"Now this person, though taught by me, refuses to believe or accept it and instead answers in opposition; he is able to comprehend everything thoroughly, which has caused me to doubt."

Nevertheless, there is another principle: the mind of a prince does not wish to accept either minor or major transgressions; yet the conduct of a Bodhisattva involves many faults. Dwelling for a long time in birth and death, coming and going through the various realms of existence, he is subject to the faults of greed, anger, and delusion. Furthermore, those who seek at an improper time may come forcefully to demand his most cherished possessions:
his head, eyes, marrow, brain, and all parts of his body.
In the conduct of a bodhisattva, there may be such faults as these; yet this prince would abandon even a slight transgression of heart, let alone many failures.
Now, if he were to hear that there are such faults within the conduct of a bodhisattva, he might perhaps regress and enter the Dharma of the Lesser Vehicle.
"One who enters nirvāṇa is still superior to this; for this would utterly destroy his mind.
Having reflected thus, he said to the prince:
"Excellent, excellent!"
As you have rightly said, it is the way of the wise that one should not associate with either those who have many faults or those who have few;
my previous statement was erroneous, as I failed to grasp your intention.

"Prince, you should know that only Nirvana is free from all faults and defects; therefore, you should seek it with single-minded diligence, and cease coming and going through the cycle of birth and death to undergo manifold sufferings."

Prince, you should know that conception is extremely painful; dwelling in the womb is painful, and emerging from it is also painful. There is the suffering of separation from what is loved and the suffering of encountering what is hated. This body is impermanent, empty, and lacks solidity; its nurturing requires diligent labor, yet its life-span is precarious and fragile. These matters of impermanence are truly terrifying; how could the boundless cycle of birth and death ever be brought to an end?
Upon hearing this, the wise develop sufficient weary detachment.

You yourself previously said: "The Buddhas are difficult to encounter; it is difficult to be free from the eight adversities; a human body is difficult to obtain; the sutras and Dharma are difficult to hear; and to have faith in them is likewise difficult."
"You have now fully attained all these matters; you should not abandon them in vain. You ought to give rise to weary detachment and enter *nirvāṇa* within this very body.
This was precisely what I intended to teach, which is why I first required you to make a firm vow before you could say to me:
'Having heard it, I shall understand.'"
The prince replied: "If you, O virtuous one, say that birth, old age, sickness, and death involve repeated suffering, it may be as you have said;
but if you say that this body shall enter Nirvāṇa, that is not possible."
Having heard this, my compassion for sentient beings increased all the more.
Sentient beings are pitiable, for they repeatedly undergo suffering through old age, sickness, and death.

When I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I shall turn the wheel of Dharma for the sake of eliminating immeasurable sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, preaching the Dharma so that they may forever be liberated from them.
"O Benevolent One, you are rare!

You have brought me great benefit; when I heard you speak of the suffering of birth and death, I immediately gave rise to a heart of great compassion toward all sentient beings, intent upon their rescue and protection."
"If this body of mine were to enter *nirvāṇa* immediately, who would be there to save others?
Furthermore, having now heard these matters from you, my great vow and its adornments have become even more firm and steadfast."
At that time, Māra the Evil One said to the prince:
"If you say that even those with minor faults should not be approached, for what reason do you now wish to enter the cycle of birth and death?"
He replied: "O virtuous one!
Within Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi there is not a single fault; therefore, one should cultivate intimacy with it."
Māra said: "O Prince!
Although there is no fault within the Unsurpassed Way, who would ever grant it to you?"
"If even I could not attain the path of the Buddha despite my seeking, how much less so you?

When I first conceived the thought that I would attain the path of the Buddha, this perverse mind arose, and immediately there were countless beggars who came to me to demand my head, eyes, marrow, brain, and various other limbs and members."
He spoke again:
"O Prince! I have given my head, eyes, hands, feet, and other limbs to various beggars, until the flowing blood formed a river."
"Do you wish to see it?
He replied, "I wish to see it, for the sake of my benefit."
Then Māra immediately had this thought:
"Does this prince’s mind perhaps waver from the unsurpassed path?
He spoke these words:
"I wish to see this for the sake of benefit.
Mara immediately manifested four great pools of blood, filled with blood;
by the sides of these pools flowed four rivers of blood, and human heads were piled up like Mount Sumeru.
Some were already decaying; some had turned blue-black, yellow, red, or white;
others had further transformed into the corpses of dead people, piled up like mountains, with hands and feet severed, eyes gouged out, ears and noses cut off, and all their limbs disjointed.
Furthermore, yakṣas and various man-eating ghosts filled the surroundings on all sides, appearing most terrifying.
Some wield swords, staves, bows, arrows, spears, and halberds; some carry mountains, vomit fire, or manifest thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts.

Others further transform themselves into the heads of various malevolent insects and beasts—such as lions, bears, brown bears, tigers, leopards, oxen, horses, camels, elephants, pigs, dogs, snakes, fish, and makaras.

These various spirits either grasp venomous snakes or spit fire from their mouths; some have two heads, five heads, ten heads, or hundreds of thousands of millions of heads; some have one tongue, two tongues, ten tongues, or hundreds of thousands of millions of tongues; and some have one eye, two eyes, five eyes, ten eyes, or hundreds of thousands of millions of eyes—each emitting a great roar that is most terrifying.
Each spoke words of wrath, staring with eyes full of anger, biting their lips and protruding their tongues as they surrounded him on all sides.
Having manifested such terrifying sights, they said to the prince:
"Do you now see these four great pools of blood from which four great rivers flow, filled with streaming gore?"
The prince said, “I see it. Māra said:

"All of this is from the blood that flowed when, in the past, when I first resolved to attain the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, various beggars came to me and asked for my head, eyes, marrow, brain, and various other limbs and members; it is from all this blood that this great river has been formed."
"Do you also see this multitude of human heads upon Mount Sumeru?
The prince replied,
"I see them."
Māra said: "All of these are the heads I severed in the past when giving to beggars.
Do you also see this heap of corpses of dead people, like the four great mountains, with their hands, feet, ears, noses, and other limbs all cut off?"
The prince replied, "I see them. Māra said:
"This, too, was my own body that I gave away when I was formerly practicing the bodhisattva path as a Buddha-to-be, bestowing it upon all who came begging.
Do you also see these yakṣas and various evil spirits on all four sides; are they not terrifying?"
The prince said, "I see him. Māra said:

"If a person resolves to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they will immediately be harassed by these various ghosts, who beg for their heads, eyes, ears, noses, hands, feet, and all manner of bodily parts."
"Since I first resolved my mind upon enlightenment in the past, I have severed such numbers of heads and various limbs.
Then Māra further manifested as a great host of rākṣasas and said to the prince:
"Do you see this host of rākṣasas?"
The prince said, "I see them. Māra said:
"If one has generated the unsurpassed bodhicitta, these evil spirits will devour their five viscera and drink seven drops from their heart, severing the life-faculty.
You should know now that if you do not abandon this bodhicitta, you shall not be liberated from this suffering."

I previously reflected that this matter was extremely difficult and ultimately unattainable; unable to endure such manifold sufferings and afflictions, I therefore regressed from the unsurpassed path.
When you regress, you shall immediately be liberated from this suffering and attain peace and happiness.
Therefore, for your benefit, I now speak these words: do not again give rise to this mind of unsurpassed enlightenment!
"If you depart, you shall receive this portion of suffering and not attain liberation.
Prince Smṛtiprāpta thought to himself:
"I have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the presence of the Buddha; yet as I am about to go to my parents, this man has obstructed and thwarted me on the way."

"This may be a māra who has transformed himself into a human body, or one sent by a māra; or perhaps it is one who has given rise to thoughts of regression and indolence regarding the Buddha-way, and thus comes to destroy me."

This person must have committed grave offenses in previous lives; for this reason, there are now so many beggars coming to demand his head, eyes, and various limbs, severing his life-force and causing him such suffering and distress.
Furthermore, these beggars can assist the Bodhisattva in accomplishing the unsurpassed path. Why is this?
These beggars come from all places, and it is because of greed, hatred, delusion, jealousy, and arrogance that they seek alms from the Bodhisattva at inappropriate times.
If I cannot fulfill the worldly aspirations of these sentient beings, how could I possibly grant them supramundane benefits?
Because such a person is indolent and unable to take deep delight in the unsurpassed path, they will consequently give rise to regression.
Seeing this now, I shall redouble my diligence in seeking the unsurpassed path.

Even if, in the space of a single breath, I were to sacrifice as many bodies as there are, continuing until my final ultimate body, and were I to constantly sacrifice as many bodies in each single thought-moment, my mind would never retreat.
I shall now make a great vow as an adornment: these sentient beings, through the power of their afflictions, give rise to such sinful karma;
I must surely attain unsurpassed bodhi and preach the Dharma for them so that they may sever their afflictions!
Having reflected thus, he spoke to Māra, saying: "Alas, O worthy one!
This is most rare; you have brought me great benefit."
He who seeks peace and secures enlightenment can manifest such matters for me.
Having seen this, I have conceived the great armor, which has become increasingly firm, and I take deep delight in enlightenment.
Then Māra thought to himself:
"Now that this prince has seen these transformations, he will redouble his diligence and take even deeper delight in Bodhi.
Having formed this thought, he spoke to the prince, saying:
“O Benevolent One!
If you do not believe my words, we shall now depart for a short while, and you shall know for yourself.
At that time, the various followers of Māra spoke thus to Māra:
"Now this prince does not heed your instructions; you may withdraw to a short distance.
I am extremely hungry and thirsty; I shall tear his body apart, devour his five internal organs, and drink the blood from his heart!"
Or again, some said:
"Go a short distance away; we shall crush and destroy this prince's body. Others said:
"Step aside for a moment; I shall seek out his head.
Or some ghosts said:
"I shall seek out his eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and various other body parts."
A rākṣasa said: "Withdraw from him for a moment;
now the time has come for this prince's life to end, yet though you wish to benefit him, he is unwilling to accept."
"I shall now slay and eat their flesh and blood.
Birth after birth—whether they are conceived, dwelling in the womb, or emerging from it—I will constantly follow them and devour them."
Other yakṣas and ghosts said to one another:
"This man has no power; he does not follow our instructions.
We must now seize him, bind him, kill him, and tear his body apart."
Then the Mara Lost Mindfulness said to the rākṣasas: "Wait a moment;
I shall cause this Prince Attaining Mindfulness to turn away from these false views, and for his sake, I will act as a virtuous friend throughout the long night."
"Wait a moment; you shall be recognized for your kindness. I now wish to cause you to give rise to a mind of right view.
If you do not abandon your evil and false views, then do as you please;
but if you can turn away from them, I shall repay your kindness, and this prince here shall likewise repay me in the future."
Then the Māra Lost Mindfulness spoke a second and third time to the prince, saying:
"You should accept these words!
I am one who seeks your benefit from the depths of my heart; for as long as you live, I shall act as your spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). You should now abandon this inverted and false view."

"Prince! You should know that this unsurpassed path is difficult to attain and difficult to realize. Furthermore, do you wish to see the places where the great bodhisattvas are reborn after their lives have ended?"
He replied, "I wish to see it. Thereupon,
the Mara Lost Mindfulness immediately manifested a great hell at that very spot and said to the prince:
"Do you now see these beings in hell undergoing various forms of torture and suffering?
The prince replied,
"I see them."

Māra said: "These people all sit [in this state] because, in their previous lives when they first resolved upon unsurpassed bodhicitta, seekers who came at an improper time forcibly demanded from them their most cherished and valued possessions."
Because of stinginess and parsimony, one gives rise to a mind of anger and resentment, thereby receiving this retribution for one's sins.
If even for the sake of external objects one is reborn here, how much more so when someone comes to demand one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain—how could one not be free from a mind of anger?
Because of a mind of anger, one receives this retribution.
If you are stingy and refuse to give, you will be born here;
even if you do give it away, if you harbor resentment and anger, you will likewise fall into this state.
Both sides cannot avoid suffering this same misery.

Prince, you should know that if one gives to a seeker without giving rise to anger, these yakṣas will likewise kill, slaughter, and dismember them while they are in the womb, at the time of birth, and after birth, severing their limbs and carrying each part away for themselves.
"Prince, you should know that this bodhisattva path has faults on both extremes; whether one gives or does not give, both are likewise unwholesome.
If you do not believe me, you should ask this man why he was born here."
The prince asked, "O, worthy ones! For what reason have you all been born in this place?"
The people replied, "In the past, when we were practicing the path of the Buddha, we gave rise to thoughts of stinginess and greed toward those who came seeking; therefore, we have been born here."
He further said:
"We originally sought the Buddha-way; yet when beggars came to cut and mangle our bodies, we gave rise to thoughts of anger and resentment at that time, and for this reason we fell into this place."
"Therefore, Prince!
You should follow what this person says; do not enter therein, lest you later feel regret.
At that time, the prince said to Māra:
"Alas, O Benevolent One!

You have deeply perceived what is beneficial by showing me the hells and this bodhisattva. From this day forward, regarding those things I hold dear, I shall have no stinginess or thoughts of not giving."
If one gives to a beggar, one never feels anger or resentment.
Why is this? Those who are born in hell do so as a retribution for stinginess and greed; it is not the fruit of giving.
"Alas, O virtuous one!
We should now go together to the Buddha Śrīkūṭarāja and inquire about this matter.
Whatever the Buddha teaches, let us all practice it together."
The demon Muṣitasmṛti said:
"What need have I now to go to the Buddha's abode?
If you wish to go, you may do as you please."
"Why is this? I fear that the Buddha will instead instruct me to resolve my mind upon the unsurpassed path.
Prince Smṛtimat spoke again to Māra, saying:

"You yourself have said that you are one who deeply seeks benefit and seeks peace and security; you must go with me to the Buddha Devarājasupratiṣṭhita, and according to what the Buddha teaches, we shall practice it together."
Thus he spoke up to three times, but Māra remained unwilling, saying:
"Prince! Let it be for now;
because I previously followed the words of the Buddha, I have already undergone all manner of sufferings, and I cannot go now."

The prince immediately took his hand and led him away together to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and related in detail everything they had previously discussed to the Buddha.
The Buddha said: “Dainian! Excellent, excellent!”
"Can you not follow what this man says?
This is the delusive deception of the Mara Lost Mindfulness (Muṣitasmṛti), who wishes to obstruct your bodhisattva path.
Thereupon, the prince addressed Lost Mindfulness, saying:
"You should now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus.
Māra said, "Stop! Do not speak thus!"
"I shall not take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha.
Having spoken thus, he fell silent.
At that time, the prince gazed intently at Māra and made a solemn vow with single-minded resolve:
"If I seek the Buddha-way with a sincere heart, may this Māra take the form of a bhikṣu!
Immediately, losing his mindfulness, he shaved his head, donned the dharma robes, took up his alms-bowl, and stood among the assembly.
Seeing himself with his hair shaven, wearing the dharma robes, holding an alms bowl and a mendicant’s staff in the likeness of a śramaṇa, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If one originally has no mind to take refuge in the Triple Gem, yet forcibly changes their form to that of a śramaṇa, is this in accordance with the Dharma?"
The Buddha said to Muṣitasmṛti:
"Who has forcibly provided you with a shaven head, the Dharma robes, and the appropriate ritual implements?
Thereupon, Māra immediately gave rise to this thought:
"Since no one will shave my head or provide me with the Dharma robes to become a śramaṇa, why should I not abandon this and depart!
He then wished to remove his own Dharma robes and alms bowl, but was unable to do so. Thereupon, he thought:
"While I remain in this assembly, I shall be constantly ridiculed by others for as long as it takes."
"You may now depart from here and return to your own palace.
Having thought this, he suddenly vanished and ascended to his celestial palace, where he said to his retinue:
"Do not think of me as a bhikṣu; I am still that very same Māra, King Lost-Mind!"
"I intended to go to the Buddha Devarājasupratiṣṭhita to cause him harm and ruin, yet instead you have transformed me into this form; it is truly laughable!
At that time, his attendants reviled him, saying: "Shaveling!..."
"Do not speak such madness; you are no longer the Heavenly King Māra, for there is now another king here in this palace.
Upon hearing this, Śambara was filled with deep distress and remorse; wailing and weeping bitterly, he returned to where the Buddha was.

By the power of his supernatural penetrations, the Buddha Virtuous King Radiance immediately manifested the Avīci Hell. Within it were hell-wardens holding glowing iron balls as large as Mount Sumeru, searching from east to west for the Māra Lost Mindfulness to identify who he was.
Someone asked, "What is the use of this?
and the wardens replied:
"I wish to place this great, glowing iron ball into his mouth.
Yet another person said:
"This Mara Lost-Mind (Pramuṣitasmṛti) has already become a śramaṇa; he shall escape hell."
"Or there may be a hell-warden who carries a great mountain of fire upon his two shoulders, searching from east to west for the Mara Lost-Mind (Vismṛta), asking:
'Who is this? Someone asks him:
'What is the use of this?'"
The hell-warden replied,
"I wish to burn and crush his body with a mountain of fire. Someone said:
"This Māra Vismṛti has already attained renunciation and escaped the suffering of hell.
Then, some wardens, with iron-sword mountains from which fierce flames burst forth placed upon their shoulders, searched east and west for the Māra Vismṛti, asking, "Which one is he?"
Someone asked, "What is it for? and the wardens replied:
"I wish to use a mountain of blades to cut his body to pieces! Someone said:
"The Mara Lost-Mind has already left the household life within the Buddha-dharma of King Virtuous Radiance and has been liberated from the suffering of hell."
"Or there may be a hell-warden who carries on his shoulder a large cauldron filled with molten copper, searching from east to west for where the demon Lost-Mind (Vismṛta) might now be.
Someone asks him: 'What will you do with it?'"
The hell-warden replied,
"I wish to pour molten copper into his mouth, burning his lips, tongue, throat, and five internal organs, so that they are scorched and rotted as it passes through."
Some people said: "This Māra Lost Mindfulness has left the household life within the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgata Virtuous King Radiance and has been liberated from the suffering of hell.
Meanwhile, some wardens, holding in their hands various weapons such as iron forks, bows, arrows, spears, and halberds, searched here and there, saying these words:
"Where is the Māra Lost Mindfulness now?
Someone asked, "What use would there be for him?"
The hell-warden replied,
"I wish to strike, pierce, cut, and mangle his body with various kinds of weapons.
Someone else said:
"This Māra Vismṛti has already attained renunciation and escaped the suffering of hell.

At that time, within the hells, Māra Vismṛti heard the terrifying voices of the hell-wardens shouting, "Seize him! Bind him! Beat, hack, pierce, and slash him! Tear his body apart! Do not let him live!"
Having heard this matter, he was struck with great terror and thought to himself:
"Now I see it with my own eyes; there is no longer any doubt.
I am certainly declining and shall lose my original celestial palace to enter the great hells."
"The various hell-wardens are shouting from all sides, seeking to capture me.
Upon whom can I now rely?
Only the Dharma of renunciation can be depended upon."
"If the Buddha would believe my most sincere heart, I shall leave the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma, hoping to escape the suffering of this great hell.
You may convey this intention to the Prince."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to De-mnian (Smṛti) and related these matters in detail, saying:
"I wish to go forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma. De-mnian replied:
"If you can, with faith, joy, and purity, give rise to the unsurpassed bodhicitta, only then may you go forth from home into the Dharma. Why is this so? "
Within the teachings of all Buddhas, it is not merely by shaving one's head and donning dyed robes that one is called "one who has gone forth";
rather, you must practice the dharmas appropriate for those who have gone forth before you can truly be considered one who has gone forth.

Lost Mindfulness, you should know that within the Buddha’s Dharma, those who harbor attachment to a self or what belongs to a self, as well as those who engage in conceptual discrimination, are not called renunciants.
Lost Mindfulness!
You should first give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment, and then correctly contemplate: by what dharma is it called "hell"?

When you investigate the essential nature of hell in this manner, you will certainly not find a fixed nature of hell, nor will you perceive any dharma that enters hell or any dharma that does not enter it.

At that time, the Mara Lost-Mind immediately gave rise to the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi; he constantly delighted in correctly contemplating such characteristics of dharmas, and before long, he attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
“Śāriputra! Prince Dṛḍhamati single-mindedly exhorted this Māra Lost-Mindfulness, causing him to abandon all evils and reach the stage of non-retrogression.
Buddha Guṇarājaprabhāsa then conferred upon him the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.”
Śāriputra! This is what is called the true bodhisattva mind.
By means of this mind, all bodhisattvas are able to gather immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
“Śāriputra! Do you think that Śīlavatī was someone else? Do not entertain such a view;
she was none other than the Buddha Kuśaṃti of the past, who, within this Bhadrakalpa, brought sentient beings to liberation and has already entered parinirvāṇa.”
"Who else could this Smṛti have been at that time?
It was none other than this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dṛḍhamati here in this assembly. Śāriputra!"
At that time, Smṛtilābha went to his parents, stood to one side, and said to them:
"I now wish to go forth into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma of King Virtuous Radiance."
Before his parents, he spoke these verses:
"I have gone forth into the Dharma; Parents, do not create obstacles.
Going forth is praised by the Buddha, For it is the root of all happiness."
If you wish to obtain the joy of a sovereign, birth in heaven, or wealth;
if you seek merit and wisdom, you should go forth into the Dharma.
That your parents are now noble and honored is due to their original practice of giving and morality.
By further cultivating the roots of merit, you shall become a Dharma King.
Having practiced giving, morality, and patience in the past, you have now attained the status of a human king.
If you wish to increase your goodness, you should now go forth into the homeless life.
When a person’s karmic rewards are exhausted, they later fall into the various evil realms;
because of having committed grave offenses, they are unable to encounter the Buddhas.
If a person relinquishes remaining worldly blessings, leaves the household life, and practices the wholesome Dharma, [they shall attain liberation].
Thus one can leave the eight difficulties behind, And always encounter the various Buddhas.
Seeing a Buddha, one quickly gains faith; Through faith, one gives rise to reverence.
With a reverent mind, one follows the Path; Swiftly one attains Bodhi.
If you wish to be free from all calamities, You should distance yourself from evil associates;
Follow me and learn to leave the household life— This is the root of all happiness.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits, As well as the gandharvas and others, [rejoice].
None shall be able to create obstacles to prevent me from leaving the home life.
Should anyone wish to create such obstacles, they will only bring upon themselves the karma of sin;
like a mighty elephant king, I shall break through their fetters at will.
I am now likewise in this way; having severed and cast off the bonds of craving, once they are severed I shall go forth into homelessness, such that no one can turn me back.
My parents, honoring his virtue, silently granted permission for him to go forth.
Having thus circumambulated him to the right, he departed and went straight to where the Buddha was.
Having approached the Buddha and gone forth into the homeless life, immeasurable sentient beings heard of it;
their hearts were filled with faith and joy, and they followed the prince to leave the household life.
The prince’s spiritual friends, immeasurable sons of elders,
having faith in the subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Buddha, all together went forth into homelessness.
When the king heard that his son had gone forth, he too abandoned the sovereign position of the kingdom.
He immediately joined eighty billion, seventy nayutas, and suchlike retinues,
all of whom together went forth into homelessness.
At that time, the King’s consort, having heard that the King had gone forth, [did likewise].
Together with eighty thousand court ladies, she likewise went forth into homelessness;
all followed this prince and gave rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna.
Thus praising the life of renunciation—who would not follow and train therein?
“Śāriputra! Do you think that the King who cultivated roots of goodness as the father of Smṛti was someone else?
Do not hold such a view; he was none other than myself.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"The king and his great ministers, The palace ladies and all their retinue,
For twenty-one thousand years, Together purely cultivated the holy life."
At the time of his death, that Buddha, standing amidst the assembly,
smiled and bestowed a prophecy upon the king, recounting his original practices and vows.
This king had cultivated the pure conduct and deeply resolved upon the Mahāyāna vow.
He shall never fall into the states of woe, but always be born in places free from hardship.
For immeasurable kalpas, this king made offerings to countless Buddhas;
in the Bhadrakalpa he became a World-Honored One, known by the name Śākyamuni.
The king’s various kinsmen, including the bhikṣus such as Smṛti,
went before Śākyamuni Buddha, left the household life to become his disciples,
