and all purely cultivated the brahma-faring; in the end, they returned to obtain human bodies.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, his relics shall be widely distributed.
In that final age, when the Buddha-dharma is about to perish,
these people shall once again be able to hear together the sūtras that I now preach.
The Buddha’s wisdom is pure and unimpeded; He proclaims the light of knowledge through his teachings.
Whatever discourses he utters Ultimately all return to the truth.
If a person hears this Dharma And believes it deeply, their hair stands on end.
Then one will not give rise to doubt, thinking, "I have not yet received the prediction.
If a person in the final age attains patience regarding the profound Dharma, they should immediately form this thought:
"I have heard the Dharma King speak; [he has predicted my future attainment]."
Bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, as well as all laymen and laywomen who can take delight in this profound Dharma— I shall bestow predictions of enlightenment upon them all.
When the Buddha spoke this Dharma, within that great assembly,
Fully eighty billion, seventy nayutas in total, have all attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī kṣānti*) and become minor Dharma-Princes.
Chapter 24: Right View (VII) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
"What is meant by 'right view'?
Śāriputra, that which is right view is without high or low; it regards all phenomena with equanimity."
Furthermore, because the seer is equal to and not different [from the seen], it is called right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*).
What is meant by "equal"?
The eye is itself *nirvāṇa*; there is no *nirvāṇa* apart from the eye.
The eye and nirvāṇa—these two are equal. Why are they equal?
Because the eye is not [identical to] the eye, and nirvāṇa is not [identical to] nirvāṇa; thus they are equal.
Why is this? Within the eye there is no eye, and within nirvāṇa there is no nirvāṇa;
within the eye there is no nirvāṇa, and within nirvāṇa there is no eye; the eye and nirvāṇa are neither two nor distinct.
Because there is no duality or distinction, it is called "equality.
The ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are themselves nirvāṇa; there is no nirvāṇa apart from the mind. Thus, the mind and nirvāṇa are equal and identical.
In what sense are they equal?
They are not the mind, yet they are equal to the mind; they are not nirvāṇa, yet they are equal to nirvāṇa. Why is this so?
In the mind there is no mind, and in nirvāṇa there is no nirvāṇa;
in the mind there is no nirvāṇa, and in nirvāṇa there is no mind; the mind and nirvāṇa are non-dual and without distinction.
If there is no discrimination regarding this dharma, it is emptiness; emptiness is equality—this is called right view.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, because it is right view, it is called "right view."
Thus, because it is precisely the center and possesses no mark of deviation, it is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, because this view is ineffable and immeasurable, it is called right view.
What is called the characteristic of destroying right view?
Śāriputra, to oppose,
disbelieve, not accept, not praise, and not practice according to the teachings of such sūtras as these is called destroying right view.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
to discriminate among various phenomena is what is called 'profoundly destroying right view. Why is this so?
One who is free from conceptual discrimination attains right view.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"If a noble disciple does not dwell upon the characteristics of earth, nor dwells upon 'this earth' or 'that earth,' nor thinks 'I am within the earth' or 'the earth is within me.'"

He does not attend to other great elements, such as water, fire, or wind; he does not attend to the Brahma-world, the Ābhāsvara realm, or the Śubhakṛtsna realm; he does not attend to the Bṛhatphala, Avṛha, Atapa, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he does not attend to nirvāṇa, nor does he attend to this or that nirvāṇa, nor to a self within nirvāṇa, nor nirvāṇa within a self.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, one who possesses right view has no views at all. Why is this?
Whatever views one may hold are all false views; the absence of all views is itself right view.
"Śāriputra, furthermore, right view is inexpressible."
Why is this? All verbal expressions are merely empty sounds, yet some people develop craving and attachment toward them. "Śāriputra!..."
Furthermore, regarding the right view known by the Tathāgata, within this view there is no wrong view.
Why is this? All verbal expressions abide within suchness (*tathatā*); since suchness is ineffable, so too are verbal expressions.
Śāriputra! All bodily actions are likewise thus: they abide within suchness, being neither correct nor erroneous, and devoid of discrimination. Śāriputra!
All karmas abide within suchness; they are neither correct nor erroneous, and are devoid of discrimination.
All karmic retributions likewise abide within suchness, as explained according to the characteristics of karma.
Therefore, when the Tathāgata speaks the truth, he says:
"If there is an action performed, there will necessarily be a retribution for that action; the retribution follows the action."
"In this way, Śāriputra, this wisdom is called the discernment of the five destinies.
The wisdom regarding the five destinies is entirely non-wisdom; all five destinies arise from non-wisdom."
"Śāriputra! Upon hearing this, a bodhisattva should not be startled or afraid, nor should they give rise to despondency or retreat. Śāriputra!"
There are four kinds of practices which, if one cultivates and pursues them, increase ignorance and do not give rise to wisdom.
What are these four? Reading and reciting the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths increases ignorance and does not give rise to wisdom; [the other three are as follows: ... [and so forth].
To associate with and cultivate various dharmas of false views increases delusion and does not give rise to wisdom;
to delight in making definitive judgments about matters increases delusion and does not give rise to wisdom;
to fail to accept, read, or correctly contemplate these profound dharmas that accord with emptiness increases delusion and does not give rise to wisdom.
These are called the four.
"Śāriputra, one should cultivate those things that, by being contrary to these four dharmas, can give rise to wisdom."
What are the four? Cultivating right view, which can sever wrong view—this is the first dharma that can destroy ignorance and give rise to wisdom.

If there is a place where non-Buddhist scriptures are being read or recited, one who practices the pure conduct should distance themselves and depart from it, and should not remain there; this is the second dharma that can destroy ignorance and give rise to wisdom.

Śāriputra! If there are those who adjudicate legal disputes in a monastic residence, practitioners of pure conduct should not dwell together with them. If one wishes to stay, one should speak only of the Right Path and not mix it with what is contrary to the Dharma, so as to extinguish such matters and practice in peace and security. This is also for the sake of subduing those who act contrary to the Dharma and for the sake of maintaining the harmony of the Saṃgha so that it is not destroyed. This is the third dharma that can destroy ignorance and give rise to wisdom.

Śāriputra! To listen to and receive these profound sūtras with a single-minded focus, to practice according to what is taught, to expound them for others, and to cause the Dharma to endure for a long time—this is the fourth dharma that can destroy ignorance and give rise to wisdom.
These are called the four.
Śāriputra, as for the Dharma of a bodhisattva: they practice shame and remorse deeply, maintaining pure ethical discipline because they do not give rise to [karmic] action;
A bodhisattva should give rise to a mind free from fear, because they adorn their vows;
a bodhisattva should constantly cultivate the conduct of a great person and initiate great progress, because they never slacken or cease.
Chapter 25: Praising the Teaching (7). Chapter Twenty-Five: Praising the Teaching. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“If a bodhisattva, for the sake of protecting the true Dharma and thoroughly understanding the authentic treatises, questions my disciples...”
At that time, the Tathāgata was deeply comforted and rejoiced.
Why is this? Because he continues the lineage of the Buddhas.

Therefore, you disciples, the śrāvakas, should expound the true Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them; in this way, you shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit.

Śāriputra! If my disciples—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—mindfully recollect the Buddha, mindfully recollect the Dharma, and likewise mindfully recollect the Tathāgata; for the sake of seeking the Dharma, they undergo various hardships through immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; and with such mindfulness, they explain even a single verse to a bodhisattva;
furthermore, they form this thought:

"When these bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, and are shown, taught, benefited, and gladdened by it, they shall plant roots of goodness and cultivate the Buddha-dharma, attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. For the sake of severing the various sufferings and afflictions of beginningless birth and death for immeasurable and boundless sentient beings, they shall preach the Dharma."

If the merit thus obtained were to have a physical form, and if all sentient beings throughout the four continents were to attain human bodies and each were to take a portion of this merit, forming a lump as large as Mount Sumeru, even then this merit would not be exhausted.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Setting aside the four continents, suppose all sentient beings within a small thousand-world system, a medium thousand-world system, or a great thousand-world system—whether with form or without form, with perception or without perception, or neither with nor without perception—were all at once to obtain human bodies. If each were to take a vessel as large as Mount Sumeru and depart filled to the brim with this merit, it would still not be exhausted."

Śāriputra! My disciples—whether bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās—who explain even a single four-line verse for the sake of a bodhisattva, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, shall obtain immeasurable and boundless merit.

Śāriputra! If these bodhisattvas know that by preaching the Dharma to this person they will gain great benefit—thereby enabling them to accomplish such qualities of the Buddha-dharma and further increase their buddha-wisdom—they [will do so].

If one were to carry all manner of articles of pleasure upon one's head or on one's shoulders to provide for them, even until the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi, one should first preach the Dharma for them, causing them to perceive the Four Noble Truths.
Śāriputra! Although these bodhisattvas provide such offerings and benefits, they have not yet repaid their debt of gratitude. Why is this?
Because of such a person, one is able to see the immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, you should know that the kindness of one who expounds the Dharma for the sake of bodhisattvas is difficult to repay.

“Śāriputra! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Samantarakṣita Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, whose lifespan was seventy thousand years.”
His assembly of śrāvakas held three great gatherings:
at the first gathering when he preached the Dharma, eighty nayutas of people all attained the Way;
at the middle gathering when he preached the Dharma, sixty nayutas of people [attained it].
Later, when he preached the Dharma, forty nayutas of people also all attained the Way.
"Śāriputra! After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained in the world for a full four thousand years."
When the Dharma was about to perish, there was a bhikṣu named Prajñāmati, who was of sharp faculties, intelligent and discerning, and possessed of great learning and wisdom.
At that time, the king of Jambudvīpa was named Nanda, and the city where the king resided was also named Nanda.
The city was twelve yojanas in length and seven yojanas in width; it was prosperous, peaceful, and teeming with people.
At that time, there was an elder in this city named Mṛdumati (Soft-Minded), who had a son named Sumati (Good-Minded). The son went to where Prajñācakra (Wondrous Wisdom) was and sat down to one side.

The Bhikṣu Wondrous Wisdom immediately preached the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas for him. Upon hearing this Dharma, the son of the elder was filled with joy; he then took a precious robe worth a billion pieces of gold as an offering and spoke these words: "Excellent!"
Dharma Master!
What you have spoken is subtle and wondrous.
We pray that you will deign to visit our home and preach such a Dharma, so that we may obtain great benefit!
The Dharma-teaching Master’s gift of the Dharma likewise yields great fruit.

From this day forward, for as long as I live, I shall provide offerings of robes, food and drink, medicinal decoctions, and all necessities of life; furthermore, I shall likewise provide offerings and support for the entire lifetime for the Dharma-teaching Master’s like-minded disciples and friends.
The bhikṣu Miaozhi may then say,
"Excellent! At that time,
the son of the elder prostrates with his head at [the bhikṣu’s] feet, circumambulates him to the right, and departs.
Thereafter, Subhūti went to his house and taught and benefited Danxi (Priyadarśana), as well as his parents and kinsmen below him, causing them all to resolve to seek unexcelled bodhi.

By virtue of this merit, this son of a householder has, throughout immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, never been separated from the Buddhas; he has always been able to hear the Dharma and encounter spiritual friends.
“Śāriputra! Do you think that Liyi was someone else?
Do not entertain such a view; he was none other than myself.”
At that time, the father of Liyi, the elder Mṛdura, was Kāśyapa Buddha. Śāriputra,
do you think that the parents of Liyi and the members of his household ever retreated from the unsurpassed path?
Do not form such a view. Why is this?

These people have all already attained certainty regarding unsurpassed bodhi; they now cultivate the pure life (brahmacarya) under me, and I shall bestow upon them the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment.
“Śāriputra! The bhikṣu Wondrous Wisdom attained parinirvāṇa within that very body.

Had this bhikṣu not entered nirvāṇa through the Hīnayāna, he would have attained the Buddha-way by virtue of the meritorious causes and conditions arising from preaching the Dharma for the sake of the single person Liyi alone; how much more so for preaching the Dharma for the sake of the elder Rūpaśānta and his retinue?”
“Śāriputra! If such a bhikṣu does not enter parinirvāṇa, no offering whatsoever found within all the worlds could repay his kindness.”
Why is this? Because I have heard the Dharma from Wondrous Wisdom, I have attained the great, pure, wondrous, and profound Buddha-dharma.
Therefore, you should know that if anyone can preach the Dharma for a bodhisattva, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them, they will certainly obtain immeasurable and boundless merit.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva generates the mind of awakening for the sake of initiating immeasurable acts of benefit. "Śāriputra!..."

For example, when the great ocean first begins to arise, one should know that it serves as the dwelling place for mani jewels of both measurable and immeasurable value, for all such jewels are born from the great ocean.

The bodhisattva’s production of the mind of enlightenment is likewise so: when it first gradually arises, one should know that it is the source from which all jewels of wisdom are born—the world and that which transcends the world, the contaminated and the uncontaminated, the conditioned and the unconditioned, whether defiled or pure—all such vessels of the Dharma.

“Śāriputra! It is like the great ocean: when it first begins to rise, you should know that it serves as a dwelling place for beings of large bodies, from which they grow, develop, and flourish in abundance.”

The bodhisattva’s generation of the mind is likewise so: when it first gradually arises, one should know that it immediately becomes the dwelling place for the bodies of immeasurable and incalculable great wisdom, the bodies of great roots of goodness, and the bodies of all sentient beings; all depend upon this mind and gradually attain growth.
“Śāriputra! For example, when the great ocean first begins to arise, you should know that it becomes the dwelling place for all the great nāga kings.
Those great nāga kings cannot be swallowed by the garuḍas, nor can they be disturbed by the winds fanned by the birds' twin wings.”

These dragon kings emerge from the great ocean, able to raise vast clouds that cover the eighty thousand continents, pouring down torrents of water so that there is nowhere it does not moisten and saturate. Śāriputra!

The bodhisattva’s generation of the mind is likewise: when it first gradually arises, one should know that it becomes the dwelling place for the great bodhisattva-nāgas at the time of attaining the Buddha-way.
Just as this great dragon king cannot be swallowed by the garuḍa,
so too a bodhisattva who dwells in the profound Buddha-dharma cannot be overcome by Māra or his followers.
This great dragon king is not troubled by the wind from the wings of the garuḍa; if it should wish to cause trouble, it is instantly extinguished.

So it is with the bodhisattva: neither Māra nor the followers of Māra can afflict or destroy them; any intent to cause affliction is immediately extinguished, and they are able to destroy the bonds of Māra, the activities of Māra, and the works of Māra.

Śāriputra! This Great Dragon King emerges from the great ocean and universally bestows the moisture of wisdom upon the four continents and the eighty thousand islands, causing all things to be thoroughly saturated. Thus, the grasses, trees, forests, the hundred grains, and medicinal plants all attain growth, and he also causes sentient beings with two feet and four feet to be free from thoughts of hunger and thirst.
Having caused this rain to fall, he returns to his original palace.

Great Bodhisattvas as dragons are also like this: emerging from the Buddha-dharma, they can rain down the great Dharma-rain upon the cities, towns, and villages of the trichiliocosm, and are able to sever the three kinds of craving—craving for sense-pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless—for immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! It is like the great ocean: when it is first about to be formed, all the flowing waters from the eighty thousand islands of the four continents, as well as the large and small rains, rivers, streams, and springs that flow into it, are all received by it without increasing or decreasing. Such is the nature of the ocean. All the various waters that enter it lose their original names and are collectively called ‘ocean water’; they lose their original tastes and become uniformly one salty taste.”

The bodhisattva’s generation of the mind is also like this: from the initial aspiration until the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they fulfill the Buddha-dharmas and are able to sever the doubts of sentient beings through wisdom; all great masters of treatises have already perfected their roots of merit and wisdom.

If they have not yet attained perfection, the Buddha, in order to sever their doubts, causes them all to lose their original titles and share a single designation: "disciples of the Buddha. Just as the waters of the great ocean are all of one salty taste, my disciples likewise all attain the single flavor of liberation through the departure from desire.
“Śāriputra! It is like the great ocean, which becomes progressively deeper.
If the waters of the great ocean were suddenly deep from the very beginning, those who seek its treasures would be unable to enter.
Because it gradually deepens until it reaches the peerless, it becomes a great ocean.
The minds of bodhisattvas are also like this: from the first moment they resolve their intent, they gradually deepen until they become peerless.
Śāriputra! That the mind of this bodhisattva gradually deepens refers to the dāna-pāramitā, śīla-pāramitā, kṣānti-pāramitā, vīrya-pāramitā, and dhyāna-pāramitā;
that which is profoundly deep is what is called the prajñā-pāramitā.
That which is incomparably profound is the Dharma of all Buddhas. Śāriputra,

if the Bodhisattva path were suddenly and immediately profound from the very beginning, such that one realized the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), then immeasurable sentient beings who seek the treasure of the Dharma would be unable to enter it.
“Śāriputra! For example, the reason the great ocean comes into being is entirely for the benefit of all worlds.
It is the same with the bodhisattva’s production of the thought of enlightenment: from the very beginning, it is always for the benefit of all worlds.”
Śāriputra! Just as the great ocean, when it first begins to arise, possesses the nature of an island of jewels;

so too is it with the bodhisattva’s production of the mind of awakening: from the very beginning, there gradually arises the nature of the jewel-islands of the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the four bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the path, as well as the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!
You are able to joyfully explain these various metaphors of the great ocean to clarify that the merit of a bodhisattva’s resolve is immeasurable and boundless.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The mind of a bodhisattva cannot be understood through the analogy of the great ocean. Why is this?
This mind is profoundly adorned by the arousal of great vows.
Even if a Tathāgata were to speak of the merit of this mind for an entire kalpa, or even beyond a kalpa, he could not exhaust it.

Why is this? Because when bodhisattvas give rise to such a mind, they are able to accomplish the great task; it is difficult to surpass and difficult to destroy, most supreme and most wondrous. It can provide all means of happiness for sentient beings, overturn the suffering of the triple world, and give birth to great wisdom—a light of great knowledge whose depths are unfathomable and which is free from all obstructions.
Śāriputra! To speak in brief, the great matters accomplished by the minds of all bodhisattvas are inexhaustible to describe. Śāriputra!
For example, when the trichiliocosm is first beginning to arise, one should know that it serves as a place of reliance for all sentient beings within it.
In this way, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one should know that it is for the sake of enabling immeasurable sentient beings to attain wisdom.
“Śāriputra! For example, when Sumeru, the king of mountains, first begins to rise, you should know that it immediately becomes a dwelling place for immeasurable devas.”
Because of this king of mountains, the various devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are able to defeat the hosts of asuras.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva first resolves to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, cultivates the path, and becomes a Buddha, they are able to serve as a place of reliance for immeasurable and incalculable disciples.
Just as the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, by means of Mount Sumeru, are able to destroy the hosts of asuras;
so too do sentient beings, by means of the Tathāgata, are able to destroy the hosts of Māra.

“Śāriputra! For example, when the king of mountains, Cakravāḍa, first begins to rise, you should know that for the sentient beings therein, it acts as a barrier against the eight *caṭaka-bhara* winds, so that they cannot cause destruction.”

In this same way, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment, it gradually ascends, becoming firm and difficult to obstruct; one should know that such a person is able to act as a protector for all sentient beings who draw near to them, warding off the winds of Māra so that they cannot cause affliction or destruction.
“Śāriputra! Just as when the King of Snowy Mountains first begins to rise, you should know that it becomes the place where all medicinal herbs, grasses, and trees depend for their growth.”

In this same way, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva is first born, he immediately practices the medicinal herbs of all dharmas for the sake of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings, in order to destroy the diseases of their afflictions. "Śāriputra!..."

For example, when the nature of a jewel first arises, one should know that it immediately becomes a source of benefit for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings.

In the same way, when a bodhisattva first gives rise to the jewel-nature of great wisdom, one should know that it immediately becomes a source of benefit for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) sentient beings.

“Śāriputra! For example, when the palace of the Sun Deva-son is first about to be completed, you should know that it is already capable of illuminating and heating the four continents and the eighty thousand islands of the world-system.”

In this way, as the Bodhisattva gradually grows from his initial arising until he reaches the state of Buddhahood, one should know that he acts as a great Dharma-light for the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm, and is also able to dry up the mire of all afflictions such as craving, hatred, and delusion.

“Śāriputra! For example, when Lake Anavatapta first begins to arise, you should know that it serves as the dwelling place for the dragon Anavatapta. From the shores of this lake flow four great rivers, all of which bring benefit to two-legged and four-legged sentient beings by eliminating their thirst and producing various precious metals and jewels, before gradually entering the great ocean.”

When this Mahāyāna Dharma first begins to arise, it is likewise so: by means of this vehicle, all bodhisattvas are able to study the Buddha-dharma; having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they are then able to flow forth the four great rivers of Dharma—namely, the unimpededness of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpededness of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), the unimpededness of eloquence (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and the unimpededness of speech (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)—as well as the flavors of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the path (*mārga*). When immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings hear these various sounds, they sever the thirst of afflictions and are enabled to realize the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) from which they are forever separated.

In this way, Śāriputra, when the minds of bodhisattvas first gradually arise, they are able to accomplish great matters— matters that are difficult to conquer, difficult to destroy, and peerless— and they also bring great benefit to immeasurable sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
“Śāriputra! Although the Tathāgata has spoken thus, he cannot exhaustively describe it.

Therefore, you should know that if there is someone who can preach the Dharma for a bodhisattva, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them, the merit obtained will be immeasurable, boundless, and beyond calculation.”
Śāriputra! With my Buddha-eye, I observe this karmic reward and see no limit to it; whichever vehicle one turns toward, one will be able to attain it.
Just as when a person plants roots of goodness by making offerings to a Buddha, they shall never be exhausted until the attainment of nirvāṇa.
“Śāriputra! In the distant past, there was a bodhisattva named Dharmarata who was born and raised in a royal family; whatever virtuous words he heard, he would transcribe, read, and recite them all.”
At that time, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, this prince traveled through various kingdoms and towns.
Then there was a man living beside a deep pit who spoke these words to one who delighted in the Dharma: "O Prince!"
"Come here, and I shall give you the verses spoken by the Buddha.
Then this bodhisattva climbed up onto the bank of the pit and called out to the man, saying: "Ho! Good son!"
"You should give me the verse spoken by the Buddha.
That person replied, "I shall not give it to you for nothing."

The Bodhisattva Delight-in-Dharma was clad in precious robes; these robes were worth twenty billion pieces of gold, and he wore a necklace of maṇi jewels as an ornament for his neck, each pearl of which was worth four billion pieces of gold.
Upon seeing this, the man conceived a greedy attachment and thought to himself:
"If this prince gives me precious robes and mani-jewel necklaces, only then will I give him the verse spoken by the Buddha."
At that time, the prince said to the man:
"Whatever you require, I shall give it to you;
you must give me the verse spoken by the Buddha."
The man’s greedy mind grew and flared up, and he said to the Bodhisattva:

"If you can give me the precious robe I am wearing and the pearl necklace, and having heard the Buddha's verse, throw yourself into this deep pit—if you can do such a thing, you must first make a vow, and then I shall recite one verse of the Buddha for you."
The prince replied, "Alas,
O benevolent one! What benefit do you seek in wishing to cast me into this deep pit?"
The man replied: "I have obtained nothing.

I only fear that now you will abandon these precious robes and pearl necklaces; having heard the verse, you may give rise to regret and, relying on your powerful influence, come back to seize them from me."
The prince replied, "Simply speak it, and I shall never regret it.
That person then said:
"If you are unwilling to take this oath, you should know that your heart has already repented.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"You need only speak it; I shall grant you the precious robe and the pearl necklace as you wish, and I shall likewise cast myself into the deep pit."
Upon hearing this vow, the man recited a single verse of the Buddha for the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately gave him a precious robe and a mani-jewel necklace, and further made this vow:

"If my heart is sincere, and I joyfully give away these precious robes and mani-jewels without regret, by this word of truth, may I now fall from this height and land safely and steadily, without any injury."
Having made this vow, he threw himself down.
Before he had even reached the ground, the Four Heavenly Kings came and gently caught him, placing him upon the earth. Setting him upright, they said:
"O man, how extraordinary! How rare!"
"The verses spoken by the Buddha are profound and subtle, and of great benefit.
Thereupon, the man descended from his high position, went to where the Bodhisattva was, and spoke these words: "O Prince!"
"It is rare!
You are capable of performing a difficult task; what dharma do you seek?
The Bodhisattva replied:
"By means of this Dharma, I shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Once I have realized the Way of the Buddha, I shall deliver those not yet delivered, liberate those not yet liberated, cause those not yet extinguished to be extinguished, and bring peace to those not yet at peace."
"Śāriputra! Having heard this, that person immediately gives rise to faith and says to the bodhisattva:
'Go back and take the precious robe and the various necklaces.'"
"Why is this? That you wear these precious robes and drape yourself with this necklace of pearls is truly most fitting.
The Bodhisattva replied:
"This is impossible!
It is like a person who has vomited; how could they possibly eat it again? This person replied:
"If you do not take it back, I pray that you accept my repentance.
When I later become a Buddha, may you be saved by me. "Śāriputra! [The Buddha said.]

Do you think that the Prince Rata at that time—who, for the sake of a single verse, stripped off his precious robes and mani-jewels to give them to that person, and furthermore cast his own body into a deep pit—was anyone else? It was none other than me.
"Do not conceive such a view;
it was I myself who was that person at that time. He spoke a verse for me, and later, having gained faith in me, he said these words:
'When you attain Buddhahood, you shall deliver me.'"
"Could this have been anyone else?
Do not hold such a view; it was none other than the bhikṣu Hāgali here now. Śāriputra!"
Once, while I was with a group of bhikṣus in a deep ravine, we were walking in meditation through the air.
At that time, Upāli was on a high bank; I called out to him, saying:
"Come, cast yourself down!"
"Because he trusted the Buddha’s words, he threw himself down without sustaining any injury and attained the six supernormal powers. Śāriputra!
Observe the power of these roots of goodness: because this person recited a single verse for me and, trusting my words, took refuge with his own body, he has now attained liberation."

Śāriputra! If such a person, taking greed as their basis, plants various roots of goodness and yet attains the exhaustion of outflows, how much more so for one who, having faith in and accepting my words, thoroughly understands the Buddha’s wisdom and explains even a single four-line verse of the Bodhisattva Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening others—I see no end to this merit, except upon entering Nirvāṇa.
26. Chapter on Destruction (VII). Chapter Twenty-Six: On Destruction. Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If someone were to explain a single four-line verse to a bodhisattva, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, thereby assisting them in attaining the Buddha-way, they would obtain such merit.”
Furthermore, if there should be someone who, wishing to destroy the bodhicitta, creates obstacles for it, how much sin would that person incur?
For what reason?
"Those who have already corrupted and disturbed [the mind], or those who will do so in the future, shall, upon hearing of these transgressions, immediately repent and reform themselves.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a person creates an obstacle and destroys the bodhisattva-mind, they incur boundless sin."
Just as a person who wishes to destroy a priceless jewel would lose immeasurable wealth and profit,
so too, Śāriputra, if a person disrupts or corrupts the mind of a bodhisattva, they destroy immeasurable Dharma-jewels.

“Śāriputra! It is like planting a medicinal tree; if someone cuts it down and prevents it from growing, that person destroys the means by which immeasurable sentient beings are treated for their illnesses, causing many sentient beings to be tormented by disease.”

In this way, Śāriputra, if anyone wishes to destroy this bodhisattva’s mind, this mind of great peace and happiness, this mind of great wisdom-medicine that extinguishes the suffering and afflictions of immeasurable sentient beings, you should know that such a person causes immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings to be afflicted by the diseases of all the defilements— greed, anger, delusion, pride, stinginess, envy, crookedness, lack of shame, and lack of remorse— and furthermore causes immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings to lose their dwelling place of the peace and happiness of nirvāṇa.

“Śāriputra! If a person destroys Lake Anavatapta and kills the Great Dragon King, you should know that such a person has ruined and lost the water of eight virtues for thirsty beings—both those with two legs and those with four.”
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
If anyone disrupts the mind of a bodhisattva, they destroy the water of the Eightfold Noble Path that can eliminate the thirst and craving of immeasurable sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! Suppose there were a person who destroyed the sun palace; that person would thereby extinguish the light for the sentient beings of the four continents.
In the same way, Śāriputra!”

If anyone should corrupt or disturb the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva, one should know that such a person destroys the great light of the Dharma for all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Śāriputra! Just as a person who destroys all precious natures should be known to destroy the treasures of immeasurable sentient beings, so it is, Śāriputra!

If a person should corrupt or disturb the mind of a bodhisattva, one should know that such a person destroys their share of the countless, incalculable treasures of the Dharma, and likewise brings about the destruction of such sutras so that they may not be heard or seen.
Śāriputra! Just as immeasurable jewels emerge from a jewel-mine to provide for and satisfy sentient beings, so it is, Śāriputra!
The minds of all bodhisattvas are the nature of the Dharma-jewel; from this Dharma-jewel arise the inconceivable supernormal powers and the power of wisdom of all buddhas. Therefore, Śāriputra!
"You should know that one who destroys the bodhicitta incurs immeasurable and boundless deep transgressions.

Śāriputra, it is as if a person with an evil mind sheds the blood of a Buddha; likewise, if another person breaks the precepts, lacks faith, destroys, or abandons this bodhicitta, their transgression is exactly equal."
Śāriputra! Setting aside the case of one with an evil mind who sheds the blood of a Buddha— which I say constitutes the full five ānantarya crimes—
if there is a person who destroys the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva, their transgression exceeds even this.

Why is this? Even the commission of the five crimes of immediate retribution cannot destroy the Dharma of a single Buddha; yet if a person destroys the bodhicitta, they sever and extinguish all the Buddhas' Dharmas.
Śāriputra! It is just as when a cow is slaughtered, its milk, curd, and ghee are already destroyed.
In the same way, Śāriputra!
If a person destroys the bodhicitta, they sever the wisdom of all Buddhas. Therefore, Śāriputra,
you should know that if a person violates the precepts, lacks faith, reviles, or slanders and destroys the bodhicitta, this transgression exceeds that of the five deeds of immediate retribution.
Śāriputra! Setting aside these crimes of immediate retribution,
suppose the four continents were filled with arhats, and a single person were to take the lives of them all.
"What do you think?
Would this person’s transgression be considered great? Śāriputra replied:
“Very many, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

"I now tell you: if someone reviles, slanders, or disrupts a bodhisattva, causing them to believe and accept such things so that they abandon this mind and lose the wisdom of a Buddha, the former offender's transgression does not approach even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part of this one; it cannot even be compared by way of analogy."

Why is this? Although one might take the lives of so many arhats, one cannot obstruct the ten powers of the Buddhas, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness and great compassion, or the non-empty conduct of a Buddha. One cannot obstruct the Tathāgata’s elephant-king-like backward glance, his lion’s majestic stride, or his invisible crown protuberance. One cannot obstruct the Tathāgata’s blowing of the conch shell of the hundred-thousandfold complete Dharma, nor can one hinder the turning of the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma. One cannot obstruct the sovereign spiritual power of the Holy Lord, nor can one obstruct his ability to know the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of sentient beings, their various inclinations and pleasures, and their diverse wisdoms.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva resolves upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and achieves the adornment of firm vows for the Great Vehicle,

and if someone should come to disrupt and confuse this mind, causing them to regress and abandon it, that person obstructs the Buddha’s ten powers, up to and including his knowledge of the various inclinations of sentient beings.
“Śāriputra! Setting aside the four continents,
suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with arhats, as dense as a forest of bamboo, reeds, rice, or hemp, and a single person were to take the lives of them all.
"What do you think?
Would this person’s transgression not be very great?
"It would be very great."
“World-Honored One!
[The Buddha replied: “Śāriputra!

If there should be another person who harbors anger, treats [the bodhisattva] with contempt, violates the precepts, or lacks faith, thereby destroying and distracting this bodhisattva’s mind—the transgression committed by such a person can only be known by the Buddha.”
Why is this? Because such a person corrupts and disrupts the profound resolve of a bodhisattva, thereby destroying all Buddha-dharma and severing the lineage of the Buddhas. Why is this?
If there were no bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], how could such Buddha-wisdom and the sovereign power of a Buddha ever appear in the world? Therefore, Śāriputra!

This unsurpassed mind, the great mind, the profound mind, and the mind of all bodhisattvas—whether it resides in bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans—all worlds should pay homage and respect to it.
Why is this? One who possesses such a mind should be known as the World-Honored One of the future. "Śāriputra!..."
What do you think?

When the Tathāgata praises this bodhisattva mind, does he therein differentiate or set limits for the names of sentient beings—such as those from the Kṣatriya class, the Brāhmaṇa class, great householders, wheel-turning kings, the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devendra, or the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, or the Brahmā heavens, or the Great Brahmā King?
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
“World-Honored One, you have spoken only of such a pure mind, a great mind, and a profound mind. “What do you think?
In this praise of the mind that I have given, have I mentioned at all whether it belongs to a great strongman such as Nārāyaṇa, or to one who is young or old, wealthy or poor, noble or lowly?”
"No, World-Honored One. "Śāriputra!"

Wherever you see this mind—whether in one who is young or old, wealthy or poor, noble or lowly, powerful or powerless—you all should respect and keep them in mind, protect them, and assist them in their accomplishment. This is the unsurpassed repayment of gratitude for a śrāvaka, for it enables them to transform bodhisattvas through the gift of the Dharma.

Śāriputra! If a śrāvaka can act in this way, they will be fully accomplishing the offering to the Tathāgata; that is to say, they are able to provide instruction and guidance so that all bodhisattvas do not regress from their aspiration for unsurpassed bodhicitta.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A bodhisattva possesses three kinds of mind:”
First, the initial arousal of the mind;
second, the transformation of the mind;
third, the fulfillment of the mind.
"Among these three types of mind, which one does the World-Honored One praise and protect?
The Buddha said, "It is so, it is so!"
As you have said, a bodhisattva has three kinds of mind:
the initial mind, the transformative mind, and the perfected mind. Śāriputra!
In this regard, the Tathāgata praises, protects, and guides those who have first resolved their minds or have turned their minds, causing them to achieve success. Why is this?
If there should be anyone who gives rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, [the Tathāgata] ensures they do not fall back or descend into the stages of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Because they do not fall [into the two extremes], they shall gradually attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva gives rise to the bodhicitta, they should contemplate this mind as having the characteristic of emptiness.
“Śāriputra! What is this mind? What is the characteristic of emptiness?”
Śāriputra! What is called "mind" is the mental consciousness; it is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), and the element of mind (manodhātu).
As for the empty characteristic of the mind: the mind has no characteristic of mind, nor does it have an agent.
Why is this? If there were an agent, then that agent would perform the action while this person would experience the result.
If the mind itself acts, then it would be the self-acting that experiences the result for itself.
“Śāriputra! This characteristic of mind is empty; there is no agent, nor is there anyone who causes an agent to act.
If there is no agent, then there is no characteristic of action.”
If a person engages in frivolous conceptualization regarding the characteristics of this mind, they are contending with the unimpeded, the empty, and the signless;
if they contend with the unimpeded, the empty, and the signless, such a person is contending with the Tathāgata;
one should know that by contending with the Tathāgata, such a person will fall into a deep pit.

Those deep pits refer to hell, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the realm of animals, as well as all views of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the view of a self, the view of a person, and the view of a sentient being.
Śāriputra! To speak briefly:
views of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, and views of nirvāṇa—all such as these are called "views of attainment.
These various views are the source of the evil realms; because sentient beings are greedily attached to these views, they fall into deep pits themselves and also cause others to fall into deep pits.
"That deep pit refers to the cycle of birth and death within the five realms of existence.
At that time, there was a beggar in the assembly named Vyavahāra who rose from his seat, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I do not wish to fall into this deep pit, nor do I wish to contend with the Tathāgata."
Since ancient times, I have harbored such a thought, desiring to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, yet I have further given rise to this reflection:

"I am a poor man with many sufferings and afflictions; my livelihood is difficult to sustain. Even these kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, and wealthy householders cannot practice for unsurpassed bodhi, let alone me, a beggar who is the most wretched and lowly!"

Now, having heard from the Buddha this praise of such a bodhisattva’s initial resolve, it is not mentioned here whether one belongs to a great kṣatriya clan, a brahmin family, or a wealthy householder family; nor is mention made of the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven; nor is mention made of the Brahma world or the Brahmā King; furthermore, there is no mention of being poor, rich, noble, or lowly.
"From this day forward, I shall firmly resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and shall not disparage myself.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
“Cintā! You are now indeed able to follow and learn from the Tathāgata, having resolutely given rise to this mind for the unsurpassed path.
At that time, Cintā spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“I do not seek praise; for praise is not the supreme excellence.
What I seek is the most excellent intention: namely, the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddha.
Among all worlds, the Buddha is likewise unsurpassed.”
For sentient beings afflicted by suffering, you are able to act as their refuge.
The Buddha has realized the untainted Dharma— subtle, wondrous, pure, and immeasurable—
and out of compassion for sentient beings, he has taught it to deliver them from the calamities of birth and death.
The Buddha’s spiritual power is unimpeded, and his radiance is likewise boundless;
having attained wisdom that reaches the shoreless, his merit is most sublime and honored.
O World-Honored One, my original aspiration was also to attain Buddhahood.
The mind again gives rise to despondency: "Who would give to one so poor and lowly?
Even kings, householders, Śakra, Brahmā, and other honored deities—the great beings among gods and humans—could not obtain it even from them."
How much more so for one as poor and lowly as I, who sustains my life by begging;
how could the Buddha’s wisdom, which is unsurpassed in the world, ever be attained?
The World-Honored One, knowing my mind, addressed Śāriputra, saying:
I say that this generating of the mind has no distinction of poor or wealthy,
noble or lowly; nor do I speak of Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, or householders,
nor of devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits— it speaks only of generating a pure mind.
Now that I have heard what the Buddha has taught, my mind has attained great strength;
I shall certainly attain Buddhahood, for I am able to give rise to this profound resolve.
Heaven and earth may change their positions, and Mount Sumeru may be ground into dust, yet my vow shall remain unshaken.
Even space may be changed, but my mind cannot be turned.
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to become demons and all came together to harass and disturb me, my mind would certainly not waver.
If someone were to speak these words before me:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is extremely difficult to attain; who would give it to one so poor and lowly?
having heard this, I would answer:
"You are one who is poor and lowly; you lack the wealth of faith. I shall become a Buddha.
The Buddhas have no inherent nature, nor do they have a fixed lineage;
yet by single-mindedly dedicating oneself toward the unsurpassed Mahāyāna,"
This is the nature of all Buddhas, And it is also the seed of the Tathāgatas.
Seeking the Buddha-way with a single mind, One attains Buddhahood through making offerings.
I do not begrudge my body or life, Nor do I crave worldly pleasures.
My sole resolve is the unsurpassed path, to deliver all sentient beings.
Now, before the Dharma King, I speak words of truth without fear;
should there be any error or mistake, may the Buddha out of compassion explain it.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
“You have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind, Riding upon the Unsurpassed Vehicle.
In this there is no error; You shall become a Buddha, a King of Dharma.”
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching, Citta attained immeasurable joy;
because his mind was so pure, he soared seven *tāla* trees high.
At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his mouth issued light of five colors.
It illuminated heaven and earth everywhere, then returned and entered through the crown of his head.
Ānanda immediately joined his palms and questioned the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings:
"O Hero of the World, whose wisdom is unimpeded, what is the cause of this?"
In this city of Rājagṛha, the most lowly of beggars,
dwelling now in mid-air, joins his palms in reverent salutation to the Buddha.
Now all the devas, nāga kings, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans—
All with single-minded devotion joined their palms and paid homage to this beggar.
I now ask the World-Honored One: for what reason do you smile and emit light?
Who is it that exclusively practices the Buddha-way, such that you wish to bestow upon them a prediction of enlightenment?
Who shall abide in the Buddha-way and resolve upon the unsurpassed mind?
Who shall realize the most supreme wisdom and deliver all beings from old age, sickness, and death?
Who shall sit at the site of enlightenment and destroy the armies of the Mara King?
Attaining the unsurpassed path of the Buddha, Turning the most wondrous wheel of Dharma?
Who shall obtain great wisdom, Reach immeasurable supernormal powers, And,
attaining universal knowledge without obstruction, Discern the faculties of all sentient beings?
Who shall obtain the Brahma-voice, whose speech is entirely extraordinary,
who, because of unimpeded true wisdom, teaches without deviation?
Who has realized the unsurpassed path and constantly dwells in subtle and wondrous concentration?
Having fully realized the mind of the three realms, you preach the Dharma out of compassion.
When you preach the Dharma, gods and humans alike rejoice;
they shall attain the practice that is not in vain—the Dharma of the elephant king’s backward glance.
Who is the guide for the great assembly, who purifies the Buddha-worlds and leaves behind all hardships, widely opening the path to nirvana?
To the World-Honored One of great divine virtue, I shall now ask about this matter.
"For what reason do you smile?
We pray that you will speak so as to bring joy to the assembly.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"It is because of this mendicant’s discernment that the Tathāgata smiles and emits great radiance.
At that moment, eighty billion nayutas of beings in the assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled bodhi."
"For these individuals, I have bestowed the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"When the Tathāgata spoke of these causes and conditions, Eighty billion nayutas were filled."
All sentient beings have resolved upon the unsurpassed mind; all of these shall attain the path of Buddhahood.

Now, this person of profound wisdom has been selected; with joy, palms joined, standing in mid-air, he reverently praises and makes offerings to me, vowing that he himself shall attain awakening just like the Buddha of today.
By virtue of the causes and conditions of this person’s merit, they shall never fall into the various evil realms;
in birth after birth, they will always remain free from the eight difficult states, and in life after life, they will constantly behold all Buddhas.
Having already encountered all the Buddhas, for the sake of attaining unsurpassed bodhi,
they offer these requisites— precious canopies, banners, pennants, flowers, and incense— to worship the Buddhas.
When the Buddhas of successive generations practiced the Way, they offered to the Buddha these requisites:
exquisite garments and various delicacies, as well as beds, couches, bedding, and medicinal decoctions.
Gradually and in succession, he shall meet Maitreya; seeking the state of Buddhahood, he will deepen his reverence by making offerings of seventy billion nayutas of mani-jewels.
The radiance of each and every mani-jewel Can illuminate within an area of eighty yojanas.
By gathering the power of the light from this multitude of jewels, They are able to universally illuminate all worlds.
Furthermore, they erected stūpas and shrines made of the seven treasures, numbering seventy billion nayutas;
each stūpa was ten li in length and breadth, adorned with various exquisite jewels.
Robes, couches, and bedding, as well as seventy billion nayutas of them—
with such various articles of adornment, he offered them to Maitreya Buddha and the assembly of monks.
Providing offerings for three months during the rains retreat, and continuing thus without weariness for a hundred years,
such a person may then go forth as a renunciant and cultivate the holy life within the Dharma of Maitreya.
With such a heart of love, joy, and reverence, He made profound offerings to Maitreya Buddha;
Gradually practicing the bodhisattva path, He beheld all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
From this, they further behold various Buddhas, Their number exceeding that of the sands of the Ganges;
Having seen them, their minds attain profound goodness and purity, And they all provide offerings while cultivating the Buddha-way.
The retribution for the merit of this person’s pure mind—I cannot fully describe it even now in brief;
its fruit is immeasurable and beyond comparison. Having heard this, who would not seek Buddhahood?
This person, coming and going within birth and death, shall seek the Buddha-way for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
in the end, they shall realize unsurpassed wisdom and attain Buddhahood under the name Jishianshi (Accumulated Solidity).

The lifespan shall be calculated as one thousand kalpas; at that time, the Buddha-world will be exceedingly pure, and the land of Jambudvīpa will also be adorned like the Trāyastriṃśa palace atop Mount Sumeru.
The World-Honored One, the Solid Accumulation, was surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas numbering more than a billion nayutas, as many as the sands of the Ganges.
Within each of these great assemblies, there were people as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
All have attained arhatship, possessing the power of sovereign supernormal faculties.
They have thoroughly mastered the Tripitaka and are clearly proficient in all questions and answers;
like my Śāriputra, they are foremost among those of wisdom.
There is a great assembly of bodhisattvas, their number twice as many as the former;
that Buddha’s great bodhisattvas are also named Ajita.
Those hosts of bodhisattvas have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
They turn back to be born in various lands, attaining Buddhahood in each place.
Within every one of these great assemblies, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges receive from those Buddhas the prediction that they shall attain the Unsurpassed Way.
After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma shall remain for a full kalpa,
and his relics shall be widely disseminated, just as they will be after my own passing.
Gathering these solid relics, they shall be venerated by devas and humans alike.
According to the inclinations of sentient beings, they manifest various supernormal powers.
These stūpas and shrines for the śarīra relics are all fashioned from the seven precious gems,
with railings and jeweled pillars, and adorned with incense, flowers, and many banners and canopies.
With these exquisite jewels as adornments, they shall embellish the stupas of the Tathāgata;
by means of these various shrines, they shall purify Jambudvīpa.
If a person holds various flowers and makes offerings at the Buddha’s stupa,
It immediately transforms into a floral canopy; such is his supernormal power.
The World-Honored One, the Solid and Firm, appears in images within all stupas;
according to the inclinations of sentient beings, he smiles and manifests radiance.
When the great light has shone everywhere, it returns to its original place;
if it enters the mark of the crown protuberance, one knows for oneself that one has received the Buddha’s prediction;
if the light enters through the mouth, one knows that one will receive the prediction for the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddha.
If the light enters through the navel, one knows for oneself that one will receive the state of a śrāvaka.
That image of the World-Honored One possesses such supernormal powers that it shall remain thus for the duration of one kalpa, and only at the end of the kalpa shall it perish.
"Conditioned phenomena are impermanent; therefore, one should diligently practice progress.
At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare!"
World-Honored One!
Although this beggar is so lowly and base, his mind has already attained the most sublime and noble Dharma; what wise person would treat him with contempt?
The Buddha told Śāriputra: “So it is, so it is!
Just as you have said, what wise person would ever hold such a person in contempt?”
Except for ordinary worldlings who lack learning and wisdom.
Śāriputra, for this reason, I have said in my sūtras:
A wise person should not underestimate others; to underestimate others is to wound oneself.
Śāriputra, do you think that this beggar Citta has ever been honored and saluted by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans?
"No, World-Honored One! Why is this? Because..."
When this poor and lowly person had not yet received a prediction from the Tathāgata, no one paid him homage or respect.
Now that he has received a prediction from the World-Honored One, all devas, humans, and asuras pay him homage and respect.
“Śāriputra! This is the unimpeded knowledge and vision of all Buddhas in future ages, which is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Therefore, Śāriputra!”

My disciples, having faith and accepting the Buddha’s words, when they expound the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, should first extol the divine virtues of the Buddha. Upon hearing this, sentient beings may be inspired to resolve to seek the wisdom of a Buddha;
because they have resolved their minds, the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.
“Śāriputra! In all worlds, there are few sentient beings who seek benefit for others; to benefit oneself and to benefit others is the most difficult of all. Śāriputra!”
Setting aside for a moment the pursuit of benefit for others,
those among sentient beings who are even able to benefit themselves are rare. Why is this?
Now, ordinary persons, desiring to seek their own benefit, instead bring harm upon themselves.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!
I do not see anyone who, while harming others, does not themselves suffer decline and affliction.
Therefore, you should know that it is difficult to abide in the cause of one's own benefit.
Furthermore, within this context, benefiting oneself and benefiting others is the most difficult of all.

Therefore, Śāriputra, if a person disparages those who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna, you should know that such a person cannot benefit themselves, nor can they benefit others; this individual is not called a practitioner of the Path.
“Śāriputra! These deluded people walk upon the path of error; they lose their own benefit and also lose the benefit of others.
For this reason, such persons shall encounter the eight conditions of decline and affliction.”
What are the eight? They are:
the loss of beloved and esteemed friends, relatives, and family;
and the decline and turmoil of one's kingdom.
Wealth is consumed daily;
it is burned by calamitous fires;
and it is encroached upon by local officials.
The faculties are impaired;
one dies and enters hell;
and the wardens of hell subject one to torture—these are called the eight.
"Furthermore, there are eight great states of insecurity.
What are these eight? They are:
being born in hell, among the hungry ghosts, or as an animal—these are the great states of insecurity;..."

If one obtains a human body, yet is always born in a frontier region where one does not recognize good or evil, and where there is no Buddha, no Dharma, and no Sangha—this is a state of great insecurity.
Even if one obtains a human body and is born in a central land, to be deaf, blind, mute, crippled, or afflicted by a hundred diseases is likewise called a state of great insecurity.

Although one is born in a central land and possesses a complete human form, to be constantly subject to decay and ruin, harboring a mind of flattery, crookedness, hypocrisy, and guile—this too is called a state of great insecurity.

To receive the teachings of external paths, to delight in heterodox arguments, heterodox views, and evil conduct, and thereby to accomplish impure karma of body, speech, and mind—such that even the Buddhas and noble sages cannot save one—this is also called a state of great unrest.

Furthermore, if one is born in a central land and possesses a complete human form, yet dies immediately on the very night the Buddha attains enlightenment, thus failing to encounter the Buddha-dharma, this too is called a state of great unrest.
This constitutes the eight conditions of unrest for one who disparages those seeking the Buddha-way.

"Śāriputra, you should know that if such a person is born in hell, they will certainly fall into the Great Avīci Hell; there they will obtain a massive body, undergo manifold sufferings, and continue to commit grave offenses."

If they fall among the animals, they become evil insects or beasts, constantly suffering from hunger and thirst; they prey upon the lives of others and sustain themselves by devouring flesh and muscle, further increasing their karmic offenses wherever they are born.

If they are born in the water as *makara* fish, they are caught by nets and hooks set by people such as the Citra, Śiśumāra, and Udraka, being sliced alive and enduring manifold afflictions, unable to seek death even when they wish for it.
If they are born on land, they may become camels, donkeys, oxen, sheep, pigs, or dogs.

If one is made into a camel or an ox and has one's nose pierced for a person, one’s body must constantly carry heavy loads while being subjected to the pain of whips; one groans and cries out loudly with no one to provide relief;
exhausted on the road, one cannot move forward;
and before life has even come to an end, one is slaughtered and flayed alive, with one’s flesh torn away and eaten, all while being reviled with insults.
"Eating too much and being fond of sleep have caused me great loss.
"Śāriputra! Observe these causes and conditions of sinful karma; were I to explain them in detail as I know them, they could not be exhausted even in the course of kalpa after kalpa."
Śāriputra! To speak in brief, if a person were to destroy the bodhicitta, it would be impossible for them to be free from the eight difficulties. Why is this?
Because these people continue to give rise to various sinful karmas, you should know that you have escaped this calamity and achieved your own salvation.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-puṣpamūla-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
The *Buddhabhāṣita-puṣpamūla-sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Twenty-Seven: Miscellaneous Matters (8). Chapter Twenty-Seven: Miscellaneous Matters.
The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“There are four methods of rescue. What are the four?
The Tathāgata can rescue sentient beings who are terrified;”
Those who have entered wrong paths can be saved by the Noble Path;
those with various evil karmas can be saved by the Foundations of Mindfulness;
and those in the eight difficult conditions can be saved by Bodhisattvas.
These are called the four.
"Śāriputra, there are four dharmas of peace.
What are the four? To be born and encounter a Buddha is called the Great Peace;
to obtain a place free from hardships is called the Great Peace.
Being able to have faith in the Buddha-dharma is called great peace;
being endowed with noble right view is called great peace; these are the four.
"Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are four dharmas that can accomplish one's undertakings. What are these four?
The harmony of the four great elements brings peace to the body;
right view gives rise to a straightforward and pure mind;
and seeing the Buddha and attaining faith serves as the cause for all forms of happiness.
"Generating the unsurpassed mind can extinguish the diseases of affliction of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings;
these are the four dharmas that can accomplish the task.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
There are four aspirations in the world. What are these four?
Those who are ill and emaciated aspire to live;
Those oppressed by hunger and thirst wish to obtain food and drink;
those tormented by suffering and affliction wish to obtain happiness;
and those traveling on perilous paths wish to attain peace and security.
These are the four vows.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are four places of attachment in the world; because of such attachment, one shall fall into the evil realms.
What are the four? First, craving for the body;
second, craving for life.
Third, the pursuit of wealth;
fourth, indulgence in sensual desire—
these are called the four.
“Śāriputra, there are seven storehouses:
namely, the wind-storehouse, the raw-storehouse, the cooked-storehouse, the cold-storehouse, the heat-storehouse, the view-storehouse, and the desire-storehouse.”
Śāriputra! Among all these treasuries, the treasury of desire is the most secure.
Upon what does this treasury of desire rely?
"It relies upon tears and saliva, phlegm and snot, pus and blood, tendons, bones, skin, flesh, heart, liver, the five viscera, intestines, stomach, excrement, and urine.
At that time, there was a lay follower in the assembly named Vyavahāra.
The householder had a wife named Māyāvarṇā, whose countenance was dignified and whose features were exceptionally striking.
The householder Citta conceived a deep attachment to her, and his afflictions burned intensely.
Having heard what the Buddha had said, he immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do not speak thus:”
The mind of lust arises from excrement and urine.
Why is this? My wife is beautiful and upright, free from all foul odors and impurities.

The Buddha, knowing that the householder’s defilement of greed was deep-seated, immediately manifested the form of a woman—exquisite, pure, and beautiful as if she were of wondrous complexion—who entered the midst of the assembly with composed features and a slow, graceful gait.
Having seen this, the householder immediately thought to himself:
"For what reason has my wife entered this assembly?
Having had this thought, he asked her:
"For what reason have you come here? He replied,
"I wish to hear the World-Honored One preach the Dharma."
The householder immediately pulled her toward him and sat upon her garment.

By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha caused this woman to defile his garment with excrement, making the householder unable to endure the stench; he covered his nose with his hand and looked around left and right, wondering, "Who has done this?"
At that time, Upananda was seated on the right side;
he spoke to the householder, saying, "For what reason do you cover your nose while looking at me? He replied:
"This place is extremely foul and filthy!
By the Buddha's spiritual power, he caused Upananda and the entire assembly to see this woman as she discarded excrement and filth, which soiled the layman’s robes.
Then, Bhaddāli said to the householder, "Behold your wife; her conduct is foul and loathsome.
The householder replied:
"I have no doubts. My wife is pure and her body is free from all impurities.
If anyone has any suspicion, they should observe for themselves."
He said to Baddhālitta, "In my opinion,
you are the one who has committed this defilement.
At that moment, Baddhālitta became greatly incensed and rose from his seat, saying to the householder:
"You have no sense of shame or modesty!
Who gave you the name 'Householder'?
You should now be called the 'Excrement Householder'!"
"Why do you not take your wife by the hand yourself and sit upon her garment?
When your wife sits there, this very excrement and filth is present; yet you sit upon it yourself, smeared with dung and feeling no shame, while instead wishing to slander others."
The assembly proclaimed:
"This 'Excrement' householder should be expelled from the assembly. They then said to him:
"A person who is impure and base should not remain among the assembly.
He then took him by the hand and led him out of the gathering.
Purifying his own mind of delusion, he said to his wife:
“I have had you sit upon my robe out of respect for you; since you are a great man, this is how it ought to be,” she said.
His wife then replied, “Since you are close to a bag of excrement, it is only natural that you should act thus.”

At that time, the householder felt a sense of revulsion; wishing to remove the excrement from his clothes lest it further defile his body, he said to Baddhananda, "By what means may I rid myself of this filth?"
Bhadanta said: "It is not merely this excrement that defiles your body; there are further misfortunes that shall be your lot.
If you wish to escape them, you must flee far away, for your wife's excrement has caused this great assembly to suffer from headaches and confusion!"
The householder replied, “All the Śākyaputrīyas are full of compassion; how can you be so foul-mouthed? Upananda said:
"How can you possibly show such compassion?
How dare you oppose the words of the Buddha by speaking in this manner!"
"My wife is dignified and beautiful, and has no foul-smelling parts.
Now, having examined yourself, are you not impure?
And yet you wish to slander me.
At that time, the householder said to his wife,
"You may return home. Having sent her away, he spoke to Upananda:

"I now clearly perceive that women are deceitful and crooked, replete with many faults and impurities; my heart gives rise to weary detachment, and I wish to leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma to practice the Way."
Bhadanta said: "Your body is currently so foul-smelling and impure!
Only after you have applied perfumes for many years and months might you perhaps be fit to go forth."
The householder replied,

“If I were to continue applying fragrant ointments for years on end, my body might perish or the Buddha might pass into parinirvāṇa, thereby destroying the causes and conditions for my renunciation and pursuit of the Way.”

If you would now grant me permission to go forth, I shall no longer frequent cities, towns, monasteries, or vihāras; instead, I will dwell as an araṇyaka, subsisting on alms and wearing robes made of discarded rags.
"In a secluded place, who would smell my odor?
The Buddha said, "Householder!"
"Do you wish to go forth in my Dharma?
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said, "Welcome! You shall be a śramaṇa; practice the holy life."
Immediately, the layman’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord; the saṃghāṭī robe was upon his body and he held an alms bowl, appearing like a bhikṣu.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Upon hearing the Four Noble Truths, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and became a Srotāpanna.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him again for his further instruction and transformation, gradually leading him to attain the fruits of Sakṛdāgāmin and Anāgāmin.

When that night had passed, he took up his robes and bowl, went to the city of Rājagṛha, and proceeded to beg for food from house to house until he reached his own former home, where he stood outside the gate.
At that time, his wife, who was of exquisite beauty, seeing her husband with shaven head and clad in dharma-robes, having left the household life to practice the Way, spoke to him, saying:
"Is it according to the Dharma that you have abandoned me to become a śramaṇa?"
Candracchāya replied, "According to the Dharma, you should have discarded your impurities upon my robes yesterday;
thus you have defiled my body. Varṇa replied:
"Are you a bhikṣu who should slander others?
From my father's house to your home, I have not even seen the outer gate; how much less could I have gone to the Bamboo Grove to reach that assembly?"
At that time, the bhikṣu said to Varṇa:
"There is one named Upananda who was my contemporary; he was seen and ordered to leave the great assembly."
At that time, an evil Māra followed Vīradatta and said to him:
"What you saw yesterday was not a truly exquisite form!
It was a magical creation intended to delude your mind; you should now return to delighting yourself with the five sensual pleasures."
"The śramaṇa Gautama has merely deceived you!
You are now false and not a true bhikṣu.
The śramaṇa Gautama constantly uses this artifice to delude many people, causing them to leave the household life, just as he has deceived you today."
Because the bhikṣu Citta had realized the true Dharma, he immediately recognized that this was the work of Māra and said: "Evil one!
You are an emanation, and I am also an emanation; this sister of exquisite form is likewise an emanation. All dharmas taught by the Buddha are empty and like emanations."

At that time, having heard this Dharma, Varṇa immediately became free from dust and defilement regarding all phenomena, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; he cast off doubt and regret, no longer following the words of others, and attained the power of fearlessness within the Buddha-dharma. He spoke these words of discernment: "What you have done is most excellent;
you are able to joyfully cultivate the holy life within the Buddha-dharma. I, too, shall go forth from home to practice the Way."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If a person resolves their mind to seek bodhi, they should distance themselves from four things. What are these four?"
To distance oneself from evil associates, wicked teachers, and unwholesome conduct—this is the first thing that should be abandoned.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a person resolves their mind to seek awakening, they should abandon attachment to the marks of women and avoid dwelling or working together with worldly people; this is the second thing that should be abandoned.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a person resolves their mind to seek bodhi, they should distance themselves from the books and treatises of non-Buddhists—namely, the doctrines of the naked ascetics (Nirgrantha), the Lokāyata, and the Makkhaliputta. One should not draw near to, listen to, or recite what was not spoken by the Buddha; this is the third dharma that should be avoided.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a person resolves their mind to seek awakening, they should not associate with wrong views or evil views; this is the fourth dharma that should be abandoned.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata does not see any other dharmas that so deeply obstruct the path to Buddhahood as these four; therefore, a bodhisattva should abandon them.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one wishes to swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi, one should cultivate four dharmas. What are these four?
A bodhisattva should follow spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); spiritual friends refer to the Buddhas.

Furthermore, if a śrāvaka can cause a bodhisattva to abide in the profound treasury of the Dharma—the various *pāramitās*—they too are a spiritual friend to that bodhisattva; they should be approached, served, and venerated.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva should draw near to those who have left the household life, and should also draw near to the dharma of the araṇya, for the sake of remaining free from female forms.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A bodhisattva should cultivate and practice the correct view of great emptiness in order to remain free from false views.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if bodhisattvas wish to swiftly attain unsurpassed enlightenment, they should cultivate these four dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Stay far away from the affairs of women, And distance yourself from evil associates;
Likewise, remain remote from the discourses of non-Buddhists, As well as all other heterodox views."
If one associates with women and various evil associates,
And accepts the discourses of non-Buddhists, One increases all manner of false views.
Because of increasing these false views, One swiftly falls into the various states of woe.
