It is difficult to escape the eight states of no-leisure, and it is likewise difficult to have faith in the Buddha-dharma.
If a person intends to do evil, they will immediately commit evil deeds;
if one commits evil deeds, one will then fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, those who seek the Way should not associate with or become intimate with women;
they should always cultivate a sense of weary detachment, viewing them as swine in a sty.
Do not draw near to evil associates who cause one to dwell in what is not the Dharma.
If one associates with those who act contrary to the Dharma, it causes one to lose their mental clarity and vision.
If one draws near to non-Buddhist paths and the various treatises of the Nirgranthas,
though their rhetoric may be finely adorned, they are capable of giving rise to manifold faults.
Completely relinquishing all these worldly affairs, one then departs from all false views;
I say that these four dharmas are the root of coming and going in birth and death.
One should distance oneself from inferior dharmas and cultivate the practice of the sublime and wondrous.
That which I have originally cultivated, I shall now practice according to this Dharma.
Leaving the household life to cultivate pure conduct and drawing near to virtuous friends—
the Buddhas and their disciples— may they cause me to abide in the Buddha-way.
I constantly practice emptiness—emptiness of emptiness and great emptiness;
though I practice these dharmas of emptiness, I do not cling to emptiness.
Whether it be dharmas or that which is attained, both are not found within emptiness.
This is called true emptiness, Which the world cannot fathom.
For the sake of the Buddha-way, I have practiced various dharmas;
these dharmas are most subtle and wondrous, Beyond the reach of ordinary wisdom.
When I sought the path of the Buddha, I personally reflected within my own mind upon all the sūtras and teachings I had heard; I did not follow the words of others.
Having attained full realization myself, I then spoke them for the sake of others.
This is called the True and Right Path—emptiness, non-obstruction, and quiescence.
Within emptiness there is no birth, nor is there any who grows old;
within emptiness there is also no death. This is called the characteristic of eternal abiding.
This is called the true mark of phenomena, which the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) has fully realized;
it destroys all demonic armies and attains unsurpassed bodhi.
The Dharma that I have attained, I shall now explain for the sake of others.
To realize the unsurpassed limit, wherein no marks of transition exist;
if one wishes to attain the Buddha-way, or wish to sit at the site of enlightenment,
or wish to destroy the hosts of Māras, one should constantly cultivate this dharma of emptiness.
If anyone wishes to turn the unsurpassed, wondrous wheel of Dharma, to deliver immeasurable sentient beings,
they should study this dharma of emptiness. If they wish to abide in the ten powers of a Buddha, as well as the four fearlessnesses, [they should study this dharma of emptiness].
To roar the lion’s roar amidst the assembly, one should practice this dharma of emptiness.
If one desires great renown that spreads widely throughout the ten directions,
one should cultivate with a rectified mind and thoroughly comprehend this dharma of emptiness.
Those wise Bodhisattvas, who follow and study my teaching on emptiness, are able to attain supreme enlightenment; this is called the most excellent wisdom.
Whether they be bhikṣus or bhikṣuṇīs, if they follow and study my practice, [they shall likewise attain it].
They, too, shall attain bodhi, just as I have now attained it.
Not only these two assemblies who are able to practice this dharma of emptiness,
but all classes of sentient beings shall likewise study to achieve the path of Buddhahood.
By means of the Eightfold Noble Path, I have practiced this dharma of emptiness;
having thoroughly realized the characteristics of all phenomena, I have attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
By cultivating this dharma, I am able to obtain unimpeded wisdom.
This is the true path of all Buddhas: namely, the constant practice of the dharma of emptiness.
Therefore, for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, all Bodhisattvas should study this dharma, which is the emptiness of all phenomena.

“Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva, through successive rebirths, does not lose right mindfulness; is able to practice according to what has been taught; attains a mind of certainty regarding all dharmas; and acquires unimpeded eloquence, sharp eloquence, profound eloquence, and incomparable eloquence. Having been known by the Buddhas, they are empowered by their spiritual authority and shall protect the city of the Dharma in future ages.”

What are the four? They are: always delighting in leaving the household life and practicing this dharma of renunciation throughout successive lifetimes; seeking the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings without weariness; preaching the Dharma without fatigue; practicing the concentration of non-reliance and destroying all marks of phenomena; and constantly and diligently cultivating the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-recollection samādhi), wherein no mark of purity arises amidst all conditions. These are called the first dharma for not losing right mindfulness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks the Buddha-way for himself while simultaneously transforming sentient beings so that they may abide therein, and constantly delights in praising the divine virtues of all Buddhas— this is the second dharma by which one does not lose right mindfulness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to accomplish the profound patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), this is the third dharma by which one does not lose right mindfulness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva is at the point of death, their mind is not distracted; they constantly keep in mind all the Buddhas and the profound Dharma. By means of this profound patience, they do not lose right mindfulness. This is called the fourth.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
“The Bodhisattva constantly seeks the Dharma, And also constantly practices the gift of Dharma;
Therefore, regarding all phenomena, He never loses right mindfulness.”
In order to transform immeasurable multitudes and cause them to abide in the Buddha-way,
in every successive life and upon changing bodies, they always attain the state of never losing mindfulness;
they practice and draw near to the profound, empty, and quiescent Dharma praised by the Buddhas.
Therefore, this bodhisattva swiftly attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
Nor does he give rise to "non-arising," for non-arising is itself non-arising.
Because of this profound patience, he never loses right mindfulness.
This wise bodhisattva does not die with a distracted mind,
but always maintains single-minded mindfulness of the Buddhas and the profound Dharma of the Buddhas.
At the time of this person’s death, their mind does not regress or sink.
Therefore, throughout successive lives and changing incarnations, one never loses right mindfulness.
For this reason, if anyone wishes to attain the unsurpassed path,
they should practice all these four dharmas in this manner.
This Dharma is the most supreme, praised by all Buddhas;
I now extol it as well—may you all practice and study it.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is for the sake of benefiting you all.
The Buddha acts for the benefit of others; it is not that he speaks to you out of force.
If you seek the wisdom of a Buddha, you should practice and study this path.
By practicing and studying this path, the wisdom of a Buddha will arise from within you.
If a person harbors indolence, or gives rise to regression and despondency, they shall never attain the Buddha-way; one should keep far away from such states.
If a person calculates with the notion of a self, or dwells upon the perception of sentient beings, [they likewise fail].
If one relies upon various phenomena, one cannot realize the Buddha-way.
One should abandon these various states of mind and constantly practice and study the mark of emptiness;
by dismantling and dispersing all phenomena, one attains profound wisdom.
Furthermore, do not rely on anything; for reliance is the mark of movement.
Because one delights in the dharma of movement, one wanders through birth and death. 28.
Chapter on the Myriad Subtleties (VIII), Chapter Twenty-Eight. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“Bodhisattvas possess four qualities that enable them to attain all the most supreme and wondrous dharmas. What are these four?

If a person has resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind and perceives that the Dharma is about to perish, they apply themselves with diligent practice for the sake of its long endurance, seeking the Dharma without weariness.”

If they see the stupas and temples of the Tathāgata falling into ruin, they diligently restore and maintain them so that they may endure for a long time; for the sake of delighting in the Dharma, they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives.
Seeing suffering beings, they give rise to great compassion and further intensify their practice, making this vow:
"When shall I attain the cultivation of the Buddha-way, sever all these sufferings, and preach the Dharma for others!"
“Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas never tire of seeking the Dharma.
For the sake of seeking the Dharma, they give rise to a great and profound resolve and produce a great aspiration.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, seeking great wisdom, possesses a spiritual virtue that is difficult to surpass, for he has destroyed all prideful thoughts.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly practices loving-kindness toward sentient beings and seeks their benefit, forming this thought:
"These sentient beings have no savior; I alone am their refuge!"
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is free from anger and resentment because he cultivates great compassion;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is free from envy because he causes sentient beings to attain the joy of true wisdom;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is free from avarice because he constantly gathers in sentient beings through the gift of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is a great giver because he delights in the Buddha-way with a profound mind;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has no attachment in his mind toward any phenomena;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is an eloquent speaker, with a serene and joyful countenance, always smiling as he speaks, and redoubling his diligent progress upon seeing suffering sentient beings.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas delight in the Buddha-dharma;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are fearless because they roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assembly;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are without alarm or dread because they abide in the Buddha-dharma.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly and diligently practice progress for the sake of cultivating roots of goodness;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have no fixed attachment to any kingdoms, cities, towns, or villages;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly and diligently teach and transform all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are intelligent and of sharp faculties, having thoroughly mastered all dharmas;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the true meaning because they contemplate all dharmas according to reality;
bodhisattva-mahāsattvas seek the true meaning within the Buddha-dharma because they desire to attain unexcelled bodhi for themselves.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are awakeners, for they are skillfully able to know the proper time to transform sentient beings.
"Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to refute the arguments of non-Buddhists in accordance with the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is one who has attained certainty regarding the meaning of all phenomena;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is the very nature of the Buddha-dharma;
and the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is a field for the Jewel of the Dharma, because they give birth to the Jewel of the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the great ocean, for he receives all dharmas without ever being satiated;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the Cakravāḍa mountains, for he can obstruct the winds of affliction of immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the waters of the great ocean, for he expounds the Dharma inexhaustibly.
The mind of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is pure and subtle, for it is like space;
the bodhisattva mahāsattva is inexhaustible, for he is equal to space;
the bodhisattva mahāsattva is like Mount Sumeru, for he accumulates wholesome dharmas.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the great earth, for he receives both hatred and love;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like a fertile field, for he plants all roots of goodness so that they are not lost;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the fierce sun, for he can bestow the light of the Dharma upon sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like the pure moon, for he destroys all darkness;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like a dense canopy, for he shields sentient beings from the heat of the afflictions such as lust, anger, and ignorance;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like a cloud-shade, for he provides peaceful rest for all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is like a great tree, for he serves as a place of refuge for sentient beings;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is the savior of the world, its refuge, its support, and the giver of fearlessness;
the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is the teacher of the world, for he has attained complete mastery over all arts and crafts.
Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas are able to bestow the happiness of this life, future lives, and nirvāṇa for the benefit of sentient beings,
all sentient beings should pay homage to these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

“Śāriputra! If all sentient beings could know that for their sake the bodhisattva performs such difficult practices and ascetic austerities, taking upon himself the heavy burden of seeking the causes and conditions for their happiness.”

As I understand it, all sentient beings should carry [this teaching] upon their heads or bear it upon their shoulders; from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, throughout that entire interval, all the gods and humans of every world should provide every kind of requisite for comfort, and they should always carry it upon their heads so that it never touches the ground.
Furthermore, when this bodhisattva proceeds to the site of enlightenment, he uses his own upper garments, or celestial robes, or various wondrous lotus flowers, to spread out a high seat;
reaching as far upward as the Peak of Existence, he uses celestial jewel-robes to form a canopy that shields him from the wind and sun.
Having attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they shall honor and serve [the Buddha] with various flowers, incense, banners, pennants, and music, as well as with their own bodies.
Even though these sentient beings thus revere and make offerings to them, they still cannot repay the Bodhisattva’s kindness.
Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva, for the sake of sentient beings, has brought forth great adornment to grant them the untainted, pure, wondrous, and unsurpassed joy of the Path.

“Śāriputra! If one were to compare the worldly desire for pleasure with this, even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part would not equal it; indeed, no analogy whatsoever can reach it.”

Why is this? The articles of pleasure offered by sentient beings to Bodhisattvas are all worldly, tainted, deceptive, impermanent, and subject to change; whereas the pleasure bestowed by Bodhisattvas upon sentient beings transcends the world, being untainted, real, free from feverish distress, free from affliction, immeasurable, limitless, and ultimately eternal bliss.
Therefore, Śāriputra, you should know that even if sentient beings were to provide all manner of articles of pleasure to a bodhisattva, they still could not repay them. Śāriputra!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva awakens those who are asleep; he inspires diligence in those who are indolent; he constantly cultivates right mindfulness for those who are deluded and confused; he serves as the sun of wisdom for those who are blind and in darkness; he acts as a great physician and medicine for those who are sick and emaciated; he shows the correct path to those with wrong views; and he is able to give rise to wholesome dharmas in sentient beings in whom they have not yet arisen, and to increase wholesome dharmas in sentient beings in whom they have not yet increased.
Śāriputra! To speak in brief, there is no other person who can serve as a refuge, a savior, or the ultimate path for sentient beings; it is only the Buddhas.
Furthermore, the Dharma of the Buddhas, the Dharma of the Tathāgatas, and the Self-Existent Dharma do not arise from elsewhere; all of them are born from the Bodhisattva path.
Chapter 29: On the Reverse and the Accordant (8). Chapter Twenty-nine: On the Reverse and the Accordant. At that time, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “It is rare!”
World-Honored One!
This bodhisattva path is subtle and profound; it is able to adorn and purify oneself while also purifying sentient beings.
World-Honored One, it is, for example, like this:

On the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are pārijātaka and kovidāra trees; when their flowers bloom, they are not only naturally majestic and beautiful, but are also able to adorn all the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

In this way, when a bodhisattva is fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas and has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, having already adorned and purified themselves, they also become a refuge for immeasurable sentient beings. Those who have accomplished the vehicle of the śrāvakas all attain playful mastery, delighting themselves through the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*), the path (*mārga*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), and liberations (*vimokṣa*). This is just like that tree whose flowers are in full bloom, providing entertainment for the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
World-Honored One!
What wise person would not mount this vehicle?

It is only because we were originally indolent and followed the words of others that, upon hearing the Dharma, we gave rise to a sense of ease and comfort, and thus claimed to have attained happiness.
"Now I understand that I myself have no power to cause even a single person to abide in this Way.
World-Honored One!
From this day forward, whenever I preach the Dharma, I shall first expound this Bodhisattva Vehicle, and only thereafter shall I speak of the various Śrāvaka teachings."
"Why is this? One such as I may repay the Buddha's kindness by causing even a single person to resolve upon the unsurpassed mind and swiftly attain perfect enlightenment.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Excellent, excellent!
That you are now able to give rise to such a mind, desiring to expound the Great Dharma and transform bodhisattvas—why is this?
For what reason?”
In future ages, there will be many who disparage this Mahāyāna Dharma, and people will have no faith or acceptance for such sūtras as these. Śāriputra!

In that time and age, if there are sons or daughters of good family who seek the wholesome Dharma, they should maintain right mindfulness, relying on the meaning and relying on the Dharma, and should not remain among the crowds.
Why is this? At that time, the assembly was not composed of those practicing the Way.
My assembly of śrāvakas, who are practitioners of the Way, do not disparage bodhisattvas or revile the Mahāyāna; how much less would they oppose such profound sūtras and dharmas spoken by the Buddha!
Why is this? If one gives rise to opposition, it is the karma of a non-practitioner, not the karma of a practitioner; it is the karma of an ordinary person, not the karma of a wise one. Śāriputra!
Therefore, you should train yourselves to initiate the deeds of the wise and abandon the conduct of ordinary persons.
If there is a bhikṣu who takes me as his teacher, he should practice in this way. "Śāriputra!

In future ages, those who seek the path of the Buddha and possess deep faith, diligence, single-mindedness, and a sense of shame and remorse, who joyfully seek the wholesome Dharma, may be disparaged by others who say:

"These indolent ones lack the power of skillful means; they cannot attain the fruits of the śramaṇa in this present life, yet for the sake of enjoying the five desires they act as kings, practicing the gates of Dharma and calling themselves Bodhisattvas, accepting the offerings of others while praising such Mahāyāna sūtras and teachings."
“The Buddha does not say that such a person is called a practitioner. “Śāriputra!
Observe this fool who, on account of a trivial cause, slanders me; I declare that such a person is a true practitioner, yet he considers himself otherwise.”
If the Tathāgata says that one who is a supreme practitioner or one who has attained superior understanding is, in fact, not a practitioner and has not attained understanding, Śāriputra!

At that time, there was a layperson who became a disciple of that [teacher] and accepted his words; upon seeing the bodhisattvas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās reading, reciting, and faithfully practicing such sutras as these, he conceived a mind of enmity and hostility toward them.
Śāriputra! Observe this foolish person—how could he possess any observance of the precepts?
In my sūtras I have said:
If one sees a stumps that resembles the form of a person, one should still not give rise to anger, let alone toward those who possess consciousness.
Such evil people constantly harbor anger and affliction! Śāriputra!

You should observe how, at that time, all were inverted: they perceived what is Dharma as non-Dharma and what is non-Dharma as Dharma; they perceived what is wholesome as unwholesome and what is unwholesome as wholesome; they conceived the notion of non-practice toward practitioners and the notion of practice toward those who do not practice; they conceived the notion of lack of realization toward those who have attained realization and the notion of realization toward those who have not attained realization.
It should be known that such a person is not called a practitioner nor is he called one who understands.

Since he neither knows the Dharma nor knows what is wholesome, he cannot accord with the teachings of the Buddha. Such a deluded person is obscured by anger, shrouded by stinginess, greed, envy, and pride; he praises himself, exalts himself, and disparages others. Consumed and harmed by greed, hatred, and ignorance, he plunges deeply into various evils and remains far removed from wholesome dharmas.

“Śāriputra! If I were to fully recount the transgressions of such a person, their accumulated karmic offenses would continue to increase beyond remedy. Such a deluded person should be avoided, just as one avoids a rogue bull.”
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is the teacher of those who possess a sense of shame and remorse, not of those who lack them;
he is the teacher of those who have faith and acceptance, not of those who lack them.
The teacher is one who accords with the Dharma, not one who destroys it;
one who exerts effort, not one who is indolent;
one who maintains mindfulness, not one whose mindfulness is distracted.
One who possesses wisdom is my teacher, not one who is deluded. Śāriputra,
such a deluded person is not my disciple, and I am not his teacher.

Observe this person: such is the Buddha-vehicle, the Tathāgata’s true wisdom, and the sphere of practice cultivated by the Tathāgata over a long period. Having practiced for a long time, he has fully realized great wisdom and attained unsurpassed bodhi; he then teaches this very Dharma to the bodhisattvas, thinking thus:

"If there are bodhisattvas who follow and study this Dharma and cultivate the Buddha-wisdom, they will be able to attain unsurpassed bodhi, rescue and deliver sentient beings, cause them to escape birth and death, and ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed."
"The Tathāgata himself also reveres this Dharma.
Yet these foolish people disparage and do not believe it; this is most unwholesome, the foremost unwholesomeness—what can be done about it?"
Therefore, you all should practice in accordance with the Dharma and not rely on persons; you should rely on yourselves and not rely on others.
Śāriputra, this is what is called the teaching of the Tathāgata.
How does a bhikṣu practice in accordance with the Dharma and not rely on persons, but rather rely upon himself and not upon others? Śāriputra,
a bhikṣu follows detachment and accords with nirvāṇa by cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the applications of mindfulness?
They consist of constant mindfulness, never abandoning it, with respect to the body, feelings, and the mind.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

To see phenomena as they truly are—having the nature of non-existence—and to maintain right mindfulness without error regarding these phenomena is called the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). This is for a bhikṣu to practice in reliance upon the Dharma and not in reliance upon persons; to always rely upon oneself and not upon others.

“Śāriputra! If one can thus cultivate the foundations of mindfulness and completely sever all greedy attachments, they are called an Arhat; they are called one whose outflows are exhausted, one who is free from afflictions, and a field of merit for the world. They are called one who has attained mastery, one who is undefiled, one who is wise, one who has reached the other shore, a guide, and a brahmin.”
“Śāriputra! An arhat is one who has distanced himself from all evil and unwholesome dharmas, takes no delight in the conditioned, and has extinguished all karma so that it shall not arise again.”
Śāriputra! It is impossible for an Arhat to give rise to karma of sin or merit. Why is this?

Because they have abandoned the three kinds of seeking and transformed the nine fetters, their minds are unattached to all phenomena; having transcended the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, they are free from craving, without feverish passion, and without affliction. Their minds are as pure as space, and thus they are called Arhats.
“Śāriputra! One who is said to have ‘fulfilled the exhaustion of outflows’ has exhausted the outflows regarding all phenomena without remainder, reaching ultimate exhaustion;
one who is ‘free from all fetters’ is because the mind of an Arhat is fundamentally and eternally empty, being stainless and pure.”

They are undefiled because their minds remain unchanged whether encountering the pleasant or the unpleasant, or praise or blame among the six sense objects, having severed all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
They are fields of merit for the world because they have severed all burning afflictions and are able to bestow the foremost gift of the pure Dharma.
They are called masters because they perceive all phenomena as empty and non-existent, having attained the further shore within the dharma of emptiness and being free from false discourse.
He who is named the Brahmin Sovereign (Vaśavartin) is so called because he obstructs all unwholesome dharmas and remains unstained by any phenomena;
he is a guide because he can preach for others the path where there is no birth-and-death;

he is named Wise because this person knows that the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as the karmic conditions and their retributions, all arise from false conceptualization, and having attained liberation therein, he is thus called Wise.

One who has reached the other shore is able to destroy all Māras and all fetters (saṃyojana), and is able to reach the further shore of all dharmas; having emerged from the mud and established themselves on dry land, they are therefore called "one who has reached the other shore."
“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata can describe, without increase or decrease, all the merit possessed by Arhats who have exhausted their outflows.
These Arhats are great fields of merit; they are free from defilement and impurity, and likewise devoid of stumps, sprouts, and all manner of gravel.”
Śāriputra! An Arhat whose outflows are exhausted does not give rise to the thought when someone slanders or reviles him:
"This person is abusing me."
If others praise him, he does not give rise to the thought, "This person is extolling me.

Free from discriminatory thoughts and without doubt or deficiency, he skillfully restrains the six sense faculties and dwells in the stage of certainty. Relying on the practice of the Dharma rather than on persons, he is able to rely upon himself and not upon others.
Therefore, Śāriputra, a practitioner such as this will never contravene the bodhi of all Buddhas, nor will they ever give rise to the karma of one who is not a practitioner.
In this way, one will not be censured by those who practice the holy life, and will also deeply protect the bodhi of all Buddhas, causing it to endure for a long time. "Śāriputra!
"An Arhat is one who has no doubt regarding any phenomena, has accomplished what was to be done, and dwells within the path of the Dharma.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
An Arhat never opposes or fails to abide in the Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? If one were to oppose it, that would be the conduct of an ordinary person, not the work of an Arhat.
The Buddha said, “So it is, Śāriputra.”
To act in opposition to the Dharma is the behavior of ordinary worldlings; it is not the work of the wise.

The Tathāgata speaks only for the sake of future generations, so that there may be elder bhikṣus of great renown whose minds find temporary stability when dwelling alone apart from the crowd and no longer beholding women, and who then say of themselves: "I am an arhat."
A sense of arrogance arose in his mind.
At that time, many among the assembly were full of faith and, believing him to be an Arhat, they revered and provided for him.
This foolish man, likewise craving fame and profit, accepted these offerings and claimed to himself, "I possess the dharma of an Arhat; the fetters do not arise within me."
This person does not understand the dharma of non-discrimination and delights in generating discrimination; because their fetters have merely subsided for a time, they claim to have attained the Way.
If they enter a village, they maintain formal decorum, yet if they dwell in solitude, they give themselves over to indulgence, behaving differently even when among the multitude.

This person delights in maintaining a large assembly of disciples and possesses many acquaintances; he receives great offerings from kings and ministers, his fame spreads abroad, and he is loved and respected by many. Yet, while all the fetters overflow within him, he claims to be free from the afflictions of the defilements.

When they hear such profound sutras and teachings corresponding to emptiness, my beloved disciples cherish them, listen to and receive them, seek to understand their meaning, and practice these dharmas with a heart of reverence;
yet this foolish person refuses to believe or accept them, wishing instead to harbor opposition, and speaks thus:
"This is not the word of the Buddha, nor the teaching of the Great Master; it is neither Dharma nor good."

This person conceives the notion of non-dharma regarding dharma, and conceives the notion of dharma regarding non-dharma; they conceive the notion of wholesome regarding unwholesome dharmas, and conceive the notion of unwholesome regarding wholesome dharmas.

“Śāriputra! These deluded people, according to whatever dharmas they have obtained, immediately praise themselves; yet regarding those dharmas they have not obtained, they disparage and hold them in contempt, becoming arrogant and haughty while deprecating others.”

Such a foolish person, though they may maintain the precepts, concentrate their mindfulness on a single point, gradually subdue their evil thoughts, and engage in extensive study and recitation; and though they gather many disciples and are venerated by others, receiving praise and respectful salutations, they give rise to arrogance, self-conceit, and overweening pride. Consequently, upon hearing such profound and wondrous sutras as these, they commit grave karmic offenses.

These deluded people do not realize that they possess such offenses; instead, their arrogance and delusion increase further. Having opposed this sutra and committed grave transgressions, they shall fall into the great hells.
The Buddha-spoken *Kusuma-hasta Sūtra*, Scroll Eight.
The Buddha-spoken *Kusuma-hasta Sūtra*, Scroll Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin, by Imperial Decree.
Chapter Thirty: On Non-Retrogression (9) The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
“The Tathāgata shall now sever your doubts, and likewise cause those who in the future read, recite, explain, or receive this sutra to all sever their doubts.”

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is called the All-Knowing One, the All-Seeing One, and the All-Speaking One. There is no phenomenon he does not see, no phenomenon he does not hear, no phenomenon he does not perceive, and no phenomenon he does not know; he thoroughly comprehends the three periods of time without any obstruction.
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is called the "Peerless One" because he has attained perfect understanding of all phenomena; he is spontaneously sovereign and has no place of dependence.
The Tathāgata now wishes to let out a lion’s roar amidst this great assembly; setting aside these ignorant people who practice the ways of false paths, there is no need for further elaboration.
If sons or daughters of good family have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they should practice with single-minded diligence within this Dharma.
Why is this? One should reflect thus:

"The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which the Buddhas have accumulated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas—if I were to give rise to indolence regarding it, I would surely fail to believe, would oppose and reject it, and would be unable to penetrate and understand it."
“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva practices four dharmas, they will destroy the unsurpassed bodhi of all buddhas.
What are these four?
To be separated from virtuous friends and to associate with evil companions, following what they learn to destroy the Mahāyāna— this is called the first dharma. Furthermore, Śāriputra,

for a bodhisattva to have views based on grasping at acquisitions and to harbor deep conceits regarding a self, such that upon hearing a profound sūtra they become greatly terrified and shall fall into a great pit— this is the second dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there is the third dharma:

a bodhisattva who studies the various scriptures of non-Buddhist paths, is skillful in debate, and is respected by many people; yet such a person cannot discipline their own mind, nor can they discipline all phenomena. Because they lack such discipline, they do not practice the Mahāyāna. This is the third dharma.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva violates the prohibitions and is unable to comply with the precepts established by the Buddha, and upon hearing this profound, empty, pure, and wondrous Dharma of the precepts, their mind fails to comprehend it; they cannot believe in or delight in it, but instead oppose it and refuse to accept it—this is the fourth dharma.
"If a bodhisattva possesses these four dharmas, they will be unable to believe and accept [the teaching], and will destroy their bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"If one associates with evil friends, And likewise follows their conduct..."
Therefore, they take no delight in the Buddha-way and destroy unsurpassed bodhi.
They study various non-Buddhist scriptures and are skillful in all forms of contentious debate;
whenever anyone speaks, they are able to refute and destroy them all.
Though they call themselves wise, they are in truth deluded;
for such reasons as these, they have no faith in bodhi.
If a person is greedily attached to a self and follows whatever views they have acquired, [they will not believe].
Hearing this most profound Dharma, they give rise to great alarm and fear.
Such people cannot understand reality as it truly is— emptiness and quiescence—
and failing to penetrate awakening, they are likewise unable to have faith or delight in it.
Due to the cause of breaking the precepts, one is able to give rise to unwholesome karma and cannot follow the training as the Buddha has taught in the precepts.
Such a person uses harsh speech and engages in double-tongued talk, delighting in exposing the faults of others.
Such unwholesome persons commit every kind of evil. Therefore, one should keep them at a distance;
those who do not believe in the path to enlightenment should always diligently practice and study the Dharma as I have praised it.
If a person wishes to see the Buddha and wishes to know such a Dharma, they should maintain the precepts with tranquility; from this, true wisdom arises.
If a person maintains the pure precepts, the bodhicitta becomes increasingly firm.
By means of profound and pure upholding of the precepts, one is able to extinguish evil thoughts and observations.
Therefore, those who seek bodhi should profoundly and purely uphold the precepts;
such persons will have no doubts or difficulties regarding the Buddha-way.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can protect the Buddha-way. What are these four?
One personally upholds the precepts, deeply generates a wholesome mind, and dwells securely within them;
one extensively studies the orthodox scriptures without mixing in heterodox doctrines;
and having heard the Buddha’s sutras and teachings, one is able to diligently recite them.
He always delights in dwelling alone and accords with the practice of seclusion. Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, he can protect the Buddha-way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When a Bodhisattva abides in the precepts, He does not exalt himself on account of those precepts;
Seeking further the most profound Dharma, He resolves upon its subtle and wondrous meaning."
Seeking unsurpassed bodhi through the foremost profound Dharma,
one should cultivate only the Buddha’s true teaching and not study the treatises of non-Buddhists.
One should never take pleasure in reading or reciting the scriptures of the Lokāyata.
One does not delight in disparaging discourse, but only protects the Buddha-dharma.
Constantly practicing the dharma of quiescence, one delights in dwelling in secluded places;
there are no sensual desires that can disturb the mind.
The four subtle and wondrous dharmas that I now praise,
for the sake of attaining the path to Buddhahood, you all should practice and study.
Throughout my successive lifetimes, I have always practiced these dharmas in this way.
Having protected the Buddha-dharma, one is thus able to achieve great wisdom.
By upholding and protecting the Buddha-dharma, one does not fall into the lowly or evil realms,
but is always born in noble and honorable places, attended and guarded by the masses.
One may attain great wealth, yet not become heedless;
one should swiftly perform meritorious deeds, knowing that wealth is impermanent.
If one gives, it belongs to oneself; if one does not give, it is not one's own property.
My body and my wealth— At the end of life, I must abandon them all.
Yet I can obtain virtuous companions And likewise find virtuous friends;
Parents and all kinsmen Can cause me to abide in the Buddha-dharma.
Always delighting in the practice of wholesome dharmas, And likewise causing others to have faith and joy,
One thereby attains great happiness, Because one has cultivated the True Dharma.
One is constantly born into this world Within families of wealth and noble lineage.
One who has given rise to heedfulness always delights in practicing wholesome dharmas.
Regarding body, life, and wealth, one does not form fixed attachments;
for Buddhas are extremely difficult to encounter, and even a place free from calamity is rare.
Seeing the Buddha brings freedom from hardship and can give rise to great benefit;
the mind always delights in leaving the household life, and through this, wisdom is born.
The heart gives rise to great joy and seeks the most supreme wisdom.
Constantly dwelling securely within the Dharma, they are able to give rise to the unsurpassed path.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva’s mind is always joyful; practicing the path with self-comfort, they are able to know for themselves that they will certainly become a Buddha, their fame heard throughout the ten directions.
What are the four? They are:
giving away all that one possesses, both internal and external;
abiding securely in the precepts while cultivating various meritorious virtues;
Among all forms of wisdom, they are the most honored and supreme;

for the sake of the profound Dharma, they do not begrudge their own bodies or lives, and toward those who read and recite this profound sutra, they are able to provide offerings, pay homage, and provide protection.
"Endowed with these four dharmas, the mind is always joyful and one can comfort oneself: 'I shall certainly become a Buddha, and my fame shall reach the ten directions.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"Having completely renounced all property and wealth, One dwells securely within the pure precepts."
Supreme among all forms of wisdom, they do not doubt the dharma of emptiness and stillness.
If one sees those who read, recite, uphold, and expound such profound sutras,
one should honor them with all manner of musical instruments and offerings.
Therefore, this bodhisattva, always practicing the Way with a joyful mind,
is able to self-proclaim that he shall become a Buddha and will forever be the Honored One among the worlds.
Whether they be Buddhas of the past, the future, or those of the present—
They all receive this prediction of enlightenment: "You shall certainly attain awakening.
If a person follows and studies this Dharma studied by all Buddhas, know that such a bodhisattva dwells securely in the unsurpassed path.
This Dharma is praised by the Buddhas and practiced by all Bodhisattvas;
because a person dwells within it, they are able to achieve the path of Buddhahood.
It is like an unbaked clay jar that falls from a great height.
If there is no obstruction along the way, one should know that [the goal] will surely be attained; it will certainly be destroyed. So too it is with the Bodhisattva:
one who can cultivate this path and remains unobstructed midway shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Just as when a person weaves, by interlacing the warp and woof without obstruction, they can quickly achieve completion;
so too is it with the Bodhisattva, who constantly cultivates this Dharma.
Remaining diligent therein until the attainment of Buddhahood—
just as when a person plants various fruit trees in fertile soil and waters them from time to time,
causing them to gradually flourish and grow.
Nurtured and protected according to the seasons, shielded from wind, cold, and heat,
this tree gradually grows, flourishing with wondrous flowers and fruit.
Its shade is most cool and refreshing, causing people to delight in resting there.
Flowers and fruits are given to sentient beings, providing them with benefit.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: first planting the bodhicitta, gradually cultivating the Bodhisattva path, and inquiring of those who are widely learned.
Bestowing gifts at the proper time, always maintaining the precepts with purity,
and likewise practicing all other bodhisattva dharmas without weariness—
by practicing in this successive order, one shall sit at the site of enlightenment.
Having shattered the armies of all Māras, he attained unsurpassed Bodhi.
In accordance with the time, he turned the Wheel of Dharma, which had never been turned before in the world.
Gradually delivering sentient beings, he leads immeasurable multitudes.
Such a person of great wisdom, having resolved upon this unsurpassed mind,
shall never regress from life to life until they attain bodhi.
Therefore, you all should now gradually cultivate this Dharma.
"When the time arrives, one shall become a Buddha and, according to the occasion, turn the wheel of Dharma. Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva never regresses from unsurpassed bodhi."
Having sacrificed his body, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), attaining blessings according to his will and a great physical strength like that of Nārāyaṇa;
as a Wheel-Turning King, he shall renounce the four continents and go forth into the homeless life;
having gone forth, he shall attain mastery and cultivate the four Brahma-abodes.
At the end of his life, he shall be reborn in the world above Brahmā and become a Great Brahmā deity.
What are these four? Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva sees that a stupa or temple is in ruin, they should restore and adorn it, even with a single brick or a lump of clay; this is the first practice, by which one may eventually become a Great Brahma King.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, at a crossroads or in a place where many people gather, erects a stūpa or temple and constructs an image to serve as an auspicious condition for the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha— whether depicting the turning of the wheel of Dharma or the appearance of renunciation, sitting at the site of enlightenment, destroying the demonic armies, manifesting supernatural powers, entering parinirvāṇa, or the descent from the heavens— this is the second dharma by which one may even attain the status of a Great Brahmā King.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva sees the bhikṣu-saṃgha split into two factions, engaged in disputes and anger, and mutually accusing one another of faults, the bodhisattva at that time diligently seeks skillful means to bring them into harmony. This is the third dharma, by which one may even attain the status of a Great Brahmā King.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva sees that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, they are able to read, recite, and explain even a single verse so as to ensure the Dharma does not cease; they diligently practice and cultivate it for the sake of protecting the Dharma, respectfully supporting the Dharma-preacher, and single-mindedly guarding the Dharma without sparing their own body or life—this is the fourth dharma.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, in every successive life they will be reborn as a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) and attain a physical strength equal to that of Nārāyaṇa; they will renounce the four continents to go forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth, they will be able to practice the four brahma-vihāras at will, and at the end of their life, they shall be reborn in the Brahma world to become a Great Brahmā King.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: "If one sees a Buddha-stūpa in ruin, And is able to diligently restore and adorn it,
By virtue of this, the bodhisattva Shall attain great physical strength."
By constructing a stupa or temple at a crossroads,
manifesting the marks of the Buddha’s virtues, and causing the minds of the multitude to attain purity,
one thereby obtains a great reward of merit, and one's fame spreads far and wide.
One shall also gain a great retinue and be praised by many people.
If one sees the Saṃgha falling into ruin or further engaging in mutual disputes and litigation,
one employs skillful means to cause them to repent their faults and restores them to harmony.
By virtue of these merits, they shall be courageous and invincible,
attaining a great physical strength like that of Nārāyaṇa.
Seeing that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish and that there are none who believe or accept it,
Able to protect with a single mind, Without begrudging body or life;
Seeing those who uphold the Dharma, One adds offerings, service, and reverence.
Thus guarded by the various devas, One is protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas.
One who protects and upholds the Dharma shall become a Wheel-Turning King;
traversing the four continents, he transforms all nations through the Dharma.
Though he governs these realms, he never succumbs to negligence.
Able to loathe and detest all worldly desires, he abandoned his kingdom to practice renunciation.
Capable of cultivating the bliss of the four dhyānas and possessing all supernormal powers,
he purely cultivated the four brahma-vihāras and constantly delighted in all wholesome merits.
Having passed away from this life, one shall be reborn in the world of Brahmā;
among the Brahmā devas, one shall become a sovereign king.
These four sublime and wondrous dharmas are praised by all Buddhas.
In the past, when I was a bodhisattva, I also drew near to and practiced them.
Whatever Dharma I heard, I practiced exactly as it was taught;
having fulfilled the perfections and reached the other shore, I attained unsurpassed bodhi.
If one can practice and study the Dharma that I originally practiced,
one will be constantly honored and noble in every lifetime, possessing great power that is difficult to destroy.
One will always be a supreme being among men and a king of the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
Furthermore, within the desire realm, one attains the status of a sovereign king;
likewise, reaching the form realm, one acts as a sovereign king.
Honored and noble in all places—who would not practice this path?
Able to purely uphold the prohibitive precepts, Possessing deep shame and remorse,
All their aspirations shall be fulfilled, Abiding in the roots of all wholesome merit.
Diligently practicing without indolence, Fully practicing patience and meditative concentration.
Having attained supreme great wisdom, they clearly understand all dharmas.
Whether there be hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, or millions of kinds of immeasurable methods of skillful means,
they are able to accomplish them all and swiftly comprehend their underlying significance.
Able to expound immeasurable meanings from within a single phrase,
Mastering all manner of skillful arts, always preeminent among them;
Constantly attaining great wisdom, with eloquence that is beyond measure.
Dedicating oneself to the practice of a bodhisattva, One abandons all other forms of wisdom.
By constantly practicing with a straightforward mind And properly cultivating right view,
One is able to encounter the various Buddhas And abandon all hardships.
This vehicle is the greatest, praised by all Buddhas;
in this subtle and wondrous vehicle, there is no limitation for those with faults,
no limitation for the blind, nor is there any limitation for the deaf.
As well as those who are humpbacked or crippled by a hundred ailments, the mute, the dumb, and all who are ugly;
nor is it limited to the poor, nor to those who have lost their merit and virtue,
nor to those who have committed evil karma, nor to those with the causes and conditions for the woeful realms.
Who, upon hearing this praise of the vehicle, would not practice and study it, free from all evils?
Only those who delight in evil are excluded.
Therefore, those who seek wisdom should seek this Buddha-wisdom;
by practicing and studying this wisdom, they reach the further shore of all phenomena.
In every lifetime I am born, I shall always dwell in a noble and honored family.
Handsome, powerful, and valiant, surrounded by a full retinue;
from the beginning I was never indolent, but practiced with diligent vigor,
able to purely uphold the prohibitive precepts, and always practiced wisdom with a single-minded focus.
In accordance with the wholesome dharmas I practiced throughout my past lives, may you all receive this retribution; observe it fully and clearly.
Through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, and countless nayutas of eons—
In all those worlds, my wisdom fully penetrates and understands them;
I also know the minds of all sentient beings therein,
as well as their actions and the inclinations of their deep-seated intentions.
I know what is appropriate for them, transforming them with the bodhicitta;
I also know how to discipline their minds and further cause them to blaze forth.
With my Buddha-eye, I behold the minds of the multitudes in this world.
Knowing those who should be taught, he delivers them from within birth and death.
He goes at the appropriate time to preach the Dharma, instructing and guiding them;
manifesting various supernormal powers, he causes them all to attain joy.
If sentient beings are greedily attached to their physical form and wealth,
he manifests various faults for them so that they may thereby attain nirvana.
If people are bound by deep fetters and rely upon various false views...
I also manifest the appearance of having views, so that they may recognize their faults.
According to what sentient beings value, I manifest various forms and colors,
appearing before them to show and lead them to know the true path.
Having attained the Dharma, this person’s heart was filled with joy and increased reverence;
they immediately thought, "This is the Buddha, who has taught and transformed me out of compassion.
Thereupon, they took refuge in me, and further took refuge in the Holy Dharma.
Thereafter, I gradually cause them to attain [liberation], pulling out the arrows of all suffering and affliction.
I preach the Dharma for these people, enabling them to attain the path of quiescence;
hearing my Dharma, these people gradually reach nirvana.
As I know the present, all phenomena are entirely without obstruction;
regarding the past and future worlds, my wisdom is likewise so.
The Buddha’s body is exceedingly vast and tall, such that it cannot be measured or limited.
Even those with great supernormal powers cannot see the crown of his head.
The Buddha’s power is immeasurable and has no limit;
by means of this limitless power, it pervades worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
What is the true form and appearance of the Tathāgata?
Among all classes of sentient beings, none are able to measure it.
If there should be a sentient being who comes, wishing to see the form and appearance of the Buddha—
They see various kinds of bodies, yet cannot grasp their fixed characteristics.
Seeing the Buddha’s transformation body, their minds attain great joy;
to praise me in such diverse ways is indeed an error.
Among all classes of sentient beings, none are able to see the Buddha’s body;
even with the divine eye, they cannot behold it.
What you now behold is the power of the Buddha’s supernormal transformations.
The physical marks of the true Buddha’s body are inconceivable.
The supernatural powers manifested by the Buddha from a single pore,
and the beings he benefits thereby, are likewise beyond thought.
From within a single pore, he emits countless billions of rays of light,
which pass beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
immeasurable in extent. You who now praise me, truly sit here before this assembly.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, each likewise says the same.
Even with my omniscience, as I speak of the power of the Buddha’s wisdom, I cannot exhaust it; how much less so for the śrāvakas!
"The Buddhas are inconceivable, and the Dharma is also inconceivable;
those who can believe this, their reward shall likewise be inconceivable.
At that time, there was a seven-year-old boy in the assembly named Vyavasthāpana. He rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“World-Honored One, I have resolved my mind: May I become like the Dharma King;
Having heard the inconceivable Dharma, I shall put on the great armor of adornment.
I invite all sentient beings To establish a great assembly for the gift of Dharma.”
Having uttered this lion’s roar, he was able to accomplish exactly what he had said:
"World-Honored One, from this day forth, I shall never again crave my family;
now, within the Buddha-dharma, I shall leave the home life to cultivate the True Path."
By practicing the conduct of one who has gone forth, as well as meditative concentration and wisdom, he attained this perfect enlightenment; now I too shall practice and study.
I have conceived a deep longing for it; I pray that you will quickly grant me permission to go forth.
Having shaved my hair and donned the dharma-robes, I shall constantly practice the supreme Dharma.
By the power of knowledge and vision, I shall discern this world;
may I become a World-Honored One—only pray, grant me permission to leave the household life.
I have no perception of a sentient being; because there are no sentient beings, having realized this Dharma, I shall preach it for the sake of sentient beings.
Having shattered the hosts of Māra’s army, I terrify all the non-Buddhists.
Tearing asunder the net of false views, you bring great benefit to the multitude.
I practice the path of peace and bliss, which leads to nirvana;
this path is characterized by non-arising, and is therefore inconceivable.
Having severed the darkness of my own ignorance, may the light of Dharma illuminate the world;
I shall preach the Dharma as it truly is, in accordance with the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
Having attained great supernormal powers, I shall manifest various rare and wondrous events.
“If sentient beings see this, they will gradually sever all doubts.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Vyūha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
"Young man!
You wish to go forth in my Dharma?
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
Thereupon, the Tathāgata spoke these verses:
"Though one does not wear the dyed robes, If the mind is free from attachment,
Then within the Buddha-dharma, This is called true renunciation."
Though one does not remove ornaments and finery, If one can sever all fetters and bonds,
With a mind neither bound nor liberated— This is called true renunciation.
Though one does not receive the prohibitive precepts, If the mind is always free from all evils, [this is true renunciation].
One who opens up the conduct of concentration and wisdom is called a true renunciant.
Though not formally upholding the Dharma, because they are able to dismantle all phenomena and remain detached from the marks of all phenomena, they are called a true renunciant.
If one does not discriminate a self, nor apprehend sentient beings,
and the mind does not sink into despondency, this is called the arousal of bodhicitta. If one arouses the mind of enlightenment,
yet does not apprehend the characteristics of the mind, [this is the true arousal of bodhicitta].
"There is nothing he has not attained and nothing that does not move;
this person cannot be destroyed. At that time, Śāriputra had this thought:
"How long has it been since this youth first resolved his mind [on enlightenment], that the Buddha now preaches such a profound Dharma for him?"
Then Śāriputra addressed the Buddha in verse:
“How much practice has this youth Cunda undertaken,
that upon hearing this most profound Dharma, his mind is not startled or afraid?”
In previous lives, how many Buddhas did this person encounter?
Having heard this most profound Dharma, how was he able to immediately believe and accept it?
From how many Tathāgatas did he hear such a deep teaching?
"Now that I have heard what the World-Honored One has said, my mind does not retreat or sink.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"This youth Cunda, in a former time within this world,"
From immeasurable Buddhas, he has heard this most profound Dharma.
I know that this youth, throughout the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha,
has heard the teachings of all the Buddhas and practices the path of a bodhisattva.
One who can clearly and thoroughly understand the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases,
as well as the three gates of liberation, what is possible and what is impossible;
and whatever Dharma is heard here in Kāśī and Kośala— [he knows all this].
I know and see them all, just as in the case of the two aforementioned kingdoms.
This youth Citta has already reached the further shore of wisdom;
because his wholesome qualities have increased to the utmost, he has attained such knowledge.
In calculation and all arts and crafts, as well as the literary compositions and verses of the world—
all such matters of knowledge— he never forgets or loses them.
There is no wisdom regarding any world that he cannot recall or retain.
The supramundane wisdom is said to be the knowledge that all phenomena are empty.
If a person can thoroughly comprehend the empty nature of all phenomena,
they shall never lose this wisdom, even after passing through immeasurable eons.
"This is called great wisdom, which can extinguish all afflictions.
Those who delight in this knowledge of emptiness have no distress or suffering regarding phenomena.
At that time, Śāriputra asked the youth:
"Do you wish to go forth into homelessness within the Buddha's Dharma? The youth replied,
"I do not wish to go forth!"
"I have now already left the household life.
Then Śāriputra asked in verse:
"I do not see you now wearing the dyed dharma-robes; [how can you say you have gone forth?]"
Nor have you shaved off your hair and beard; how can you say you have left the home life?
You possess no alms bowl, nor do you have a preceptor or an acharya, and you have not received the prohibitive precepts; how can you be called one who has left the home life?
In what assembly was the precepts received? Who performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*)?
This is the sequential method for going forth within the Buddha-dharma.
Since you lack these communal requirements, how can you be called one who has gone forth?
"Regarding all such questions as these, you shall see me answer them according to reality.
Then the youth Vītaśoka replied in verse:
"If one does not wear the saṃghāṭī robe, nor wear what is not the saṃghāṭī robe,"
Not abandoning nor grasping at phenomena, one is said to wear the true kāṣāya.
I have received the kāṣāya of wisdom; it gives rise to no afflictions or distress.
This robe is pure and stainless; I always wear this garment.
Having severed all fetters and latent tendencies, one is thus shaven of hair and beard;
because they are severed by the power of wisdom, they shall not arise again.
My vessel is inconceivable, for it is able to receive all dharmas.
Neither increasing nor decreasing, one constantly maintains all wholesome dharmas.
Practicing wholesome dharmas by oneself, never receiving them from another,
and personally attaining all-encompassing wisdom— this is the full ordination.
The Buddha performed the *karmavācanā* for me; because he contemplates the equality of all phenomena, he constantly practices the Buddha-way and follows after all Buddhas.
This is called my renunciation, and it is also my precept-dharma.
These are my robes and bowl, and they are also the white *karmavācanā*.
My practices are immeasurable; performing deeds within the Honored Dharma, I go from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-land.
"Abiding securely in the site of enlightenment, I shall practice inconceivable giving;
I will never eat alone, but shall always share with immeasurable multitudes.

At that time, the World-Honored One gazed intently at the youth; immediately, the youth’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the saṃghāṭī robe was draped upon his body, as if he had just shaved his head.
After seven days, he attained the five supernormal powers and suddenly vanished from that place.

At that time, this world shook with a great earthquake; sentient beings were filled with fear, celestial drums resounded spontaneously, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments played in unison;
a great radiance shone everywhere, illuminating heaven and earth.

At that time, the Buddha smiled, and from his mouth issued forth immeasurable flames of light in various wondrous colors. They circled the world three times and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
Then Ānanda, baring his right shoulder and joining his palms toward the Buddha, asked him in verse:
"O Supreme Tamer among the Multitudes, Exalted Honored One of sublime merit and virtue, Whose conduct is most excellent— Why do you manifest such a smile?"
With wisdom that penetrates all without obstruction, you now ask about the All-Knowing, Unsurpassed Awakening.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you smile?
The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must be a reason.
Who should receive the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha?
I only pray that the World-Honored One will sever my doubts.
From the mouth of the World-Honored One, a great radiance issued forth, its light universally illuminating all worlds.
Having circled this world-system on all sides, he re-entered through the crown of his head and vanished.
For whom will he bring benefit?
Who shall receive the prophecy of their attainment of the Buddha’s wisdom?
Therefore, the World-Honored One manifests a smile, And a great radiance shines universally upon the Buddha-worlds.
Now this world is entirely adorned, And all sentient beings are filled with joy;
Their minds are tranquil and free from negligence, As he displays such supernatural powers as these.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Do you see this youth Candra, who was clad in the dharma robes, suddenly vanish from this very spot?”
Ānanda replied, “Indeed, I have seen it.

“Ānanda, you should know that once this youth has passed away here, he will immediately appear in the world-system of Abhirati, the buddha-field of Akṣobhya Buddha. There, he will practice the pure conduct of brahmacarya for the full duration of his lifespan, and within that very body, he will further increase his life-span.”
In this way, Śakra Devānām-indra increases his lifespan even within his current body;
the youth Cunda likewise travels from one buddha-field to another in this very body, and continues to increase his lifespan in all those lands.
In this manner, passing through successive eons of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he was never separated from the Buddhas.
In the presence of each Buddha, he manifested his body to further extend his lifespan.
After immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, he shall thereafter attain unsurpassed bodhi and become a Buddha named Mahājñānavicaya; that Buddha-world shall be called Nityāvabhāsa.
Ānanda! The sentient beings of that land never undergo birth from a womb; they are all born by transformation, sitting cross-legged upon lotus flowers.
That Buddha-land is thus adorned with various such wondrous merits and blessings.

“Ānanda! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva, upon changing bodies, shall become a *svāgata-bhikṣu* (a monk who has come well), never again receiving birth from a womb but being born through transformation within a lotus flower, and immediately extending his lifespan in that very body.”
What are the four? One personally delights in leaving the household life, encourages others to do so, and assists them with the causes and conditions for leaving the household life;
having left the household life, one preaches the Dharma for them, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening them—this is called the first dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda,

when a bodhisattva is able to personally and diligently practice the quest for all Buddha-dharmas, and also transforms others to diligently practice the quest for the Dharma, this is the second dharma.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
A bodhisattva practices harmony and patience themselves, and also transforms others, causing them to abide in patience;
this is the third dharma. Furthermore, Ānanda!

The Bodhisattva is able to personally practice skillful means and deeply resolve great vows, and also transforms others, causing them to practice skillful means and resolve great vows; this is the fourth dharma.

Ānanda! If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, upon changing bodies he shall become a "Welcome" (Svāgata) bhikṣu; he will never again undergo conception, but will be born by transformation within a lotus flower, and his lifespan shall continue to increase in this very life.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will never fall back or lose unsurpassed bodhi.
What are these four?
The bodhisattva firmly and deeply resolves upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;
they always delight in seeing the Buddhas and never tire of hearing the Dharma.
One always practices truthful speech and takes no pleasure in deception. Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will never regress from unsurpassed bodhi.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Resolutely and deeply resolve the mind; Always delight in seeing all Buddhas;
Listen to the Dharma without weariness; And always abide within true speech."
Seeing sentient beings in suffering and affliction, he gives rise to a heart of deep compassion;
having understood the minds of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma according to their needs.
This person constantly listens to the Dharma, their mind never weary or satisfied.
Constantly exerting oneself in practice, for the sake of increasing wisdom;
always being sincere and trustworthy, abiding securely within truthful speech,
whatever one says shall never be erroneous.
If one practices and studies these four dharmas according to the occasion,
one shall attain the Bodhi of the Buddha and turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
I declare that within these dharmas, one obtains immeasurable karmic rewards.
Who, having heard such a Dharma as this, would not practice and study it? "Furthermore, Ānanda,
if a bodhisattva mahāsattva accomplishes four dharmas, he will never forget or lose the unsurpassed bodhi, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits will all come to encourage and assist him."
One is never separated from the field of merit of the assembly of noble ones;
if there are no noble ones present, one then becomes a field of merit for oneself within the assembly. What are these four?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva practices with diligent perseverance without slackening, teaching and transforming sentient beings so that they may resolve to attain unexcelled bodhicitta;
he practices with diligent perseverance without slackening in making offerings to the Tathāgatas for the sake of seeking the Dharma;
and with a heart of reverence, he makes offerings to the Dharma-preachers.
If one sees sentient beings who are terrified and afflicted by suffering, one bestows fearlessness upon them. Ānanda!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they shall not lose the thought of awakening in every lifetime.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Serve and honor all Buddhas; Revere and respect the Buddha-dharma; And with a respectful heart, serve and honor the Dharma Master.”
Seeing all beings afflicted by suffering and filled with fear, he immediately bestows fearlessness and rescues them from their distress.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, he constantly succeeds in seeing the Buddhas; the devas exhort him, saying, "You should diligently practice cultivation."
If one does not see the Buddha, nor his disciples, nor the Pratyekabuddhas—
the field of merit for all sages—
one may nonetheless leave the household life by oneself, cultivate the wisdom of cessation, enter profound meditative concentration, and give rise to the five supernormal powers.
Having attained the supernormal powers, he travels through various worlds and enters all villages, causing the multitudes to abide in the Dharma. Upon hearing this,
sentient beings distance themselves from what is unwholesome, refrain from committing evil deeds,
and instead treat one another with mutual respect and compliance.
Sentient beings, by following this, all attain peace and happiness; because he honors the Dharma, I do likewise.
When a person practices the Dharma themselves, they obtain such merit; benefiting both self and others—who would not practice goodness?
Therefore, those who seek the Buddha-way Should practice this Dharma; In the end, they shall not lose the Buddha’s Inconceivable wisdom.
“I originally cultivated this Dharma To cross to the other shore of merit and virtue.”
Having thoroughly realized this Dharma, I have attained unsurpassed Bodhi.
I am truly the Hero of the World and the most supreme in all worlds;
furthermore, I can bestow upon the world unsurpassed, wondrous wisdom.

“Ānanda! For this reason, you should know that when a bodhisattva is able to practice these dharmas for the benefit of sentient beings, they are then able to cultivate and fulfill the Buddha-dharmas.”
Ānanda! In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, right here in this world-system at Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Fangyin (Varṇasvara).
The King’s chief consort gave birth to a crown prince, at which time all the heavenly deities raised their voices in unison, proclaiming:
"A person who practices the Dharma of goodness has now appeared in the world!
When the King heard these words, he was immediately struck with wonder and astonishment.
"What is called 'Dharma' and what is called 'non-Dharma'?
"Ānanda! [the Buddha said.]
As the prince gradually grew up, he reached the age of seven and went to his father the king. He prostrated himself at the king's feet, stood to one side, and asked his father:
"What is the Dharma?"
"What is unrighteousness? Then King Fangyin replied in verse:
"Practicing generosity and upholding the precepts while severing desire, Practicing patience and firmly abiding in all wholesome merits,"
"Avoiding killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these are the dharmas praised by all the noble ones.
At that time, the Prince asked in verse:
"Regarding the dharma taught by my parents, if one remains at home to govern the kingdom..."
Can it be said to be omnipresent?
I pray that you will answer this matter at this time.
Whether it is applicable or not applicable, I only wish for a response in accordance with reality.
Truthful speech crosses over the evil paths; one need not fear falling into hell.
False speech leads to the miserable realms, where one shall suffer the pains of Avīci.
Therefore, do not speak falsely; tell me according to the facts.
Then King Fangyin replied in verse:
"If one rules the country while remaining at home, One cannot fully cultivate all virtues;
Using swords, staves, and whips to harm others— How could there be any Dharma in such a thing?"
If people do not obey my commands, I give rise to anger and harsh speech;
I forcibly seize their wealth and property, imprison them, and inflict cruel punishments upon them.
When I go abroad on excursions, the masses are all struck with fear.
They all thought: "The King is now coming out; what crime have we committed?
If I am sitting in my proper place, the officials will bring the culprit before me and say, 'Treat him as Your Majesty pleases.'"
I have carefully examined their transgressions and have immediately inflicted punishments upon them;
yet, for the sake of others' affairs, I myself give rise to a multitude of karmic offenses.
If I were to be lax, they would obstruct one another, and the realm would fall into chaos and ruin.
Therefore, I govern with rigorous severity, and the people are filled with fear.
It is said that Your Majesty’s majesty is so formidable, and you are so harsh and devoid of compassion,
that who would dare to remain in this kingdom without obeying your commands?
At that time, Prince Dharmacārin, having heard this verse from the king,
conceived a sense of world-weariness and said to the king:
"I wish to practice the Dharma in its entirety."
I do not crave the throne; for another’s sake I have committed sinful karma.
I shall abandon my parents and leave the household life to practice the Dharma.
If the King will not grant me his permission, I shall now take my own life.
"Drink poison, throw yourself from a height, or take your own life with a blade.
Having heard his son's vow, the king was immediately filled with great sorrow and distress, saying:
"Enjoy yourself as you please; I shall attend to the affairs of state."
I shall let you enjoy your wealth at will and sport in the various groves and pavilions;
why must you leave the household life to be mocked by others?
Enjoy the five desires during your prime years; when old age arrives, you may then leave the household life.
"Life is fleeting and its duration cannot be trusted; yet you strive on without ever conceiving a mind of weariness. He replied:

"To experience worldly pleasures without satiety only increases anger and affliction; by leaving the home life and departing from all defilements, one constantly practices loving-kindness and sympathetic joy."
Dwelling alone in the empty wilderness, I shall there give rise to pure joy;
I will rely upon this place to uphold the precepts and cultivate the holy life.
O King, you may go forth together with me—what benefit is there in the multitude of the people?
Having created evil karma for others’ sake, one undergoes the suffering of hell oneself!
Swallowing glowing iron balls and drinking boiling, molten copper—
having given rise to sinful karma through perverse conduct, one wallows within the hells.
Iron nails are driven into their bodies, and they are bound with glowing iron sheets;
furthermore, with iron plows and oxen, their bodies are furrowed and torn asunder.
The hell-wardens are most terrifying, with blue eyes and yellow heads.
They cast the person into the cauldron of boiling water, where they are turned over with iron forks.
Having passed through ten million years, they endure all manner of suffering;
because their karmic offenses are so deep and heavy, they seek death but cannot find it.
If one emerges from the boiling cauldron, one enters again the great fire pit;
fierce flames arise upon the body like the burning of a dry bamboo grove.
If one manages to escape the fire pit, one immediately falls back into a mountain of fire.
Emerging from beneath the volcanic mountain, they enter again the pit of boiling excrement.
Within it, boiling flames arise, and iron-beaked insects devour their bodies for immeasurable billions of years, surging up and sinking down therein.
Having escaped from this, they enter again the forest of bamboo thorns,
where fierce fires and great flames arise, and glowing coals scorch their bodies.
As they enter this forest, great winds blow from all four directions.
They agitate this bamboo forest, piercing and lacerating their bodies.
Having emerged from here, they immediately enter again the Forest of Blades,
where the branches and leaves are like swords and halberds, as well as knives, spears, and pikes.
As soon as one enters this forest, violent winds arise from all four directions,
raining down various sharp blades that slice the body into pieces.
As these swords and spears rain down, they sever the physical form.
For immeasurable billions of years, the bitter poison is unbearable.
