Even if one escapes from this, one immediately enters the River of Ashes;
skin and flesh are completely rotted away, leaving only a chain of skeletal bones.
Having passed through immeasurable eons, they undergo all manner of suffering and distress;
though they may emerge from this, they enter again the River of Molten Copper.
The molten copper overflows and fills the expanse, its surging waves crashing with a thunderous roar.
Whirling around a hundred thousand times, surging like waves and tossing up the spray;
the river flows through the moat of hell, and all the sinners enter within it.
As soon as they fall into this place, they are overturned by the billows.
Unable to reach the bottom of the abyss, one drifts and sinks in the middle of the current;
though perhaps emerging from this, a rākṣasa stands upon the shore.
Yellow-eyed and with long teeth, he seizes and binds them once again.
Having seized him, he asked, "What do you seek? He replied:
"I am famished; food is my foremost need.
Immediately, the wicked rākṣasa placed him upon the ground of glowing iron and forced him to swallow hot iron balls, which scorched and rotted his five internal organs.
Burned from both within and without, they see from afar a great river of ash and mistake it for a cool spring; they rush toward it and cast themselves in.
Even if they should escape from this, they enter again the land of boiling excrement.
The mountain of blades and the pit of fire—through these one revolves in manifold sufferings.
A king’s wealth and nobility are impermanent; before long they shall fall into ruin.
Both life and physical existence, as well as honor and status—the Buddha taught that all are impermanent.
Therefore, you should accept my words: renounce the kingdom together and go forth from home.
At the end of your lives, you shall be reborn in heaven and likewise attain liberation from all sufferings.
Dwelling in seclusion after leaving the household life, cultivate pure precepts and meditative concentration.
Always delighting in the practice of compassion, And cultivating emptiness and cessation;
At that time, one shall know for oneself That there is no one equal to such a person,
Who has attained the peace and bliss of cessation, Just like the Great Brahmā King.
When the Prince spoke thus, neither the King and Queen nor any of the rest of the assembly were able to obstruct him.
Having renounced the household life, the Prince sought the Dharma and practiced meditative concentration.
Endowed with the five supernormal powers, he expounds the Dharma for the multitude.
Cultivating a mind of tranquil extinction, he delights in preaching emptiness and non-self;
that all phenomena are neither bound nor liberated—such is the Dharma he shall proclaim:
"All you people should now, with a single mind, correctly contemplate the Dharma:
within these aggregates, elements, and sense bases, where is there a self or what belongs to a self?
Having heard the Dharma, hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings have gone forth into homelessness."
The father king and his consort likewise went forth into the Dharma.
Having gone forth, this person made such a vow, saying:
"May I attain all those dharmas that the prince seeks."
Those bodhisattvas who followed his teachings all gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve;
according to the Dharma they preached, they attained buddhahood and entered nirvana.
Ānanda, that prince sought the Dharma to transform his parents.
Those who have been established in the Buddha-dharma—do you think they were others?
Ānanda, do not harbor doubts: it was I myself who, for the great benefit of the multitude, established them within the path of the Buddha.
From the time I first resolved my mind upon it, I have always sought the Dharma with single-minded focus;
with diligence and firm resolve, I have never known weariness or rest.
I constantly cultivate this Dharma, never allowing a heart of indolence or exhaustion.
Never giving rise to doubt as to whether one will attain the Buddha-way,
always setting one's mind on and delighting in bodhi, practicing supreme diligence,
and seeking the Dharma with a joyful heart— thereby one attains the most excellent wisdom.
If a person seeks awakening, they should practice and study as I have;
never shall they fall back or suffer loss, for they will become a Buddha and turn the wheel of Dharma.
31. Chapter on the Dharma (9). Chapter Thirty-one: On the Dharma. The Buddha addressed Ānanda:

“Bodhisattvas possess four qualities by which they understand the intended meaning of the teachings they hear, attain wisdom, become capable of receiving the Dharma, achieve firm mindfulness, and become fully endowed with both the meaning and the Dharma.”
What are these four? They are:
to exert diligent effort in practice and seek such profound sūtras and dharmas;
and having obtained these dharmas, to abide in accordance with what has been taught.
Abiding themselves in the Dharma, they are also able to exhort and guide many sentient beings to enter this Dharma;
having entered the Dharma, they are able to explain it for them, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Bodhisattva seeking the profound Dharma Is able to attain unsurpassed bliss;
Until such a Dharma is attained, He shall never grow weary midway.”
Having heard this most profound Dharma, one should contemplate it in solitude;
thus, regarding the Dharma as heard, one should always practice and study with a single mind.
One should be able to transform others, causing them to abide as one does oneself.
"It is not merely by means of words that one guides others through bodily conduct. Furthermore, Ānanda,
for the sake of this Dharma, a bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly follows a Dharma teacher, thinking thus:"
"I might not hear or know the Dharma, and thus it may be inconsistent; I might lose the benefit of this Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If there is a person of much learning, Who always follows and stays close to [the teacher],"
One should regard him as a Dharma King for the sake of cultivating and gathering the Dharma.
If one has not heard the Dharma previously, does not understand its meaning and intent,
or if the causes and conditions are mistaken, then one will lose the benefit of this Dharma.
Generating firm diligence, abandon all desires;
constantly seek the definitive Dharma to increase true wisdom.
Associate with those who possess knowledge, who are learned, and of sharp faculties.
"He shall be revered by the multitude who is able to uphold this sutra. Furthermore, Ānanda,
when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva extensively expounds for others the Dharma as he has heard it, he will not be harmed by that Dharma."
Ānanda! What is it that harms a Dharma?

If there is a bhikṣu who is greedy for various gains and offerings—namely, reputation, robes, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites—and yet praises to others practices such as dhūta, profound pure precepts, and teachings corresponding to emptiness, while being unable himself to practice according to what he has taught, this is called a bhikṣu being harmed by the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“When a bodhisattva hears this Dharma, They should expound it extensively for the great assembly;
They should act as the Buddha acts, And not be harmed by the Dharma.”
Do not speak for the sake of livelihood, nor for the sake of praise;
always with a heart of compassion, preach the unsurpassed Dharma.
Toward suffering sentient beings, give rise to great compassion.
One should preach the Dharma with a single-minded focus for the sake of benefiting sentient beings.
If a person preaches the Dharma to the great assembly for the sake of gain and offerings,
relying on worldly profit, they will be harmed by the Dharma.
One should follow the wise and train according to their instructions;
not being harmed by the Dharma, this is called "upholding the Dharma.
The World-Honored Ones of the ten directions all praise such a person.
“Excellent is your ability to preach the Dharma; you likewise abide within this Dharma.

Furthermore, Ānanda, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva seeks the Dharma, he does not take to heart the faults of the Dharma-preacher—such as his harsh glares, frowning, contempt, or arrogance—but always seeks the Dharma with single-minded devotion, exactly as is appropriate.”
Ānanda! How does a bodhisattva seek the Dharma as it truly is?

If there are teachers and preceptors who instruct according to the Dharma, he dwells within that [instruction], diligently practices to fulfill the Dharma, and serves them with all necessary requisites such as clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal decoctions; this is called a bodhisattva seeking the Dharma as it truly is.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"When a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma, He does not seize upon the faults of the Dharma teacher;
He explains it for others as he has received it, And likewise abides within it himself."
When a bodhisattva seeks the Dharma, they should abide as instructed;
seeking the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, they dwell securely within that Dharma.
Therefore, one who seeks the Dharma should abide as instructed.
This is called the first dharma: namely, being able to practice according to what has been taught.
Thus one can realize nirvāṇa, just as I have explained.
I originally studied this dharma and was thereby able to attain this bodhi.
One should always diligently seek the Dharma and cultivate a heart of reverence for it;
toward those from whom one hears the Dharma, one should conceive the thought that they are the World-Honored One.
One should form this reflection: "This person is my Great Teacher."
This person has guided me, causing me to abide within the path of the True Dharma.
He is my World-Honored One; I shall always accord him with the highest reverence.
Because of this Great Teacher, I have renounced worldly pleasures.
Ānanda, you should know that in a past age,
beyond immeasurable and boundless, inconceivable kalpas ago,
there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Sumeruśikhara-rāja.
After this Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa, there will be a disciple named Viśruta,
of keen faculties and great wisdom. He will preach the Dharma for the sake of the assembly,
definitively resolving the most profound meanings and thoroughly understanding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
Able to reach the other shore of the precepts, Discerning the Abhidharma,
Skillfully cultivating the dharmas of the three trainings, And firmly upholding the treasury of the Buddha-dharma—
The Buddha, King of Mount Sumeru, Empowered him with his supernormal powers.
Seeking the great wisdom of all Buddhas, he thoroughly realized the most profound Dharma.
The merit of this bhikṣu cannot be fully described.
At that time, in the city of Mahāpuṣpa, there was a wealthy and noble elder.
Possessing abundant wealth and property, he is lofty and eminent due to his merit;
his name is "One Who Delights in Goodness," revered and honored by many.
Upholding the precepts and possessing virtuous conduct, his fame spreads far and wide.
At one time, this elder went to the place of Viśvāmitra;
with the wisdom of his vast learning, [the teacher] preached the Dharma to him as was appropriate.
Having heard the Dharma, the elder spoke these words with a joyful heart:
"Whatever wealth I possess, I shall provide it all for you.
Then that bhikṣu said, "Excellent!
You are truly capable of great generosity."
Hearing the Dharma and attaining faith and understanding is the root of the Buddha’s teachings.
Having offered all one's wealth and possessions to the Dharma teacher,
one should constantly follow and serve them for twenty years.
When this Elder Sukṣetra followed the Dharma Master,
he heard various teachings and his mind was never satiated.
He further gave rise to this thought, desiring to provide various offerings and gifts.
When making such offerings and gifts, his mind never grew weary or indolent.
Once, when going to inquire after his health, he took twenty billion pieces of gold and presented them to the Dharma Master, who accepted them all for his own use.
Constantly and repeatedly in this manner, he provided for them according to the occasion;
because of these provisions, his heart attained great joy.
The Dharma Master Viśula and the various disciples he led—
Furthermore, they all provided offerings, each with a thousand taels of gold.
Having presented such amounts of gold, they also each offered three robes;
the value of each individual robe was twenty billion taels of gold.
Furthermore, for the sake of Vīra and the assembly of bhikṣus,
they each constructed dwellings, lofty, vast, and most magnificent.
For each and every stūpa, they expended twenty billion pieces of gold.
The couches and all the bedding were fully provided and magnificently adorned.
The Dharma Master, according to the seasons, constantly preached the Dharma therein,
performing great benefit for the multitude until the end of his life.
This Layman Sukṛta further made offerings to the remains,
cremating them with a multitude of fragrant woods and erecting a stūpa one hundred yojanas in height.
He constructed seven stūpas of the seven precious gems to enshrine the Teacher’s śarīra.
He enshrined [the relics] within a great stūpa, constantly making offerings of flowers and incense.
This Layman Shanle, having made such offerings,
will eventually encounter immeasurable Buddhas and never again fall into the evil realms.
By virtue of these roots of goodness and merit, for eighty billion kalpas he was constantly a Great Brahmā King, and he also always beheld the Buddhas.
Furthermore, for eighty billion kalpas, he was the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
They constantly behold all Buddhas and make various kinds of offerings.
Furthermore, throughout those kalpas, they act as universal monarchs (cakravartin),
always able to see all Buddhas and likewise making profound offerings to them all.
From this point on, in succession, he further encountered immeasurable,
countless, asaṃkhyeya, and nayuta Buddhas. Having encountered these immeasurable Buddhas,
he likewise made immeasurable offerings and services to them.
He was able to inquire about the path of the Buddhas, and the Buddha likewise answered according to the meaning.
Ānanda, do you think that the elder of great renown in the city of Mahāpuṣpa was some other person?
Do not harbor such doubts; it is I myself who am here now.
At that time, in order to fulfill the Buddha-dharma, I served the Dharma Master Viśruta and made such offerings as these.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, one attains unsurpassed bodhi.
The various foundations of merit I have cultivated by providing for the Dharma Master can yield a great fruit and reward that remains inexhaustible even to this day.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, In life after life, I have become increasingly exalted and honored.
I have encountered immeasurable Buddhas And have also heard the teachings of all those Buddhas.
The answers given by those Buddhas Were just like what I am saying now.
"This is called the true path of the Buddha; you all should practice and study it.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary! How rare!"
The Tathāgata, having long ago deeply accumulated the roots of virtue, has always attained honor and nobility throughout past lives.
World-Honored One!
Is the bhikṣu Viśruta still living in the present?
"Is he entering nirvana?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This bhikṣu has not yet entered nirvana; he practices the bodhisattva path within my Dharma."
Ānanda spoke again:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!

That the householder Sukhaśīla, by serving the Dharma-master and through this root of merit, shall attain unsurpassed bodhi, while that Dharma-master has only just now begun to practice the bodhisattva path.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“This Viśvāmitra was unable to resolve upon bodhicitta as I have; he has always sought bodhi by delighting in the Way and has abandoned these ascetic practices.”
Ānanda! Throughout the long night, I have constantly sought anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi by means of the path of suffering.
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I made this vow:

"If there are sentient beings who, having largely followed evil karma, fall into the three evil realms and undergo all manner of sufferings, at that time I shall attain perfect enlightenment and deliver these sentient beings from their afflictions!"
“Ānanda! The vows and practices cultivated by this Viśvāmitra are inexhaustible to describe; they cannot be clarified even by calculation or metaphor.
Having practiced great acts of giving, he deeply resolved his mind upon unsurpassed bodhi, and by means of these roots of goodness, he made such a vow:”

"If, while I am practicing the path to enlightenment, there are sentient beings who have not yet entered the stage of the Dharma, as well as those seeking the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, may all these sentient beings be able to see my body."
"If they hear my name,
they shall all attain the certainty of unsurpassed bodhi.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is this Dharma Master Viśruta, who received those superior offerings of joy and goodness, present now within this great assembly?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The bhikṣu Viśvāmitra, who was among this assembly, is the one standing here before me now.
Chapter 32: Praising the Assembly (9). Chapter Thirty-Two: Praising the Assembly. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
"Now this great assembly is a gathering for those who practice purity.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Ānanda! It is as you have said.
This assembly consists entirely of those who practice purity; that is to say, this assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Ānanda! This great assembly is a lion assembly, a fearless assembly, a great dragon assembly, an extraordinary assembly, and an incomparable assembly.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason is this called the Assembly of Great Beings?”
"Is it the Lion Assembly?
"Ānanda! Because it shatters great ignorance regarding all phenomena, benefits immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, and gives rise to great vows, it is called the Great Being’s Assembly."
Because these bodhisattvas have donned the great armor and are able to encompass all the teachings of the Buddhas, this assembly is called the "Lion Assembly.
Furthermore, Ānanda!
Just as when the lion king dwells within a deep valley, no small insects or beasts can approach his location, for they cannot endure the power of his breath or the sound of his roar.
If anyone should come near, upon hearing their breath or voice, they would all immediately fall prostrate on the ground. Ānanda!

This assembly of Bodhisattvas, this assembly of great beings, this assembly of great lions, this extraordinary assembly, and this peerless assembly is likewise so; wherever it may be, Māra, or the gods of Māra, or those sent by Māra, shall not be able to harass or approach them. Should any come near, they will immediately experience suffering and affliction; struck with fear and remorse, they will retreat and vanish, unable to endure the great spiritual power and virtue of the Bodhisattvas.
“Ānanda! Just as when the lion king roars three times, his voice is heard throughout one yojana, penetrating one yojana both above and below.
Ānanda! This lion’s roar causes even the young lions to be filled with fear, let alone other birds and beasts!
Even the white fragrant elephant kings, upon hearing its roar, are likewise struck with terror; they cannot control themselves and let out great, piercing cries.

Ānanda! This assembly of bodhisattvas, this great assembly of lions, this assembly of those who are fearless—those who are newly trained and merely nominal bodhisattvas are like young lions who, upon hearing a great roar, immediately crouch down and hide away.

“Ānanda! Among this great assembly, there are many evil bodhisattvas who are greedily attached to gain and offerings and who seek wide renown. Upon hearing the profound Dharma spoken by the Great Bodhisattva, they are all greatly terrified and fall into deep pits and ravines.”

Why is this? Because these great bodhisattvas proclaim the sounds of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, whereas the lesser bodhisattvas are attached to the self, the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases; they are also attached to morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom; they are attached to the fruits of the various paths, and they are likewise attached to nirvana and the Buddhas, and thus they are unable to endure or receive [this teaching].
“Ānanda! Within the Buddha-dharma, what are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
Although I speak of emptiness, therein no dharma is empty, nor does anything belong to it; there is nothing by which it is made empty, nor is there any location for it.”

Ānanda! When I speak of the signless, herein there is no dharma that can be named "signless," nor is there anything to which it belongs, nor is there any dharma that serves as the signless, nor is there any location.

Ānanda! When I speak of "non-action," there is no dharma therein that can be named non-action; it belongs to nothing, nor is there any dharma that constitutes non-action, nor does it have any location.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of dharmas that can be abandoned, herein there is no dharma to be abandoned, nor is there one who abandons; there is no use for abandoning, nor is there any place where abandonment occurs.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of this Dharma that can be realized, within it there is no Dharma to be realized, nor is there one who realizes; there is no Dharma used for realization, nor is there any place where realization occurs.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of this as a dharma that can be cultivated, within it there is no dharma to be cultivated, nor is there a cultivator; there is no utility for cultivation, nor is there a place for cultivation.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of this as a dharma that is dispersed and destroyed, therein there is no dharma that can be destroyed, nor is there any destroyer; there is no dharma used for destruction, nor is there any place of destruction.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is no phenomenon that is conditioned; furthermore, there is nothing to which it belongs and nothing for which it is used that constitutes a conditioned phenomenon.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of these unconditioned dharmas, within them there is no unconditioned dharma; nor does this unconditioned dharma have any belonging, nor does it have any function.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of defiled phenomena, therein is no phenomenon that is defiled, nor is there anything to which it belongs, nor is there any function of such a defiled phenomenon.

Ānanda! Although the Tathāgata speaks of the pure dharma, within it there is no dharma that is pure; nor is there anything to which it belongs, nor anything for which it is used—this is the pure dharma.
Ānanda! This is called the seal of all dharmas, the indestructible seal; it is unchangeable, and within this seal there is no mark of a seal.
“Ānanda! If bodhisattvas are able to attain this seal, they are called true lions among men, those who can walk alone, and those who are without fear.”
With the lion’s roar, they terrify all non-Buddhists, causing them to cower and hide;
they subdue the hosts of Māras, reaching beyond the grasp of those who are greedily attached;
they frighten those of overweening pride and shake those with views of self, while remaining unswayed by the emissaries of Māra and bringing joy to the sons of the Buddhas.

They are able to open the treasury of the Buddha-dharma for all sentient beings of the ten directions; they can erect the banner of the Dharma, beat the great Dharma drum, and blow the great Dharma conch, enabling all the sons of the Buddha to drink the flavor of the Dharma, discern the gift of Dharma, expound the teaching, and enter it with sufficiency and skill.
“Ānanda! Just as the lion king emerges from his dwelling and roars three times,
the lion’s cub, having heard this sound, leaps with joy and without fear, looking toward the four quarters.”

Ānanda! This assembly of great wise lions, this assembly free from fear, this assembly of great wise men, consists of true bodhisattvas who have deeply resolved upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment;

even if their roots of goodness are not yet matured, should they hear such a lion’s roar regarding the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, they will not be startled or afraid, but will further increase in joy.
“Ānanda! Just as the lion king strides alone without fear wherever he dwells, so too is this Great Assembly of Lions, the Fearless Assembly.
Therein, those who have conceived the great armor for the Buddha-dharma, who have conceived peerlessness, and who possess non-dual armor, form this thought:”
"I shall alone attain unexcelled bodhi; I shall have no equal companion as I realize all Buddha-dharmas. "Ānanda!
It is like a lioness of the lion king who, when she is pregnant, conceives only once and not twice."

Ānanda! This is the Assembly of Lions, the Assembly Free from Fear, the Great Bodhisattva Assembly; all the bodhisattvas therein have resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind and shall never again give rise to thoughts of the two vehicles.
Ānanda! Just as when the lion king wishes to harm various beasts, whether large or small, he exerts his strength equally against them all. Ānanda!

All the teachings spoken in this assembly of lions, this assembly free from fear, and this assembly of great bodhisattvas, are intended to cause all to understand equally with a single mind. Therefore, Ānanda!
"This great assembly is called the Lion Assembly.

Chapter 33: On Supreme Firm Virtue (9). Chapter Thirty-Three: On Supreme Firm Virtue. At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Dṛḍhamati. He rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Because I wish to make offerings to this Dharma of the sutra, and because I also wish to make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time as well as to all bodhisattvas who study this Dharma, and because I also wish to encourage and assist them so that their roots of goodness may increase.
"For this reason, I now offer what I hold most precious to the World-Honored One!
He immediately scattered his upper robe over the Tathāgata, and then, holding his middle robe, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I now offer this robe to the World-Honored One; may it be that in future lives, wherever I hear this Dharma from others, I shall likewise offer this robe to them out of respect for the Buddha’s intention."
Immediately, Dṛḍhamati went to the bhikṣu Tāraka and said: "O virtuous friend!
Because the Buddha has praised me, let us together offer this robe to the Tathāgata."
He then took this robe together with Xingde, desiring to offer it to the Buddha in order to increase their roots of goodness.
At that moment, the Tathāgata manifested great supernormal powers, and Ānanda, along with the fourfold assembly, all beheld within the robe the various miraculous transformations of the Tathāgata.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “It is rare,
World-Honored One!”
Although the Tathāgata already knew this, he asked: "Ānanda,
what meaning do you see that you call it 'rare'?"
At that time, Ānanda, wishing to clarify this matter, addressed the Buddha in verse:
"In these robes we see immeasurable bodhisattvas, Who, with courageous hearts, have resolved upon bodhicitta; Having praised the Buddha, they have flown away."
Furthermore, they see all the bodhisattvas taking from within this robe immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *asaṃkhyeya* kinds of robes;
having taken these various robes, they immediately offer them to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
I have seen in various places those who, through immeasurable supernormal powers,
offered robes to the Buddha; the Buddha bestowed predictions upon them all,
saying that these people shall gradually practice the Path and all shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Wherever they may dwell, they are all able to purify Buddha-fields;
each and every sentient being thinks, "The Buddha has attained enlightenment in this very place.
Furthermore, they behold immeasurable billions of various kinds of musical performances.
From this, the sound of the Dharma issues forth; in the air, I hear the voice of the Buddha.
I behold the three thousandfold world-system, filled entirely with Buddhas.
World-Honored One, as I now reflect, I consider myself no longer a śrāvaka.
The power of your supernormal faculties is rare and wondrous, dazzling the eyes and minds of me.
Now, by means of noble wisdom, I contemplate that the three realms are entirely empty;
regarding this wisdom of emptiness, as well as the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising, [I am now liberated].
Among such manifold wisdoms, he never loses right mindfulness;
yet, due to the faculties resulting from karmic retribution, there may be errors therein.
The fourfold assembly is filled with joy as they fly through the air.
They all sit upon thousand-petaled lotus flowers made of various jewels.
Furthermore, within these robes, one sees the Buddhas,
the World-Honored Teachers of the ten directions, surrounded by their great assemblies.
Furthermore, I see various superior beings practicing inconceivable giving;
for the sake of seeking Bodhi, they constantly draw near to all Buddhas.
Knowing that through these causes and conditions they are able to bring great benefit to sentient beings, [I rejoice].
They are able to manifest themselves throughout the ten directions, preaching the Dharma everywhere.
What I see within my robe is inexhaustible; seeing the Bodhisattvas therein, I rejoice and pay them reverent homage.
Like the Brahma King in his sovereignty, they have fully realized the power of supernatural penetrations;
possessing great learning and vast eloquence, they have all attained dhāraṇīs.
Turning the wheel of the Buddha’s true wisdom, they do so throughout the ten directions.
Furthermore, I see all the bodhisattvas, In all the worlds where they roam,
Which have all been transformed into various jewels, Adorned with flowers, incense, and every ornament.
I see the Buddhas seated at the site of enlightenment, Turning the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Thus, through the Buddha’s supernatural power, all these appear within his robes;
able to manifest various forms throughout all worlds,
he preaches the Dharma for the benefit of beings, causing them all to abide in Bodhi.
What we see now is rare; this matter is difficult to believe.
The Buddha’s spiritual power is immeasurable, able to manifest for all sentient beings.
The Buddha is a supreme field of merit, the foremost among those who receive offerings.
The giver obtains great fruit and is able to sever all suffering.
Even if I were to praise this for ten million kalpas, I could never exhaust it.
For whose sake did you manifest such deeds of supernatural power?
Who shall purify the Buddha-fields and cultivate this bodhisattva path?
Who has attained such supernormal powers?
I pray that the Buddha will sever my doubts.
Lotus flowers made of the seven treasures, as large as chariot wheels,
with various bodhisattvas seated upon them, travel through the air to the ten directions;
having paid homage to the Buddhas, they return here and immediately attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
The world is vast, pure, and serene, manifesting inconceivable power.
Within this world, I see a bodhisattva who diligently advances toward enlightenment, standing with a robe held in his hand.
I pray that the Buddha will explain this matter: how should one practice and train?
It must be that in the past they practiced immeasurable giving, and also cultivated immeasurable hearts of sympathetic joy;
wishing to share these with all sentient beings, they now see that all have attained happiness.
The World-Honored One has explained this matter for me, severing all doubts in the minds of the assembly;
therefore, O Bhikṣu, you have made this vow: "Shall I become the Star-Attainer of Firm Resolve?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Wait a moment! The Bodhisattva Resolute Mind wishes to ask a question; I shall answer this later."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a question; if the Buddha would grant me leave, I would venture to consult you.”
The Buddha told Dṛḍhamati:
"Ask whatever you wish; I shall explain it for you so that you may attain joy.
Then Dṛḍhamati said:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called ‘entering the Dharma-gate,’ what is meant by ‘Dharma’ and what is meant by ‘gate’?”
How does one enter?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this in full detail: what is called the Dharma, what is called the gate, how one thus enters, and who is called the one who enters.
At that time, Resolute Mind (Dṛḍhamati) asked in verse:
"What is the supreme Dharma?
What is the gateway to the Dharma?"
How does one enter this gate?
I pray that you will answer this meaning:
how does one enter this gate so as to be able to attain the Buddha’s bodhi?
How is it that when preaching the Dharma, your eloquence is inexhaustible?
From where does this Dharma come, and where does it now abide?
How is it that regarding all phenomena, your mindfulness is never mistaken?
What is called "entering the signs"?
What is called "having entered"?
And when teaching the Dharma, how do all phenomena appear before one?
When preaching various dharmas, how is it that the mind is not distracted?
How is it that for immeasurable kalpas, their eloquence never falters?
What is the aspiration and pursuit of such bodhisattvas?
How is it that this bodhisattva, having preached the Dharma boundlessly, remains free from overweening pride? How did he dedicate his past offerings so that,
in every lifetime when he preaches the Dharma, his eloquence never falters?
How does one uphold the precepts?
How does one purely cultivate the precepts?
How does one dedicate the precepts so that the mind does not become weak or inferior?
How does one practice patience?
How does one cultivate patience?
By means of this, one is able to reach the inexhaustible, unsurpassed limit.
How does one arouse diligence?
How should one practice cultivation?
So that, throughout every successive life, one may never be separated from the Buddha’s bodhi.
How does one give rise to meditative concentration? How does one cultivate it?
By contemplating what dharma within concentration can one attain inexhaustible eloquence?
How does one seek wisdom and cultivate it through close association?
Where does this wisdom reside so that one attains uninterrupted eloquence?
Abiding in the unsurpassed wholesome dharmas, one proclaims the true reality of all phenomena.
They contemplate the Buddha’s wisdom, Profound, quiescent, and empty.
Though they recite various sūtras And resolve their definitive meanings,
They do not wish to expound them, Because they are devoid of true knowledge.
I ask the Buddha about this meaning, so that he may sever all the doubts of the multitude.
In future ages, there will be various Dharma masters;
how should one draw near to them?
What is the Dharma of inquiry?
What is the practice of the Dharma?
What is the protection of the Dharma?
"By means of the power of the possible and the impossible, please explain this meaning for me,
so that I may sever all doubts regarding the future for all sentient beings.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind:
“Excellent, excellent! You are able to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this most profound meaning.
In the presence of immeasurable Buddhas of the past, you have long planted the roots of virtue, making offerings, paying homage, inquiring, and posing questions.”

Dṛḍhamati! I recall that in the past, within the expanse of space in this world-system, you once questioned sixty-eight thousand Buddhas regarding such a meaning. When those Buddhas answered the meaning of your questions, immeasurable sentient beings attained great benefit.
Therefore, you should know that you have deeply planted roots of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgatas of the past.
Resolute Mind!

In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Ratnarcis Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, whose lifespan was half a kalpa.
There was an assembly of seven billion arhats, all of whom had exhausted their outflows and attained mastery over their minds.
The Buddha Ratnārcis, together with this great multitude, traveled through various kingdoms and towns, dwelling together in retreat.
At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was vast and expansive, measuring seventy thousand yojanas in length and breadth.
At that time, there was in the world a consecrated Kṣatriya universal monarch named Uttarakūṭaśrī, who ruled over the four continents.

“Dṛḍhamati! At that time, there were eight billion cities in Jambudvīpa, all of which were vast and expansive, forty yojanas long and thirty yojanas wide; they were peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, with a flourishing population.”

Within Jambudvīpa there is a great city, eighty yojanas in length and breadth, equal on all sides; its streets and lanes are straight and their alignments are symmetrical, and each individual street or lane is five li wide.
Within it was a small city named An-yin (Peaceful Security), where King Śūradatta resided. "Firm Mind!
Beside this great city were seventy thousand groves that belonged to no one, where sentient beings gathered to sport and enjoy themselves."
There was a great garden, eighty yojanas square in extent, where the king went for excursions and observation.
It was surrounded on all sides by seven tiers of jewel trees, and it was likewise covered above by seven tiers of nets made of the seven precious gems.
Between the trees were seven layers [of railings], likewise made of the seven treasures, and seven layers of walls and seven layers of precious moats surrounded them on all sides.
At that time, the Buddha Ratnārcis, respectfully surrounded by a multitude of seventy billion arhats, traveled through various kingdoms and arrived at the city of Kṣemavatī.

When King Dṛḍhadharman heard that the Buddha and his great assembly were traveling through various kingdoms and had arrived at this city, his heart was filled with great joy. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.

At that time, that Buddha, observing the king’s profound mind and the causal conditions of his past conduct, immediately preached for him the *Bodhisattvapitaka Sūtra* titled "Severing the Doubts of Sentient Beings and Causing the Multitude to Rejoice."
Upon hearing the Dharma, King Adṛśyadharman was filled with joy and thought to himself:
"I should now adorn this garden with all manner of exquisite things and offer it to the Tathāgata, so that he may accept and enjoy it."
Thereupon, he constructed seventy billion monastic dwellings within that place, with exquisite robes covering the ground.
There were seventy billion places for walking meditation (caṅkrama), as well as seventy billion beds, couches, and bedding.
Having completed all these preparations, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet,
and said to him: “I pray only that the World-Honored One,
out of compassion for me and for the great assembly, will accept my invitation for tomorrow.”
The Buddha Ratnārcis silently granted his permission.
Knowing that he had accepted, the king prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him to the right, and departed.
That very night, for the sake of the Buddha and the Sangha, he prepared various offerings and diverse delicacies—the flavors of food enjoyed by a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin).
"At dawn he went to the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
'The meal is prepared; we pray that you will know the time.
Then the Buddha Ratnārcis put on his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded with reverence by seven billion great arhats, proceeded to the garden and sat down in due order."

When King Uttarakṣema saw that the Buddha and the assembly of monks were seated, he personally served various kinds of delicious foods, providing whatever they required until everyone was fully satisfied.
Knowing that the Buddha and the Sangha had finished their meal, washed their hands, and set aside their bowls, he offered a robe each to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Having made this offering, he personally took a golden vessel, washed the Tathāgata’s hands, and spoke these words:

"I offer this garden, along with all the dwellings, places for walking meditation, couches, bedding, and the park-keeper, to the Buddha and the Sangha; may you please accept and use them. Furthermore, I shall provide for the Buddha with my own person."
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:

“King Adhimātradhara provided for the Buddha Ratnarcis, coming regularly morning and evening at all times to listen to the Dharma. This continued for half an eon, during which he questioned that Buddha regarding the causal continuity of all phenomena; the Buddha answered each question, benefiting immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.”
Dṛḍhamati! Do you think that the one who was then the Cakravartin King Uttamadṛḍhaguṇa was anyone else?
Do not entertain such a view; he was none other than yourself.

Dṛḍhamati! I recall that in a past life, because you heard this Dharma, you made unsurpassed offerings to a thousand Buddhas. Now, the Tathāgata shall likewise preach this Dharma-gate for you, so that you may enter into the characteristics of phenomena.
The Flower Hand Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Nine.
The Flower Hand Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin Dynasty, by Imperial Decree.
34. Chapter on the Dharma-Gates (10). Chapter Thirty-Four: On the Dharma-Gates.
The Buddha addressed Resolute Mind:

"Dharma is named as being without thought, without deliberation, without marks, without action, without recollection, and without mindfulness; it is pure, subtle, and without conditions; it possesses no letters and is beyond verbal expression, and cannot be demonstrated."
Dṛḍhamati! All dharmas do not conjoin with the faculties; they cannot be known by wisdom, nor can they be known by the absence of wisdom; they are neither knowable nor unknowable.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
The Dharma is called that which is formed by a multitude of conditions; the Tathāgata is able to know this, yet the Tathāgata’s knowledge is ineffable.
Nevertheless, by means of these ineffable dharmas, the Tathāgata speaks of all these dharmas; whatever path is spoken is itself a Dharma-gate."
Why is this? Because the seal of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) stamps all dharmas, causing them to become of one single flavor.
Resolute Mind!
All phenomena are inexhaustible, because the limit of exhaustion itself is inexhaustible.
Resolute Mind!
All phenomena ultimately neither increase nor decrease, for they enter the limit of exhaustion.
For this reason, the Tathāgata provides analytical explanations through language and written characters. "Dṛḍhamati!
The letter-gateway 'A' enters into all phenomena; by means of the letter-gateway 'A,' one analytically discerns all phenomena."
First one enters the gateway of the letter A, and thereafter the other letters follow in succession.

For this reason, it is said that all letters emerge from the side of the letter A, and all phrases are formed by the conjunction of these letters; because of these phrases, all meanings can be established. Therefore, the Tathāgata taught that the gateway of the letter A enters into all phenomena.
Dṛḍhamati! This is a Dharma-gate. What is this Dharma?

Dṛḍhamati! That which is called "Dharma" is, from the very beginning, without action, without speech, and without demonstration; it is known because there is no knowing, spoken because there is no speaking, and demonstrated because there is no demonstrating.
In this way, the letter A can produce all speech; this is called a Dharma-gate.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family enters this gate, they will attain inexhaustible wisdom and inexhaustible eloquence.

That which is inexhaustible is exhaustless in the past; within this exhaustless exhaustion there is no mark and no teaching. All that is known is non-knowing, all that is shown is non-showing, and all that is differentiated is non-differentiation; therefore, it is called inexhaustible.
Dṛḍhamati! This is called a gate. What gate is it?
These are the gateways to the Dharma. What is this Dharma?
It is that which the Buddha did not attain.
Furthermore, this gate consists of contemplating all phenomena as entering into the state beyond thought. Why is this?
Because all speech is not speech; all verbal expressions are inexhaustible; all words are like suchness and do not depart from suchness; and all wisdom is not wisdom.
"Vīradatta! These are called vajra-words.
For what reason are they called vajra-words?"
If a phenomenon is without action, it cannot be destroyed; because it cannot be destroyed, it is called a "vajra phrase.
All phenomena are without karma; if there is no karma, there is no retribution.
Therefore, the Tathāgata says that all phenomena are without karma and without retribution—this is called the Seal of the Dharma.
Whatever karma the Tathāgata has taught and whatever retribution he has taught, all are sealed with this seal; this seal cannot be destroyed.
Resolute Mind!
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to know the retribution of karma, they should enter through this gate.
“Dṛḍhamati! All dharmas neither come nor go; this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate.
By means of this gate, I preach the distinctions of birth and death for the sake of sentient beings.”

Dṛḍhamati! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family wishes to enter into the wisdom regarding the birth and death of sentient beings, they should enter by means of this seal. This is called the Dharma-seal; it is called the seal of no-letters and the seal of non-obstruction.
Dṛḍhamati! Whatever the Tathāgata speaks is all sealed with this seal:
that all who possess bodies are the body of the Tathāgata.

Why is this? Because the natures of these bodies do not conflict with one another; the Buddha, by means of this seal, explains the characteristics of the bodies of sentient beings, and this is called the "body-seal" (kāyamudrā).
Furthermore, by means of this seal, he reveals and expounds upon all bodily characteristics.
Why is this? Resolute Mind!
All dharmas have no gate, for they cannot be entered.
The Dharma cannot be entered because it does not emerge;
all phenomena have no emergence because they cannot be entered.

Therefore, whatever the Tathāgata may teach, it never departs from this teaching on the limit of non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇakoṭi*). He teaches all phenomena by means of this limit of non-obstruction, and through this very limit, he knows all sentient beings and teaches them according to their needs.

“Dṛḍhamati! That which is the limit of non-obstruction is the limit of the boundless; that which is the limit of the boundless is the nature of all sentient beings. This is called the gateway of the limit.”
Upon entering this gateway of the ultimate limit, one is able to expound upon ten trillion treasuries of Dharma.
These treasuries of Dharma, however, are not treasuries at all.
Resolute Mind!
Within the Tathāgata’s treasury of all dharmas, whatever teachings are spoken, they all speak of this limit (koṭi).

Furthermore, there is the treasury of form, and the treasuries of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these treasuries, non-treasuries, and non-sovereign treasuries—these are called the various treasuries entered through the gateway of the letter A.
At that time, Resolute Mind addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This gate is profoundly deep.”
The Buddha said,
“Dṛḍhamati! I do not give rise to the thought that this is deep or that is shallow.”
“World-Honored One!
Does the Buddha preach the Dharma? “Firm Mind!
It is not as it is described by the attachments of ordinary people; rather, it accords with what the wise understand, and is thus called the Tathāgata’s teaching of the reality of dharmas.
That which the Tathāgata knows according to reality cannot be demonstrated, nor can it be spoken.
Why is this? All dharmas possess an ineffable nature, which only the wise can know.
If ordinary beings have any knowledge, they are all attached to words and phrases.
Therefore, the Buddha said that words and speech are not speech.
The Buddha further addressed Resolute Mind:
“All dharmas are as bright and pure as the sun; according to one’s correct contemplation of them, they all enter the boundless.”
Dṛḍhamati! All dharmas are capable of illuminating, for they can give rise to the light of all wisdom. Dṛḍhamati!
All dharmas are without obstruction, for they are like space.
Resolute Mind!
Following after dualistic dharmas, therein the Tathāgata exercises his unobstructed eye. Resolute Mind!
This is called the Dharma-eye.
With this eye, the Buddha perceives all phenomena without any obstruction. Resolute Mind!
This is called the gate of non-obstruction of all phenomena.

If good sons or good daughters enter this gate, all that they speak will be beneficial, free from all obstructions, revealing the essential meaning, expounding profound significance, and being devoid of any attachment.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
All dharmas are stainless, neither defiled nor separate [from purity].
Resolute Mind!"
Dharmas have no ownership, because they are not grasped.
Resolute Mind!
All dharmas are boundless, for their beginning and end cannot be apprehended.
Dṛḍhamati! You should know that regarding all that is spoken in terms of written characters and speech, within these there are no written characters and no speech. Dṛḍhamati!
"How is there entry into this gateway of letters?
It is simply by explaining that these dharmas are without obstruction; this is called 'entry.
Resolute Mind!"
One who enters in this manner is said to be "non-entry," because they enter into the dharma-nature.
"Resolute Mind!
As for the various gates of samādhi spoken of by the Tathāgata, what are they?"
Dṛḍhamati! There is the samādhi of a single characteristic and the samādhi of manifold characteristics.
Regarding the samādhi of a single characteristic: there is a bodhisattva who hears that in a certain world there is a certain Tathāgata currently preaching the Dharma.

The Bodhisattva takes the form of a certain Buddha and brings it before him—whether that Buddha is seated at the site of enlightenment having attained unsurpassed bodhi, or turning the wheel of Dharma, or preaching the Dharma surrounded by a great assembly.

Taking such a form, with undistracted mindfulness he restrains his sense faculties; his mind does not wander, but remains single-mindedly focused on that one Buddha without abandoning this object of focus, while also recollecting the characteristics of that Buddha’s world-system.
Furthermore, this bodhisattva thoroughly realizes the signlessness of both the marks of the Tathāgata and the marks of the world.

Constantly practicing in this way and constantly contemplating in this way, never departing from these conditions, at that time the image of the Buddha will appear before them and preach the Dharma for them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva gives rise to profound reverence and listens to and receives this Dharma; according to their faith and understanding—whether deep or shallow—they further increase their devotion and honor toward the Tathāgata.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they hear it taught that all dharmas possess the characteristic of decay and disintegration.
Having heard this, they receive and uphold it; then, arising from the samādhi, they are able to expound this Dharma for the fourfold assembly.
"Resolute Mind!
This is called entering the gate of the samādhi of the single characteristic.
Furthermore, Resolute Mind!"
When a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, he is further able to destroy and eliminate these signs of a Buddha that serve as objects of perception, as well as his own body;
by means of this destruction of signs, he destroys all dharmas.
Because he destroys all dharmas, he enters the samādhi of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa-samādhi*).
Arising from this samādhi, one is able to explain this Dharma for the sake of the fourfold assembly.
Resolute Mind!
This is called the skillful means for entering the gate of the samādhi of the single characteristic.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
A bodhisattva, taking this image of the Buddha as an object of focus, forms this thought:
'From where has this image come?'"
"Where am I going? He then realized that the Buddha-image had come from nowhere and that he himself had gone nowhere.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:
"All dharmas are likewise thus: they come from nowhere and go nowhere.
When a bodhisattva practices and contemplates in this manner, before long they shall attain the unimpeded Dharma-eye;
having attained the Dharma-eye, they will be known and remembered by all Buddhas, and all profound dharmas will manifest before them.
By means of this profound Dharma, one attains unimpeded eloquence; though one expounds the Dharma, one does not perceive any dharma.
Resolute Mind!

The Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom regarding past lives, as well as his wisdom regarding all marks, is without obstruction. With respect to past lives, he does not create conditions, yet it is not that he lacks knowledge; he does not follow after recollections or conceptualizations.
Dṛḍhamati! It is the same for a bodhisattva: while abiding in this samādhi, although they expound the Dharma, they do not perceive these dharmas as real entities.
Because the bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi and practices it deeply, according to the causes they have heard, they take up the signs of a second Buddha, which appear before them.

Whether the Buddha sits at the site of enlightenment and attains unsurpassed bodhi, or turns the wheel of Dharma, or preaches the Dharma while surrounded by a great assembly, the Bodhisattva likewise upholds this second Buddha-dharma; he does not abandon the original marks of the Buddha, yet he also perceives this [second] Buddha. Thus, the Bodhisattva takes both Buddhas as objects of focus, apprehending their forms as manifest before him, and listens to and receives the preaching of the Dharma.
“Dṛḍhamati! This is also called ‘entering the gate of the samādhi of the single characteristic.
Furthermore, Dṛḍhamati!”

Because a bodhisattva has skillfully cultivated the marks of a single Buddha, they attain mastery according to their will; whenever they desire to see all Buddhas, those Buddhas can appear before them.
Resolute Mind!

It is, for example, like a bhikṣu who has attained mastery of mind: when he contemplates the "all-entrances" (kṛtsnāyatana) by grasping the mark of the color blue, he is able to attain faith and understanding that all worlds are a single blue mark.

The object of focus for this person is solely the color blue; they perceive all internal and external phenomena as being uniformly blue because they have attained mastery over that object of focus, O Resolute Mind!

The Bodhisattva is also like this: according to the names of the Buddhas he hears and the worlds in which they reside, he immediately grasps the characteristics of those Buddhas and their worlds, all of which appear before him as objects of focus.
Because the Bodhisattva skillfully cultivates this object of mindfulness of the Buddha, he perceives all worlds as being entirely composed of Buddhas;
because he constantly and skillfully cultivates the power of this contemplation, he is able to comprehend that all conditions are but a single condition—namely, the condition of the present Buddha.
"This is called attaining the gate of the samādhi of one characteristic.
Resolute Mind addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
“By what skillful means can this samādhi be attained?
The Buddha told Resolute Mind:
“In this regard, the Buddha focuses his mindfulness upon an object, neither scattering nor departing from that object; this is called the gateway to samādhi.”

Dṛḍhamati! By means of this single condition, one thoroughly comprehends all dharmas and perceives that all dharmas possess an identical characteristic; this is called the Samādhi of the Single Characteristic.

When a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, they further enter a dharma-gate: namely, that all speech is the speech of the Tathāgata, and all embodied beings are the body of the Tathāgata, for they do not depart from suchness.
"Furthermore, Dṛḍhamati!

When a bodhisattva hears the names of various Buddhas—whether two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, or more than that number—if they single-mindedly recollect them all at once, they will appear before them; as well as the worlds and the numbers of their assemblies of disciples, all appearing before them, whom they revere and respect.
They also recollect these Buddhas as possessing complete and wondrous bodies, with their physical forms, marks, and signs, all appearing before them, whom they revere and respect."

Furthermore, one takes each of the thirty-two marks of a great man, as well as the mark of non-empty conduct, the mark of the lion’s majestic stride, the mark of the invisible crown of the head, the mark of the elephant king’s gaze, and the mark of great radiance, and through the contemplation of resolute belief, transforms them into immeasurable marks;
likewise, one takes the marks of the buddha-fields and, through the contemplation of resolute belief, transforms them into immeasurable pure marks;
and likewise, one takes the assembly of disciples and, through the contemplation of resolute belief, transforms them into immeasurable marks.
At that time, he reflected thus:
"From where have these Buddhas come? And where shall I go?"
He immediately realizes that all Buddhas as well as his own body come from nowhere and go nowhere.
Observing and knowing thus, and understanding with faith thus, the Bodhisattva then reflects:
"In such matters, there is no fixed dharma called 'Tathāgata'."

When observing in this way, one knows that all phenomena are empty and non-existent, characterized by a single mark which is marklessness. By employing the gate of marklessness, one enters into all phenomena; through such faith and understanding, one penetrates and realizes that all dharmas possess a single mark.
“Dṛḍhamati! When a bodhisattva is able to take all buddhas as objects and bind their mindfulness to a single point, this is called the samādhi-door of manifold signs. Dṛḍhamati!”
If a bodhisattva enters this samādhi and thoroughly realizes that all dharmas are of one mark, which is the markless, this is called the Samādhi of All Marks.
When a bodhisattva abides in this samādhi, everything known and seen is none other than the Tathāgata, yet they neither see nor know the Tathāgata;
everything known and seen is none other than the Dharma, yet they do not see the Dharma.
All that is known and seen consists of the Buddha’s disciples, yet one neither sees nor knows the assembly of the Buddha’s disciples;
all that is known and seen is nothing other than the teaching of the Dharma, yet one likewise neither sees nor knows the teaching of the Dharma;
all that is seen and known is nothing other than conditions, yet one does not see conditions.
All that is seen or known is none other than eloquence, yet one does not perceive eloquence;
all that is seen is none other than a buddha-field, yet one does not perceive a buddha-field;
all that is seen is none other than a world-system, yet one does not perceive a world-system.
All views whatsoever are not other than the assembly, yet one does not perceive an assembly.

There is no dharma that is not spoken, yet there is nothing spoken; no dharma that is not manifested, yet there is nothing manifested; no lack of faith-and-understanding, yet no faith-and-understanding; no lack of discernment, yet no discernment; no dharma that is not destroyed, yet nothing destroyed; no dharma that does not emerge, yet nothing emerged; no dharma that does not illuminate, yet nothing illuminated.
Dṛḍhamati! These are called the gateways to the samādhis of all bodhisattvas.
Those who enter these gateways shall attain unimpeded wisdom regarding all phenomena.
To be able to contemplate in this way is called the unimpeded eye;
to be without greedy attachment toward these matters is called the Dharma-eye.
Resolute Mind!
“By means of this samādhi, a bodhisattva is able to attain unimpeded and boundless eloquence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How many bodhisattvas will, in a future age, accomplish this samādhi and be able to attain immeasurable and boundless eloquence?
What kind of bodhisattvas will, in a future age, accomplish this samādhi and be able to attain immeasurable and boundless eloquence?

“Dṛḍhamati! If, in a future age, a bodhisattva hears this samādhi from a bhikṣu, you should know that this bhikṣu has accomplished this samādhi and is able to attain boundless and immeasurable eloquence.”
Dṛḍhamati! Regarding what you have asked:
"How many bodhisattvas have accomplished this samādhi and attained boundless eloquence?"
If a person constantly cultivates this samādhi, they will be able to accomplish it.
Having attained this samādhi, they will also attain immeasurable and boundless eloquence.
Resolute Mind!
This gate can open the treasuries of the Dharma numbering eight hundred; the bodhisattvas currently in the land of the Buddha Akṣobhya constantly employ this gate.
Resolute Mind!
In this way, a single gate encompasses all gates of the Dharma and all gates of samādhi; this is called the "Gate of Repeated Phrases.
Therefore, Resolute Mind!
If a person wishes to enter the gates of the Dharma according to the Dharma—namely, these gates of samādhi and gates of repeated phrases—they should draw near to spiritual friends and ask:
"How does one practice?
How does one observe?
How does one cultivate?"
"You should follow their instructions and practice according to what they have taught. Resolute Mind!
If there are four qualities, you should know that such persons are spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra)."
What are the four?
First, they enable people to enter into wholesome dharmas;
second, they can obstruct all unwholesome dharmas.
Third, they are able to cause others to abide in the True Dharma;
fourth, they are always able to provide instruction in accordance with [the needs of others].
Possessing these four qualities, one should know that such persons are indeed spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"One should draw near to virtuous friends who can obstruct unwholesome dharmas;
those who can speak what is praised by the Buddha—such persons one should associate with."
Following the teachings of the Buddha to transform and guide others, one can give rise to wholesome dharmas in people;
abiding securely in what has been heard, one is able to increase wisdom.
One should approach the dharmas that are to be approached and distance oneself from those dharmas that should be avoided.
Having departed from unwholesome dharmas, one should practice that which is praised by the Buddhas.
If you desire eloquence and wish to manifest your own wisdom,
you should swiftly cultivate this samādhi and always follow virtuous friends.
Practice according to the instructions received, and do not harbor secrecy or stinginess regarding the Dharma;
you should also speak of the wholesome dharmas you have attained yourself to others.
Practice this Dharma with a profound mind, abandoning all forms of flattery and crookedness.
Constantly draw near to virtuous friends and practice such dharmas as these. Therefore,
by drawing near to virtuous friends and distancing oneself from evil associates,
one will gain great learning and swiftly attain this samādhi.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
If there are four qualities, you should know that these are the characteristics of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). What are the four?
Skillfully knowing how to teach and transform others;
skillfully knowing how to cultivate the path;
and knowing the errors in teaching and transforming others.
One knows the faults of the path of cultivation. Vīradatta!
If these four qualities are present, you should know that such a person is a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"Knowing how to teach and transform others and how to cultivate the path, And likewise knowing these faults,
Having already understood these dharmas, I now abide in the unimpeded dharma."
“Dṛḍhamati! Furthermore, there are four qualities by which one should know the characteristics of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra). What are these four?
One knows the ground, one knows the teaching, one knows the person, and one knows the practice.
What is knowing the ground?
It is to know the ground according to the person.

How does one know persons? One knows them according to their conduct: "This person dwells in a state of much desire; this person dwells in a state of much hatred; this person dwells in a state of much delusion; this person dwells in a state of fixed desire; this person dwells in a state of fixed hatred; this person dwells in a state of fixed delusion; this person dwells in a state of fixed desire and hatred; this person dwells in a state of fixed desire and delusion; this person dwells in a state of fixed hatred and delusion; this person dwells in a state of fixed desire, hatred, and delusion."
If sentient beings are in any of the three unwholesome states or other such stages, he knows them all; having known them, he teaches and transforms them according to the stage in which they abide.
He also knows all the various inclinations and desires of the bodhisattvas.
"Resolute Mind!
If a person accomplishes these four dharmas, you should know that they are a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Resolute Mind!"
Furthermore, there are four qualities by which one should know the characteristics of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
What are these four? They are the ability to speak with words that are capable of subduing [the mind].
They cause people to abide within the profound Dharma;
they are able to teach according to the occasion; and they adjust their guidance according to the occasion.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Knowing that the various stages differ according to the conduct of beings,
And knowing how to teach and transform according to those stages, One is thus able to achieve success swiftly."
He is able to preach the Dharma and subdue them, causing them to abide in the profound Dharma;
he reprimands them at the appropriate time and provides counsel at the appropriate time.
Even if there are words that are skillful and good, they will not be accepted if spoken at an improper time.
Therefore, the wise, according to the occasion, practice both adoption and relinquishment. "Firm Mind!
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that should be known as the characteristics of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), which can cause people to cultivate this samādhi."
What are these four? They are:
being able to cause disciples to leave the household life and practice detachment;
and being able to lead others to enter into the contemplation of the profound Dharma.
It can cause one to abide in meditative concentration;
it is unimpeded regarding all objects of perception and is free from all marks.
Resolute Mind!
"If one possesses these four qualities, know that such a person is a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"If a person praises renunciation, And practices departing from fixed dwellings,"
To cause disciples to abide in the Middle Way— this is called a virtuous friend.
To cause them to abide in the ultimate truth, within the profound and wondrous Dharma,
and to cause them to abide in the signless samādhi— this is a true virtuous friend.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they can cultivate this samādhi. What are the four?
Abandoning one's own mind, one follows the teacher’s intent;
remaining free from all conditions,
one constantly exerts diligent effort for this samādhi, never becoming weary or lax.
Furthermore, desiring to attain this samādhi, one should delight in dwelling in secluded places, far removed from the clamor and bustle of crowds.
If a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they will be able to practice this samādhi.
“Dṛḍhamati! Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can swiftly attain this samādhi.
What are these four?
They skillfully grasp the marks of the Buddha, seeing all Buddhas even in their dreams;
they skillfully grasp the marks of the teaching of the Dharma, hearing the Dharma even in their dreams;
and they preach for the sake of sentient beings without weariness.

Because they have attained the profound patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) and thus destroy all phenomena, they practice the concentration of non-reliance (*anālambana-samādhi*), following the departure from the mind.
Dṛḍhamati! A bodhisattva who possesses these four dharmas can swiftly attain this samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"This person does not abandon the marks of all World-Honored Ones; constantly taking the Buddha’s marks as their object, they never depart from before their eyes."
Fully beholding the Buddha, with his thirty-two marks, and hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they attentively grasp these characteristics.
Established in profound certainty, they attain patience within the Dharma; not relying on meditative concentration, they delight in following a mind of detachment.
Because it is not a phenomenon that can be extinguished, it shatters and tears asunder all phenomena; that all phenomena are non-phenomena is what this person delights in.
When contemplating all marks, they are without discrimination; they have faith and understanding that all phenomena are the Buddha-body.
Not clinging to words, not following the speech of others, one knows these marks for oneself and also explains them to others.
If a bodhisattva attains such patience regarding dharmas (dharmakṣānti), they are called a wise one who has reached this samādhi.
Associating with virtuous friends, practicing the Buddha’s praise of the Dharma, teaching and transforming sentient beings, and abiding in the dharma of profound meditative concentration—
Bodhisattva Resolute Mind, if one possesses these four dharmas, one will be able to practice and attain this samādhi.
"What are the four? They are: skillfully knowing the characteristics of conditions;
skillfully discerning conditions;..."
One who well understands the transformation of conditions and well understands fundamental practice—
possessing these four dharmas, one can swiftly accomplish and penetrate this samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“A bodhisattva who is learned and wise Should expound this samādhi to others;
Furthermore, having heard the sublime Dharma from the Buddhas, They should likewise proclaim it for the sake of others.”
Taking the marks of the Buddha’s body as the object of focus, one cultivates this wondrous samādhi of quiescence;
furthermore, regarding the physical characteristics of all World-Honored Ones, one deeply grasps their various distinct features.
The thirty-two marks and the physical characteristics, the features of form, the characteristics of color, and the radiance;
with a face where the white tuft between the eyebrows stands prominent—one should grasp the marks of such a Honored One among Men.
Taking these various marks as manifest before one, one should constantly observe their distinct characteristics;
likewise, one should take each individual part of the body as an object of focus, rather than regarding a single dharma as the Buddha-body.
By means of the mind, one analyzes the bodies of all Buddhas; this mind is formless and pure by nature.
Though it appears variegated as it follows conditions and perishes moment by moment, it arises through the convergence of conditions, each manifesting distinct characteristics.
Since one knows that mental characteristics do not remain for even a moment, one should know that these conditions likewise arise and perish;
all such phenomena are born from conceptual discrimination, and the absence of discrimination is the supreme bliss.
One well understands that the nature of the mind is a phenomenon of transformation, and likewise understands that all conditions are phenomena of transformation;
knowing that the world is empty and like a mirage, once this is understood, mindfulness remains undisturbed.
One who can thus know the meaning of all phenomena is able to manifest the forms of many Buddhas,
yet remains unattached to these Buddha-forms, for they know that all worlds are empty.
Not grasping at signs among any conditions, one should know that body and mind are merely shifting appearances;
by thus thoroughly understanding these phenomena, one can swiftly attain this samādhi.
When preaching the Dharma, he manifests supernatural powers, and there is no error or contradiction in what he says;
he can cause sentient beings to give rise to wholesome merit, and they too can swiftly attain such a Dharma.
“Dṛḍhamati! There are four dharmas by which a bodhisattva can accomplish this samādhi, and having accomplished it, can explain it to others. What are the four?
In order to attain this samādhi, one practices diligently without ceasing, walking in meditation day and night;
when wishing to sit, one first recollects that all Buddhas are seated at the site of enlightenment and are now present before one;
one bestows the Dharma upon sentient beings without any stinginess, regarding the speaker of the Dharma as if he were the World-Honored One himself.
Analyzing oneself, one does not rely on dharmas, and preaches the Dharma to the assembly by means of non-reliance.

When a bodhisattva can practice in this way, contemplate in this way, and take this as their object of focus, they sit upon the Dharma-seat and extensively practice the gift of Dharma, thereby attaining this samādhi; or, there may be a bodhisattva who rises from the Dharma-seat and attains this samādhi.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
If a bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will attain this samādhi. What are these four?
The bodhisattva is one who has gone forth as a renunciant, practicing the conduct of seclusion because he has abandoned clamor and bustle;
he maintains only the three robes because he is free from greedy attachment;
and he does not engage in various worldly affairs with either the laity or the monastic community because he is free from the fault of untimely activity.
Because they have attained profound dharma-patience and delight in emptiness and stillness.
Resolute Mind!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they attain this samādhi.
“Dṛḍhamati! If a lay bodhisattva accomplishes four dharmas, they will be able to attain this samādhi. What are the four?
If a bodhisattva lives as a householder, they uphold the five precepts;
they eat but one meal per day and rely upon stupas and temples;
they study extensively and hear much, thoroughly understanding all treatises.
Furthermore, one should also associate with spiritual friends who are well able to teach and transform others in this samādhi.
Resolute Mind!
A lay bodhisattva who possesses these four dharmas can attain this samādhi.
"Furthermore, Resolute Mind!
If bodhisattvas, whether householders or those who have left the home life, accomplish four dharmas, they will attain this samādhi. What are these four?
Fully maintaining the precepts, living a life of pure conduct, and being free from all doubt and regret;
for the sake of this samādhi, not craving body or life and not relying on dharmas;
regarding those from whom one has heard it and those who can teach this samādhi as the World-Honored One;
When practicing this Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha, one should abandon the mind of stinginess.
Resolute One! If there are lay or ordained bodhisattvas who possess these four dharmas, they will attain this samādhi.
“Dṛḍhamati! If a person has resolved upon the Mahāyāna mind and wishes to attain this samādhi, they should cultivate four beneficial dharmas. What are these four?
One should contemplate the body in accordance with reality, so that no perception of a body arises;
one should contemplate feelings in accordance with reality, so that no perception of feelings arises;
one should contemplate the mind in accordance with reality, so that no perception of a mind arises.
One should contemplate phenomena in accordance with reality and not give rise to the perception of phenomena.
Resolute Mind!
When a bodhisattva accomplishes these four dharmas, they assist this samādhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“A bodhisattva should practice The foundations of mindfulness praised by the Buddha, The sphere of practice for bhikṣus; Thus they can attain this samādhi.”
One should constantly analyze the body and likewise not rely upon it;
with a mind free from reliance, one shall attain this samādhi.
Within feelings, mind, and phenomena, there is likewise nothing to rely upon.
This Dharma is inconceivable; one shall attain this samādhi.
One should practice the four dhyānas and cultivate the four right efforts;
without relying on these dharmas, one shall attain this samādhi.
Regarding the four bases of psychic power and the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge,
one should cultivate these dharmas without giving rise to a mind of stinginess.
One should abide firmly in the precepts and draw near to virtuous friends.
Regarding those who speak of this samādhi, one should conceive of them as the World-Honored One.
Taking extensive learning as the foundation, one gives rise to this samādhi from it;
following what all Buddhas have taught, one practices and trains according to their instructions.
This is called the supreme eye; the Dharma-eye is unsurpassed.
Within it there is no obstruction, for it teaches and transforms sentient beings.
It is the root of all sutras, capable of giving rise to the dharma of great learning.
Enlightenment is accomplished from this; therefore, one should constantly practice and study.
All that belongs to the Buddhas of the ten directions, as well as the four types of unimpeded knowledge, all emerge from within this; therefore, one should practice and study.
