The Bodhisattva who is able to attain this samādhi spoken by the Buddha,
when such a person preaches the Dharma, their eloquence shall be inexhaustible.
Regarding all phenomena, such a person is able to penetrate and know their equal characteristics.
Like the ocean, it neither increases nor decreases, and no one can exhaust it.
If one attains this samādhi, one does not follow the instructions of others;
when listening to and receiving the Dharma, one does not scrutinize the words of others.
The devas, ghosts, and dragon kings, yakṣas, kinnaras, and the multitudes of humans and non-humans—all gaze upon what the Bodhisattva speaks.
[In the Dan and Xiang editions, there follows: "All say: 'How does he abide?'"
How should one practice and train?
From where is this Dharma obtained?
Please explain this for us now.
By abiding in this samādhi, one knows the deep minds of sentient beings and also knows what their hearts delight in,
and thus preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate.
Now, within this sūtra of mine, all the Buddhas who have been spoken of—
By dwelling in this samādhi, one knows all their names;
one can also know the various teachings spoken by all Buddhas,
and according to whatever thoughts arise in the mind, one knows them all instantly.
All the World-Honored Ones and all their assemblies of disciples,
because they abide in this samādhi, are all able to see and know them.
They know the various worlds of the Buddhas and all manner of their adorned features.
They also know the measure of those feelings, because they have attained this samādhi.
They know the number of kalpas and years, as well as days, months, and seasons;
and throughout the worlds of the ten directions, they know all the Buddhas, the Honored Ones among two-legged beings.
They know all these Buddhas, and they also know these Buddha-lands;
they know the various distinct names of the World-Honored Ones.
Because they have skillfully cultivated this samādhi, they are able to know and see them all.
They also know all the World-Honored Ones and their entire assemblies of disciples;
they are able to fully know and see the teachings spoken for the sake of the multitudes,
as well as all the practices of the Buddhas and all their profound and wondrous Dharmas.
Because they have well practiced samādhi, they are able to know and see,
within future ages, all the immeasurable World-Honored Ones;
their names, their titles, and their clans— they see and know them all.
They also know their lifespans, as well as their assemblies of disciples;
they are able to fully understand all the sūtras and dharmas they preach,
and they know the various buddha-worlds and their manifold adornments.
After the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, regarding the duration for which the Dharma remains—
by dwelling within this samādhi, one knows all such matters. Therefore,
those who seek extensive learning should cultivate this samādhi.
Constantly cultivating this samādhi, one thoroughly understands all meanings and purposes.
You should know that this samādhi is the initial gateway for entering the Buddha’s wisdom;
from it arise sentient beings, and from it also arises the Buddha’s wisdom.
Furthermore, from within this, immeasurable merits and virtues arise.
If there is a person who resolves their mind to seek unsurpassed enlightenment,
and exhaustively makes offerings to all past Buddhas as well as their assemblies of disciples, [the merit is even greater].
To make offerings to each and every Buddha, as well as to their assemblies of disciples,
one could give away enough precious treasures to fill a great trichiliocosm;
with such wealth and jewels, filling it for the duration of an entire eon—
Thus providing for all, the Buddhas and the noble assemblies;
throughout the future ages, for all the World-Honored Ones,
one shall likewise provide for them all, as well as for their assemblies of disciples.
Dṛḍhamati, you should know that the merit obtained by such a person—
who seeks the unsurpassed Dharma of the Buddha and the inconceivable wisdom— is vast.
If a person seeks the path of the Buddha and cultivates this samādhi, [they shall attain it].
Because of this samādhi, one’s extensive learning becomes increasingly sublime.
Having attained such extensive learning, one explains it widely for the sake of sentient beings.
This merit surpasses the former; it cannot be measured by thought.
This merit is immeasurable, capable of increasing wisdom.
If one cultivates this samādhi, there is no need to make offerings to the Buddhas—
whether with incense, fragrant unguents, clothing, food, or medicinal decoctions.
To offer these to the Buddhas is not called a true offering.
The subtle and wondrous Dharma attained by the Tathāgata while seated at the site of enlightenment—
if a person can practice and study it, this is the true offering to all Buddhas.
If one seeks the path of the Buddha and wishes to behold all Buddhas,
one should diligently practice this Dharma to swiftly attain this samādhi. If,
upon hearing of this samādhi, one can give rise to a heart of joy, [one shall likewise attain it].
"You should know that these sentient beings have already seen thousands of Buddhas.
Furthermore, Resolute Mind!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family who seeks the Buddha-way provides offerings and adorns the stūpas and temples of the Tathāgata, they will attain the fulfillment of four great pure vows."
What are these four?
One is able to attain a supreme, pure, and wondrous physical body;
one is able to be constantly born in places free from all calamities; and one is also able to maintain a firm resolve to receive and uphold the wholesome Dharma.
They are able to see all Buddhas and attain indestructible faith;
they shall gradually attain unsurpassed bodhi and turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma—
these are called the four.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke in verse:
"The wise are able to provide offerings To the stūpas and shrines of the Honored Buddhas;
They are able to fulfill the four kinds of great pure dharmas Praised by the Sages."
May they always be born in places free from hardship, Attain correct and true vision, And always be able to see all Buddhas; Having seen them, their minds shall also be purified.
May they attain firm and steadfast deep faith, Unshakable like Mount Sumeru.
They will certainly attain the Buddha-wisdom And swiftly turn the unsurpassed wheel.
35. Entrustment Chapter (10). Entrustment Chapter, the Thirty-fifth: "Furthermore, Resolute Mind!

If a son or daughter of good family resolves upon the Mahāyāna mind, whether the Buddha is currently present or has entered parinirvāṇa, they should offer various flowers, necklaces, or superior flowers and incense as an act of worship.
By virtue of these conditions, one attains eight kinds of perfection:

perfection of the physical form through merit, perfection of wealth and resources, perfection of retinue, perfection of ethical discipline, perfection of meditative concentration, perfection of extensive learning, perfection of wisdom, and perfection of one's aspirations;
these are called the merits of the eight perfections.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If there are those who seek the Buddha-way, And provide offerings to the stupas and shrines, They shall obtain meritorious rewards in every lifetime; You should listen with single-minded attention."
Always possessing a perfect physical form, those who see them find their minds purified;
they attain great merit, vast wealth, and virtuous kinsmen.
Abiding securely within the precepts, they are able to enter deeply into meditative concentration.
Possessing great learning and wisdom, immeasurable as the great ocean;
whatever aspirations one may seek, all can be fully accomplished.
The most honored and supreme among those in the world, the foremost field of merit.
By virtue of these roots of goodness, he attains the thirty-two marks;
each mark is distinct and brilliant, adorning his body.
Each and every one of these marks is further embellished by the various secondary signs.
Within each and every mark, there are eighty rays of light;
within each of these rays, the brilliance is exceedingly clear and penetrating,
and from each of the eighty secondary signs, further rays of light also emerge.
Arising from the conditions of various wholesome karmas and also born of vows,
one attains such marks according to the distinctions of those vows. The mark of the wheels on the soles of the feet,
adorned with all manner of exquisite features, is formed by a single finger’s breadth.
Listen with a single mind to this power of merit:
within my toes there is a beautiful one named Illumination;
there is a light named Utmost Height, which dwells therein.
He is able to manifest radiance, like a precious jewel of surpassing beauty;
this light is like a crescent moon situated upon Mount Sumeru.
He possesses a mark named "Firm Accumulation," and there are eighty billion rays of light.
Each ray of light has its own name, and each also has its own luminous color.
From the edge of one ray, I emit a thousand kinds of radiant colors that encircle the great trichiliocosm, performing buddha-work in the regions below.
If I were now to radiate everywhere the light obtained through my wholesome karma,
all worlds, whether large or small, would be utterly bewildered and distressed.
From this light shall appear immeasurable Buddhas, who will be dispatched to all the worlds throughout the ten directions.
Extensively transforming sentient beings and performing the work of Buddhas—such are his supernormal powers.
I possess a samādhi capable of universal illumination; by means of this samādhi I behold the worlds.
This samādhi is named "Sumeru-Aspect," and within it there is a light called "Wholesome Dharma."
There is a samādhi named Śūraṅgama, which is the most supreme among all;
because of a pure mind, it can be attained, penetrating the ten directions without obstruction.
Some see the Buddha manifesting his parinirvāṇa; some see him first entering the womb;
some see him born, fearless, his mind serene as he takes seven steps;
or some see him sitting at the site of enlightenment, thinking, "I have now just attained Buddhahood."
Furthermore, they see me turning the wheel of Dharma, And they see me practicing the bodhisattva path;
You all observe this power of samādhi, In which the Buddha dwells and attains mastery.
Some know the number of kalpas of my lifespan; some know my lifespan to be half a kalpa;
some see my lifespan as one small kalpa, or two, three, four, or even more than that;
some see my lifespan as one hundred million years, or even more than that, or less again.
The people of this Jambudvīpa world know my lifespan to be eighty years;

yet others see my lifespan as a single day and night. Furthermore, some people know my lifespan to be vast and long, even as long as a trichiliocosm, while others say my lifespan is a single day and night of the devas.
I know the hearts and inclinations of these people; according to what they delight in, I preach the Dharma for them.
According to what each assembly requires, I manifest various teachings; each person thinks, "He is speaking to me.
Seeing this, they rejoice and give rise to faith and understanding—this is the Buddha’s rare power of supernatural penetration.
If I were to reveal to you the deeds I perform, all ordinary beings would fall into madness and delusion;
as for the conduct and deeds of the Tathāgata, even if you were to see them, you would not recognize them.
If a bodhisattva understands my profound practice, that person will be able to turn the wheel of Dharma.
Each of those who preach the Dharma has their own preferences, yet they cannot fully know my practice;
if one cannot know the practice of universal wisdom, what that person says is extremely trivial and shallow.
If, upon hearing this Dharma, their mind retreats and sinks, for this reason I have nothing further to say.
If a person can know the conduct of universal wisdom, that person’s mind will never regress or sink;
knowing that all phenomena are entirely equal, such a person accords with my practice.
Dṛḍhamati, you should know that in future ages these sutras will have no one to receive them,
except for these eight bodhisattvas in this assembly who now stand before me with palms joined.
Dṛḍhamati, you should know that such a person as this is able to understand my profound conduct;
they shall also be a leader among the assembly of the Dharma in former gatherings, constantly able to illuminate the torch of the Buddha-dharma,
always teaching sentient beings the bodhicitta, and always being praised by all the Buddhas.
Now they stand before me; likewise before the Buddhas of the past, as many as the sands of the Ganges—all these World-Honored Ones stand manifest before them.
Then five hundred people rose from their seats, joined their palms, and said: "We shall protect the Dharma;
all of us who have been permitted by the Buddha to protect the Dharma—you, Resolute Mind, are also included among their number."
Furthermore, eighty bodhisattvas arose, all for the sake of protecting the Buddha-dharma:
"World-Honored One, in future ages, we shall receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma and practice according to its teachings;
amidst the turbid and chaotic evil world, we shall extensively explain and disseminate these seeds of the Dharma."
The World-Honored One immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy; he then flew into the air to the height of seven tala trees.
Eight hundred million people attained profound joy, each hearing for themselves that they had received the prophecy.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Will you be able to receive, uphold, and preserve such sūtras as these in the evil age to come? He replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am not capable.
Knowing this, the Buddha asked Kāśyapa:
“Are you able, after my parinirvāṇa, to receive, uphold, and maintain such sutras as these? He replied:
“World-Honored One!”
I am not capable; though I can sustain the trichiliocosm, The waters of the great oceans, the mountains and forests,
And all other heavy burdens, I cannot protect and uphold the Dharma in this evil age.
In this world, bhikṣus are for the most part corrupt and evil; they do not follow the teachings taught by the World-Honored One.
How much more so after the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa—who will be able to believe in and accept this profound sūtra?
They must surely have spoken these words to me: "You are old and senile, lacking in wisdom;
how can you, in turn, instruct us who possess sharp faculties, eloquence, and the ability to understand the meaning?"

"Bhagavān! Such base and evil persons delight in worldly verses and the treatises of non-Buddhists; they abandon the joy of profound meditative concentration and instead take pleasure in and become attached to all mundane affairs."
With many desires, difficult to satisfy and never content, they are greedily attached to fine flavors and seek gain and honor;
I cannot save such evil people, and seeing them only increases my sorrow and distress.
While I was dwelling in seclusion and solitude, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas came to me and said:
"Our World-Honored One has taught such a Dharma that it causes many sentient beings to abide in the Noble Path;
such-and-such a bhikṣu has attained the state of outflow-free realization, and such-and-such one has attained supernormal powers and reached the further shore."
Having heard this, my heart was filled with joy, and I replied to Śakra: "What is there to marvel at!
Later, in the evil age, Śakra and Brahmā will come to my dwelling and weep, saying:
'Venerable One, you should know that the Buddha-dharma is being destroyed.'"
Unable to explain extensively the conditions of this offense, Nor able to uphold this sutra,
Nor able to act as a witness for it— It is difficult to speak with such bhikṣus in an evil age.
At that time, all the devas wept and wailed. Then the Buddha addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"I also knew beforehand that you would be unable to receive, uphold, and protect my Dharma-seed;
none of my śrāvaka disciples are capable of upholding such a sūtra as this."
Yet all bodhisattvas, relying on the power of the Buddha, are able to receive and uphold such a Dharma;
lest those in future evil ages should give rise to doubt, I shall now sever the delusions of these people.
Why has this sutra not existed from the beginning? Is it merely something fabricated by bhikṣus themselves?
Or, seeing that this sutra is so vast and immeasurable, do they feel fear and trepidation toward its recitation?
This sutra is so extensive and full of manifold details—who could possibly recite it to completion?
If anyone now sees you questioning me, and also hears me now speaking for your sake,
that person will, in the future, during the most evil age, be able to hear this sutra and attain joy.
When the Buddha spoke these words on protecting the Dharma, immeasurable multitudes gave rise to the bodhicitta.
All these sentient beings thought to themselves:
"In the future, we shall serve and honor all the World-Honored Ones, seeking with single-minded devotion the Great Wisdom of the Buddhas."
"Providing for the śarīras and stūpas, and adorning the venerable forms with all kinds of ornaments.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What should this sutra be named?
How should it be received and upheld?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Compendium of All Roots of Goodness,' and it is also titled 'The Basis of Merit,' and also titled 'Consoling the Minds of All Bodhisattvas,' and also titled 'The Questions of the Bodhisattvas,' and also titled 'Severing the Doubts of All Sentient Beings'; you should uphold it thus."

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the Bodhisattva Resolute Mind, and the entire great assembly—including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, humans, and non-humans—all rejoiced greatly and faithfully accepted the Buddha’s words.
